title: Covering Points with Rectangular Boundaries
summary:
Geometric covering problems ask for a small family of geometric objects whose union covers a given point set. We study the more restrictive \emph{boundary covering} variant, where every point must lie on the boundary of a chosen object. Motivated by the framework of Langerman and Morin\,[Discret.\ Comput.\ Geom., 2005] for hyperspheres, we initiate the study of boundary covering by axis-parallel rectangles.
  We first consider the \emph{discrete} setting, where rectangles must be selected from a given family. We define \bcdaprfull\ (\bcdaprshort): given a point set \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^2\), a family \(\mathcal{R}\) of axis-parallel rectangles, and an integer \(k\), decide whether \(P\) can be covered by the boundaries of at most \(k\) rectangles from \(\mathcal{R}\). We prove that \bcdaprshort\ is \(\mathrm{W}[1]\)-hard parameterized by \(k\).
  We then study the \emph{continuous} variant, \prbcfull\ (\prbcshort), where rectangles may be placed freely. Given \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^2\) and \(k\), the goal is to decide whether \(P\) can be covered by the boundaries of at most \(k\) axis-parallel rectangles. In contrast to the discrete case, we show that \prbcshort\ is fixed-parameter tractable, with running time \(2^{\cO(k\log k)}\cdot n^{\cO(1)}\), where \(n=|P|\). Our algorithm relies on a structural analysis of how \(k\) rectangles interact with the point set, reducing \prbcshort\ to at most \(2^{\cO(k\log k)}\) instances of \ddmtcsp, each solvable in polynomial time. On the hardness side, we prove NP-completeness for boundary covering by axis-aligned \(L\)-shapes and use this reduction to establish NP-completeness of \prbcshort.

AI.tldr: The paper studies boundary covering by axis-parallel rectangles in two models. Discrete setting (rectangles must come from a given family) is W[1]-hard when parameterized by k. Continuous setting (rectangles can be placed freely) is fixed-parameter tractable with running time 2^{O(k log k)} poly(n), via reducing to a small number of instances of a CSP, while NP-hardness is shown for related L-shapes, implying NP-hardness of the continuous variant as well.
AI.motivation: Extend the boundary covering framework of Langerman and Morin (hyperspheres) to axis-parallel rectangles, separating discrete and continuous variants and identifying their parameterized complexity, to understand how allowing free placement changes tractability.
AI.method: Discrete: establish W[1]-hardness (likely via a reduction from a known W[1]-hard problem). Continuous: perform a structural analysis of how k rectangles interact with the point set, reduce to at most 2^{O(k log k)} instances of a constraint satisfaction problem (DDMT-CSP), each solvable in polynomial time. Hardness: show NP-completeness for boundary covering by axis-aligned L-shapes and transfer to the rectangle setting.
AI.result: Discrete boundary covering with restricted rectangle families is W[1]-hard in k. Continuous boundary covering with freely placed rectangles is FPT with 2^{O(k log k)} poly(n) time. NP-completeness is established for boundary covering by L-shapes, and this is used to prove NP-hardness of the continuous variant.
AI.conclusion: There is a sharp complexity dichotomy: discrete boundary covering is intractable in the parameter k (W[1]-hard), while the continuous variant is FPT. Moreover, related L-shape problems yield NP-hardness results that inform the hardness landscape for boundary covering problems in the rectangle setting.

title: Context Graphs for Proactive Enterprise Agents
summary: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) and agentic frameworks have advanced enterprise AI considerably, yet agents remain fundamentally reactive: they wait for a human query before acting. This paper argues that genuine enterprise productivity gains require proactive agents: systems that surface relevant, actionable information to workers before they ask. We propose the Context Graph, a live relational data structure that models enterprise entities, their relationships, and state transitions over time. Built on this graph, we define a Delta Detection Engine that continuously monitors state changes, a Proactivity Scorer that ranks candidate insights by urgency, relevance, and persona-fit, and a Surfacing Layer powered by an LLM that delivers ranked notifications with grounded explanations. We formalize each component, derive a unified Proactivity Score function, and provide a complete end-to-end Python implementation using NetworkX and the Anthropic Claude API. Evaluation across three generic enterprise case studies (contract lifecycle management, engineering incident response, and sales pipeline hygiene) demonstrates that context-graph-driven proactivity achieves Precision@5 of 0.83, a false positive rate of 0.11, and reduces mean time to surface from 47 minutes (reactive baseline) to under 30 second.

AI.tldr: Proactive enterprise agents surface actionable insights via a live Context Graph, Delta Detection Engine, and Proactivity Scorer, enabling timely, persona-aligned notifications. Evaluated on three enterprise domains with Precision@5 of 0.83, false positive rate 0.11, and MTTS reduced from 47 minutes to under 30 seconds.
AI.motivation: Current RAG/agentic systems are largely reactive, waiting for user queries. To realize genuine productivity gains, enterprise agents must proactively surface relevant information to workers before they ask, enabling faster, more informed actions.
AI.method: Introduce a Context Graph—live relational data structure of entities, relationships, and state transitions over time; build a Delta Detection Engine to monitor state changes; develop a Proactivity Scorer to rank insights by urgency, relevance, and persona-fit; implement a Surfacing Layer with an LLM to deliver ranked notifications with grounded explanations. Formalize each component, derive a unified Proactivity Score function, and provide an end-to-end Python implementation using NetworkX and the Anthropic Claude API.
AI.result: Proactivity driven by the context graph yields Precision@5 of 0.83, a false positive rate of 0.11, and reduces mean time to surface from 47 minutes (reactive baseline) to under 30 seconds across three enterprise case studies (contract lifecycle management, engineering incident response, and sales pipeline hygiene).
AI.conclusion: Context-graph-driven proactivity offers a viable path to substantial productivity gains in enterprise AI by pre-surfacing relevant insights with grounded explanations; future work should explore scalability, robustness, and domain-generalization across additional workflows.

title: SASGeo: Stability-Aware Semantic Map Localization for GNSS-Denied UAVs -- A Framework and Synthetic Proof of Concept
summary: GNSS-denied unmanned aerial vehicles require occasional absolute position fixes to bound the drift of visual-inertial odometry. Cross-view image retrieval can provide such fixes, but raw appearance is sensitive to season, illumination, viewpoint, map age, and sensor modality. We propose \sas, a semantic map-localization framework that represents the environment through persistent structures such as roads, buildings, waterways, railways, intersections, and field boundaries. The method combines semantic raster alignment, relational graph evidence, feature stability and geographic distinctiveness, explicit positive/contradictory/unknown observations, and integrity-aware rejection of ambiguous fixes. Unlike a broad architecture-only proposal, this paper specifies concrete weighting and decision models and reports a reproducible synthetic proof of concept. In 220 randomized retrieval trials with rotation, scale changes, partial crops, occlusion, simulated map changes, and hard semantic decoys, a global semantic descriptor achieved 58.6\% Recall@1, while spatial semantic matching variants achieved 94.5-95.5%. Wilson 95\% intervals separate the global descriptor from the spatial variants but overlap among the spatial variants, so the experiment supports semantic geometry rather than a definitive benefit from each proposed module. The preliminary experiment does not validate real-flight navigation; rather, it demonstrates that structured semantic geometry can discriminate locations under controlled cross-view perturbations and identifies the harder aliasing, map-aging, and rejection tests required next.

AI.tldr: Semantic map-localization (SAS) uses persistent semantic structures for GNSS-denied UAV localization, combining semantic raster alignment, relational graphs, and integrity-aware decision rules; shows strong spatial matching in synthetic tests but no real-flight validation.
AI.motivation: GNSS-denied navigation requires occasional absolute fixes to bound drift in visual-inertial odometry. Raw appearance is sensitive to season, illumination, viewpoint, map age, and sensor modality. Semantic geometry aims to provide robust, view-invariant localization using persistent map structures.
AI.method: Represent environment with persistent semantic primitives (roads, buildings, waterways, railways, intersections, field boundaries). Use semantic raster alignment, relational graph evidence, feature stability, geographic distinctiveness, and explicit observations (positive/contradictory/unknown). Apply integrity-aware rejection of ambiguous fixes and concrete weighting/decision models. Provide a reproducible synthetic proof-of-concept with controlled perturbations.
AI.result: In 220 randomized retrieval trials with rotation, scale changes, partial crops, occlusion, simulated map changes, and semantic decoys, a global semantic descriptor achieved Recall@1 of 58.6%, while spatial semantic matching variants achieved 94.5–95.5%. Wilson 95% intervals separate the global descriptor from spatial variants but overlap among spatial variants. The results support semantic geometry rather than a specific benefit from individual modules. The study is a preliminary, synthetic demonstration, not real-flight navigation validation.
AI.conclusion: Structured semantic geometry can discriminate locations under controlled cross-view perturbations. However, further work is needed to address aliasing, map aging, and rejection tests, and to validate performance in real-flight navigation.

title: DreamCharacter-1: From 3D Generative Foundation Models to Product-Ready Character Generation
summary: We present DreamCharacter-1, a lightweight post-adaptation framework that calibrates pretrained 3D foundation models toward high-fidelity, production-ready 3D character generation. Building upon a 3D foundation backbone, our pipeline incorporates three task-oriented components: (1) geometry post-training, which enhances fine-grained surface details through geometric preference optimization; (2) texture post-training, which synthesizes high-resolution textures and refines the appearance of occluded regions; and (3) inference acceleration, which enables scalable deployment. Extensive quantitative and qualitative experiments demonstrate that DreamCharacter-1 produces visually compelling and structurally robust 3D character assets, consistently surpassing state-of-the-art character generation methods.

AI.tldr: A lightweight post-adaptation framework (DreamCharacter-1) that refines pretrained 3D foundation models for high-fidelity, production-ready 3D characters via geometry post-training, texture post-training, and inference acceleration, outperforming existing methods.
AI.motivation: To bridge the gap between pretrained 3D foundations and production-quality character generation by enhancing geometry detail, texture quality, and deployment scalability.
AI.method: Three components built on a 3D foundation backbone: (1) geometry post-training with geometric preference optimization; (2) texture post-training to synthesize high-res textures and improve occluded regions; (3) inference acceleration for scalable deployment.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show DreamCharacter-1 yields visually compelling and structurally robust 3D character assets and consistently surpasses state-of-the-art methods.
AI.conclusion: DreamCharacter-1 provides an effective, lightweight pipeline for production-ready 3D character generation with improved fidelity and deployment efficiency.

title: Towards the Explainability of Temporal Graph Networks via Memory Backtracking and Topological Attribution
summary: Temporal graphs are ubiquitous in real-world applications and Temporal Graph Networks (TGNs) have achieved superior predictive accuracy. Understanding which historical events drive model predictions can enhance trustworthiness of TGNs. Existing explanation methods overlook the memory module, the core component that records and updates node histories, leaving the influence of past events unexplored. To address this, we attribute TGNs predictions through the topology attribution tree and memory backtracking tree. The topology attribution tree captures the influence of neighbors and their memory vectors, then the memory backtracking tree quantifies how historical events shape node memory vectors. We apply the LRP in TGNs, ensuring that the total contribution of events equals the logits of model. Finally, top-k selection may be unfaithful due to the nonlinear mapping from logits to probabilities, we design optimization objectives to identify the important events. Experiments on nine temporal graph datasets, spanning node property prediction, link prediction tasks and graph classification tasks, show that our method provides faithful explanations and outperforms state-of-the-art baselines. The code is available at https://github.com/yazhengliu/MemExplainer

AI.tldr: Introduces MemExplainer, a faithfulness-driven explanation framework for Temporal Graph Networks (TGNs) that uses a topology attribution tree and a memory backtracking tree to attribute predictions to neighbor interactions and historical events; applies LRP with conservation to logits, and optimizes event-level importance; validated on nine temporal graph datasets across node property, link prediction, and graph classification tasks, outperforming baselines; code released.
AI.motivation: Explainability of TGNs is hindered by the overlooked memory module; understanding how past events and memory updates influence predictions is essential for trust and debugging.
AI.method: Construct a topology attribution tree to quantify the influence of neighboring nodes and their memory vectors; build a memory backtracking tree to trace how historical events shape node memory vectors; apply Layer-wise Relevance Propagation (LRP) to TGNs with a conservation constraint so the total event contributions match the model logits; address potential unfaithfulness of top-k explanations via optimization objectives that identify important events.
AI.result: The approach yields faithful explanations that align with the model's logits and surpass state-of-the-art baselines across nine temporal graph datasets spanning node property prediction, link prediction, and graph classification tasks.
AI.conclusion: MemExplainer provides a faithful, event-centric explanation for TGNs by decomposing predictions into topology (neighbor/memory) contributions and event histories, enabling more trustworthy model interpretations; code is available at the provided GitHub link.

title: AI-integrated models for assessing agricultural resilience
summary: Agricultural supply chains are vulnerable to disruptions through linked biophysical and economic systems. We develop an AI-powered tool that integrates economic models (GTAP) with biophysical models (APSIM) to analyze supply chain shocks, enabling policymakers and market participants to assess cross-disciplinary impacts through queries and responses written in natural language.

AI.tldr: An AI-powered framework integrating GTAP and APSIM to analyze agricultural supply-chain shocks via natural-language queries.
AI.motivation: Agricultural supply chains are vulnerable due to coupled biophysical and economic systems; a cross-disciplinary tool is needed to assess shocks and policy implications.
AI.method: Integrates GTAP (global trade/economy model) with APSIM (crop biophysical model) and provides a natural-language query interface for users to explore cross-domain impacts and scenario analyses.
AI.result: Enables cross-disciplinary impact assessment of supply-chain shocks and supports natural-language querying, facilitating scenario analysis for policymakers and market participants.
AI.conclusion: The approach offers a scalable, AI-assisted framework for integrated economic-biophysical analysis of agricultural disruptions, bridging complex models and user-friendly querying.

title: Physics-Guided Biomechanical Gait Adaptation for Humanoid Locomotion on Extreme Sloped Terrains
summary:
Model-free reinforcement learning has enabled impressive humanoid locomotion; however, control on steep slopes remains largely unexplored. Unlike flat or discrete terrains, sloped terrains impose a persistent gravitational bias that demands simultaneous stability and posture control. Consequently, under generic reward formulations, policies can converge to slow, conservative low-center-of-mass (CoM) crouched gaits.
  In this work, we propose a novel two-stage physics-guided framework, dubbed HumoSlope, dedicated to robust humanoid locomotion on diverse sloped terrains. Specifically, Stage I establishes a terrain-consistent balance prior by introducing a slope-adaptive Zero Moment Point (ZMP) regularizer evaluated directly on the local inclined support plane rather than a world-horizontal reference. To prevent the resulting policy from defaulting to a crouched posture, Stage II introduces the Biomechanical Slope Gait Adapter (BSGA). Utilizing extracted macroscopic terrain descriptors as privileged, training-only signals, BSGA dynamically gates soft reward priors to modulate CoM height and lower-limb coordination based on the estimated slope geometry -- encouraging hip-dominant uphill propulsion and knee-oriented downhill braking. Crucially, the deployed actor remains entirely proprioceptive, requiring no online exteroceptive sensing.
  Extensive Sim-to-Real experiments demonstrate that our framework effectively mitigates posture degeneration and enables blind, continuous traversal of outdoor grass slopes up to 62.7% ($32.1^\circ$), validating a physics-guided approach to challenging slope terrain adaptation.

AI.tldr: Two-stage physics-guided RL framework (HumoSlope) for robust humanoid slope locomotion: Stage I uses a slope-adaptive ZMP regularizer on the inclined plane; Stage II deploys a Biomechanical Slope Gait Adapter with privileged terrain descriptors to modulate CoM height and limb coordination, while keeping the policy proprioceptive. Demonstrates sim-to-real traversal on grass slopes up to 32.1° (62.7% gradient).
AI.motivation: Model-free RL often yields slow, crouched gaits on slopes due to persistent gravitational bias, lacking balance and posture control on diverse terrains.
AI.method: Stage I: introduce slope-consistent ZMP regularizer evaluated on the local inclined support plane. Stage II: Biomechanical Slope Gait Adapter (BSGA) uses privileged terrain descriptors to gate soft reward priors, modulating CoM height and hip/knee coordination based on slope geometry; actor remains proprioceptive with no online exteroception.
AI.result: Extensive sim-to-real experiments show reduced posture degeneration and enable blind, continuous traversal of outdoor grass slopes up to 32.1° (62.7% incline).
AI.conclusion: A physics-guided two-stage framework effectively improves slope robustness in humanoid locomotion, enabling higher-gradient terrain traversal with minimal reliance on exteroceptive sensing.

title: GIRAF: Towards Generalizable Human Interactions with Articulated Objects
comment: 12 pages, 6 figures, 3 tables. Accepted at the Third Workshop on Human Motion Generation (HuMoGen), CVPR 2026
summary: Synthesizing realistic full-body human interactions with articulated objects is a fundamental challenge for embodied AI and graphics, with applications in robotics training and virtual agents. Existing models remain limited: some focus on simple activities with static objects, while others restrict attention to hand-only manipulation. This leaves open the problem of generating coordinated full-body motion that approaches, manipulates, and moves articulated objects in a realistic and generalizable way. The key difficulty lies in reasoning jointly about locomotion, fine-grained contact, and object articulation. Models must capture subtle hand-object correspondences that transfer across object geometries, while also producing seamless transitions from navigation to manipulation. At the same time, the scarcity of large-scale paired motion-scene data makes it difficult to generalize across diverse object positions and shapes. We introduce a text-conditioned diffusion model that addresses these challenges through three core ideas: an object-centric representation that unifies hand-object contact with object surfaces, a mixed-domain training strategy that balances locomotion and interaction, and a contact-based augmentation scheme that expands training diversity. Through experiments, our method demonstrated strong generalization to unseen object configurations, surpassing current state-of-the-art methods.

AI.tldr: A text-conditioned diffusion model for realistic full-body human-object interactions with articulated objects, using object-centric representation, mixed-domain training, and contact-based augmentation; demonstrates strong generalization to unseen object configurations and outperforms SOTA.
AI.motivation: To address the challenge of synthesizing coordinated full-body motion that can approach, manipulate, and move articulated objects—requiring joint reasoning about locomotion, fine-grained contact, and object articulation—while avoiding reliance on static objects or hand-only manipulation and overcoming data scarcity for diverse object geometries.
AI.method: Introduce a text-conditioned diffusion model with (1) an object-centric representation that unifies hand-object contact with object surfaces, (2) a mixed-domain training strategy that balances locomotion and interaction, and (3) a contact-based augmentation scheme to expand training diversity.
AI.result: Empirical experiments show strong generalization to unseen object configurations and performance that surpasses current state-of-the-art methods.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework advances realistic, generalizable full-body interactions with articulated objects, enabling improved robotics training and virtual agents; it addresses data scarcity and integration of locomotion with manipulation, paving the way for broader object categories and more complex scenes.

title: Who Gets Missed in the Tail? Thresholded Subgroup Underdiagnosis in Long-Tailed Chest X-ray Classification
summary: In chest X-ray (CXR) classification, acceptable ranking performance can still leave rare-positive patients below threshold, especially within subgroups. We study this pre-deployment fairness problem as an audit question: after a long-tailed multi-label CXR model is converted from scores into decisions, who is missed? Across VinDr-CXR and MIMIC-CXR/CXR-LT, we use a diagnostic ladder to separate class-level long-tail losses, subgroup-aware weighting, group robustness, and threshold selection. On VinDr-CXR, group-tail weighting followed by tail-aware thresholding reduces tail FNR from 0.665 to 0.269, sex worst-group FNR from 0.705 to 0.157, and age worst-group FNR from 0.822 to 0.133, while macro-mAP increases from 0.611 to 0.635. On MIMIC-CXR/CXR-LT, the same score-to-threshold comparison reduces tail FNR from 0.866 to 0.741 and lowers worst-group FNR across sex, age, race, and insurance; residual missed-positive rates nevertheless remain high. Paired bootstrap contrasts on VinDr support the thresholded FNR reductions, and GroupDRO reference runs indicate that aggregate group robustness alone does not remove rare subgroup misses in this setting. The study supports a narrow audit claim: rare-label fairness in CXR depends jointly on the finding, subgroup, and operating threshold, not on label frequency or ranking metrics alone.

AI.tldr: Audit-focused analysis of long-tail, multi-label chest X-ray classification shows that converting scores to decisions with subgroup-aware weighting and thresholding reduces rare-missed positives (FNR) but residual misses persist; group robustness alone does not eliminate rare-subgroup misses; rare-label fairness depends on finding, subgroup, and threshold rather than label frequency or ranking metrics.
AI.motivation: Address pre-deployment fairness for rare-positive misses in long-tail, multi-label chest X-ray classification by auditing how decisions are made and thresholds affect different subgroups.
AI.method: Apply a diagnostic ladder to separate class-level long-tail losses, subgroup-aware weighting, group robustness constraints (GroupDRO), and threshold selection. Evaluate on VinDr-CXR and MIMIC-CXR/CXR-LT by comparing score-to-threshold conversions.
AI.result: VinDr-CXR: tail FNR 0.665 -> 0.269; sex worst-group FNR 0.705 -> 0.157; age worst-group FNR 0.822 -> 0.133; macro-mAP 0.611 -> 0.635. MIMIC-CXR/CXR-LT: tail FNR 0.866 -> 0.741; worst-group FNR across sex, age, race, insurance reduced; residual missed positives remain high. Paired bootstrap confirms FNR reductions; GroupDRO indicates aggregate robustness alone does not remove rare-subgroup misses.
AI.conclusion: Rare-label fairness in CXR requires jointly considering the finding, subgroup, and operating threshold; relying solely on label frequency or ranking metrics is insufficient for preventing misses in rare-positive subgroups.

title: Adversarial Social Epistemology for Assemblies of Humans and Large Language Models
summary: We outline an adversarial social epistemology (ASE) for densely interactive communicative landscapes in which public assertions are scaffolded by chains of testimony, inference, institutional certification, and tacit trust. In such landscapes, agents have incentives and affordances to distort, color, omit, fabricate, or strategically under-specify information for private, reputational, rhetorical, or material gains. We argue that these phenomena are not adequately captured by familiar descriptions of epistemic bubbles, echo chambers, or misinformation diffusion. What requires explanation is how communicative agents exploit the commitments and entitlements that normally make scaffolded assertions trustworthy. We provide language that delivers the requisite analysis, outline mechanisms that subvert trust in scaffolded public communications, and outline machinery for auditing and redressing trust breaches arising from subverting the auditability of inferential chains, drawing on epistemic networks, enriched with an inferentialist semantics for interpreting assertions.

AI.tldr: Proposes adversarial social epistemology (ASE) to model manipulation of scaffolded public assertions in densely interconnected discourse. Introduces inference-network auditability and inferentialist semantics to detect, explain, and redress trust breaches beyond traditional echo-chamber or misinformation models.
AI.motivation: Standard descriptions of epistemic bubbles and misinformation diffusion fail to capture how communicative agents exploit commitments and entitlements that ordinarily make scaffolded assertions trustworthy. The work aims to explain and counteract deliberate distortion in chains of testimony, certification, and tacit trust.
AI.method: Develops a theoretical framework combining epistemic networks with inferentialist semantics. Identifies subversion mechanisms, proposes auditing/redressing machinery for breaches, and outlines how to operationalize auditing in scaffolded inferential chains.
AI.result: A conceptual framework (ASE) with terminology and mechanisms for analyzing and correcting trust breaches in scaffolded public communications, grounded in networks and inferentialist interpretation.
AI.conclusion: ASE provides a richer explanatory toolkit than standard diffusion models, enabling auditing and remediation of trust breaches arising from subverting inferential chains in densely interactive epistemic ecosystems.

title: Shift & Drift: A Zero-Shot Benchmark for Generalizable and Robust Autonomous Driving Motion Planning
comment: Accepted at 2026 IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS 2026)
summary: While closed-loop motion planners trained on large-scale, object-level datasets, e.g., nuPlan, demonstrate strong in-distribution (ID) performance, their generalization to novel urban topologies and recovery mechanisms following execution perturbations remain under-explored. To address this, we present Shift & Drift, a novel dual-track benchmark designed to rigorously stress-test motion planners across two critical axes of distribution shift: (1) The Semantic Shift Track leverages a novel conversion pipeline that transforms the aerial, DeepScenario Open 3D dataset into the nuPlan simulation framework. This enables zero-shot evaluation of planners trained on North American and Singaporean data against 1,182 scenarios spanning four German cities and the US city of San Francisco featuring dense pedestrian-cyclist interactions. (2) The State-Distribution Drift Track injects stochastic perturbations into the ego vehicle's dynamics to quantify robustness against compounding execution errors. Based on this, we systematically evaluate the failure modes of diverse planning paradigms under semantic and state-distribution shifts. While imitation learning methods achieve high scores in ID benchmarks, they exhibit significant failures under semantic shift, particularly in pedestrian-dense environments, and suffer from persistent drift when subjected to temporally correlated actuation noise. In contrast, the evaluated reinforcement-learning-based planner demonstrates more graceful degradation, maintaining higher safety and progress metrics across both tracks. Our findings reveal an empirical trade-off between imitation fidelity and closed-loop resilience, providing the community with a rigorous benchmark to evaluate progress toward reliable deployment.

AI.tldr: Shift & Drift offers a dual-track benchmark to test motion planners under semantic distribution shifts and state-distribution perturbations, revealing a robustness gap for imitation learning (IL) and relative resilience for reinforcement learning (RL).
AI.motivation: Evaluate generalization and robustness of closed-loop motion planners beyond standard in-distribution benchmarks, addressing topological/semantic shifts and execution perturbations.
AI.method: Two tracks: (1) Semantic Shift Track converts the aerial DeepScenario Open 3D dataset into the nuPlan simulation framework for zero-shot evaluation across 1,182 scenarios in four German cities and San Francisco; (2) State-Distribution Drift Track injects stochastic perturbations into ego dynamics to measure robustness to compounding actuation errors; compare planning paradigms.
AI.result: Imitation learning methods excel in in-distribution benchmarks but fail under semantic shifts, especially in pedestrian-dense environments, and accumulate drift under temporally correlated actuation noise. Reinforcement-learning-based planners degrade more gracefully, maintaining higher safety and progress metrics across both tracks.
AI.conclusion: There is an empirical trade-off between imitation fidelity and closed-loop resilience; the benchmark provides a rigorous platform to quantify progress toward reliable deployment of autonomous motion planners.

title: 3D Reconstruction of deciduous Trees using low-cost UAV- and Crane-based Photogrammetry for Monitoring Shoot Elongation across entire Canopies
comment: Accepted to ISPRS Congress 2026, camera-ready version
summary: Tree growth determines how much CO2 is sequestered from the atmosphere and temporarily stored in woody biomass. At the same time tree growth is affected by increasing temperatures, more frequent drought periods, late frosts and other extreme events associated with climate change. While continuous measurements of radial (secondary) tree growth using dendrometers are well established, monitoring of shoot elongation (primary growth) has largely been neglected because suitable measurement techniques are lacking. As a result, the effects of climate change on primary tree growth remain insufficiently understood. This work aims at reconstructing native deciduous trees in 3D as a basis for measuring and monitoring shoot elongation over entire tree canopies. Here we explored the use of low-cost UAV photogrammetry and of a multi-camera CraneCam system under real-world conditions. Data were collected in two study areas over an entire growing season. We present sensor evaluations, photogrammetric data acquisition and processing strategies. A special focus is placed on the analysis of the resulting photogrammetric 3D point clouds in terms of accuracy, resolution and completeness. Results demonstrate 3D point accuracies of 5-6 mm for entire trees using consumer-grade UAVs weighing less than 250 g and a 3D reconstruction completeness between 92% and 98% depending on the UAV type. The paper introduces a novel 3Dprinted ground-truth branch to evaluate the capability to reconstructing fine-detail structures such as thin tree shoots. Finally, we discuss operational challenges and initial experiments towards a skeletonization of entire trees based on photogrammetric point clouds.

AI.tldr: Low-cost UAV photogrammetry and CraneCam enable whole-tree 3D reconstruction for monitoring shoot elongation; achieves ~5–6 mm point accuracy and 92–98% completeness; introduces a 3D-printed ground-truth branch and explores skeletonization.
AI.motivation: Address the gap in understanding primary (shoot) growth under climate change and its interaction with factors like temperature and drought, by enabling canopy-wide 3D measurements beyond conventional radial growth dendrometers.
AI.method: Data collected over a growing season in two study areas using consumer-grade UAVs (<250 g) and a multi-camera CraneCam; generate 3D point clouds, evaluate accuracy and completeness; introduce a 3D-printed ground-truth branch; explore skeletonization of trees from photogrammetric data.
AI.result: 3D point accuracy 5–6 mm for entire trees; completeness 92–98%; demonstrates feasibility and provides baseline for shoot-elongation analyses; identifies operational challenges and initial steps toward skeletonization.
AI.conclusion: Feasibility shown for cost-effective canopy-scale measurement of primary growth; potential to quantify climate-change effects on shoot elongation; further work needed on processing pipelines, accuracy, and skeletonization robustness.

title: LLT: Local Linear Transformer for PDE Operator Learning
summary: Neural operators have become a common approach for learning PDE solution maps and accelerating numerical simulations. Transformer-based neural operators are of particular interest, since attention can learn long-range dependencies in the computational domain. However, standard attention has two major limitations when applied to PDEs: it scales quadratically with the number of computational nodes, and it lacks an explicit bias toward local interactions. To address these issues, we introduce Local Linear Transformer (LLT) for PDE operator learning. The architecture combines linear global attention with local spatial mixing, and incorporates coordinate and geometry information. We evaluate LLT on several PDE problems, including elasticity, plasticity, airfoil flow, pipe flow, and Darcy flow. The reference data for these problems span finite-element, finite-volume, and finite-difference discretizations on structured and unstructured meshes. Compared with other neural-operator and transformer baselines from prior studies, LLT achieves competitive or lower relative $L_2$ error across these problems. On matched structured discretizations, wall-clock time per training iteration is reduced by factors of 1.8 to 2.5 relative to Transolver. We also scale the approach and apply it to a three-dimensional car aerodynamics dataset with 32,186 unstructured mesh points per sample. Together, these results indicate that LLT provides an accurate and computationally efficient operator for PDE problems across discretizations, mesh types, and problem settings.

AI.tldr: Local Linear Transformer (LLT) combines linear global attention with local spatial mixing and geometry-aware embeddings to learn PDE operator maps efficiently across discretizations, achieving competitive accuracy and faster training than Transolver, and scaling to large 3D unstructured meshes.
AI.motivation: Standard attention in Transformer-based neural operators is quadratically expensive in the number of spatial nodes and lacks an explicit bias toward local interactions, which are critical for PDEs. There is a need for scalable, accurate PDE operators that work across mesh types and discretizations.
AI.method: LLT integrates linear global attention with local spatial mixing and coordinate-geometry embeddings. It processes PDE solution maps on structured and unstructured meshes, trained on data from finite-element, finite-volume, and finite-difference discretizations. It is evaluated on elasticity, plasticity, airfoil flow, pipe flow, Darcy flow, and a 3D car aerodynamics dataset with 32k+ unstructured nodes per sample, comparing to neural-operator and transformer baselines (e.g., Transolver).
AI.result: LLT achieves competitive or lower relative L2 error across the tested PDE problems. On matched structured discretizations, training time per iteration is reduced by about 1.8–2.5x relative to Transolver. It scales to large 3D unstructured meshes, indicating robustness across discretizations and mesh types.
AI.conclusion: LLT provides an accurate and computationally efficient operator for PDE problems across discretizations and mesh types, representing a promising alternative to existing neural operators and transformer-based methods for science and engineering simulations.

title: Aligning Clinical Needs and AI Capabilities: A Survey on LLMs for Medical Reasoning
summary: Large language models (LLMs) have emerged as important tools in healthcare, showing growing potential for clinical reasoning and patient care. This survey examines recent progress in medical LLMs, focusing on reasoning applications and requirements. We present a dual-view approach that connects clinical practice with computational methods. On the clinical side, we establish a five-level competency scheme following Miller's Pyramid, progressing from knowledge recall to dynamic case management. On the computational side, we link deductive, inductive, and abductive reasoning patterns to common medical goals and tasks. We also introduce a benchmark dataset spanning five levels of medical reasoning capability and report results on 18 state-of-the-art models, revealing that medical specialist models excel in diagnosis-centric tasks while general models lead in decision support and dialogue. We conclude by discussing current progress and open challenges, including data limitations, hallucination, and grounding issues, and outline directions toward safer, more reliable, and workflow-ready systems.

AI.tldr: Introduces a dual-view framework tying clinical practice to AI reasoning, a Miller's Pyramid-based five-level clinical competency model, and a five-level medical reasoning benchmark evaluated on 18 LLMs; finds specialist models excel in diagnosis, general models in decision support/dialogue; highlights data, hallucination, and grounding challenges with safety-oriented directions.
AI.motivation: To unify clinical practice with AI reasoning, evaluate medical LLMs across reasoning levels, and chart a path toward safer, workflow-ready systems in healthcare.
AI.method: Proposes a dual-view framework linking clinical competency (Miller's Pyramid) with computational reasoning (deductive, inductive, abductive) patterns; introduces a five-level medical reasoning benchmark and a dataset; evaluates 18 state-of-the-art models and analyzes performance across tasks.
AI.result: 18 models evaluated; medical specialist models outperform in diagnosis-centric tasks, while general models outperform in decision support and dialogue; the benchmark reveals limitations related to data, hallucination, and grounding.
AI.conclusion: Highlights progress and open challenges in medical LLMs, and outlines directions toward safer, more reliable, and workflow-ready systems, with emphasis on data quality, robust grounding, and mitigation of hallucinations.

title: STEMbot: A Compliant Robot for Under-Canopy Plant Navigation
comment: Accepted to the 2026 IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS 2026). Project page: https://um-arm-lab.github.io/stembot-site/
summary: The scalability of organic agriculture is partially limited by the labor costs associated with monitoring for pests. While drones and rovers are well-suited for agricultural monitoring from above or next to plants, many pests live on the underside of leaves or on plant stems, making them detectable only after they have caused significant damage. To enable early pest detection we present STEMbot, a miniature climbing robot system designed for autonomous navigation under plant canopies. Unlike existing climbing platforms that lack on-board perception or are restricted to unbranched vertical trunks, STEMbot integrates a fully geometric PIN-SLAM pipeline with a semantic OcTree to achieve robust localization and mapping while climbing the plant. To plan STEMbot's motion we propose a manifold-constrained A* planner along with ray-tracing goal specification to enable branch-aware traversal and the inspection of occluded targets. We validate our system through hardware experiments, demonstrating reliable traversal of stems ranging from 7-33mm and autonomous navigation across four distinct plant specimens. Quantitative evaluations show that our system achieves high-fidelity geometric reconstructions with an average Chamfer distance of less than 1cm relative to an offline photogrammetry baseline, confirming that STEMbot maintains the globally consistent odometry needed for autonomous navigation.

AI.tldr: STEMbot enables autonomous climbing under plant canopies with PIN-SLAM and semantic OcTree for branch-aware perception and planning; validated with <1 cm Chamfer distance and traversal on 7–33 mm stems across four plants.
AI.motivation: Labor-intensive pest monitoring in organic agriculture limits scalability; pests on leaf undersides and stems require close-up inspection under canopies.
AI.method: A miniature climbing robot STEMbot with on-board PIN-SLAM and semantic OctTree; manifold-constrained A* planner; ray-tracing goal specification for branch-aware traversal and occluded target inspection; hardware experiments on four plant specimens; Chamfer-distance-based evaluation against offline photogrammetry.
AI.result: High-fidelity geometric reconstructions with average Chamfer distance < 1 cm relative to offline photogrammetry; globally consistent odometry enabling autonomous navigation; successful traversal of stems 7–33 mm; navigation across four plant specimens.
AI.conclusion: STEMbot demonstrates robust on-board perception and planning for autonomous climbing under plant canopies, enabling early pest detection and scalable monitoring in organic agriculture.

title: Adversarial Decoys: Misdirecting Attention-Based Defenses in ViT
summary: Vision Transformers (ViTs) remain vulnerable to localized adversarial attacks, e.g., adversarial patches, while recent test-time defenses mitigate them by suppressing image tokens with abnormally high attention scores. These defenses exploit a strong coupling between attention and adversarial effectiveness: adversarial tokens often need to attract substantial attention to influence the prediction. We introduce adversarial decoys, independently optimized image patches that redirect the attention, and therefore related defenses, toward selected target tokens. Rather than jointly optimizing misclassifications and defense evasion, our approach decouples the two objectives: the original adversarial region induces the incorrect prediction, while a separate decoy manipulates the attention ranking used by the defense. A layer-wise objective increases target-token attention and promotes these tokens above competing non-target ones. Since the decoy is optimized independently of the underlying attack, the method is attack-agnostic and can be easily integrated with any existing adversarial patch attack. Experiments on ImageNet across multiple ViT architectures and attacks show that decoys can redirect high attention scores away from the true adversarial region while preserving much of the attack effectiveness. These results reveal a fundamental limitation of using attention magnitude as an indicator of adversarial relevance.

AI.tldr: Proposes adversarial decoys for ViTs: independently optimized patches steer attention to target tokens, decoupling misclassification from attention manipulation; attack-agnostic and compatible with existing patch attacks; demonstrates attention magnitude is an unreliable defense signal.
AI.motivation: Localized adversarial patches threaten ViTs; current test-time defenses rely on suppressing tokens with high attention. The key vulnerability is the coupling between attention and adversarial effectiveness, which can be exploited to evade defenses.
AI.method: Introduce adversarial decoys: independent patches optimized to raise attention on chosen target tokens, while the original attack region remains responsible for misclassification. A layer-wise objective elevates target-token attention above competitors. Decoy optimization is independent of the attack, enabling attack-agnostic integration with existing patch attacks.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation on ImageNet across multiple ViT architectures and attacks shows decoys redirect high attention away from the true adversarial region while preserving most attack effectiveness.
AI.conclusion: Attention-magnitude is an unreliable indicator of adversarial relevance in ViTs; defenses relying on attention scores can be circumvented by decoys, highlighting a fundamental limitation and prompting rethinking of attention-based defenses.

title: ReCoLoRA: Spectrum-Aware Recursive Consolidation for Continual LLM Fine-Tuning
summary: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning adapts a large language model to one task cheaply, but across a task sequence LoRA-style methods keep stacking low-rank updates on the same frozen weight, so each new task tends to overwrite the previous ones. We present ReCoLoRA (Recursive Consolidation of Low-Rank Adapters), a spectrum-aware framework for continual fine-tuning: adapters are initialized from a randomized SVD of the pretrained weight, per-layer effective ranks are selected by an elbow criterion, and the principal subspace is adapted before residual capacity is opened. Before each new task, ReCoLoRA re-decomposes the current effective weight, rather than the original one, into a frozen residual, a slowly updated principal component, and a fresh adapter (recursive consolidation), so every task starts from the model that has already absorbed its predecessors. On a six-task continual GLUE sequence over four 7-8B backbones, ReCoLoRA attains the best final average score on three of the four backbones against rank-swept LoRA, PiSSA, AdaLoRA, and DoRA baselines while training fewer parameters; an oracle-routed task-bank variant serves as an upper bound under full task isolation. Code: https://github.com/bhqy666/ReCoLoRA.

AI.tldr: ReCoLoRA enables continual fine-tuning with recursive, spectrum-aware low-rank adapters, initializing from a randomized SVD, selecting per-layer ranks by an elbow criterion, and re-decomposing weights before each new task to preserve past knowledge while learning new tasks.
AI.motivation: Overcoming catastrophic forgetting and task overwriting in sequential parameter-efficient fine-tuning (LoRA-style) by leveraging a spectrum-aware, recursive consolidation of adapters.
AI.method: ReCoLoRA initializes adapters from randomized SVD of the pretrained weight; per-layer ranks are chosen via an elbow criterion; the principal subspace is adapted before enabling residual capacity. Before each new task, the current effective weight is re-decomposed into a frozen residual, a slowly updated principal component, and a fresh adapter (recursive consolidation).
AI.result: On a six-task continual GLUE sequence across four 7–8B backbones, ReCoLoRA achieves the best final average score on three backbones versus rank-swept LoRA, PiSSA, AdaLoRA, and DoRA baselines, while updating fewer parameters. An oracle-routed task-bank variant provides an upper bound under full task isolation.
AI.conclusion: Spectrum-aware recursive consolidation improves parameter-efficient continual fine-tuning by absorbing predecessors into a frozen residual and progressively updating a principal subspace, enabling better performance with fewer parameters across tasks and backbones.

title: Alignment Plausibility: A New Standard for Assuring AI in Healthcare
summary: Large language models (LLMs) have become significant providers of mental health support, yet they remain products of an attention economy whose operational and commercial targets favour sustained engagement over the friction that effective psychological support often requires. Developers' safety responses have been largely reactive, addressing the most visible and acute harms while subtler, longer-term patterns of risk (e.g., dependency, boundary erosion, the amplification of distorted beliefs) receive less attention. We contend that making LLMs structurally safe requires alignment organised at three levels that mirror how society assures the safety of human clinical practice: 1) explicit value specification grounded in the codified normative commitments of clinical practice; 2) training that embeds those values in the model; and 3) oversight that detects drift and longer-term harm during deployment, much as clinical supervision does for human practice. Organising alignment in this way yields a construct we call alignment plausibility - a structured demonstration that a system's values, training regime, and oversight mechanisms are together consistent with safe and positive outcomes. We propose alignment plausibility as a regulatory construct (by drawing analogy to the established construct of biological plausibility) for AI in health: a principled way to argue for, or against, trust that systems are aligned to positive health outcomes, will cause no harm even where capable of doing so, and will ultimately lead to patient benefit.

AI.tldr: Proposes alignment plausibility as a three-level, regulator-friendly framework to ensure LLMs in health are aligned with safe, beneficial patient outcomes (explicit values, training, and deployment oversight).
AI.motivation: Address the shortfall of reactive safety measures in AI health applications and the risk of long-term harms (e.g., dependency, distorted beliefs) in an attention-driven system.
AI.method: Conceptual analysis that defines a three-tier alignment model and introduces 'alignment plausibility' as a regulatory construct; draws analogies to clinical practice and supervision.
AI.result: A structured construct (alignment plausibility) and regulatory framing that links explicit values, model training, and ongoing oversight to safe, positive health outcomes.
AI.conclusion: Alignment plausibility offers a principled basis for trust in AI health systems and a pathway for governance to ensure no harm and patient benefit, even when systems are capable of causing harm.

title: Time-to-Collision Based Dynamic Obstacle Avoidance Using Pretrained Vision Models for Robots in Unstructured Environments
summary: Dynamic obstacle avoidance in unstructured outdoor environments remains a critical challenge for autonomous mobile robots, particularly when large-scale robot-specific training data and simulation-based policies are impractical. We present a data-efficient, interpretable method for vision-based dynamic obstacle avoidance that operates entirely on real-world data, avoiding the sim-to-real transfer problem inherent in simulation-trained policies. Our approach leverages UniDepth, a large pretrained monocular depth estimation model, to produce dense depth maps from RGB video without requiring stereo cameras or LiDAR at inference time. Dynamic obstacle avoidance is achieved by extending the SuperPoint and SuperGlue feature correspondence pipeline to track keypoints across long frame sequences, projecting their 2D pixel-space positions into 3D using camera intrinsics and predicted depth, running bundle adjustment initialized from these 3D keypoints, and computing per-keypoint time-to-collision (TTC). A 2D motion primitive in the ground plane is then selected to move the robot away from the closest point of approach of the minimum-TTC keypoint. Evaluated on real-world data from the M3ED dataset, our pipeline achieves a precision of 0.49 and a recall of 0.38 in identifying frames with a ground truth TTC below 1 second, and correctly generates the evasive motion direction in 84\% of true positive detections. Crucially, it detects at least one frame with TTC less than 1 second for 20 out of 22 unique physical obstacles present in our test sequences. Unlike end-to-end learned methods that demand thousands of hours of robot-specific training data, our approach eliminates model training entirely, requiring only 74 seconds of data for hyperparameter tuning. This demonstrates exceptional data efficiency while preserving interpretable and generalizable behavior across diverse obstacle types.

AI.tldr: A data-efficient, interpretable framework for vision-based dynamic obstacle avoidance in unstructured outdoor environments using monocular depth (UniDepth) and long-term keypoint tracking with bundle adjustment to estimate per-keypoint time-to-collision, selecting a ground-plane 2D motion primitive to evade the closest approach. It achieves non-training-based deployment with real-world data and minimal tuning, showing competitive detections without large robot-specific datasets.
AI.motivation: Address dynamic obstacle avoidance without large robot-specific training datasets or sim-to-real transfer, enabling practical deployment with monocular vision.
AI.method: Leverage UniDepth to obtain dense depth from RGB; extend SuperPoint/SuperGlue to track keypoints over long frame sequences; project 2D keypoints into 3D via intrinsics and predicted depth; perform bundle adjustment initialized from these 3D points; compute per-keypoint time-to-collision (TTC); select a 2D ground-plane motion primitive to steer away from the point of closest approach with minimum TTC.
AI.result: On real-world M3ED data: precision 0.49 and recall 0.38 for frames with TTC < 1s; evasive direction correct in 84% of true positives; detects at least one frame with TTC < 1s for 20 of 22 obstacles; requires only 74 seconds of tuning data and no robot-specific model training.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates data-efficient, interpretable obstacle avoidance without training, avoiding sim-to-real transfer and end-to-end learning; generalizes across obstacle types with minimal tuning.

title: Beyond Thermal Imaging: Inferring Thermophysical Properties from Time-Resolved Thermal Observations
summary:
Inferring latent physical properties from sensory observations is a fundamental challenge in machine perception. Among available sensing modalities, thermal imaging is particularly promising because temperature evolution is directly governed by heat-transfer physics and therefore encodes information about underlying thermophysical properties of a scene. Recovering spatially resolved thermophysical properties from thermal observations could transform applications ranging from digital twins and infrastructure monitoring to robotics and scientific imaging. However, existing thermal scene reconstruction methods can recover temperature fields in complex 3D environments without identifying the thermophyiscal properties that govern thermal evolution, whereas inverse methods provide physically interpretable parameter estimation but typically rely on simplified geometries and controlled experimental conditions.
  Here we introduce ThermoField, a framework that unifies thermal scene reconstruction and thermophysical parameter estimation through differentiable heat-transfer simulation. The proposed framework represents these quantities as spatially varying neural fields and constrains them through scene geometry, governing heat-transfer physics, and temporal thermal observations. We demonstrate that ThermoField jointly reconstructs geometry, estimates spatially varying thermal diffusivity, and predicts thermal evolution under previously unseen environmental conditions. By integrating neural scene representations with differentiable heat-transfer solver, the framework enables physically interpretable parameter inference in complex 3D scenes. Our results establish a bridge between thermal scene reconstruction and inverse heat-transfer analysis, providing a unified approach for geometry reconstruction, thermophysical property estimation, and predictive thermal simulation from thermal observations.

AI.tldr: ThermoField unifies 3D thermal scene reconstruction with spatially varying thermophysical property estimation (diffusivity) via differentiable heat-transfer simulation, enabling predictive thermal evolution from observations.
AI.motivation: Thermal data encodes heat-transfer physics and underlying properties, yet existing methods either recover temperature fields without properties or rely on simplified geometries; a unified, physics-informed approach for geometry and property inference in complex 3D scenes is needed.
AI.method: Represent geometry and thermal diffusivity as spatially varying neural fields; employ a differentiable heat-transfer solver constrained by scene geometry, physics, and temporal thermal observations; jointly optimize to recover geometry, diffusivity, and future thermal evolution.
AI.result: Jointly reconstructs scene geometry, estimates spatial diffusivity, and predicts thermal evolution under unseen environmental conditions; demonstrates interpretable, physics-grounded parameter inference in complex 3D scenes.
AI.conclusion: ThermoField provides a unified, physics-informed framework for geometry reconstruction, thermophysical property estimation, and predictive thermal simulation from thermal observations, bridging thermal scene reconstruction and inverse heat-transfer analysis.

title: Omni-Sleep: A Sleep Foundation Model via Hierarchical Contrastive Learning of CNS--ANS Dynamic
summary: Sleep physiology arises from the coordinated dynamics of the central nervous system (CNS) and autonomic nervous system (ANS), as reflected by multimodal polysomnography signals including EEG, EOG, EMG, ECG, and respiration. However, existing sleep foundation models often fuse heterogeneous biosignals in a topology-agnostic manner, overlooking their physiological organization. We introduce Omni-Sleep, a sleep foundation model that uses the CNS/ANS partition as a physiological prior for topology-constrained representation learning. Omni-Sleep learns structured representations through three objectives: intra-system consistency, which captures shared subsystem-level factors within neural and cardio-respiratory signals; inter-system synchronization, which aligns subsystem trajectories to model brain--body dynamics; and latent-space masked temporal modeling, which captures long-horizon sleep dynamics. Pre-trained on over 100,000 hours of multi-center multimodal PSG data, Omni-Sleep is evaluated on sleep staging and multi-disease classification. Across datasets and modality-ablation settings, Omni-Sleep outperforms strong foundation-model baselines, showing improved label efficiency, cross-dataset generalization, and robustness to missing modalities. These results highlight the value of physiological hierarchy for generalizable sleep representation learning. Code is available at https://github.com/AutoBrain-sleep/OmniSleep.

AI.tldr: Omni-Sleep is a topology-constrained sleep foundation model that uses CNS/ANS physiological hierarchy to learn structured representations from multimodal PSG (EEG, EOG, EMG, ECG, respiration). Pre-trained on 100k+ hours and evaluated on sleep staging and multi-disease classification, it outperforms baselines, with better data efficiency, cross-dataset generalization, and robustness to missing modalities.
AI.motivation: Current sleep foundation models fuse heterogeneous biosignals without respecting physiological organization, potentially limiting generalization and robustness. A CNS/ANS partition provides a principled topology prior to capture brain–body dynamics.
AI.method: Omni-Sleep imposes topology-constrained representation learning via three objectives: (1) intra-system consistency to capture shared factors within neural and cardio-respiratory signals, (2) inter-system synchronization to align subsystem trajectories and model brain–body dynamics, and (3) latent-space masked temporal modeling to capture long-horizon sleep dynamics. It is pre-trained on 100k+ hours of multi-center multimodal PSG data and evaluated on sleep staging and multi-disease classification; performance is tested across datasets and modality ablations.
AI.result: Omni-Sleep outperforms strong foundation-model baselines across datasets and modality-ablation settings, showing improved label efficiency, cross-dataset generalization, and robustness to missing modalities.
AI.conclusion: Encoding physiological hierarchy (CNS/ANS) in sleep foundation models yields more generalizable, data-efficient representations and robust performance under modality gaps, supporting topology-aware approaches for biomedical multimodal learning.

title: Idiobionics: The Unification of Privacy and Intelligent Robotic Prostheses
summary: The human body is at the center of a growing family of technologies designed to tightly and persistently couple biological and digital systems. Robotic prostheses are a representative example of this tight coupling. Also referred to as bionic limbs, robotic prostheses are devices that support people who have lost limbs in pursuing daily life activities such as walking and grasping objects. Bionic limbs are now perceptive and responsive owing to their integration with advanced sensors and artificial intelligence-based control approaches. Consequently, such robotic prostheses can now be viewed as semiautonomous wearable robotic systems that can co-adapt with their users. However, the same sensing and control advancements that increase the capability of robotic prostheses also introduce threat vectors that could be exploited by malicious entities to violate the privacy of users. To fully realize the benefits of next-generation bionic limbs, we maintain it is important to directly understand and address these privacy risks and the barriers they might present to user adoption. This paper therefore introduces a new line of inquiry we term idiobionics to holistically investigate issues at the intersection of privacy and intelligent bionic limbs. As the main contribution of this paper, we define idiobionics, ground it in related literature, and provide preliminary evidence showing and discussing potential adversarial attacks that could exploit intelligent bionic limb designs. We then contribute a curated list of open research questions within idiobionics that are relevant to researchers in wearable robotics and other human-facing autonomous systems. We expect that idiobionics research will help unlock the full potential of robotic prostheses and related bionic devices.

AI.tldr: A conceptual paper defining idiobionics, integrating privacy considerations into intelligent bionic limbs, and presenting preliminary attack vectors alongside a research agenda for future work.
AI.motivation: Growing integration of sensors, AI, and bidirectional control in prosthetic limbs creates privacy and security risks that can affect user adoption and safety; a holistic framework is needed to address these risks.
AI.method: Grounded in privacy, cybersecurity, HCI, and human-robot interaction literatures; defines idiobionics; provides preliminary evidence of potential adversarial attacks; and curates open research questions for researchers in wearable robotics and related autonomous systems.
AI.result: Defines idiobionics, situates it within existing literature, presents initial adversarial scenarios affecting bionic limbs, and offers a structured research agenda.
AI.conclusion: Idiobionics is a necessary research direction to unlock the full benefits of intelligent bionic limbs; addressing privacy risks will facilitate user trust, safety, and broader adoption, and calls for interdisciplinary investigation.

title: Monocular Vision Based Control Framework for Grasping
comment: This paper is accepted at IEEE/ASME International Conference on Advanced Intelligent Mechatronics 2026 (AIM 202^)
summary: Grasping in unstructured environments requires handling objects with widely different mechanical properties, from soft and deformable items to rigid everyday objects. Most existing approaches address these categories separately and often rely on tactile sensing, object-specific models, or specialized grippers. In this paper, we present a unified monocular vision-based grasping framework that targets both soft and rigid objects within a single control pipeline, using only RGB input and a position-controlled gripper. The proposed system combines open-vocabulary object detection, image segmentation, boundary-aware point assignment, real-time point tracking, and monocular depth estimation to recover object motion and geometry from visual observations. A key component of the framework is a language-based stiffness estimation model that infers an object's expected compliance from its semantic description and provides an object-level prior for selecting the grasping strategy before contact. For deformable objects, grasp adaptation is governed by a Procrustes-based dissimilarity measure computed from tracked keypoints, which acts as a visual proxy for deformation. For rigid objects, the gripper width is regulated through the scaling of tracked point distances. We validate the proposed method in real-world pick-and-place experiments on a Franka Emika Research 3 arm using objects with substantially different mechanical properties, including lettuce, fresh mozzarella cheese, croissants, paper towels, and hard plastic bottles. Results demonstrate that the framework achieves stable grasping across both soft and rigid objects using visual feedback alone, highlighting a practical, sensor-efficient, and generalizable approach for food handling and household manipulation.

AI.tldr: A monocular RGB-based grasping framework unifying soft and rigid object manipulation via open-vocabulary detection, segmentation, boundary-aware point assignment, tracking, and depth estimation, with a language-guided stiffness prior. Deformable objects use a Procrustes-based deformation proxy; rigid objects scale gripper width via tracked point distances. Validated on a Franka Emika arm across diverse items, achieving stable, vision-driven grasping without tactile sensing.
AI.motivation: Achieve unified, sensor-efficient grasping for objects with widely varying mechanical properties using only RGB input and a position-controlled gripper, eliminating the need for tactile sensing or specialized grippers.
AI.method: Combine open-vocabulary object detection, image segmentation, boundary-aware point assignment, real-time point tracking, and monocular depth estimation to infer object motion/geometry; introduce a language-based stiffness estimation model to predict object compliance from semantic description; use a Procrustes-based dissimilarity of tracked keypoints for deformable objects and scale tracked point distances to regulate gripper width for rigid objects; closed-loop visual feedback for grasp execution.
AI.result: Demonstrates stable grasping across soft and rigid items in real-world pick-and-place with a Franka Emika robot, using only RGB input; objects include lettuce, mozzarella, croissants, paper towels, and hard plastic bottles; validates sensor-efficient, generalizable approach.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides a practical, generalizable solution for food handling and household manipulation by unifying grasping strategies for varying mechanical properties through monocular vision and object-level priors without tactile sensing.

title: LOGOS: Language-guided Oriented Object Detection in Aerial Scenes
summary: Object detection in geospatial scenes, such as satellite and aerial imagery, poses significant challenges due to the varying orientations and densities of objects, as well as the complex backgrounds inherent to remote sensing imagery. Traditional methods for oriented object detection have struggled to address issues such as angular discontinuity, fixed query sizes, and inefficiencies in handling sparse or cluttered scenes. In this paper, we propose LOGOS, a novel transformer-based approach that leverages textual prompts to guide the detection of oriented objects in aerial scenes. In particular, our proposed approach incorporates prompt-modulated content queries to dynamically adjust the model's focus based on the provided text, thereby improving object detection accuracy in complex environments. Empirically, extensive experiments on the DOTA dataset demonstrate that LOGOS outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods, particularly in densely packed and rotated object scenarios. Our approach offers a significant step forward in improving the robustness and scalability of oriented object detection in remote sensing applications.

AI.tldr: LOGOS introduces prompt-modulated content queries in a transformer-based oriented object detector for aerial imagery, achieving superior performance on DOTA by leveraging textual prompts to adapt detection focus to object orientation and density.
AI.motivation: Address core challenges in remote-sensing oriented object detection: angular discontinuity, fixed query sizes, and difficulty in sparse/cluttered scenes, which hinder robustness of existing detectors.
AI.method: A transformer-based detector (LOGOS) that uses textual prompts to guide content queries. Prompts modulate the queries to dynamically adjust focus based on text, enabling better handling of rotated objects and dense scenes.
AI.result: On DOTA, LOGOS outperforms existing SOTA methods, particularly in densely packed and rotated-object scenarios, indicating improved robustness and scalability for oriented detection in remote sensing.
AI.conclusion: Prompt-guided content queries provide a viable and effective mechanism to improve oriented object detection in aerial imagery, offering better adaptability to varying orientations and scene densities.

title: Uncertainty-gated selection for block-sparse attention
summary: Block-sparse attention scales long-context language models by replacing the O(N^2) softmax with a per-query top-k selection over key blocks. This cutoff is myopic: when the k-th and (k+1)-th blocks are nearly tied in score, the selector commits without spending extra budget, and a dropped block carrying answer evidence is unrecoverable downstream. We propose a value-of-information router that measures, for each query, how decisively the top-k cut was made, and doubles the kept set for the queries where that gap is smallest; the rule is backbone-agnostic and stacks with existing block-scoring methods such as Quest. On LongBench-v2 medium at n=215 (the entire dataset subset), router-on-Quest reaches paired recall 0.75 vs. top-k 0.47 -- +28 pp over the SSA-style baseline (McNemar p<0.01) -- and lands within 2 pp of dense on RULER NIAH multikey at the same context. The lift reproduces on four models from three architectures (Qwen2.5, Mistral-Nemo, Qwen3.6). At 128K, the router preserves 0.81 and 0.89 of dense accuracy on Qwen2.5-7B-1M and Qwen3.6 (vs. SSA-style top-k at 0.09 on the former) while the fused selection-plus-kernel pipeline runs at 0.62x and 0.80x dense wall time.

AI.tldr: A value-of-information router enhances block-sparse attention by adaptively expanding the kept key set per query, mitigating myopic cutoffs and improving recall while preserving most of dense accuracy and improving speed.
AI.motivation: Block-sparse attention with a fixed top-k cutoff can miss evidence when the top-k boundary is near-tied, causing irreversible errors. A measure of decision decisiveness (value of information) can identify queries that need more keys and adjust accordingly.
AI.method: Introduce a value-of-information router that, per query, assesses the decisiveness of the top-k cut and doubles the kept set for the smallest gaps. The approach is backbone-agnostic and compatible with block-scoring methods (e.g., Quest). Empirically evaluated on LongBench-v2 medium at n=215, various architectures on multiple models; comparisons against SSA baseline and dense baselines; McNemar tests; speed-accuracy metrics.
AI.result: Significant recall gains: LongBench-v2 medium at 215 tokens: paired recall 0.75 vs 0.47 (top-k), +28 pp; near-dense performance on RULER NIAH multikey; consistent lift across Qwen2.5, Mistral-Nemo, Qwen3.6; at 128K contexts, preserves 0.81 and 0.89 of dense accuracy for Qwen2.5-7B-1M and Qwen3.6; speedup: fused selection-plus-kernel ~0.62x–0.80x dense wall time.
AI.conclusion: The value-of-information router effectively mitigates myopic block-cutoffs, delivering substantial recall improvements with modest speed costs and broad transfer across models and architectures; it complements existing block-scoring methods and approaches dense-model accuracy in practical settings.

title: Infinity-Parser2 Technical Report
summary: We present Infinity-Parser2, a large multimodal model that couples a controllable data-synthesis pipeline with multi-task reinforcement learning for end-to-end document parsing, addressing the persistent scarcity of faithfully annotated parsing corpora. Our contributions are threefold. First, we build a scalable synthesis engine, pairing a controllable rendering framework with an iterative refinement loop, and use it to construct and open-source Infinity-Doc2-5M: a 5-million-sample bilingual (Chinese/English) corpus spanning diverse document types, annotated with element bounding boxes, canonical content forms (Markdown, HTML, LaTeX, SMILES, structured charts), and full-page reading order. Second, we introduce a verifiable, multi-task reward system that enables Joint Reinforcement Learning across eight co-trained objectives (document parsing, layout analysis, table parsing, math formula parsing, chart parsing, chemical formula parsing, document VQA, and general multimodal understanding), unifying perception, structure, and reasoning in a single optimization signal. Third, we release two variants under a shared architecture: Infinity-Parser2-Flash, optimized for low-latency inference with a $3.68\times$ throughput gain over Infinity-Parser-7B, and Infinity-Parser2-Pro, engineered for precision-critical settings. Infinity-Parser2-Pro reaches state-of-the-art 87.6% on olmOCR-Bench and 74.3% on ParseBench, surpassing DeepSeek-OCR-2, PaddleOCR-VL-1.5, and MinerU2.5, with strong generalization to charts, chemical formulas, and document VQA.

AI.tldr: Infinity-Parser2 is a multimodal document parsing model built on a scalable synthetic data engine and multi-task reinforcement learning, introducing Infinity-Doc2-5M (5M bilingual annotations) and two efficient variants (Flash and Pro); it achieves state-of-the-art results on olmOCR-Bench and ParseBench with strong generalization.
AI.motivation: Scarcity of richly annotated end-to-end document-parsing corpora and the need for unified perception, structure, and reasoning across diverse document types.
AI.method: Develop a scalable synthesis engine combining controllable rendering with iterative refinement to create Infinity-Doc2-5M; implement a verifiable multi-task reward system for joint RL across eight objectives; release two model variants (Infinity-Parser2-Flash for low latency and Infinity-Parser2-Pro for precision) and train them in a joint framework.
AI.result: Infinity-Parser2-Pro achieves 87.6% on olmOCR-Bench and 74.3% on ParseBench, surpassing several baselines (DeepSeek-OCR-2, PaddleOCR-VL-1.5, MinerU2.5); 3.68x throughput gain for Flash variant; strong generalization to charts, chemical formulas, and document VQA; open-sourced Infinity-Doc2-5M dataset (5M samples, bilingual).
AI.conclusion: A unified end-to-end document-parsing framework that leverages synthetic data and multi-task RL yields state-of-the-art performance and broad generalization, with practical trade-offs between speed and precision and an emphasis on end-to-end perception, structure, and reasoning.

title: Towards Soft Robotic Exogloves for Musculoskeletal Manipulation to Reduce Pain and Spasticity
comment: 8 pages, 15 figures. To be published in the IEEE RAS/EMBS 11th International Conference on Biomedical Robotics and Biomechatronics (BioRob 2026)
summary: Hand spasticity and resulting pain affect 12 million people worldwide, including stroke survivors, arthritis patients, and those with other muscle and nerve deficiencies. Soft robotic exogloves are being introduced to help patients enhance mobility or manage pain; however, there are no current solutions that address both pain and mobility. We present preliminary development of a soft robotic exoglove that both aids in mobility and administers massage-like compression to relax spastic muscles. The glove consists of soft pneumatic actuators that are personalized to an individual's hand topology and kinematics, allowing for optimal conformability and targeted mobility. Novel soft actuators were designed, analyzed, fabricated, assembled into an exoglove, and experimentally tested. Actuators were 3D modeled and analyzed with finite element modeling under pressures of 100 and 200 kPa. Geometries were optimized to minimize stress before fabrication and testing. A dorsal finger actuator was successfully customized to a participant's hand topology, providing full conformal contact and maximal force distribution. A ventral finger actuator was successfully fabricated that can be drastically compressed in size to fit into the tight space of a hyperflexed spastic finger. A palmar actuator was successfully printed with stereolithography, showing potential for 3D-printed soft actuators with more complex geometries. The glove was assembled and successfully worn by a pilot user to validate initial findings in comfort and effectiveness.

AI.tldr: A preliminary soft robotic exoglove prototype that combines mobility assistance with massage-like compression to relax spastic muscles; custom-fit actuators, 3D-printed and FEM-analyzed, with initial user validation.
AI.motivation: Address pervasive hand spasticity and pain worldwide; existing solutions insufficiently address both mobility and pain simultaneously.
