AI.method: Design and fabrication of soft pneumatic actuators personalized to hand topology; 3D modeling and finite element analysis at 100 and 200 kPa to optimize stress; dorsal actuator customized for full conformal contact; ventral actuator miniaturized for tight spaces; palmar actuator produced via stereolithography; assembly and pilot user testing.
AI.result: Actuators successfully customized to participant hand topology with conformal contact and rational force distribution; ventral actuator compacted for hyperflexed fingers; palmar actuator 3D-printed; glove worn by a pilot user validating comfort and preliminary effectiveness.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates feasibility of an integrated soft exoglove for mobility support and spasticity relief; supports further development toward personalized, multi-actuator soft devices with larger-scale testing and long-term evaluation.

title: FedTR: Federated Learning Framework with Transfer Learning for Industrial Visual Inspection
comment: Author's accepted version. Published in Proceedings of the Great Lakes Symposium on VLSI 2024 (GLSVLSI '24)
summary: Federated learning (FL) is a collaborative learning scheme to train deep learning models, where collaborating parties can consolidate their models without sharing local data with other parties, hence preserving data privacy. Nevertheless, when implementing FL in Industrial visual inspection (IVI), the constraints posed by limited data availability and the intricate nature of the inspection tasks significantly impact the performance of the resulting model. This paper introduces FedTR, a novel FL framework incorporating transfer learning designed for Autonomous IVI, focusing on the challenging task of identifying label defects through end-to-end text recognition. Transfer learning is a method that leverages the knowledge of a pre-trained model to adapt to a different dataset. FedTR initially trains the model using a publicly available dataset, after which performs the essential federated learning process with model fine-tuning on the distributed and limited private data. Extensive experiment results demonstrate the effectiveness and feasibility of FedTR on private ink cartridge datasets for label defect identification. FedTR achieves an end-to-end text recognition word-level accuracy of 95.5% and 94.2% on homogeneous and heterogeneous data respectively. Additionally, it attains performance levels that are on par with those achieved through centralized training.

AI.tldr: FedTR: a federated learning framework with transfer learning for autonomous industrial visual inspection, using end-to-end text recognition to identify label defects; achieves near-centralized performance on ink cartridge datasets with high word-level accuracy in both homogeneous and heterogeneous data.
AI.motivation: Address data scarcity and privacy concerns in industrial visual inspection by combining transfer learning with federated learning to enable effective end-to-end text recognition for label defect identification.
AI.method: Pre-train on a public dataset, then perform federated learning with model fine-tuning on distributed, private data (FedTR). End-to-end text recognition is optimized for identifying label defects in autonomous IVI.
AI.result: Word-level accuracy of 95.5% (homogeneous) and 94.2% (heterogeneous); performance comparable to centralized training.
AI.conclusion: FedTR is an effective privacy-preserving transfer learning framework for autonomous IVI, achieving centralized-level performance on private datasets for label defect identification.

title: SHIFT: Survival Prediction from Incomplete and Heterogeneous Genomic Data
summary: Genomic prediction models often fail to transfer across institutions because sequencing panels differ across sites, creating structural feature missingness at deployment. Existing approaches to this challenge typically restrict analysis to genes shared across cohorts, exclude patients with incomplete profiles, or rely on test-time imputation, all of which can reduce robustness and limit the use of multi-center data. We propose Survival prediction Handling Incomplete Features using Transformer (SHIFT), a missingness-aware survival model that directly predicts from incomplete genomic inputs without test-time imputation. SHIFT represents each genomic feature separately and uses masked self-attention, along with a feature-availability mask, so that predictions are based only on observed inputs. Further, we introduce variable-rate feature masking during training to improve robustness to heterogeneous missingness patterns. We evaluate the approach on glioblastoma and lung squamous cell carcinoma with external validation across multiple cohorts, including a challenging setting with severe cross-cohort panel mismatch. Across these settings, SHIFT shows strong generalization and compares favorably with standard survival baselines and imputation-based approaches, while using a single model across differing feature sets. We also find that incorporating patients from incomplete cohorts during development can improve performance on external data, suggesting that partially observed cohorts need not be excluded from model building. These results support missingness-aware modeling as a practical strategy for multi-center survival prediction in precision oncology.

AI.tldr: A missingness-aware transformer-based survival model (SHIFT) handles incomplete genomic data without imputation, enabling cross-institution predictions and robust multi-cohort performance.
AI.motivation: Genomic prediction models struggle to transfer across institutions because sequencing panels differ, causing feature missingness that is not well addressed by standard approaches.
AI.method: Represent each genomic feature separately and apply masked self-attention with a feature-availability mask; introduce variable-rate feature masking during training; avoid test-time imputation and support a single model across differing feature sets.
AI.result: External validation on glioblastoma and lung squamous cell carcinoma with challenging cross-cohort panel mismatch shows SHIFT generalizes well, outperforming standard baselines and imputation-based methods, and enabling use of incomplete cohorts.
AI.conclusion: Missingness-aware modeling is a practical strategy for multi-center survival prediction in precision oncology, and incorporating partially observed cohorts during development can improve external performance.

title: VectorizationLLM: Smart Vectorization Based AI Assistant
summary: VectorizationLLM is a specialized Large Language Model based on Google open-weight LLMs. The model is designed to assist students to learn smart vectorization, time/wave vector analysis, piecewise functions, Fourier analysis, and differential equations in MATLAB. The course application is CTEC 247: Applied Computational Analysis II by the Department of Electrical & Computer Engineering Technology at New York Institute of Technology Old Westbury. The LLM model is designed to be an instructive assistant, providing detailed explanations of concepts with examples from in-class notes without providing direct answers to questions. The model is designed with a RAG (Retrieval Augmented Generation) knowledge base and system prompt architecture. Examples in both code, text, and images are provided in the LLM responses.

AI.tldr: A specialized LLM (VectorizationLLM) built on Google open-weight models to support MATLAB-based learning in vectorization and analysis, using RAG and a course-aligned prompt system to provide instructive explanations with examples from notes, without giving direct answers.
AI.motivation: Address the need for scaffolded, grounded instruction in vectorization, time/wave analysis, piecewise functions, Fourier analysis, and differential equations, leveraging in-class notes to ground responses and improve learning outcomes.
AI.method: Use Google open-weight LLMs; implement a Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) knowledge base and system prompts; deliver responses with code, text, and images; constrain to not provide direct answers and rely on in-class notes as sources.
AI.result: A designed instructional LLM with RAG integration intended to serve as an educative assistant for the CTEC 247 course, capable of detailed explanations and multimodal examples derived from class notes.
AI.conclusion: The framework aims to enhance students' conceptual understanding and problem-solving skills in MATLAB-related vector analysis and differential equations by grounding explanations in course material and providing multimodal examples.

title: Soft Robotic Exogloves for Dexterous Mobility -- Towards Personalized Rehabilitation
comment: 8 pages, 14 figures. To be published in The IEEE RAS/EMBS 11th International Conference on Biomedical Robotics and Biomechatronics (BioRob 2026)
summary: Soft robotic exogloves can provide hand rehabilitation and assistance. Fitting these gloves often relies on standardized measurements not tailored to the individual, limiting their effectiveness, especially for fine articulation necessary for dexterous manipulation. We present the design, fabrication, modeling, and testing of a personalized pneumatically-actuated soft robotic exoglove. The glove was fit to a user's hand with topological scans and fabricated with silicone mold casting. Finite element analysis (FEA) was performed to evaluate actuator bending and forces from physical human-robot interaction (pHRI) between an actuator and a simplified personalized biomechanical finger model. Pneumatic pressure control experiments were conducted to flex the user's finger with static and dynamic references. Fabrication results show that topological scans enable precise tailoring to hand anatomy. Simulations showed that anatomical personalization enables analysis of pHRI contact forces, and results indicate sufficient joint mobilization with non-ideal compression on the proximal phalanx. Pneumatic testing indicates that pressure control allows accurate and targeted mobility of the metacarpophalangeal (MCP) and proximal interphalangeal (PIP) joints with intrinsic stiffness. Testing of multiple designs showed that relaxing the strain-limiting layer improves actuator-to-finger joint alignment during actuation. This work presents personalization to the human hand in structural conformability, joint topology, modeling of pHRI contact, and time-dependent actuation-deformation profiles. This lays a groundwork for informing exoglove design optimization to enable assistance in dexterous manipulation and neuromuscular rehabilitation of fine motor skills.

AI.tldr: Personalized, pneumatically actuated soft exoglove designed from hand topology scans; demonstrates improved fit, pHRI modeling, and controllable MCP/PIP articulation for rehabilitation and dexterous use.
AI.motivation: Standardized fit methods do not account for individual hand anatomy, limiting precision and effectiveness in rehabilitation and fine-motor manipulation.
AI.method: Integrates hand-topology scanning and silicone mold casting for personalized fabrication; uses finite element analysis to assess actuator bending and pHRI forces with a simplified biomechanical finger model; conducts pneumatic pressure-control tests under static and dynamic references; evaluates multiple designs and a strain-limiting layer optimization.
AI.result: Topological scans enable precise hand-tailoring; personalization enables analysis of pHRI contact forces; results show sufficient joint mobilization despite non-ideal proximal phalanx compression; pressure control enables accurate MCP and PIP mobility with intrinsic stiffness; relaxing the strain-limiting layer improves actuator-to-finger alignment.
AI.conclusion: The work establishes a framework for hand personalization across structural conformity, joint topology, pHRI modeling, and time-dependent actuation, informing exoglove design optimization to support dexterous manipulation and neuromuscular rehabilitation of fine motor skills.

title: LightCrafter: PBR-Conditioned Video Diffusion Refinement for Controllable and Consistent Relighting
summary: Video relighting requires balancing long-form temporal consistency with a physically grounded understanding of light transport, which depends on accurate estimation of intrinsic scene properties such as materials, geometry, and illumination. Existing methods follow two paradigms: (1) reconstruct a video's photometric properties via inverse rendering and relight them to a target illumination via forward rendering, using physically-based rendering (PBR) or a neural renderer; these suffer from noisy reconstructions and struggle with hard-to-model effects such as global illumination. (2) Frame the task as generative video-to-video translation conditioned on relighting targets (a target environment map or text); this limits relighting control and temporal stability, since diffusion models struggle to translate long-form videos, and is constrained by the availability of input/relit training pairs. We propose LightCrafter, a hybrid pipeline that reformulates video relighting as video translation of a proxy video: rather than translating the input video directly to the target, we translate a PBR rendering of the input under the target illumination to the final target. This bakes illumination targets into the PBR proxy, removing the need to teach the diffusion model illumination concepts like environment maps, and enables more intricate lighting control while naturally providing long-form temporal consistency. We show PBR renders alone already outperform some prior art but struggle with effects like global illumination; to capture these, we leverage photometric priors in video generation models by post-training CogVideoX on synthetic video pairs and real-world unpaired videos. We outperform prior state-of-the-art on existing real-world relighting benchmarks and contribute a synthetic benchmark for further analysis. We will release our dataset, benchmark, metrics, and code.

AI.tldr: Hybrid video relighting via translating a PBR proxy render to the target illumination, improving temporal consistency and lighting control beyond inverse rendering or pure video-to-video translation.
AI.motivation: Current relighting approaches either rely on inverse rendering, which yields noisy reconstructions and struggles with global illumination, or frame-to-frame diffusion-based translation, which lacks long-form temporal stability and requires paired data. A hybrid approach can leverage physics-based proxies to embed illumination targets while enabling learned refinement.
AI.method: LightCrafter reframes relighting as translating a proxy video: first render the input under the target illumination with a physically-based renderer (PBR), then apply diffusion-based translation to map this proxy to the final target. It leverages photometric priors via post-training of CogVideoX on synthetic video pairs and unpaired real videos to capture global illumination effects. A synthetic benchmark is created, and datasets, metrics, and code are to be released.
AI.result: PBR renders alone already outperform some prior art; still limited by global illumination effects. Incorporating photometric priors via diffusion-based refinement improves results, achieving state-of-the-art performance on existing real-world relighting benchmarks. A synthetic benchmark is provided for deeper analysis.
AI.conclusion: The proposed hybrid pipeline combines physics-based proxy rendering with learned refinement to achieve better illumination control and long-form temporal consistency in video relighting, supported by a synthetic benchmark and public-release resources.

title: Jet-Long: Efficient Long-Context Extension with Dynamic Bifocal RoPE
summary: Modern LLMs are increasingly deployed in long-context applications such as retrieval-augmented generation, repository-level coding, and agentic workflows whose accumulated reasoning and tool traces routinely push the input an order of magnitude past the pretraining window, making zero-shot context extension the dominant deployment path for open-weight checkpoints. Most existing zero-shot methods fix a single rescaling factor up front, so an aggressive factor sacrifices short-context fidelity while a conservative one breaks down at long contexts. We propose Jet-Long, a tuning-free zero-shot method that pairs a local RoPE-faithful window with a long-range window whose rescaling factor adapts dynamically to the current sequence length, recovering the base model exactly at short inputs while extrapolating cleanly at long ones. An inclusion-exclusion attention merge and an on-the-fly RoPE correction rotation make the bifocal construction essentially free at inference; fused into a single CuTe kernel, long-context prefill reaches up to $1.39\times$ FA2 throughput on H100 (approaching the Hopper-only FA4), and single-batch generation incurs $\le 4\%$ overhead at every length. On Qwen3-1.7B/4B/8B up to 128K context, Jet-Long leads RULER by $+4.79$/$+2.18$/$+2.03$~pp over the strongest baseline at 1.7B/4B/8B, achieves the best overall accuracy on HELMET-RAG (a benchmark identified by HELMET as the most efficient predictor of downstream long-context performance) and attains the lowest PG-19 perplexity. Jet-Long also generalizes to hybrid attention architectures such as Jet-Nemotron for further long-context improvement without retraining, and remains hyperparameter-resilient for ease of deployment.

AI.tldr: Jet-Long is a tuning-free zero-shot long-context method that uses a dynamic, bifocal attention window (local RoPE-faithful and long-range with adaptive rescaling) to preserve short-context fidelity while extrapolating cleanly to very long sequences; it is efficient, hyperparameter-resilient, and generalizes to hybrid attention (Jet-Nemotron).
AI.motivation: Enable robust, zero-shot long-context extension for open-weight LLMs without retraining or manual tuning, balancing short-context fidelity with long-context extrapolation while maintaining efficiency.
AI.method: Jet-Long pairs a local RoPE-faithful window with a long-range window whose rescaling factor adapts to current sequence length. It uses an inclusion-exclusion attention merge and a RoPE correction rotation to realize a bifocal construction, fused into a single CuTe kernel for efficiency. It supports hybrid attention (Jet-Nemotron) and is hyperparameter-resilient.
AI.result: On Qwen3-1.7B/4B/8B with contexts up to 128K, Jet-Long improves RULER by +4.79/+2.18/+2.03 points, achieves best HELMET-RAG accuracy, and has the lowest PG-19 perplexity. Throughput reaches up to 1.39x FA2 on H100 (approaching FA4), with ≤4% overhead for generation across lengths. Generalizes to hybrid attention without retraining.
AI.conclusion: Jet-Long is a tuning-free, efficient long-context solution that preserves short-context fidelity while enabling scalable long-context extrapolation; it is broadly applicable and deployment-friendly, with strong empirical gains and robustness.

title: A Graph Neural Network Model for Real-Time Gesture Recognition Based on sEMG Signals
summary: For seemless control of advanced hand prostheses and augmented reality, accurate and immediate hand gestures recognition is essential. Surface electromyography (sEMG) signals obtained from the forearm are commonly employed for this purpose. In this paper, we present a novel approach for sEMG representation that utilizes graph networks which contain information about muscle activation patterns in the forearm. Based on these graph networks, we have developed a machine learning algorithm capable of real-time hand gesture recognition using a graph neural network. The algorithm's performance was evaluated using sEMG signals acquired from myoband, which has 8 electrodes placed around the forearm, involving 8 healthy subjects. The proposed method demonstrated an average classification accuracy of 99\%, surpassing the performance of state-of-the-art techniques. The average time for both graph construction and prediction stood at 48ms utilizing a M1 pro CPU, rendering the approach well-suited for real-time applications.

AI.tldr: Graph-based sEMG representation and GNN-based classifier achieve near-perfect real-time hand gesture recognition on forearm sEMG data.
AI.motivation: Deliver accurate, low-latency hand gesture decoding for advanced prosthetics and AR by leveraging structural information in sEMG signals.
AI.method: Represent sEMG signals as graphs encoding muscle activation patterns; train a graph neural network to perform real-time gesture classification; evaluate on 8-subject dataset from MyoBand with 8 channels; measure end-to-end latency.
AI.result: Average classification accuracy 99%; average graph construction + prediction time 48 ms on M1 Pro CPU; outperforms state-of-the-art.
AI.conclusion: Graph-based sEMG representation via GNNs is effective for real-time, high-accuracy gesture recognition and suitable for prosthetic/AR control.

title: In vivo feasibility study of humanoid robots in surgery
summary: Recent advances in actuation, control and learning have rapidly pushed humanoid robots from a distant vision towards near-term real-world deployment. Healthcare is a particularly pressing domain, in which staffing shortages and increasing care demand are widening the gap between clinical workload and available skilled labour. Although current automation has largely focused on digital and logistical tasks, much hospital work remains embodied, requiring mobility, manipulation and safe interaction in human-designed environments. Humanoid form factors offer unique potential, particularly for assisting with surgical tasks. Traditionally, robotic systems for surgery are purpose-built platforms such as Intuitive Surgical's da Vinci Surgical System, and it remains unclear how close current humanoid systems are to meeting the precision, control and safety requirements of minimally invasive surgery. Here we present a systematic evaluation of contemporary humanoid technology for laparoscopic surgical tasks. We develop a humanoid-based laparoscopic teleoperation framework using general-purpose instruments and assess its abilities through benchtop characterization, dry-laboratory user studies spanning diverse surgical experience levels and in vivo porcine studies. Across these evaluations, we quantify technical feasibility, task performance and clinical readiness relative to established surgical platforms. Together, our study provides an evidence-based assessment of current humanoid abilities and limitations for surgical applications, highlighting both their promise and key technical challenges that must be addressed before clinical deployment.

AI.tldr: Develops a humanoid-based laparoscopic teleoperation framework and evaluates its feasibility and readiness for clinical use across benchtop, dry-lab, and in vivo porcine tests, highlighting promise and key challenges.
AI.motivation: Healthcare staffing shortages and rising care demand; the embodied nature of hospital tasks benefits from humanoid platforms, especially for surgical assistance; assess whether humanoid robots can meet precision, control, and safety requirements of minimally invasive surgery compared to dedicated platforms.
AI.method: Implement a general-purpose humanoid laparoscopic teleoperation framework using standard instruments; perform benchtop characterization, dry-lab user studies across surgeons of different experience, and in vivo porcine trials; compare performance and readiness to conventional systems.
AI.result: Demonstrates technical feasibility and provides metrics on task performance and clinical readiness; finds evidence of promise but also significant technical gaps relative to established platforms; identifies specific limitations and challenges that must be addressed before clinical deployment.
AI.conclusion: Current humanoid systems show potential for laparoscopic assistance but are not yet clinically ready; systematic evaluation delineates what remains to be solved (precision, control realism, safety, reliability) and guides future research toward achieving clinical deployment.

title: SAGA: Stable Acceleration Guidance for Autoregressive Video Generation
summary: Autoregressive video diffusion enables efficient streaming and long-horizon video generation, but repeatedly reusing generated latents as causal context can amplify temporal errors, resulting in flickering, motion jitter, and structural drift. In this paper, we investigate this failure mode from a spectral kinematic perspective and identify discrete latent acceleration as an effective signal for revealing unstable high-frequency temporal perturbations. To this end, we propose SAGA, a training-free \textbf{\textit{s}}table \textbf{\textit{a}}cceleration \textbf{\textit{g}}uidance approach for \textbf{\textit{a}}utoregressive video generation. SAGA integrates an acceleration domain spectral guidance objective based on finite-window Slepian projections with a structured autoregressive noise initialization strategy that suppresses short-range temporal correlations while preserving long-range motion structure. Without retraining or modifying the backbone, SAGA can be directly applied to existing chunk-wise autoregressive diffusion models, which is the prevalent setting for high-quality generation. Extensive experiments show that SAGA consistently improves temporal quality across multiple autoregressive diffusion models. On Self-Forcing, SAGA improves Temporal Quality from 97.30 to 97.91 and Image Quality from 69.60 to 70.51. Moreover, spectral analysis and human preference studies demonstrate that SAGA reduces temporal instability while maintaining visual fidelity.

AI.tldr: A training-free spectral acceleration guidance method (SAGA) for autoregressive video diffusion that reduces high-frequency temporal errors by operating in an acceleration spectral domain and using structured autoregressive noise initialization; it plugs into existing chunk-wise diffusion backbones without retraining and improves temporal quality while preserving image fidelity.
AI.motivation: Temporal instability (flicker, motion jitter, structural drift) emerges when latent states are repeatedly reused as causal context in autoregressive video generation. A lightweight, retrain-free approach is sought to suppress short-range temporal perturbations without harming long-range motion.
AI.method: SAGA introduces an acceleration-domain spectral guidance objective based on finite-window Slepian projections and a structured autoregressive noise initialization. The approach is plug-and-play and does not require retraining of the backbone diffusion model; it modulates latent dynamics during generation to damp high-frequency temporal perturbations while preserving long-range motion structures.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show consistent temporal quality improvements across multiple autoregressive diffusion models. On Self-Forcing, Temporal Quality rises from 97.30 to 97.91 and Image Quality from 69.60 to 70.51. Spectral analysis and human studies indicate reduced temporal instability with preserved visual fidelity.
AI.conclusion: SAGA provides a practical, training-free stabilization technique for autoregressive video generation by focusing on latent acceleration in the spectral domain. It can be applied to existing chunk-wise diffusion models to improve temporal consistency without sacrificing image quality.

title: Architecture Generalization with MetaNCA
comment: 9 pages, 6 figures. To appear in the proceedings of the Artificial Life Conference (ALIFE 2026)
summary: Self-organization is an emergent property of life, driven by the collective behavior of individual components acting on local information. Biological neurons, through local interactions transmitted through synapses, are able to learn efficiently and can adapt their connections over an organism's lifespan. Motivated by these desirable properties of adaptability and local interaction, neural cellular automata (NCA) models have been successful at learning morphogenesis solely through local update rules, demonstrating stability over many updates and robustness to perturbations. In this work, we introduce Meta Neural Cellular Automata (MetaNCA), a framework that learns local rules which self-organize the weights of artificial neural networks. A learned rule network iteratively updates the weights of a task network using only local interactions on the computation graph. We propose a novel Weight Transformer architecture for the local rule network, which uses linear attention to aggregate signals from neighboring weights and hidden states. Once trained, the rule network generates task networks of diverse architectures without backpropagation. We show that MetaNCA generates weights for feedforward MLPs, CNNs, and ResNets on MNIST and CIFAR-100, scaling to networks of 2 million parameters. We further show that MetaNCA generalizes to architectures not seen during meta-training, and that architectural diversity in the training phase strengthens this generalization.

AI.tldr: MetaNCA learns local update rules to self-organize neural network weights, using a Weight Transformer with linear attention; it can generate MNIST/CIFAR-100 models without backpropagation, generalizes to unseen architectures, and benefits from architectural diversity during meta-training.
AI.motivation: Inspired by self-organization in biology and the success of neural cellular automata, the work aims to achieve adaptable, locally governed weight generation for diverse neural architectures.
AI.method: Proposes Meta Neural Cellular Automata (MetaNCA) where a rule network iteratively updates the weights of a task network via local interactions on the computation graph; introduces a Weight Transformer that uses linear attention to aggregate signals from neighboring weights and hidden states; after meta-training, the rule network can generate task networks without backpropagation.
AI.result: MetaNCA can generate weights for feedforward MLPs, CNNs, and ResNets on MNIST and CIFAR-100, scaling to networks of ~2M parameters; generalizes to architectures not seen during meta-training, with architectural diversity in training strengthening generalization.
AI.conclusion: Local, local-rule derived weight generation via MetaNCA offers a backpropagation-free pathway to synthesize diverse, robust neural networks, highlighting the potential of learned local rules for neural architecture synthesis and adaptation.

title: Agentic AI and Retrieval-Augmented Models in Straight-Through Underwriting
summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) is beginning to reshape actuarial practice, particularly in domains that require reasoning over unstructured documents, heterogeneous data sources, and regulated decision workflows. Actuaries now face a design space that ranges from traditional rule-based automation to large language models (LLMs), retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), and multi-agent ``agentic'' systems that plan, retrieve, call tools, and reflect. This paper examines how these emerging architectures can support actuarial priorities such as transparency, auditability, and human-in-the-loop governance, with a focus on straight-through decision processes. To make these ideas concrete, we develop and analyze an agentic AI framework for straight-through underwriting of small commercial Business Owner Policies (BOPs). We construct a synthetic but realistic experimental environment and compare three underwriting pipelines: (i) a single-LLM baseline, (ii) a naive RAG system, and (iii) a multi-agent ``Agentic RAG'' pipeline that combines targeted retrieval, third-party data checks, and explicit multi-step rule evaluation. The agentic system performs best overall, with the largest gains in multi-step and missing-information scenarios, where structured retrieval and reflection help the model avoid unsupported straight-through decisions.

AI.tldr: Agentic RAG pipeline for straight-through underwriting of small commercial BOPs, combining targeted retrieval, third-party checks, and explicit multi-step rule evaluation, outperforms a single-LLM baseline and naive RAG, especially in multi-step/missing-information scenarios.
AI.motivation: Address transparency, auditability, independence, and governance in AI-assisted actuarial decision-making; explore a design space spanning rule-based automation, LLMs, retrieval-augmented generation, and multi-agent systems for regulated workflows.
AI.method: Construct a synthetic yet realistic experimental environment and compare three underwriting pipelines: (i) a single-LLM baseline, (ii) a naive RAG system, and (iii) an agentic RAG pipeline that integrates targeted retrieval, third-party data checks, and explicit multi-step rule evaluation.
AI.result: The agentic system achieves the best overall performance, with the largest gains in multi-step and missing-information cases; structured retrieval and reflection help prevent unsupported straight-through decisions.
AI.conclusion: Agentic RAG demonstrates promise for transparent, auditable, and governance-friendly actuarial AI in regulated underwriting; combining retrieval, third-party checks, and explicit multi-step rule evaluation improves decision quality in complex decision workflows.

title: D-CLIPSE: Distributed Consensus-based Localization with Passive Listening on Shared State Exchange
comment: 8 pages, 7 figures, 1 table. Submitted to IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters
summary: Multi-robot localization that is accurate and consistent is imperative for downstream tasks such as planning and control. Centralized filtering approaches optimally fuse all available sensor measurements of the team. However, a centralized solution is rarely implementable due to hardware, communication, and computational constraints. Distributed approaches deploy a filter on each robot to estimate their own state and neighbours' states using inter-robot communication. This paper proposes a consistent, communication-efficient, and consensus-based distributed filtering framework that shares both preintegrated odometry and relevant shared states among communicating robots. The proposed method is validated in simulated and experimental scenarios, showing near centralized performance in accuracy, and especially in consistency, compared to the current state-of-the-art decentralized approach.

AI.tldr: A distributed, consensus-based multi-robot localization framework that shares preintegrated odometry and relevant shared states to achieve near-centralized accuracy and strong consistency with reduced communication.
AI.motivation: Centralized filtering is optimal but impractical for multi-robot systems due to hardware, communication, and computation constraints; distributed filters must estimate own state and neighbors' states while remaining consistent.
AI.method: Introduce a consistent, communication-efficient, consensus-based distributed filtering framework that exchanges preintegrated odometry and relevant shared states among communicating robots to fuse information.
AI.result: Simulation and real-world experiments show near-centralized accuracy and, notably, improved consistency compared to the current state-of-the-art decentralized approaches.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework offers a practical, scalable solution that attains centralized-like performance in distributed multi-robot localization while maintaining strong consistency and reduced communication

title: APIVOT: Adaptive Planning with Interleaved Vision-Language Thoughts
summary: Long-horizon robot planning requires jointly reasoning over semantic task structure and geometric feasibility. To successfully execute a task, a robot must decompose goals, select task-relevant objects, and sequence actions, while ensuring that plans satisfy spatial constraints such as limited free space and object collisions. In this work, we propose APIVOT, a VLM-based planner that adaptively interleaves language and visual thoughts for long-horizon planning. APIVOT learns to leverage language for semantic reasoning, while using visual thoughts as imagined future states for internal verification of geometric feasibility. On long-horizon kitchen tasks, APIVOT outperforms general-purpose VLMs and prior planning frameworks, achieving the largest gains in spatially constrained settings. We find that APIVOT learns meaningful modality selection behavior, demonstrating that adaptive interleaving of vision-language thoughts improves both planning success and reasoning efficiency.

AI.tldr: APIVOT is a VLM-based planner that adaptively interleaves language and visual reasoning for long-horizon robotic planning, using language for semantic task reasoning and imagined visual states for geometric feasibility checks, showing strong gains in spatially constrained kitchen tasks.
AI.motivation: Long-horizon robot planning demands integrating semantic task structure with geometric feasibility, balancing high-level planning with spatial constraints; existing VLMs and planners struggle to jointly optimize these aspects, especially under tight free-space and collision constraints.
AI.method: APIVOT employs a vision-language model (VLM) that alternates between language-based thoughts for semantic reasoning and visual thoughts as imagined future states to verify geometric feasibility, enabling adaptive modality selection during planning for long-horizon tasks.
AI.result: In long-horizon kitchen tasks, APIVOT outperforms general-purpose VLMs and prior planning frameworks, achieving the largest gains in spatially constrained settings and showing that the model learns meaningful modality selection to improve planning success and efficiency.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive interleaving of language and visual thoughts enables better semantic-geometry reasoning in long-horizon robotic planning, improving success rates and planning efficiency while reducing unnecessary computation via modality selection.

title: LiST: Lipschitz Scaling Training for Robust and Calibrated Neural Networks
summary: While accuracy, robustness, and calibration are all essential for reliable neural networks, they are often studied separately; developing models that satisfy all three simultaneously remains a central challenge. Lipschitz-constrained models guarantee robustness by design, yet the manual selection of the Lipschitz constraint L governs the resulting accuracy-robustness trade-off, and their calibration properties remain largely underexplored. In this work, we highlight a theoretical and empirical link between the enforced Lipschitz constraint and Temperature Scaling, a state-of-the-art calibration method. Specifically, we find that for a given training scheme, there exists a non-trivial value L* that yields an out-of-the-box calibrated network, and that calibration acts as a principled criterion to select a well-defined operating point on the accuracy-robustness Pareto front. Leveraging these insights, we introduce Lipschitz Scaling Training (LiST), a novel training paradigm that iteratively adjusts the global Lipschitz constant to reach this operating point. Through a margin parameter in the training loss, LiST further enables the construction of a fully calibrated Pareto front, allowing users to navigate the accuracy-robustness trade-off while remaining calibrated throughout. At convergence, LiST also enables the reintegration of calibration data into training, improving sample efficiency without sacrificing calibration. We validate LiST on CIFAR-10/100 and Tiny-ImageNet, demonstrating competitive accuracy and robustness against constrained and unconstrained baselines, while remaining calibrated out of the box. Code is available at GitHub.

AI.tldr: A study connecting Lipschitz constraints with calibration shows there exists an optimal Lipschitz value L* that yields a calibrated network. The paper introduces Lipschitz Scaling Training (LiST) to iteratively adjust L to reach this point, using a margin in the loss to construct a calibrated Pareto front between accuracy and robustness. LiST can reintegrate calibration data during training to improve sample efficiency. Empirical validation on CIFAR-10/100 and Tiny-ImageNet demonstrates competitive performance and out-of-the-box calibration; code is released.
AI.motivation: Calibrated, robust, and accurate neural networks are desirable but challenging to achieve simultaneously. Lipschitz constraints aid robustness but introduce an accuracy-calibration trade-off governed by the constraint L, which is not well understood. Temperature Scaling provides a calibration lens to pick operating points along the accuracy-robustness Pareto front.
AI.method: The authors provide theoretical and empirical analysis linking the global Lipschitz constant to Temperature Scaling calibration. They propose Lipschitz Scaling Training (LiST) that iteratively tunes the global L during training to reach a calibrated operating point on the Pareto front. A margin parameter in the training loss is used to generate a fully calibrated Pareto front. At convergence, calibration data can be reintegrated into training to improve sample efficiency without harming calibration.
AI.result: There exists a non-trivial L* yielding an out-of-the-box calibrated network. LiST can construct a fully calibrated Pareto front, enabling navigation of the accuracy-robustness trade-off while maintaining calibration. The approach achieves competitive accuracy and robustness compared to baselines and remains calibrated without extra calibration steps. Reintegrating calibration data improves sample efficiency.
AI.conclusion: Calibration considerations can guide the optimization of Lipschitz-constrained models to achieve balanced accuracy and robustness. LiST provides a practical training paradigm to reach calibrated operating points and explore calibrated Pareto fronts, with empirical validation on standard datasets and available code.

title: Feedback Manipulation Regularization: Enabling Offline Agent Alignment for Imitation Learning
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) research has increasingly shifted focus towards alignment, ensuring agents learn behaviors adhering to human values. While human demonstrations and feedback have proven crucial for alignment, existing approaches predominantly combine these signals using multi-stage pipelines designed for the contextual bandit framing of language generation. Yet little work explores how these complementary inputs can serve as a richer, interconnected signal for single-stage offline training in fully sequential decision-making environments. We propose Feedback Manipulation Regularization (FMR), an algorithm-agnostic method that harnesses evaluative feedback as a corrective signal to improve the alignment of imitation learning policies. We adapt Safety Gymnasium environments to be a principled testbed for alignment evaluation, demonstrating improved aptitude and up to a 98\% reduction in misalignment across a range of imitation learning algorithms. FMR remains robust in limited data regimes, even when learning from scarce aligned and uninformative noisy demonstrations.

AI.tldr: A unified, algorithm-agnostic regularization (FMR) that uses evaluative feedback to correct imitation policies, enabling single-stage offline training for sequential RL and achieving up to 98% reduction in misalignment in Safety Gymnasium tests.
AI.motivation: Address the gap between multi-stage input fusion (demonstrations + feedback) designed for contextual bandits and the need for single-stage offline training in fully sequential RL; improve alignment robustness with limited/noisy data.
AI.method: Introduce Feedback Manipulation Regularization (FMR): an algorithm-agnostic regularization term that treats evaluative feedback as a corrective signal to steer imitation-learning updates. Compatible with various imitation learning objectives and robust to scarce aligned and noisy demonstrations; evaluated by adapting Safety Gymnasium environments for alignment tests.
AI.result: Demonstrates improved alignment aptitude and up to 98% reduction in misalignment across multiple imitation-learning algorithms; robust in low-data regimes with scarce aligned and noisy demonstrations.
AI.conclusion: FMR provides a principled, single-stage alignment mechanism that leverages evaluative feedback to improve imitation-learning policies, showing strong cross-algorithm robustness and promising applicability to sequential RL alignment.

title: Factors Influencing Conversational Engagement in Robot-Delivered Individual Cognitive Stimulation Therapy (iCST) for Dementia in Home Settings
comment: Accepted for publication at the IEEE RO-MAN Conference 2026
summary: Social robots offer a promising means of supporting cognitive therapies for dementia care by guiding structured conversation and therapeutic activities. However, little is known about the conversational dynamics that emerge during robot-delivered cognitive stimulation therapy (CST) sessions. This study analysed the interaction patterns from robot-delivered individual CST (iCST) sessions conducted with people living with dementia in home settings. Our Co-STAR (Cognitive Stimulation Therapy by an Autonomous Robot) system was deployed in the homes of eight PwDs for one week, who completed 30-minute sessions. Conversational metrics, including words per turn, speech production rate, response duration, response latency, and self-referential language, were analysed to examine how conversational engagement is shaped by prompt personalisation, interaction phase, and participant characteristics. The findings highlight three key interactional properties of robot-delivered iCST. First, personalised prompts significantly increase response duration, self-referential language, and overall engagement compared to generic prompts. Second, conversational behaviour changes within sessions, with a reduction in the verbal output and autobiographical engagement observed during later interaction phases, which suggests cognitive fatigue. Third, first-session conversational metrics were associated with long-term participation, while living situation influenced conversational engagement patterns. These findings provide empirical insights into the factors that shape conversational engagement in robot-delivered iCST. They inform the design of adaptive conversational robots for dementia therapy.

AI.tldr: Personalized prompts in robot-delivered cognitive stimulation therapy (CST) for dementia increased engagement and autobiographical language; engagement declined within sessions, suggesting cognitive fatigue; first-session engagement predicted longer-term participation, with living situation influencing patterns.
AI.motivation: To understand how conversational dynamics emerge in robot-delivered CST for dementia in home settings and to inform the design of adaptive robotic interventions.
AI.method: Eight people with dementia used the Co-STAR autonomous robot for one week in their homes, performing 30-minute iCST sessions. Conversational metrics were analyzed: words per turn, speech production rate, response duration, response latency, and self-referential language, examining effects of prompt personalization, interaction phase, and participant characteristics.
AI.result: Three key properties emerged: (1) personalized prompts significantly increased response duration, self-referential language, and overall engagement versus generic prompts; (2) conversational behavior changed across interaction phases with reduced verbal output and autobiographical engagement in later phases, indicating cognitive fatigue; (3) first-session metrics were associated with long-term participation, and living situation influenced engagement patterns.
AI.conclusion: Insights illuminate factors shaping engagement in robot-delivered iCST and support designing adaptive conversational robots for dementia therapy.

title: Post-Training in End-to-End Autonomous Driving
summary: End-to-end models that map multimodal inputs directly to future trajectories/maneuvers have emerged as an increasingly prominent research paradigm in autonomous driving. This class of models includes both Vision-Language-Action models and trajectory-generative planners. Unlike classic machine learning applications, autonomous vehicles operate in safety-critical and interaction-intensive environments where traditional open-loop imitation of expert demonstrations is not sufficient to ensure reliability. In particular, small execution errors can accumulate over time, while recovery behaviors are scarce in training data. In addition, long-horizon objectives such as safety and driving comfort are not captured by pointwise labels either. These limitations have motivated a shift toward post-training techniques, which further refine driving policies beyond pure imitation. This survey presents a unified view of post-training for autonomous driving by defining its scope and organizing the existing literature into four major families based on the form of supervision they use. For each family, we discuss its capabilities, limitations, and open challenges. We aim to facilitate a systematic understanding of this emerging area and stimulate future research on reliable and efficient post-training for autonomous driving.

AI.tldr: End-to-end autonomous driving benefits from post-training techniques; the surveyed work categorizes four supervision-based families, analyzes capabilities/limits, and outlines open challenges to improve reliability and efficiency.
AI.motivation: Address safety-critical, interaction-rich driving where imitation learning alone fails due to error accumulation, scarce recovery data, and long-horizon objectives not captured by pointwise labels.
AI.method: This survey defines the scope of post-training for autonomous driving and organizes existing literature into four families based on the form of supervision; it discusses capabilities, limitations, and open challenges for each family.
AI.result: Provides a unified, systematic understanding of post-training approaches in autonomous driving and guidance for future research directions.
AI.conclusion: Post-training is essential to achieve reliable and efficient autonomous driving, complementing imitation learning and enabling long-horizon, safety- and comfort-oriented objectives.

title: Selective Left-Shift: Turning Test-Time Compute and Difficulty-based Curation into Training Data for Low-Resource Code Generation
summary: Large Language Models achieve strong code generation for high resource languages like Python and Java but suffer sharp performance drops on Low-Resource Programming Languages~(LRPLs) such as Julia. Improving Small Language Models~(SLMs) for these languages faces a trilemma: Supervised Fine-Tuning~(SFT) is bottlenecked by data scarcity, inference-time scaling is too expensive for deployment, and Reinforcement Learning from scratch yields near zero advantages. We propose a three-phase pipeline that resolves this trilemma by decoupling syntax acquisition from algorithmic reasoning. First, we \emph{left-shift} inference-time compute to an offline data synthesis engine that uses iterative compiler and test feedback to generate verified training examples. Second, we fine-tune an SLM on this synthetic, verified data to embed strong syntactic priors. Third, we apply Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Reward~(RLVR) grounded by language-agnostic Input/Output tests, where the SFT prior constrains exploration away from syntax errors. Applied to Qwen3-8B, our pipeline improves pass@1 by up to +7.6 points on MultiPL-E and +14.2 points on the Agnostics LiveCodeBench for Julia compared to SOTA results. Furthermore, the pipeline only used $\frac{1}{3}$ data and $\frac{1}{6}$ cost over the previous state-of-the-art. We further demonstrate that the pipeline generalizes to Ballerina achieving 49.7\% MultiPL-E Pass@1, a language with near-zero pretraining representation. Ablations confirm that both the SFT phase and execution-grounded rewards are necessary for stable training.

AI.tldr: A three-phase pipeline decoupling syntax acquisition from algorithmic reasoning to boost small-language model performance on low-resource programming languages, achieving strong gains with reduced data and cost.
AI.motivation: Large language models excel on high-resource languages but underperform on low-resource programming languages (LRPLs). For small language models (SLMs), data scarcity bottlenecks supervised fine-tuning (SFT), inference-time scaling is costly for deployment, and reinforcement learning from scratch yields limited benefits. A method that acquires strong syntactic priors offline and grounds reasoning with execution-based signals could alleviate the trilemma.
AI.method: Phase 1: offline data synthesis using iterative compiler/test feedback to generate verified training examples (left-shift inference). Phase 2: SFT on synthetic, verified data to encode strong syntactic priors. Phase 3: RL with Verifiable Reward (RLVR) using language-agnostic IO tests to ground rewards, with the SFT prior guiding exploration away from syntax errors. Evaluation on Qwen3-8B across Julia and Ballerina; ablations to validate components.
AI.result: On Julia (MultiPL-E and Agnostics LiveCodeBench): pass@1 improvements of +7.6 and +14.2 points respectively over state-of-the-art. Data and cost efficiency: approximately 1/3 data and 1/6 cost relative to prior SOTA. Generalizes to Ballerina achieving 49.7% MultiPL-E Pass@1 (despite near-zero pretraining representation). Ablations indicate both the SFT phase and execution-grounded rewards are necessary for stable training.
AI.conclusion: The proposed three-phase pipeline effectively decouples syntax acquisition from reasoning, enabling substantial performance gains with reduced data/cost and demonstrating cross-language generalization to at least one additional LRPL (Ballerina). The approach hinges on offline verified data synthesis and IO-grounded rewards to stabilize RL.

title: Nigeria Machinery: A Low-Resource Industrial Dataset with a Domain-Grounded Reasoning Layer
summary: There is relatively little, public, and model-ready data on industrial machinery for African economies. This makes it hard to do quantitative analysis or to train language models on numeric tasks grounded in that setting. We release two things to help with part of this problem. The first is the Nigeria Machinery Usage and Failures Dataset: 89 machine-level records across 28 indicators, covering Nigeria's manufacturing and oil and gas sectors from 2006 to 2025. Every record names a public source and is decoded by a codebook. The second is a method for building chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning examples from these sparse numeric values. The result is 94 prompt, completion, and reasoning-trace rows. In every row, the prompt names the real indicator, subsector, year, and source of the record it comes from. The data adaptation work was carried out by Adaption Labs. Along the way we describe a problem that is common when language models are used to build datasets. The prompts can match the real numbers while saying nothing about the real domain. We show that fixing this raises the share of domain-grounded prompts from 1 out of 78 in an earlier release to 94 out of 94, and that every retrieval answer now matches its source value (84 out of 84). We release the data, the reasoning layer, and a per-row provenance file under CC-BY-4.0. We are clear about the limits. With 89 records and 17 indicators that have only one observation, this is a reference and seed dataset, not a large training set. Most reasoning rows are retrieval rather than multi-step computation.

AI.tldr: Release of the Nigeria Machinery Usage and Failures Dataset (89 records, 28 indicators, 2006–2025) plus a chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning dataset (94 rows) to support domain-grounded numeric reasoning for African industrial data. Improved prompt-domain alignment; data provenance included; licensing CC-BY-4.0.
AI.motivation: Tackle the scarcity of public, machine-readable, domain-grounded industrial data for Africa, enabling quantitative analysis and language-model tasks on numeric data grounded in Nigeria's manufacturing and oil/gas sectors. Provide reproducible datasets and a provenance framework.
AI.method: Two artifacts: (1) a dataset of 89 machine-level records with 28 indicators and a detailed codebook linking each record to a public source; (2) a method to convert sparse numeric values into chain-of-thought prompts with associated completions and reasoning traces, producing 94 prompt/completion/reasoning-trace rows. The prompts explicitly name the real indicator, subsector, year, and source to ensure domain grounding, addressing a leakage issue where prompts could mirror numbers without domain meaning. Adaption Labs conducted the data adaptation; per-row provenance is provided; licensing is CC-BY-4.0.
AI.result: Public release of the Nigeria Machinery Usage and Failures Dataset and a CoT reasoning dataset, with improved domain grounding (all prompts domain-relevant) and verified source-value matches in retrieval responses (84/84).
AI.conclusion: The work provides a seed/reference dataset for economic machinery data in Nigeria and a reproducible CoT workflow, useful for LM evaluation and numeric-grounded tasks, while noting limitations: small size (89 records, 17 indicators with single observations) and a predominance of retrieval over multi-step reasoning.

title: RadLoc: Radar-based 3-DoF Global Localization via Fast, Robust, and Lightweight Spatial Descriptor Across Diverse Environmental Scenarios
summary: While global localization using spinning radar has gained attention for its robustness to adverse weather and challenging environments, many studies have focused on individual components such as place recognition or pose estimation. In this paper, we take a holistic view of radar sensor-based global localization and present RadLoc, a fast, robust, and lightweight end-to-end pipeline from place recognition to 3-DoF pose estimation. RadLoc accelerates pre-processing using 1D CA-CFAR filtering and leverages the near-range dominance in spinning radar images to design a compact descriptor and an efficient hierarchical coarse-to-fine retrieval strategy. Moreover, coupled with phase correlation-based 3-DoF pose estimation, it forms a versatile global localization module applicable to SLAM and multi-session SLAM systems. Extensive experiments on 15 sequences across 5 datasets demonstrate that RadLoc achieves robust performance while maintaining the smallest descriptor size and fastest retrieval time among state-of-the-art approaches. The supplementary materials are available at https://sparolab.github.io/research/radloc/.

AI.tldr: RadLoc is a fast, robust end-to-end radar-based global localization pipeline that uses 1D CA-CFAR pre-processing, compact descriptors exploiting near-range features, hierarchical coarse-to-fine retrieval, and phase correlation for 3-DoF pose estimation, achieving state-of-the-art efficiency and robustness across multiple datasets.
AI.motivation: To provide a holistic, end-to-end radar global localization solution instead of addressing isolated components like place recognition or pose estimation.
AI.method: 1) 1D CA-CFAR filtering for fast pre-processing; 2) descriptor design leveraging near-range dominance of spinning radar; 3) compact descriptor; 4) hierarchical coarse-to-fine retrieval; 5) phase correlation-based 3-DoF pose estimation; 6) integration into an end-to-end pipeline for SLAM/multi-session SLAM.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on 15 sequences across 5 datasets show robust performance, with the smallest descriptor size and fastest retrieval time among state-of-the-art approaches.
AI.conclusion: RadLoc provides a versatile, fast, and robust global localization module suitable for SLAM and multi-session SLAM, with a lightweight descriptor enabling real-time operation.

title: UAV-OVVIS: Unmanned Aerial Vehicles Also Need Open-Vocabulary Video Instance Segmentation
summary: Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) videos are widely used in traffic monitoring, urban management, and emergency rescue. However, existing UAV video perception mainly relies on box-level localization and trajectory association under predefined categories, making it difficult to simultaneously support flexible queries and fine-grained instance-level dynamic understanding in open scenarios. To this end, we introduce a new task, UAV Open-Vocabulary Video Instance Segmentation (UAV-OVVIS), which discovers targets in UAV videos according to open-vocabulary queries and outputs instance-level segmentation trajectories with globally consistent identities. Considering the scarcity of instance-level annotations in UAV scenarios, we propose AeroTrack, a training-free unified framework. AeroTrack centers on periodic open-vocabulary detection, short-segment mask propagation, and cross-segment identity unification, reusing existing visual foundation models to enable UAV-OVVIS. Based on this framework, we instantiate five AeroTrack variants and construct AeroVIS, an evaluation benchmark for UAV-OVVIS containing 9 UAV object categories and 8,279 trajectories. Experiments show that AeroTrack substantially outperforms existing general video instance segmentation methods in UAV scenarios and demonstrates strong open-vocabulary robustness and generalization. To support future research, we release AeroTrack and AeroVIS as a unified framework and benchmark for UAV-OVVIS.

AI.tldr: Proposes UAV Open-Vocabulary Video Instance Segmentation (UAV-OVVIS) and a training-free AeroTrack framework that uses open-vocabulary detection, short-segment mask propagation, and cross-segment identity unification to achieve instance-level segmentation trajectories with open-vocabulary queries; validates on AeroVIS benchmark and shows strong open-vocabulary robustness.
AI.motivation: UAV videos demand flexible, open-vocabulary querying and fine-grained, instance-level tracking in open scenarios, but there is a scarcity of instance-level UAV annotations. A unified, training-free approach leveraging foundation models could enable open-vocabulary, cross-frame instance understanding without heavy labeling.
AI.method: Introduce AeroTrack, a training-free unified framework for UAV-OVVIS built around periodic open-vocabulary detection, short-segment mask propagation, and cross-segment identity unification. Reuse existing visual foundation models to enable open-vocabulary video instance segmentation in UAV contexts. Instantiate five AeroTrack variants.
AI.result: Outperforms existing general video instance segmentation methods in UAV scenarios, demonstrating strong open-vocabulary robustness and generalization. The AeroVIS benchmark contains 9 UAV object categories and 8,279 trajectories, and AeroTrack and AeroVIS are released for future research.
AI.conclusion: AeroTrack effectively enables UAV-OVVIS in a training-free manner by reusing foundation models and a simple yet strong pipeline; the framework and benchmark provide a solid basis for future research in open-vocabulary UAV video understanding.

title: A Transdiagnostic Space of Disorder Like Phenotypes in Reinforcement Learning Agents
summary: Modelling psychological disorders in artificial agents offers both a testbed for computational psychiatry and a lens on the failure modes of affective control. Prior work induces one or two disorders in a reinforcement learning (RL) agent by hand-tuned reward shaping, labels the behaviour post hoc, and reports single runs. We recast disorder modelling as dose-controllable manipulation of cognitive appraisal signals in an appraisal-guided PPO agent, expressing seven disorders (anxiety, mania, obsessive-compulsive checking, depression, impulsivity, addiction, and post-traumatic stress) each as a single knob grounded in a computational psychiatry account, with each symptom measured by a preregistered assay mapped to a recognised paradigm. Across more than a thousand runs (10 seeds, four controls, 95% confidence intervals) every disorder shows a graded, monotone dose-response that no control reproduces. Beyond these induced effects, three findings emerge that were not written into the reward: the disorders self-organise into a two-dimensional affective space in which mania mirrors anxiety; removing a knob remits reward distortion disorders (mania, checking, addiction) but not avoidance disorders (anxiety, PTSD), which instead recover under a graded exposure curriculum; and two simultaneous knobs interact nonadditively, yielding testable comorbidity predictions. Appraisal weights thus parameterise a controllable space of affective phenotypes in which the same knobs that induce a disorder can model its treatment. We also show that three disorder knobs (depression, addiction, anxiety) transfer to a three-dimensional pixel environment (MiniWorld) with a standard convolutional agent and no appraisal critic, with cross-assay dissociation confirmed across both domains, indicating the framework is not specific to grid worlds or to PPO's appraisal critic.

AI.tldr: Recasting disorder modelling in RL as dose-controllable manipulation of cognitive appraisal signals in an appraisal-guided PPO yields seven graded, monotone dose-responses across disorders with reproducible controls; disorders self-organize in a two-dimensional affective space; removing knobs affects symptom domains differently and two knobs interact nonadditively, yielding comorbidity predictions; transfer across domains suggests a general framework for modelling and potential treatment.
AI.motivation: Provide a principled, quantitative, and transferable framework to model psychiatric disorders in artificial agents, moving beyond ad hoc reward shaping and post hoc labeling, enabling systematic study of mechanisms, interactions, and potential treatments across environments.
AI.method: Use appraisal-guided PPO with seven disorder knobs, each altering appraisal weights to represent anxiety, mania, OCD checking, depression, impulsivity, addiction, and PTSD. Assess via preregistered assays mapped to recognized paradigms. Run >1000 trials (10 seeds, 4 controls, 95% CIs). Examine two-domain grid-world and MiniWorld transfer with standard CNN agent, with and without appraisal critic.
AI.result: Each disorder shows a graded, monotone dose-response not reproduced in controls. Disorders self-organize into a 2D affective space where mania mirrors anxiety. Removing a knob remits reward distortion disorders (mania, checking, addiction) but not avoidance disorders (anxiety, PTSD), which recover under graded exposure. Two knobs interact nonadditively, yielding testable comorbidity predictions. Three knobs transfer to MiniWorld with cross-domain dissociation, indicating domain-general applicability.
AI.conclusion: Appraisal weights parameterize a controllable space of affective phenotypes; the same knobs that induce disorders can model their treatment. The framework is not specific to grid worlds or PPO's appraisal critic, and yields testable predictions about comorbidity and treatment across domains.

title: Persona Cartography: Charting Language Model Personality Traits in Weight Space
summary: Large language models exhibit recurring behavioural patterns -- personas -- that shape generalisation and safety, but we lack reliable tools for decomposing, measuring, and controlling them. Our central insight is to treat personas as positions in a space of behavioural traits, using the OCEAN framework to describe model personas in terms of Openness, Conscientiousness, Extraversion, Agreeableness, and Neuroticism. We train low-rank adapters to amplify or suppress individual traits, and evaluate their effects using an LLM-judge calibrated against a human-validated panel, trait-specific multiple-choice benchmarks, and standard capability evaluations. Across six models from three families (4B-32B), we find that each adapter moves its target trait largely monotonically with scale, combines approximately additively with other adapters to construct mixed personas, and preserves performance on capability benchmarks at moderate scales. We further show that the induced trait axes affect safety-relevant behaviour in downstream evaluations: for example, moving along neuroticism and agreeableness axes affects frustration and sycophancy respectively. We also introduce an unsupervised psychometric pipeline that recovers four interpretable behavioural factors (tone, initiative, didacticism, epistemic caution) from model rollouts. Persona control can then be considered in terms of learning, scaling, and composing traits in weight space, providing a bridge between personality measurement, model editing, and safety.

AI.tldr: Treats LLM personas as positions in an OCEAN trait space; uses low-rank adapters to modulate traits; shows monotonic scaling, additive fusion of traits, and safety implications; adds an unsupervised psychometric pipeline.
AI.motivation: Addresses the lack of reliable tools to decompose, measure, and control model personas. Proposes a trait-based framework (OCEAN) to study generalization and safety, enabling systematic editing and evaluation of behavior.
AI.method: Experimentally train low-rank adapters to amplify or suppress each OCEAN trait across six models (4B–32B). Evaluate with a calibrated LLM-judge, trait-specific multiple-choice benchmarks, and standard capability tests. Analyze monotonic scaling, additivity between adapters, and safety-related behavior. Develop an unsupervised psychometric pipeline that extracts four interpretable factors (tone, initiative, didacticism, epistemic caution) from rollouts.
AI.result: Adapters drive target traits largely monotonically with scale; trait effects combine approximately additively to form mixed personas; capability performance is preserved at moderate scales. Trait axes influence safety-relevant behavior (e.g., neuroticism affects frustration; agreeableness affects sycophancy). The unsupervised pipeline recovers four interpretable factors from rollouts.
AI.conclusion: Viewing persona control as learning, scaling, and composing trait weights enables a bridge between personality measurement, model editing, and safety. Trait-based manipulation offers a path to design, measure, and regulate model behavior in a decomposable, scalable way.

title: X-ACTA: eXtended Analytic Center Tension distribution Algorithm for fixed and mobile cable-driven-parallel-robot
summary: Steering Cable-Driven Parallel Robots (CDPRs) beyond their Wrench-Feasible Workspace (WFW) augments their capabilities in challenging scenarios such as during aggressive maneuvers or following a cable failure. In this context, although the determination of cable tensions is a well-studied topic, only a few approaches address these scenarios. Therefore, this paper introduces an extended version of the Analytic Center method as a criterion for selecting cable tensions outside the WFW while maintaining differentiability and including non-linear constraints. Notably, the proposed method maintains continuous and differentiable tension profiles, ensures fast real-time convergence to a unique solution, and, in contrast to other slack-based formulations, relegates wrench errors to a negligible area of the WFW. Its superiority in terms of smoothness and wrench error is confirmed via Pareto dominance with respect to the leading state-of-the-art method. Lastly, the effectiveness of the method is demonstrated through numerical experiments.

AI.tldr: Extended Analytic Center method for selecting outside-WFW tensions in cable-driven parallel robots (CDPRs), yielding smooth, differentiable tension profiles with non-linear constraints, fast convergence to a unique solution, and improved wrench performance (Pareto-dominant vs state-of-the-art). Demonstrated by numerical experiments.
AI.motivation: CDPRs are limited by a wrench-feasible workspace (WFW). In aggressive maneuvers or cable failures, operating outside WFW requires tension allocation that remains smooth and differentiable while respecting non-linear constraints. Existing slack-based methods can produce non-smooth tensions and larger wrench errors.
AI.method: Extend the Analytic Center approach to optimize tensions outside the WFW, enforcing differentiability and non-linear wrench constraints, ensuring continuous tension profiles and fast real-time convergence to a unique solution. Compare against leading methods using Pareto-dominance analysis.
AI.result: The proposed method achieves smooth, continuous, differentiable tensions with fast convergence to a unique solution. Wrench errors are confined to a negligible portion of the WFW, and the method Pareto-dominates the leading state-of-the-art in terms of smoothness and wrench performance, as shown by numerical experiments.
AI.conclusion: An extended Analytic Center method provides a viable, differentiable, non-linear-constrained criterion for tension selection outside the WFW in CDPRs. It offers improved smoothness and wrench behavior with proven Pareto dominance in simulations, supporting real-time applicability and robustness in challenging operating scenarios.

title: LDFE: Laplacian Decoupled Feature Enhancement Block for Dual-Stream CNN-based RGB-IR Object Detection
summary: The complementary information between RGB and IR images can significantly enhance object detection performance under extreme conditions. Existing methods prefer dual-stream CNN backbones built upon YOLO for feature extraction and focus on the design of feature fusion. In this paper, we introduce the Laplacian Decoupled Feature Enhancement block (LDFE) to fuse features from different stages of the dual-stream CNN backbone. By design, LDFE simultaneously considers the characteristics of modalities and structures for feature fusion by employing global-local decomposition, denoising, fusion, and reconstruction, sequentially. The LDFE first separates features into global and local components based on Laplacian Pyramid, and then performs denoising and fusion based on Global State Space Enhancement module (GS2E) and Local Convolutional Correlation Enhancement module (LC2E) separately. Specifically, the GS2E conducts a two-branch architecture for the main and auxiliary modalities. It dynamically suppresses noise in the main modality through cross-modal attention derived from the auxiliary modality, while employing a State Space Model to capture long-range dependencies within the global feature representations of the main modality. To obtain bidirectional interaction, the two modalities systematically alternate their main/auxiliary roles. Moreover, the LC2E suppresses noise in local features and leverages spatial and channel dimension along with triple convolution to extract fine-grained details for fusion. These innovative designs achieve a significant performance improvement, with mAP surpassing the SOTA methods 6.2%, 3.7%, 4.7%, 2.3%, 4.1% and 2.0% on M3FD, DroneVehicle, LLVIP, FLIR-Aligned, KAIST and VEDAI datasets,respectively.

AI.tldr: Introduces Laplacian Decoupled Feature Enhancement (LDFE) for RGB-IR fusion in object detection, fusing multi-stage features via global-local decomposition, GS2E and LC2E modules, achieving notable gains across diverse datasets.
AI.motivation: RGB-IR complementary information can boost detection under extreme conditions, but existing dual-stream backbones mainly focus on feature fusion design. A structured fusion block that handles global and local features with denoising and cross-modal interaction is needed to improve robustness.
AI.method: LDFE fuses features from different stages of a dual-stream CNN backbone. It uses a Laplacian Pyramid-based global-local decomposition, followed by denoising and fusion with two modules: Global State Space Enhancement (GS2E) and Local Convolutional Correlation Enhancement (LC2E). GS2E employs a two-branch cross-modal attention to suppress noise in the main modality using information from the auxiliary modality and captures long-range dependencies with a State Space Model; roles of main/auxiliary are alternated to enable bidirectional interaction. LC2E denoises local features and uses spatial and channel-wise processing with triple convolution to extract fine-grained details for fusion, with reconstruction to fused representations.
AI.result: The approach yields significant improvements, with mAP gains over SOTA on six datasets: M3FD (6.2%), DroneVehicle (3.7%), LLVIP (4.7%), FLIR-Aligned (2.3%), KAIST (4.1%), and VEDAI (2.0%).
AI.conclusion: LDFE provides an effective, modular fusion mechanism for RGB-IR feature fusion, producing robust performance gains across diverse benchmarks and demonstrating the value of global-local decomposition, cross-modal denoising, and bidirectional interaction in multi-modal object detection.

title: Image classification via a quantum-inspired strategy involving a mixture of experts
summary: Pattern recognition problems arise in a variety of physical image processing situations, and convolutional neural networks are a popular scheme for the required feature extraction and classification tasks. The classical networks use diffusion-based smearing and block-wise pooling to downsample the image data and capture important structural features. In this work, we propose and demonstrate a more efficient quantum-inspired strategy involving a mixture of experts. It is a hybrid classical-quantum framework. The quantum part consists of amplitude encoding of the images, convolution using local unitary operations, multiple experts processing the same image with different parameters, and feature extraction using quantum stabiliser codes. The classical part then jointly processes the features extracted by different experts using a standard fully connected neural network for image class prediction. Using MNIST and Fashion-MNIST datasets as benchmarks, we demonstrate that the joint expert analysis outperforms the individual expert one, as well as reduces the failure rate of image class prediction by around a factor of two. The overhead of our quantum-inspired strategy is only moderate on GPU workstations, which makes our proposal a practical alternative to existing classical schemes. We also point out how the quantum part of our framework can be executed on a quantum processor.

AI.tldr: Hybrid classical-quantum mixture-of-experts for image classification using amplitude-encoded inputs, local-unitary convolution, and stabilizer-code features. Joint analysis of multiple experts outperforms single expert and reduces classification failure rates, with moderate GPU overhead and potential quantum-processor implementation.
AI.motivation: Address inefficiencies of diffusion-based downsampling in classical networks and explore whether quantum-inspired features can improve recognition performance and robustness on standard benchmarks.
AI.method: Amplitude encoding of images; convolution via local unitary operations; multiple experts processing the same input with distinct parameters; feature extraction using quantum stabilizer codes; a classical fully connected network aggregates features for final classification.
AI.result: Joint analysis across experts yields better accuracy than any single expert and reduces failure rate by approximately a factor of two on MNIST and Fashion-MNIST. GPU overhead is moderate, suggesting practicality relative to purely classical schemes.
