Bubeck and Sellke proved a universal version of this law for Lipschitz-parameterized classes, but under a polynomial bound on the parameters; at depth three that boundedness hypothesis is genuinely necessary. The two-layer unbounded-weight case requires a different argument. We prove the conjectured law, up to one logarithmic factor, for every continuous piecewise-linear activation, in particular for ReLU networks. For data drawn uniformly from $\mathbb{S}^{d-1}$, $d\ge3$, or from $N(0,I_d/d)$, labels in $[-1,1]$ with noise level $σ^2>0$, and any width-$m$ two-layer network with arbitrary real weights, biases and affine skip connection, fitting the data $\varepsilon$ below the noise floor forces $\mathrm{Lip}(f)\ge c\,\varepsilon\sqrt{n/(\bar m\log(C\bar m nd/\varepsilon))}$, $\bar m=(K-1)m+1$, with high probability. A realized-kink-count version holds on the same event: every realized two-layer piecewise-linear function with $k(f)\le n$ distinct kink hyperplanes obeys the bound with $\bar m$ replaced by $k(f)+1$, irrespective of how many redundant hidden units parameterize it. The proof replaces parameter-space covering, impossible for unbounded weights, by a function-space covering. The central deterministic ingredient is a rigidity lemma: on $B_2$, and on $\mathbb{S}^{d-1}$ for $d\ge3$, the coefficient of each canonical kink is controlled by the Lipschitz constant of the realized function, because kinks on distinct hyperplanes cannot cancel at generic points. Rigidity genuinely fails at $d=2$, and an explicit two-layer ReLU interpolant with $O(1)$ Lipschitz constant at width $2n$ matches the law at the overparameterized endpoint.

AI.tldr: Proves a Lipschitz lower bound for width-m two-layer ReLU networks that fit n noisy labels, with unbounded weights, matching the conjectured law up to a log factor; uses function-space covering and a rigidity lemma; applies to data on the sphere (d≥3) or Gaussian, with noise σ^2>0; bound scales as Lip(f) ≥ c ε sqrt(n/(m-bar log(C m-bar n d / ε))) where m-bar = (K-1)m+1; a realized-kink-count version ties Lip to the number of kink hyperplanes k(f). Result fails in d=2; shows explicit interpolant with O(1) Lipschitz at width 2n matches the law at overparameterization.
AI.motivation: Resolve whether unbounded two-layer networks can achieve the same Lipschitz trade-off as bounded-parameter universal laws when fitting noisy data, removing the polynomial-bounded parameter assumption.
AI.method: Replace parameter-space coverings with function-space coverings due to unbounded weights; prove a rigidity lemma bounding canonical kink coefficients by the realized Lipschitz constant on the sphere and in B2; analyze realized two-layer piecewise-linear functions with kinks; derive Lipschitz lower bounds in probabilistic data models (uniform on S^{d-1} with d≥3 or N(0,I/d)); handle affine skip connections and arbitrary weights; establish a log-factor relaxation.
AI.result: With high probability, any width-m two-layer network with arbitrary real weights, biases, and skip connections that fits ε below the noise floor must have Lip(f) ≥ c ε sqrt(n/(m-bar log(C m-bar n d / ε))); m-bar = (K-1)m + 1; a realized-kink-count version holds with m-bar replaced by k(f)+1; rigidity holds for d≥3; fails for d=2; there exists a 2n-width ReLU interpolant with O(1) Lipschitz achieving the bound at the overparameterized endpoint.
AI.conclusion: Extends the Bubeck-Li-Nagaraj conjecture to the unbounded-weight setting up to a log factor for common piecewise-linear activations, clarifying the role of data geometry (d≥3) and kink structure in controlling Lipschitz complexity; provides a roadmap for function-space analysis when parameter norms are unbounded.

title: PARA-PV: Physics-Aware Retrieval-Augmented PV Prediction Based on Frozen Foundation Model and Distribution Shift Correction
summary: Accurate photovoltaic (PV) power forecasting is essential for reliable grid dispatch and renewable energy integration, yet it remains challenging because PV generation is jointly shaped by weather variability, day-night transitions, regime-dependent dynamics, and strict physical constraints. We propose PARA-PV, a Physics-Aware Retrieval-Augmented framework that embeds physical knowledge throughout the forecasting process. The framework first encodes multivariate PV observations into patch-level representations and, through a physics-aware retrieval-augmented learner, retrieves historical patches and analog trajectories that are consistent with the current window in temporal shape, power level, PV operating state, and intra-day period; this yields a physically grounded base forecast. To supplement local memory with broader temporal knowledge, the base forecast is then calibrated against a frozen Chronos time-series foundation-model prior through a lightweight residual adapter, so that general temporal regularities are adapted to PV-specific dynamics without overriding the physically grounded prediction. Because residual conditional distribution shifts persist when weather and diurnal regimes change, a physics-aware distribution shift correction module subsequently adjusts the preliminary forecast using power, weather, timestamp, and day/night conditions, applying gated mean-shift and scale corrections selectively. Finally, a physics-constrained loss function partitions the samples into peak, ramping, night-time, and regular regimes and adaptively reweights their error contributions, preventing the dominant regular regime from suppressing learning of operationally critical states. Our code is available at https://github.com/weican1103/PARA-PV.

AI.tldr: Para-PV is a physics-aware, retrieval-augmented framework for PV forecasting that integrates patch-level encoding, physics-consistent retrieval, a Chronos-based time-series prior with a light residual adapter, physics-aware distribution-shift correction, and a regime-aware loss to handle peak/ramp/night/regular states.
AI.motivation: PV forecasting accuracy is hampered by weather variability, day-night transitions, regime shifts, and physical constraints; there is a need to embed physics knowledge throughout forecasting and to leverage both local and broader temporal information while handling distribution shifts.
AI.method: Encode multivariate PV observations into patch-level representations; use a physics-aware retrieval-augmented learner to retrieve historical patches and analog trajectories consistent with the current window in temporal shape, power level, PV operating state, and intra-day period to form a physically grounded base forecast. Calibrate this base forecast against a frozen Chronos time-series foundation-model prior via a lightweight residual adapter to inject broader temporal regularities without overwriting physics-grounded predictions. Apply a physics-aware distribution shift correction module to adjust the preliminary forecast using power, weather, timestamp, and day/night conditions with gated mean-shift and scale corrections. Employ a physics-constrained loss that partitions samples into peak, ramping, night-time, and regular regimes and adaptively reweights their errors to prevent dominance by the regular regime.
AI.result: The abstract outlines the framework and provides a code repo; it does not report quantitative experimental results within the abstract.
AI.conclusion: The work proposes a modular, physics-informed, retrieval-augmented PV forecasting pipeline that integrates local patch-based representation learning, physics-consistent retrieval, foundation-model calibration, distribution-shift correction, and regime-aware loss to improve forecasting across varying operational conditions.

title: FabriVLA: A Lightweight Vision-Language-Action Model for Precise Multi-Task Manipulation
summary: We present FabriVLA, a lightweight Vision-Language-Action model for Precise Multi-Task Manipulation. FabriVLA combines an InternVL3.5 vision-language backbone with a flow-matching action head featuring gated self-attention across action tokens and shallow VLM layer fusion for enriched spatial context. The model is trained via single stage joint optimization from a pretrained VLM and randomly initialized action head. On the Meta-World MT50 benchmark spanning 50 diverse manipulation tasks, FabriVLA achieves a tier-average success rate of 90.0%, demonstrating that a compact VLA built on a 1B scale VLM can achieve strong performance without relying on multi billion parameter VLA backbones.

AI.tldr: FabriVLA is a compact Vision-Language-Action model for precise multi-task manipulation. Built on a 1B-scale VLM (InternVL3.5) with a flow-matching action head and gated self-attention across action tokens, it uses shallow VLM layer fusion and single-stage joint optimization from a pretrained VLM to achieve strong results on 50 MT tasks, achieving 90.0% tier-average success on Meta-World MT50, indicating strong performance without giant backbones.
AI.motivation: Reduce reliance on multi-billion-parameter VLA backbones while maintaining high performance in robotic manipulation; leverage pretrained vision-language models and single-stage training to enable efficient multi-task capabilities.
AI.method: Architecture combines an InternVL3.5 vision-language backbone with a flow-matching action head that uses gated self-attention over action tokens; incorporates shallow VLM layer fusion to enrich spatial context; trained in a single-stage joint optimization from a pretrained VLM and a randomly initialized action head.
AI.result: On Meta-World MT50 (50 manipulation tasks), FabriVLA achieves a tier-average success rate of 90.0%, demonstrating that a compact (≈1B parameter) VLM-based VLA can match performance typically attributed to much larger backbones.
AI.conclusion: A compact VLA built on a 1B-scale VLM can deliver strong, multi-task manipulation performance without relying on multi-billion-parameter backbones, highlighting efficiency gains and practical deployment potential.

title: Continual Test-Time Adaptation in Computer Vision: Methods, Benchmarks, and Future Directions
summary: Deep neural nets achieve remarkable performance when training and test data share the same distribution, but this assumption frequently breaks in real-world deployment, where data undergoes continual distributional shifts. Continual Test-Time Adaptation (CTTA) addresses this challenge by adapting pretrained models to non-stationary target distributions on-the-fly, without access to source data or labeled targets, while mitigating two critical failure modes: catastrophic forgetting of source knowledge and error accumulation from noisy pseudo-labels over extended time horizons. In this comprehensive survey, we formally define the CTTA problem, analyze the diverse continual domain shift patterns that characterize different evaluation protocols, and propose a hierarchical taxonomy that categorizes existing methods into three families: optimization-based strategies (entropy minimization, pseudo-labeling, parameter restoration), parameter-efficient methods (normalization layer adaptation, adaptive parameter selection), and architecture-based approaches (teacher-student frameworks, adapters, visual prompting, masked modeling). We systematically review representative methods within each category and present comparative benchmarks and experimental results across standard evaluation settings. Finally, we discuss limitations of current approaches and highlight emerging research directions, including adaptation of foundation models and black-box systems, providing a roadmap for future research in robust continual test-time adaptation. We encourage visiting our repository at [https://github.com/sarthaxxxxx/Awesome-Continual-Test-Time-Adaptation](https://github.com/sarthaxxxxx/Awesome-Continual-Test-Time-Adaptation)

AI.tldr: A formal survey of Continual Test-Time Adaptation (CTTA): defines the problem, proposes a three‑domain taxonomy, surveys optimization-, parameter‑efficient, and architecture‑based methods, presents benchmarks, discusses limitations, and outlines future directions including foundation models and black‑box adaptation.
AI.motivation: To maintain high performance of pretrained models under non-stationary data distributions encountered at deployment, without access to source data or labels, while preventing catastrophic forgetting and error build-up from pseudo-labels.
AI.method: Formally define CTTA, analyze continual domain-shift patterns, and introduce a hierarchical taxonomy. Systematically review representative methods within optimization-based, parameter-efficient, and architecture-based categories, and compare methods using standard benchmarks and protocols.
AI.result: A structured survey with a three‑part taxonomy, curated method reviews, and benchmark results. It highlights where existing approaches succeed or fail under various shift patterns, and provides empirical comparisons and a consolidated overview.
AI.conclusion: CTTA is a crucial, emerging research area. The survey offers a roadmap including improved adaptation for foundation models and black-box systems, and calls for standardized benchmarks and future research directions to build robust continual test-time learners.

title: Predicting Pseudo-nitzschia harmful algal blooms along the Portuguese Coast using satellite-derived predictors
comment: 33 pages, 16 figures. Submitted to Harmful Algae (Elsevier)
summary: Pseudo-nitzschia diatoms pose recurrent risks to coastal ecosystems and shellfish harvesting along the Portuguese Atlantic coast. Here we develop and evaluate a spatio-temporal machine-learning framework to predict harmful algal bloom (HAB) occurrence using exclusively satellite-derived predictors under realistic forecasting constraints. We characterised environmental and biological variability across shellfish production zones (L1-L9) using 5,882 observations, providing system-wide context. Predictive models were developed for zones L1-L2, a hotspot for Pseudo-nitzschia and domoic acid events, using a decade-long dataset (2013-2023; 1,440 observations; more than 1,000 satellite-based predictors including sea surface temperature, an upwelling index, chlorophyll-a, and plankton functional types). Sampling locations were partitioned into ecologically meaningful sub-regions using a river-aware spatial clustering scheme. A stringent spatio-temporal cross-validation strategy that simultaneously withholds entire years and spatial clusters prevents leakage and closely mimics real-world forecasting conditions. HAB occurrence proved moderately predictable across model classes and feature configurations. Ensemble tree-based methods achieved the strongest discrimination: Random Forest reached 0.74 +/- 0.05 with environmental predictors; Extra Trees reached 0.77 +/- 0.06 with biological variables added. Feature-importance analyses revealed that seasonal structure, spatial context, and lagged environmental conditions dominate model decisions, while biological indicators refine bloom likelihood within physically favourable periods. The framework demonstrates operationally relevant skill for satellite-supported HAB early-warning systems along eastern boundary upwelling coasts.

AI.tldr: A satellite-derived, spatio-temporal ML framework predicts HAB (Pseudo-nitzschia) along Portugal's Atlantic coast with cross-validated forecasts; ensemble trees perform best; framework supports operational early warning.
AI.motivation: Harmful algal blooms threaten shellfish industries; conventional in-situ monitoring is limited in timeliness and coverage. The study leverages exclusively satellite predictors to enable realistic, forecast-ready HAB predictions over an upwelling coast.
AI.method: Data from 5,882 observations across shellfish zones L1-L9 (focusing on L1-L2) from 2013–2023 (~1,440 observations for that subset) with >1,000 satellite predictors (SST, upwelling index, chlorophyll-a, plankton functional types). Locations partitioned using river-aware spatial clustering. Spatio-temporal cross-validation withheld entire years and spatial clusters to mimic forecasting. Compared model classes, with emphasis on ensemble tree methods (Random Forest, Extra Trees). Evaluated with discrimination metrics; conducted feature-importance analyses.
AI.result: Ensemble tree methods yielded strongest discrimination: RF 0.74 ± 0.05 with environmental predictors; Extra Trees 0.77 ± 0.06 when biological variables were included. HAB occurrence is moderately predictable across models. Feature-importance shows seasonal structure, spatial context, and lagged environmental conditions drive decisions; biological indicators refine bloom likelihood within favorable periods.
AI.conclusion: The framework demonstrates operationally relevant skill for satellite-supported HAB early-warning systems along eastern boundary upwelling coasts, enabling forecast-informed management of shellfish harvesting.

title: CausalDS: Benchmarking Causal Reasoning in Data-Science Agents
summary: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly act as integrated data-science agents, combining abstract reasoning with advanced tool use. Yet the relevant benchmark landscape largely divides into symbolic causal reasoning benchmarks without realistic data analysis or data analysis benchmarks without a principled causal data-generating structure. Furthermore, existing causal evaluation datasets are often restricted to curated examples from existing sources, with diversity coming from limited templatized variations rather than from systematic generation of novel synthetic causal structures. We introduce CausalDS, a benchmark for evaluating causal reasoning in agentic data-science workflows. Each benchmark instance is a scene consisting of a sampled structural causal model (SCM) with generated observational data and an accompanying synthetic natural-language story grounded in a realistic domain. We optionally ground the composition of the benchmark components in empirical distributions obtained from real-world datasets, thus retaining empirical structure while reducing the "causal parrot" risk through completely synthetic generation. From each scene, we then derive tasks spanning all three of Pearl's rungs, with typical data-science prediction tasks appearing as Rung 1. Most tasks include a data science coding component, where the model typically needs to use several tools to arrive at the final answer due to the frequent presence of imperfect observations, which are generated by an observation model. Additionally, recognizing when a question admits no warranted answer and abstaining is treated as a first-class scored outcome. The benchmark thus jointly evaluates symbolic causal reasoning, data science, uncertainty quantification, abstention, and tool use/coding.

AI.tldr: CausalDS introduces a synthetic, SCM-based benchmark with natural-language stories and observational data to evaluate causal reasoning in data-science agents, covering Pearl’s rungs and including coding, tool use, uncertainty, and abstention.
AI.motivation: Fill gaps between symbolic causal benchmarks and realistic data-analysis benchmarks, addressing limited diversity and overreliance on templated data by providing a scalable, principled, synthetic generation pipeline with optional empirical grounding.
AI.method: Generate scenes by sampling a structural causal model (SCM), produce observational data via an observation model, and create synthetic NL stories grounded in a realistic domain. Optionally ground benchmark components in empirical distributions. Derive tasks across Pearl’s three rungs, include data-science prediction tasks, typical coding/tool-use steps, and treat abstention as a scored outcome.
AI.result: Proposes the CausalDS benchmark design and pipeline. It defines components (SCM, data, NL story), grounding options, and task derivation across Pearl’s rungs, emphasizing evaluation of symbolic causal reasoning, data science, uncertainty, abstention, and tool use.
AI.conclusion: CausalDS offers a comprehensive, scalable framework for evaluating causal reasoning in agentic data-science workflows, aiming to reduce causal parrot risk and support multi-faceted assessment of LLMs in data science contexts.

title: A New Human-Likeness and Comfort Index for Robot Movements Along Prescribed Paths
comment: 14 pages, 5 figures, accepted for IEEE Transactions on Cybernetics
summary: As human-robot interaction rapidly spreads in numerous fields, the subject of robot acceptance gains increasing importance. Visual similarity to the human body, as occurs for humanoids, is generally not enough to ensure acceptance in physical interaction, as acceptance directly links to comfort and ergonomics, which are measured in terms of the quality of the robot movement perceived by the human. This paper discusses the connection between comfort and similarity of the robot movement to the human one. By considering the kinematic characterization of human movement, this paper focuses on the time laws of such movements, wherein the end-effector path is prescribed. Based on the lognormality principle for modeling human movements, a human-likeness index is defined and used to provide an a priori characterization of trajectories. Such an index can be used to evaluate the performance of trajectory generation algorithms in producing human-like movements before they are actually executed. For validation purposes, 68 subjects are required to judge their comfort. The results of three experimental campaigns involving a physical interaction with a robot demonstrate a globally consistent trend between the preference in terms of perceived comfort and the distribution of the suggested human-likeness index.

AI.tldr: A lognormal-based human-likeness index is proposed to predict comfort in human-robot movement interactions; validated with 68 participants across three experiments, showing alignment between perceived comfort and the index.
AI.motivation: Acceptance of physical robots hinges on comfortable, ergonomic movements; visual similarity alone is insufficient; need a priori trajectory metrics to gauge human-likeness prior to execution.
AI.method: Model human movement using lognormal time laws for end-effector trajectories; define human-likeness index from this model; use it to evaluate trajectory generation algorithms; validate with 68 subjects in three physical-interaction experiments.
AI.result: A globally consistent trend between comfort judgments and the index distribution; trajectories characterized as more human-like correspond to higher comfort.
AI.conclusion: The human-likeness index is a valid a priori metric for evaluating and guiding trajectory generation toward more human-like movements, potentially improving robot acceptance; supported by subject-based experiments.

title: Attention-Based Segmentation of WMHs and Differentiation of Vascular vs. Demyelinating Lesions
summary: White Matter Hyperintensities (WMHs) are commonly observed in brain Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) scans. They are associated with various neurological conditions, including vascular and inflammatory demyelinating diseases. Despite differing in etiology, WMHs from these conditions often appear similar on Fluid Attenuated Inversion Recovery (FLAIR) images. This similarity makes differential diagnosis challenging. In this work, we highlight the potential of combining attention-based segmentation with feature-driven classification. This approach supports more accurate and efficient classification between vascular and demyelinating white matter pathologies. For segmentation, we evaluate the effectiveness of attention mechanisms, specifically the Bottleneck Attention Module (BAM) and the Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM). We also test different architectures, particularly Attention U-Net. In addition, we explore advanced training strategies, such as patch-based learning and a 2.5D approach, to enhance lesion detection. After segmentation, we extract morphological features from the lesion masks. We then use them to classify WMHs based on their underlying cause. Our experiments utilize five publicly available datasets with diverse imaging protocols to promote model generalizability, despite limited sample sizes. The results suggest that attention-based segmentation and feature-driven classification offer a promising direction for discriminating vascular and demyelinating white matter lesions. Further validation in larger clinical cohorts is still needed.

AI.tldr: Attention-based segmentation (BAM/CBAM, Attention U-Net) combined with feature-driven classification to distinguish vascular vs demyelinating white matter hyperintensities (WMHs) on FLAIR. Uses patch-based and 2.5D training; morphological features from lesion masks; evaluated on five public datasets; promising but needs validation in larger cohorts.
AI.motivation: WMHs arise from diverse etiologies but appear similar on FLAIR, complicating differential diagnosis. A combined segmentation-classification framework leveraging attention models and morphology may improve discrimination and generalizability across heterogeneous imaging protocols.
AI.method: Evaluate attention-based segmentation modules (BAM, CBAM) within Attention U-Net; explore patch-based and 2.5D training strategies; after segmentation, extract lesion-morphology features from masks and train a classifier to determine WMH etiology (vascular vs demyelinating). Validate on five publicly available datasets with varied imaging protocols to assess generalizability despite small sample sizes.
AI.result: The approach is promising: attention-based segmentation and subsequent feature-driven classification show potential for discriminating vascular and demyelinating WMHs. The use of diverse datasets supports generalizability, though the study notes limited sample sizes and calls for validation in larger clinical cohorts.
AI.conclusion: Attention-based segmentation plus feature-driven classification is a promising direction for WMH etiological discrimination. Further validation in larger, diverse clinical cohorts is needed to confirm robustness and clinical utility.

title: Explaining Near-Zero Hessian Eigenvalues Through Approximate Symmetries in Neural Networks
summary: The Hessian of the training loss governs the local geometry of the loss landscape, yet despite existing explanations for its largest eigenvalues, the origin of the vast multitude of vanishingly small eigenvalues remains elusive. We argue that the bulk consists of the weakly lifted pseudo-Goldstone modes of the continuous symmetries of the network parametrization. In deep linear networks these symmetries are exact: they generate flat directions and hence exact zero modes, whose eigenvectors we construct explicitly. Introducing a ReLU nonlinearity as a perturbation, we show that it breaks these symmetries weakly and explicitly. Resolving the spectrum at the level of eigenvectors, we find that the high-curvature directions are orthogonal to the symmetry subspace, while the bulk lies almost entirely within it. We demonstrate the mechanism in a two-layer ReLU student--teacher model and in a network trained on CIFAR-10. A convolutional example demonstrates that the same diagnostic extends beyond fully connected layers. Together, these results link the Hessian bulk to weakly broken symmetries and clarify the origin of near-zero modes.

AI.tldr: Bulk of Hessian eigenvalues in deep nets arises from weakly broken continuous symmetries (pseudo-Goldstone modes) of network parametrization; exact zero modes exist in linear networks and are lifted perturbatively by nonlinearities; spectrum at the eigenvector level shows high-curvature directions are orthogonal to the symmetry subspace while the bulk lies within it; demonstrated in a two-layer teacher–student model and CIFAR-10 with additional convolutional example.
AI.motivation: Explain the origin of the vast number of near-zero Hessian eigenvalues and relate the Hessian spectrum to the symmetries of network parametrization, offering a unifying mechanism for loss-landscape geometry.
AI.method: Theoretically construct exact zero modes in deep linear networks (due to continuous symmetries); treat a ReLU nonlinearity as a perturbation that weakly breaks these symmetries; perform eigenvector-level resolution of the Hessian spectrum; validate with a two-layer teacher–student model and experiments on CIFAR-10; extend analysis to convolutional networks.
AI.result: Identification of a symmetry-based decomposition of the Hessian spectrum: high-curvature directions lie outside the symmetry subspace, while the bulk remains inside it, consisting of weakly lifted pseudo-Goldstone modes; near-zero eigenvalues explained as Goldstone-like modes lifted by nonlinearities; practical demonstrations across architectures provide evidence for the mechanism.
AI.conclusion: The Hessian bulk can be attributed to weakly broken continuous symmetries of network parametrization, clarifying the origin of near-zero modes and offering a diagnostic for loss-landscape geometry applicable from fully connected to convolutional architectures.

title: Answer Set Programming Energised! End-to-End Neurosymbolic Reasoning and Learning with ASP and Energy Based Models
summary: We present a general neurosymbolic reasoning and learning methodology based on a modular integration of answer set programming with an energy based model substrate. Key contributions are: (1) supporting joint optimisation in the continuous latent space through explicit ASP-based declarative semantics fully incorporating background knowledge, constraints, non-monotonic inference; and (2) advancing recent works at the interface of answer sets, probabilistic logic, and answer set modulo theories by providing a generalised model and practical platform for ASP-centric robust, end-to-end training for applications in dynamic domains (e.g., involving perception and interaction). We provide a practical implementation, and demonstrate basic use and application (with MNIST), and evaluate with the visual question-answering benchmark Clevr and the multi-object tracking benchmark MOT.

AI.tldr: General neurosymbolic framework integrating ASP with energy-based models for end-to-end training in dynamic perception tasks; demonstrated on MNIST, CLEVR, and MOT.
AI.motivation: Bridging non-monotonic symbolic reasoning with differentiable learning to handle dynamic environments and perception-driven tasks; extending the interface between answer sets, probabilistic logic, and answer-set modulo theories with a practical ASP-centric training platform.
AI.method: Modular integration of answer set programming with an energy-based model substrate to enable joint optimization in a continuous latent space. The approach uses explicit ASP-based declarative semantics that incorporate background knowledge, constraints, and non-monotonic inference, enabling robust end-to-end training in dynamic domains.
AI.result: A practical implementation is provided, with demonstrations on MNIST and evaluations on visual question answering (CLEVR) and multi-object tracking (MOT).
AI.conclusion: The work advances neurosymbolic integration by uniting ASP semantics with differentiable energy-based learning and offers a platform for ASP-centric end-to-end training in perception-rich, dynamic applications; scalability and comparative performance remain areas for future work.

title: Native Video-Action Pretraining for Generalizable Robot Control
summary: The advent of video-action models offers a promising path for robot control. Nevertheless, we argue that repurposing video generative models designed for digital content creation is inherently inadequate for physical environments. To bridge this gap, we present LingBot-VA 2.0, a video-action foundation model built from the ground up for embodiment. Four core design principles showcase its evolution from LingBot-VA. (1) Departing from traditional reconstruction-focused VAEs, we introduce a semantic visual-action tokenizer, which aligns visual representations with both semantics and actions, improving instruction following and action precision in subsequent policy learning. (2) Given the strictly causal nature of temporal dynamics, we adopt a causal pretraining paradigm, training from scratch to circumvent the catastrophic forgetting that frequently occurs when adapting bidirectional architectures. (3) To meet the demands of high-frequency inference, our model employs a sparse MoE backbone, expanding model capacity without compromising efficiency. (4) Real-time closed-loop control is realized through an enhanced asynchronous inference scheme, which predicts future latents in parallel with action execution while re-grounding each rollout on the latest observation via learned forward dynamics. Real-world deployment validates LingBot-VA 2.0 as a robust foundation model, as evidenced by its few-shot generalization across complex manipulation tasks.

AI.tldr: LingBot-VA 2.0 proposes a video-action foundation model for embodied robotics, built from scratch with a semantic visual-action tokenizer, causal pretraining, sparse MoE backbone for high-frequency inference, and asynchronous closed-loop control for real-time planning; it claims strong few-shot generalization in real-world manipulation tasks.
AI.motivation: Repurposing video generative models designed for digital content creation is inadequate for physical robots due to misalignment with semantics, actions, and real-time control; there is a need for an embodiment-aware foundation model with action-grounded representations and appropriate temporal dynamics.
AI.method: Introduce a semantic visual-action tokenizer that aligns visual representations with semantics and actions;train from scratch using causal pretraining to avoid catastrophic forgetting; employ a sparse Mixture-of-Experts backbone for scalable capacity and efficiency; implement an enhanced asynchronous inference scheme that predicts future latents in parallel with action execution and re-grounds each rollout with learned forward dynamics.
AI.result: Real-world deployment demonstrates few-shot generalization across complex manipulation tasks, indicating robustness of the model for embodied control.
AI.conclusion: LingBot-VA 2.0 demonstrates that an embodiment-focused video-action foundation model, designed with semantic action alignment, causal temporal dynamics, scalable inference, and real-time closed-loop control, can effectively support physical robot manipulation and task generalization.

title: LEEVLA: Seeing What Matters in Latent Environment Evolution for Vision-Language-Action
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models aim to map multimodal inputs to robot actions. However, most existing approaches struggle to cover complex dynamic scenarios due to treating all visual tokens uniformly and reasoning with human-selected factors, which lack mechanisms to emphasize task-critical evidence and ignore underlying factors. To address this issue, we propose LEEVLA, a VLA architecture for seeing what matters in Latent Environment Evolution that explicitly guides the model toward informative regions while preserving the structured evolution of latent world representations. To identify salient and instruction-relevant regions, we introduce drift-guided dynamic prioritization (DGDP), which combines dynamic position prioritization (DPP) with semantic drift guidance (SDG) to guide the VLA agent where to attend during training. On top of this, we introduce structured feature flow generation (SFFG), which models how these prioritized features should evolve in latent space via prototype-to-periphery (P2P) prediction, and a mutual-neighborhood contrastive (MC) loss to maintain topological consistency among neighborhoods. Together, DGDP and SFFG form a task-aware "where-how" training framework. Extensive experiments on VLA benchmarks show that LEEVLA consistently outperforms prior methods, confirming that explicit task-evidence guidance and structured latent reasoning are both crucial for scalable VLA. Our code is available at https://github.com/LyuQi127/LEEVLA.

AI.tldr: LEEVLA presents a task-aware VLA framework that guides attention to informative regions and models latent environment evolution, achieving consistent gains on VLA benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Address the inability of existing VLA models to handle complex dynamic scenarios due to uniform visual token treatment and reliance on manually selected factors, by introducing explicit task-evidence guidance and structured latent reasoning.
AI.method: Introduce LEEVLA architecture with drift-guided dynamic prioritization (DGDP) combining dynamic position prioritization (DPP) and semantic drift guidance (SDG); propose structured feature flow generation (SFFG) with prototype-to-periphery (P2P) prediction and a mutual-neighborhood contrastive (MC) loss, forming a 'where-how' training framework.
AI.result: LEEVLA consistently outperforms prior methods on VLA benchmarks across extensive experiments, validating the importance of guided attention and structured latent reasoning.
AI.conclusion: Explicit task-evidence guidance and structured latent reasoning are crucial for scalable vision-language-action in dynamic environments; the approach advances VLA by focusing on informative evidence and modeling latent evolution.

title: When Does Continual Learning Require Learning
summary: As large language models (LLMs) become increasingly capable, the next question is how can we enable models to continually learn? Today, the field largely frames this as a problem of context management and mitigating forgetting. We argue this framing is incomplete: continual learning is fundamentally about increasing model competence as the world changes. We disentangle this change along two axes -- space, where the model encounters new domains, and time, where the underlying data drifts under a fixed task. This framing lets us study continual learning under realistic conditions: new domains arrive over time, facts drift past their training cutoff, and agentic interactions accumulate state across episodes. To evaluate methods under this setting, we recast widely used LLM benchmarks as sequential problems and introduce a single mechanism-agnostic protocol that compares prompt-based methods (GEPA, ACE), supervised learning (SFT, SDFT), reinforcement learning (GRPO, SDPO), and context compression (Cartridges, In-place TTT). Prompt-based methods fit each new stage quickly but degrade on future tasks. Distillation-based methods accumulate knowledge stably but struggle to update outdated facts. Context compression improves efficiency without substantially improving the ability to learn new tasks. Online reinforcement learning adapts most effectively to knowledge updates but remains sensitive to noisy reward signals. Overall, our results suggest that continual learning is not a single capability: different patterns of environmental change require fundamentally different update behaviors, determining when adaptation must be learned inside model weights and when it can be achieved through external scaffolding. We hope that understanding where each method succeeds and fails will guide the design of stronger continual learning systems.

AI.tldr: Continual learning for LLMs requires more than avoiding forgetting; it is about increasing competence as the world changes, framed along space (new domains) and time (data drift). A mechanism-agnostic protocol evaluates prompt-based, distillation, RL, and context compression methods on sequential tasks, revealing diverse strengths and limitations across environmental changes.
AI.motivation: To move beyond treating continual learning as context management; to formalize how world changes in space and time affect model competence and evaluation under realistic scenarios.
AI.method: Recast widely used LLM benchmarks as sequential problems; propose a single protocol that is mechanism-agnostic and compares multiple update paradigms: prompt-based methods (GEPA, ACE), supervised fine-tuning (SFT, SDFT), RL (GRPO, SDPO), and context compression (Cartridges, In-place TTT).
AI.result: Prompt methods adapt quickly but forget future tasks; distillation stabilizes knowledge but fails to update outdated facts; context compression improves efficiency without strong gains in learning; online RL adapts to knowledge updates but is sensitive to noisy rewards.
AI.conclusion: Continual learning is not a single capability; different environmental changes require different update behaviors, requiring both internal weight updates and external scaffolding; understanding strengths/weaknesses informs design of stronger continual learning systems.

title: Overthinking: Amplifying Reasoning Weights to Extract Learned Secrets
summary: Black box auditing of language models is an essential pre-deployment tool, but it may miss subtle forms of misalignment and hidden information. To better elicit hidden information during an auditing process, we introduce \emph{overthinking}: the process of using reasoning task vectors to amplify the propensity to think out loud of reasoning models. Given the parameters of a non-reasoning instruct model $M$ and reasoning-distilled model $R$, we define the \emph{overthinking model} as $\boldsymbolθ_{\mathcal{O}_α} = \boldsymbolθ_{\mathcal{M}} + α(\boldsymbolθ_{\mathcal{R}} - \boldsymbolθ_{\mathcal{M}})$, where $α> 1$ amplifies reasoning beyond the pure reasoning model $R$. Additionally, we introduce new layer-wise attenuation strategies that selectively amplify reasoning without losing quality and coherence of model outputs. We demonstrate that overthinking models are more likely to reveal hidden information across four experimental settings, across 2B-32B models. Our findings suggest that reasoning amplification may surface secrets or unintended behaviors acquired during training up to $10\times$ more frequently than the original reasoning model. How secrets surface depends on the secret type: some require perturbation along the reasoning direction, while others yield to any sufficiently large weight perturbation.

AI.tldr: Overthinking amplifies reasoning directions to elicit hidden information from language models. It uses parametric interpolation between a base model and a reasoning-distilled model with alpha>1, plus layer-wise attenuation to preserve output quality. In four experimental setups across 2B–32B models, this approach reveals hidden information up to 10× more often than the original reasoning model, with the surface type depending on the secret requiring perturbation along the reasoning axis or large weight perturbations.
AI.motivation: Black-box auditing of language models may miss subtle misalignments or hidden information. There is a need for strategies that reliably elicit such hidden information during pre-deployment auditing.
AI.method: Define an overthinking model θ_Oα = θ_M + α(θ_R − θ_M) with α>1 to amplify reasoning beyond the pure reasoning model R. Introduce layer-wise attenuation strategies to selectively amplify reasoning while preserving output quality. Evaluate across four experimental settings on 2B–32B models, comparing the frequency of surface of secrets relative to base models.
AI.result: Overthinking models more effectively surface hidden information, up to ~10× more frequently than the original reasoning model. The surface of secrets depends on secret type: some secrets require perturbation along the reasoning direction, while others emerge under any sufficiently large weight perturbation.
AI.conclusion: Reasoning amplification via overthinking can reveal hidden secrets or unintended behaviors acquired during training. While promising for audits, it raises considerations about safety, robustness, and the boundaries of elicitation, and warrants further evaluation across architectures and secret categories.

title: Learning Adaptive Solvers for Distributed Factor Graph Optimization on Matrix Lie Groups
summary: Modern robotic perception increasingly involves large-scale geometric optimization problems distributed across multiple robots or sessions. However, existing distributed solvers often depend on brittle hand tuning and primarily target rigid body pose graphs. To address this, we present DeepCORD, a learning-augmented framework for distributed factor graph optimization on general matrix Lie groups. By unfolding a parallel and accelerated Riemannian optimizer into differentiable iterations, DeepCORD learns a self-supervised feedback policy that dynamically adapts solver parameters according to the optimization phase and communication status. The resulting method enables adaptive distributed optimization over matrix Lie groups under both synchronous and asynchronous communication regimes. Extensive experiments on real-world $\mathrm{SE}$(3) pose graph optimization and $\mathrm{SL}$(4) projective submap alignment show that our method achieves lower objective values than existing distributed baselines on most benchmarks across realistic operating scenarios.

AI.tldr: DeepCORD is a learning-augmented distributed optimization framework for matrix Lie groups that unfolds a parallel Riemannian solver into differentiable steps and learns a self-supervised policy to adapt solver parameters, improving objective values on SE(3) pose graphs and SL(4) submap alignment under synchronous and asynchronous communication.
AI.motivation: Current distributed solvers for pose graph optimization rely on brittle hand-tuning and mostly target rigid-body (pose) graphs; there is a need for a general framework on matrix Lie groups with robust performance across varying communication regimes.
AI.method: Unfold a parallel and accelerated Riemannian optimizer into differentiable iterations and train a self-supervised feedback policy that dynamically adjusts solver parameters based on the optimization phase and communication status; supports distributed optimization over general matrix Lie groups with both synchronous and asynchronous communication.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation on real-world SE(3) pose graph optimization and SL(4) projective submap alignment shows that DeepCORD achieves lower objective values than existing distributed baselines on most benchmarks across realistic operating scenarios.
AI.conclusion: DeepCORD provides a general, learning-augmented approach for distributed optimization on matrix Lie groups, yielding improved performance and robustness to communication regimes compared with traditional distributed solvers.

title: Leveraging Color Naming for Image Enhancement
comment: Project page: https://namedcurves.github.io. arXiv admin note: text overlap with arXiv:2407.09892
summary: Enhancing images to make them visually appealing is a persistent challenge in computer vision. Many deep-learning methods train models on paired datasets to replicate expert editing styles. However, these approaches struggle with two key issues: (1) interpretability and (2) a parametrization suitable for user adjustments. To address these challenges, we present NamedCurves+, an approach inspired by the concept of Color Naming, a universal set of familiar colors widely used in software tools for intuitive editing. Our method integrates color names into a learning-based framework, enabling global adjustments for each named color through tone curves. To address local image variations, we incorporate a transformer block that captures spatial dependencies, enabling context-aware edits across the image. NamedCurves+ enhances the retouching process's interpretability and supports user interaction, allowing flexible modifications of individual tone curves to refine the retouched image according to personal preferences. Extensive experiments on tasks such as image retouching, tone mapping, and exposure correction demonstrate that NamedCurves+ outperforms state-of-the-art methods. Notably, our approach is both explainable, as the tone curves explicitly represent how each color name contributes to the enhancement, and interactive, allowing users to customize the retouching process and achieve results tailored to their liking.

AI.tldr: Introduces NamedCurves+, a learning framework that uses color-name-inspired tone curves and a transformer for context-aware image enhancement, enabling interpretable, interactive edits and improved results over SOTA.
AI.motivation: To address two core issues in learned image enhancement: interpretability and intuitive user control, which are limited in models trained on paired datasets.
AI.method: Integrates a universal set of color names into a learning framework, using global tone curves per named color; incorporates a transformer block to capture spatial dependencies for context-aware edits; supports user-interactive adjustment of individual curves.
AI.result: Demonstrates superior performance to state-of-the-art methods on image retouching, tone mapping, and exposure correction, with enhanced interpretability.
AI.conclusion: NamedCurves+ provides explainable mappings from color names to edits and enables interactive, customizable, context-aware retouching.

title: NFTR: From Provable Mode-Averaging to Geodesic Subgoal Selection in Offline Goal-Conditioned RL
summary: Hierarchical Implicit Q-Learning (HIQL), an offline goal-conditioned RL method, selects subgoals by value-function advantages alone. This rule has two coupled failure modes. Optimistic bias treats lucky stochastic outcomes as skillful choices, and mode collapse reduces a multi-modal subgoal distribution to a single Gaussian mean that often falls in unreachable regions. We propose NFTR (Normalizing Flows subgoal policies with Triangle-slack Reweighting). A conditional Normalizing Flow replaces the Gaussian policy, and a closed-form mode-averaging result identifies NFs as the minimal generative class for AWR-based subgoal selection. A triangle slack score, built on the architectural triangle inequality without relying on distance accuracy, multiplicatively corrects the AWR weight to downweight subgoals whose detour cost exceeds average reachability. Triangle-slack vanishes on geodesics in deterministic MDPs and remains a conservative upper bound on composability violation under stochastic dynamics. The RWDR objective preserves AWR's population-level monotonic improvement and admits a three-term suboptimality decomposition. Together, these two ingredients yield subgoal selection that provably avoids the Gaussian collapse described above and remains stable under stochastic dynamics. GitHub page: https://github.com/erdemtbao/NFTR

AI.tldr: NFTR introduces Normalizing Flows for subgoal policies with triangle-slack reweighting to fix two failure modes of Hierarchical Implicit Q-Learning (HIQL): optimistic bias and Gaussian mode collapse. It replaces the Gaussian subgoal policy with a conditional normalizing flow, and uses a triangle inequality-based slack score to correct AWR weights, ensuring subgoal selection remains stable under stochastic dynamics and avoids collapse. It provides a closed-form mode-averaging result, a RWDR objective with a three-term suboptimality decomposition, theoretical guarantees, and a GitHub implementation.
AI.motivation: Address two coupled failure modes in offline goal-conditioned RL using HIQL: (1) optimistic bias where lucky stochastic outcomes are mistaken for skillful actions, and (2) mode collapse where a multi-modal subgoal distribution collapses to a single Gaussian mean that may be unreachable.
AI.method: Replace Gaussian subgoal policy with a conditional Normalizing Flow (NF) to represent multi-modal subgoal distributions. Derive a closed-form mode-averaging result showing NF as the minimal generative class for AWR-based subgoal selection. Introduce a triangle slack score, computed from an architectural triangle inequality, to multiplicatively adjust AWR weights so subgoals with detour cost exceeding average reachability are downweighted. The triangle slack vanishes on geodesics in deterministic MDPs and provides a conservative upper bound on composability violation under stochastic dynamics. Maintain AWR-like population-level improvement via RWDR objective, which admits a three-term suboptimality decomposition.
AI.result: The NFTR framework yields subgoal selection that avoids Gaussian collapse and remains stable under stochastic dynamics. It preserves population-level improvements and offers theoretical guarantees (triangle slack behavior, suboptimality decomposition). Provides a GitHub page for implementation: https://github.com/erdemtbao/NFTR
AI.conclusion: NFTR successfully addresses HIQL's failure modes by using conditional normalizing flows for subgoal policy and triangle-slack reweighting, delivering a provably more robust and stable subgoal selection mechanism in offline goal-conditioned RL, with theoretical guarantees and practical code available.

title: ASMR: Agentic Schema Generation for Ship Maintenance Report Writing
comment: Accepted at the DASHSys 2026 workshop (Systems for Data-centric Agents with Human-in-the-loop), co-located with VLDB 2026
summary: In this paper, we study the automatic schema generation problem: given a collection of historical ship maintenance and operational reports across multiple form categories, automatically discover compact and informative schemas that capture the essential information requirements of each report type. To address this challenge, we propose ASMR, a modular agentic framework consisting of two specialized agents. A Field Generation Agent extracts semantic concepts from historical narratives and generates candidate schema fields through adaptive multi-granularity clustering, while a Structural Optimizer Agent employs reinforcement learning to identify compact, informative, and non-redundant schema representations. The resulting schemas can guide report authors toward producing more complete, consistent, and actionable reports. Preliminary results demonstrate the promise of the proposed approach and highlight several open research challenges at the intersection of data management, agentic AI, and human-centered AI.

AI.tldr: ASMR proposes a modular, agentic framework to automatically generate compact schemas for ship maintenance/operational reports, using Field Generation and Structural Optimization agents with adaptive clustering and reinforcement learning; preliminary results show promise and highlight open challenges.
AI.motivation: Need to automatically discover compact, informative schemas from heterogeneous historical reports to improve completeness, consistency, and actionability of downstream reports.
AI.method: Two specialized agents: Field Generation Agent extracts semantic concepts from narratives and generates candidate schema fields via adaptive multi-granularity clustering; Structural Optimizer Agent uses reinforcement learning to select compact, informative, and non-redundant schema representations.
AI.result: Preliminary results demonstrate promise; the paper outlines open research challenges at the intersection of data management, agentic AI, and human-centered AI.
AI.conclusion: The work introduces a novel, modular agentic approach to schema discovery with practical implications for improving report quality, while recognizing substantial open questions in evaluation, generalization, and human-in-the-loop design.

title: ContactMimic: Humanoid Object Interaction via Contact Control
summary: Keypoint tracking alone is insufficient for object interaction tasks such as sitting on a chair, wiping a board, or pushing furniture, where the robot can reach the correct pose without making meaningful physical contact with the object. We present CONTACTMIMIC, a learning framework that tracks explicit partlevel binary contact commands alongside keypoint trajectories. CONTACTMIMIC is made possible through the use of contact-following rewards and a trajectory augmentation scheme aimed at breaking the correlations between keypoint trajectories and contact labels. The resulting policy successfully decouples contact behavior from keypoint geometry, and achieves precise physical contact as well as contact-controllability (produce or suppress contact during deployment as desired). Simulation experiments across 10 diverse human-object interaction motions confirm that CONTACTMIMIC exhibits contact controllability that enables it to complete manipulation tasks without task-specific rewards, while also outperforming keypoint-only trackers on contact-relevant tasks. Ablations confirm the necessity of the proposed trajectory augmentation scheme and sim2real deployment validates contact controllability in the real world across 5 different motions. Video results are available on https://lixinyao11.github.io/contactmimic-page/.

AI.tldr: CONTACTMIMIC augments keypoint tracking with explicit part-level contact commands, using contact-following rewards and trajectory augmentation to decouple contact from geometry, yielding controllable contact and improved performance on contact-relevant tasks in both sim and sim-to-real.
AI.motivation: Keypoint tracking alone cannot handle object interactions requiring meaningful physical contact; tasks like sitting, wiping, or pushing require controllable contact beyond pose estimation, motivating a framework that can learn when to contact an object.
AI.method: Jointly track keypoint trajectories and binary contact signals for object parts. Use contact-following rewards to incentivize desired contact behavior. Apply a trajectory augmentation scheme to decorrelate keypoint motion from contact labels, encouraging decoupled contact control. Train policies that can both enable and suppress contact during deployment (contact controllability). Validate in simulation across 10 human-object motions and perform sim-to-real transfer across 5 motions.
AI.result: The policy achieves precise physical contact and the ability to control contact during deployment, enabling manipulation without task-specific rewards and outperforming keypoint-only trackers on contact-relevant tasks. Ablations confirm the necessity of the augmentation scheme; sim-to-real deployment demonstrates contact controllability in real-world 5-motion tasks.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling contact behavior from keypoint geometry enables controllable contact in manipulation, allowing contact-enabled actions without task-specific rewards and improving performance over traditional keypoint trackers on contact-sensitive tasks.

title: Dual-Correlation Hypergraph Network for Unaligned RGBT Video Object Detection and A Large-scale Benchmark
summary: RGB-Thermal (RGBT) Video Object Detection (VOD) has gained significant traction due to its ability to overcome the limitations of conventional RGB-based VOD under challenging conditions. However, spatial misalignment commonly exists between RGBT image pairs. To address this, we propose a Dual-Correlation Hypergraph Network (DHNet) that captures high-dimensional complementary information by explicitly modeling two types of correlations: temporal correlation across consecutive frames and spatial correlation from cross-modal features. Specifically, we first design a Patch-based Spatial Alignment Module (PSAM) to sequentially align the multimodal features at the local region level. Subsequently, we introduce a Dual Hypergraph Fusion Module (DHFM), which constructs separate temporal and multimodal hypergraphs to enhance object discriminability through dual-correlation learning. Furthermore, the field currently lacks a large-scale, scene-diverse benchmark dataset for comprehensive evaluation. To address this gap, we construct DVT-VOD1000, a large-scale RGBT VOD dataset containing 1,000 video sequences with 103,464 RGBT image pairs. The dataset covers diverse scenarios, including campuses, parks, transportation, rural areas, night scenes, rain, and snow. Comprehensive experiments on VT-VOD50 and our DVT-VOD1000 demonstrate that DHNet achieves state-of-the-art detection accuracy. The dataset and source code will be made publicly available on https://github.com/tzz-ahu/ to support academic research.

AI.tldr: Proposes DHNet for RGB-T VOD with Patch-based Spatial Alignment Module (PSAM) and Dual Hypergraph Fusion Module (DHFM); introduces DVT-VOD1000 dataset; achieves state-of-the-art results on VT-VOD50 and the new dataset; code will be released.
AI.motivation: To address spatial misalignment between RGB and thermal modalities in video object detection and to leverage both temporal and cross-modal correlations. Additionally, to fill the lack of large-scale, diverse RGB-T VOD benchmarks by introducing a new dataset.
AI.method: PSAM aligns multimodal features at local regions to mitigate misalignment; DHFM constructs two hypergraphs—one temporal and one multimodal—to perform dual-correlation learning for feature fusion and improved discriminability.
AI.result: DHNet achieves state-of-the-art detection accuracy on VT-VOD50 and on the new large-scale DVT-VOD1000 dataset, demonstrating strong cross-modal and temporal reasoning in RGBT VOD.
AI.conclusion: The approach validates the effectiveness of dual-correlation hypergraph learning for RGBT VOD and provides a large, diverse benchmark to support future research; source code and dataset will be publicly released.

title: Physics-Informed Machine Learning Under Small-Data Constraints: Lessons from Abrasive Waterjet Milling
comment: 2 figures, 5 tables, Accepted for publication; to be published in the Proceedings of ICANN 2026, Springer LNCS
summary: In physically dominated machining processes, experimental datasets are small, expensive, and material-specific; in this regime, data curation, evaluation design, and the form of physics integration can matter as much as the learning algorithm. Using an abrasive waterjet milling dataset ($n{=}155$, Inconel\,718), we make three methodological contributions. First, we separate physics-based data \emph{cleaning} from statistical \emph{curation} and treat the latter as competing modelling hypotheses rather than silent preprocessing. Second, we find that model rankings from a 15-point hold-out set can be unstable: the single-split winner drops from rank~1 to rank~7 under 10-fold cross-validation, while Gaussian Process (GP) variants occupy the top ranks. Third, we study a spectrum of physics integration levels and find that residual learning on a compact physics baseline is competitive for GP, yielding lower variance and an interpretable decomposition, but degrades tree-based models. Bayesian hyper parameter tuning improves parameter-sensitive baselines such as gradient boosting and SVR, yet harms multi-stage hybrid pipelines at this sample size. GP uncertainty intervals are approximately calibrated ($86\%$ empirical coverage at nominal $90\%$). The resulting picture is methodological: for small, expensive process datasets, our results suggest that, in this setting, reliable model comparison benefits from explicit curation hypotheses, robust evaluation, and careful choices about how physics enters the model.

AI.tldr: Small, expensive machining dataset analysis reveals that explicit data curation, robust evaluation design, and thoughtful physics integration are crucial; Gaussian Process models with residual physics offer stable performance and interpretable decompositions, but results vary with evaluation design and model type.
AI.motivation: In physically dominated machining, data are scarce and costly, so how data cleaning, evaluation design, and physics integration affect learning is critical for reliable modeling.
AI.method: The study (i) separates physics-based data cleaning from statistical curation and treats curation as competing modeling hypotheses, (ii) analyzes stability of model rankings under hold-out versus cross-validation, (iii) evaluates a spectrum of physics integration levels and compares GP and tree-based models, with Bayesian hyperparameter tuning, on a small abrasive waterjet milling dataset (n=155, Inconel 718).
AI.result: Key findings: single-split rankings can be unstable (hold-out top might drop from 1 to 7 under 10-fold CV). Gaussian Process variants tend to occupy top ranks. Residual learning on a compact physics baseline yields competitive GP performance with lower variance and interpretable decomposition, but degrades tree-based models. Bayesian hyperparameter tuning helps parameter-sensitive baselines (e.g., GB, SVR) but harms multi-stage hybrids at this sample size. GP uncertainty intervals are approximately calibrated (86% empirical coverage at nominal 90%).
AI.conclusion: For small, expensive process datasets, reliable model comparison benefits from explicit curation hypotheses, robust evaluation, and careful physics integration, with GP-based residual physics offering a favorable balance of interpretability and uncertainty quantification.

title: A First-Principles Theory of Slow Thinking and Active Perception
comment: Published on 2026/05/11 in Journal of Machine Learning
summary: As part of a series on first-principles modeling of cognitive functions, this paper attempts to provide a mathematical formulation of thinking and perception. It formally derives slow thinking or more generally, active perception, and encompasses the design, training and inference of slow thinking large language models. Our starting point is the lifting and projection of probability distributions on the observable and latent spaces, with the objective of representing complex data distributions by simple function families such as neural networks. A theory called "active lifting" is proposed, based on the sampling of latent sequences and an intrinsic drive to reduce uncertainty with maximum rate. It derives a large design space, containing the slow thinking models in a subspace that we call the static theory. These models are positioned on the representation hierarchy and sampler hierarchy induced by the static theory, and can be upgraded by climbing the two hierarchies. Active lifting further derives an inference process with an internal time axis, and a training objective that resembles minimum-length coding as well as the invention of languages. Thus, it characterizes the agency of perception, including the emergence of the slow thinking formats. Technical by-products of this theory include a three-stage pathway for improving slow thinking models, a unified approach to constructing encoders and generative models for all data modalities, a priori formation of human-like visual representations, and a possible solution to policy collapse.

AI.tldr: Proposes 'active lifting' as a first-principles framework for cognitive functions, formalizing slow thinking and active perception via lifting/projection of probability distributions between observable and latent spaces, deriving a training/inference paradigm for slow-thinking LLMs and outlining a design space and practical by-products.
AI.motivation: To provide a mathematical, principled formulation of thinking and perception, unify encoders, generative models, and language emergence, and address challenges in slow-thinking AI such as policy collapse.
AI.method: Introduce active lifting: sampling latent sequences with an intrinsic drive to minimize uncertainty at maximum rate; construct a static theory with representation and sampler hierarchies; derive an internal time axis for inference and a minimum-length coding-like training objective; propose a three-stage pathway and a unified modality-agnostic approach.
AI.result: Characterizes the agency of perception, identifies slow-thinking models as a subspace (static theory), grants a design space for slow thinking models, and yields concrete by-products including a three-stage improvement pathway, unified encoders/generative models, human-like visual representations, and a potential policy-collapse solution.
AI.conclusion: The active lifting framework grounds slow-thinking AI in a principled, hierarchical, probability-based formalism, enabling systematic development of slow-thinking LLMs and perceptual agents with broader applicability across modalities.

title: DexVerse: A Modular Benchmark for Multi-Task, Multi-Embodiment Dexterous Manipulation
summary: Building general-purpose dexterous manipulation policies requires benchmarks that go beyond isolated tasks to systematically evaluate policies across diverse interaction modes, sensory conditions, and robot embodiments. However, existing benchmarks remain limited in task and data diversity, embodiment coverage, or controllable visual variation, hindering studies of cross-task and cross-embodiment generalization. We present DexVerse, a large-scale and modular benchmark for dexterous manipulation. DexVerse includes 100 tasks spanning a broad range of manipulation skills, including object grasping and relocation, articulated-object interaction, functional tool use, bimanual coordination, non-prehensile control, contact-rich behaviors, multi-goal execution, and long-horizon multi-stage task completion. It supports 3 robot arms and 6 dexterous hands, and is extensible to new tasks, assets, and embodiments. To evaluate visuomotor generalization, DexVerse provides configurable visual variations in textures, background, lighting, and camera viewpoints. We further provide a VR-based teleoperation interface and 3,180 demonstrations with synchronized proprioceptive, RGB, depth, point-cloud, and state observations. We benchmark representative methods, including Diffusion Policy, DP3, OpenVLA, and $π_{0.5}$, across 19 tasks. Results reveal substantial challenges in task generalization and visuomotor robustness, establishing DexVerse as a promising testbed for general-purpose dexterous manipulation. Project page: https://ycyao216.github.io/DexVerse.site

AI.tldr: DexVerse is a large-scale, modular benchmark for dexterous manipulation with 100 tasks, multiple embodiments (3 arms, 6 hands), configurable visual variation, VR teleoperation, and 3,180 demonstrations, designed to study cross-task and cross-embodiment generalization; baseline results show sizable generalization and visuomotor robustness challenges.
AI.motivation: Current dexterous manipulation benchmarks suffer from limited task/embodiment diversity and insufficient control over visual variation, hindering systematic study of generalization across tasks and embodiments.
AI.method: DexVerse defines 100 tasks across diverse manipulation skills (grasping, articulated-object interaction, tool use, bimanual coordination, non-prehensile control, contact-rich behaviors, multi-goal, long-horizon tasks); supports 3 robot arms and 6 dexterous hands; extensible to new tasks/assets/embodiments; offers configurable visual variation (textures, background, lighting, camera viewpoints); provides VR teleoperation; includes 3,180 demonstrations with synchronized proprioceptive, RGB, depth, point-cloud, and state data; benchmarks methods (Diffusion Policy, DP3, OpenVLA, and π0.5) over 19 tasks.
AI.result: Experiments reveal substantial challenges in cross-task and cross-embodiment generalization as well as visuomotor robustness, validating DexVerse as a valuable testbed for evaluating and improving general-purpose dexterous manipulation.
AI.conclusion: DexVerse delivers a scalable, extensible benchmark suite enabling systematic study of generalization across tasks and embodiments in dexterous manipulation, and provides a foundation for developing and evaluating future general-purpose policies.

title: Dive Into the Implicit Biases of Low-rank Vision-language Alignment
summary: Vision-language alignment, the stage that bridges pretrained vision encoders and large language models, is widely treated as a form of pretraining requiring full-parameter updates. We challenge this view and investigate what happens when low-rank adaptation is applied to the LLM during this stage instead. We find that low-rank alignment not only reduces computational costs but also outperforms full-parameter alignment on most benchmarks. To understand this phenomenon, we systematically characterize the implicit biases introduced by low-rank adaptation during alignment. Empirically, we find that low-rank alignment shifts model behavior from hallucinatory to conservative and preserves per-token linear separability of visual features that full-parameter alignment disrupts, a phenomenon we term LS-curse. Geometrically, low rank aligned models exhibit more homogeneous and structurally stable visual representations, maintaining modality-specific knowledge rather than prematurely fusing entity-level semantics. Theoretically, we establish two theorems showing that low-rank alignment induces preferences for parameter subspaces with flat gradients and feature subspaces robust to perturbations, providing a principled explanation for the observed structure-preserving behavior. Extensive experiments cover ablation over 100 alignment configurations, three families of low-rank operators, and various rank, encoder, and other settings.

AI.tldr: Low-rank adapters for vision-language alignment can beat full-parameter updates, cutting costs while preserving or improving performance. They produce stable, structure-preserving representations and are supported by theory (flat gradients, robust features).
AI.motivation: Reconsider whether vision-language alignment between vision encoders and LLMs must rely on full-parameter fine-tuning; explore low-rank adaptation at alignment stage for efficiency and bias control.
AI.method: Apply low-rank adapters during the alignment stage between pretrained vision encoders and LLMs, across extensive ablations (100 configurations, 3 low-rank operator families, varied rank/encoders). Compare to full-parameter alignment. Analyze implicit biases: hallucinatory vs conservative behavior, LS-curse (loss of per-token separability when aligning), geometry of representations. Prove two theorems: (i) preferences for parameter subspaces with flat gradients, (ii) feature subspaces robust to perturbations. Provide empirical and theoretical explanations for structure-preserving behavior.
AI.result: Low-rank alignment reduces computational cost and often surpasses full-parameter alignment on benchmarks. It shifts model behavior toward conservatism, preserves per-token linear separability, and maintains modality-specific knowledge. Visual representations become more homogeneous and structurally stable, resisting premature fusion of entity-level semantics. Theoretical results explain these observations via flat-gradient and robust-subspace preferences. Comprehensive experiments cover wide configurations and aligners across ranks and encoders.
AI.conclusion: Low-rank adaptation offers an efficient, principled approach for vision-language alignment that preserves structure and bias characteristics while improving performance on average. The dual empirical-theoretical framing explains why rank-constrained updates yield stable, interpretable representations, guiding future exploration of subspace biases and alignment strategies.

title: Optimal Learning Rate Scaling Depends on Data in Deep Scalar Linear Networks
summary: In this short note we consider the gradient descent dynamics of deep scalar linear networks, $f(x) = \prod_{l=1}^L w_l x$, which enjoy exact time-course solutions for any integer depth. We show that even in this minimal model, the optimal depth-wise learning rate scaling depends on data, whereas data-agnostic scaling rules fail to transfer across depths. Under the data-dependent optimal scaling, the learning dynamics is independent of data and weakly dependent on depth, resulting in a constant linear convergence rate across all depths including infinity. We further show similar data-dependent effects in deep scalar linear networks with residual connections.

AI.tldr: Gradient descent on deep scalar linear networks admits exact time-course solutions for any depth. Optimal learning-rate scaling depends on data; data-agnostic scaling does not transfer across depths. With data-dependent scaling, dynamics become depth-robust: data-independent and with a constant linear convergence rate across depths, including infinite depth. Residual connections exhibit similar data-dependent effects.
AI.motivation: To understand how depth and data influence learning dynamics in deep linear networks, and whether simple, depth-agnostic learning-rate rules can generalize across depths.
AI.method: Derives exact time-course solutions for gradient descent on the product-form model f(x)=∏_{l=1}^L w_l x, analyzes depth-wise learning-rate scaling, and studies residual connections; investigates data-dependent versus data-agnostic scaling rules.
AI.result: Shows: (1) optimal per-depth learning-rate scaling depends on data; (2) data-agnostic scaling fails to transfer across depths; (3) with data-dependent scaling, dynamics are data-independent and weakly depth-dependent, yielding a constant linear convergence rate across depths including infinity; (4) similar data-dependent effects in networks with residual connections.
AI.conclusion: Data-dependent learning-rate scaling can achieve depth-robust, depth-agnostic convergence behavior in deep scalar linear networks and their residual variants, revealing that transferability of training dynamics hinges on data-aware hyperparameter scaling.

title: Playing ZendoWorld: Challenging AI Agents on Active Visual Concept Induction
summary: A central challenge in building intelligent systems is enabling agents to jointly perceive complex inputs, form hypotheses about hidden patterns, and design informative experiments to test them. To study this problem, we propose ZendoWorld, a controlled interactive environment in which agents must infer a logical rule about visual game observations, acquire information by proposing new scenes, and refine their hypotheses based on feedback from the game environment. We evaluate several agents spanning pure VLM reasoning, Bayesian particle filtering, dynamic concept discovery, and neuro-symbolic methods. Our main findings are: (1) high accuracy in predicting labels for observed examples does not imply recovery of the underlying rule; (2) perception and induction are distinct bottlenecks for different agent classes; and (3) VLM-based agents propose near-uninformative experiments, failing to actively reduce hypothesis uncertainty. To compare these results, we collect human data on the task, which reveals a gap in inductive reasoning, particularly for more complex rules. Overall, ZENDOWORLD takes an important step toward evaluating intelligent agents and identifies concrete avenues for improvement, particularly in domains like scientific discovery.

AI.tldr: ZendoWorld provides an interactive testbed for agents to infer logical rules from visual observations, design informative scenes, and refine hypotheses; key findings show that predicting observed labels with high accuracy does not guarantee rule recovery, perception and induction are bottlenecks that vary by agent type, and VLM-based agents struggle to propose informative experiments.
AI.motivation: To study the joint problem of perception, hypothesis formation, and experiment design in intelligent agents, and to identify bottlenecks and avenues for improvement in tasks requiring scientific-like inductive reasoning.
AI.method: Introduce ZendoWorld, a controlled interactive environment where agents infer a logical rule from visual game observations, acquire information by proposing new scenes, and update hypotheses based on feedback. Evaluate multiple agent classes (pure VLM reasoning, Bayesian particle filtering, dynamic concept discovery, and neuro-symbolic methods) and compare with human data.
