AI.result: Main findings: (1) high accuracy in predicting labels for observed examples does not imply recovery of the underlying rule; (2) perception and induction are distinct bottlenecks for different agent classes; (3) VLM-based agents propose near-uninformative experiments and fail to actively reduce hypothesis uncertainty. Human data reveal gaps in inductive reasoning for more complex rules.
AI.conclusion: ZendoWorld offers a valuable benchmark for evaluating intelligent agents on joint perception, hypothesis testing, and experiment design, highlighting concrete avenues to improve active learning and inductive reasoning—crucial for advances in domains like scientific discovery.

title: Unpaired Joint Distribution Modeling via Multi-Scale Image Representations
summary: This paper studies the problem of learning a joint distribution from marginal observations, which is inherently ill-posed due to the ambiguity of feasible couplings. We propose LUD-MSR, a latent-variable probabilistic framework that models the joint distribution via auxiliary representations and optimizes evidence lower bounds using only marginal data. Under mild assumptions, we establish an upper bound on the distribution approximation error. This analysis reveals a trade-off in representation learning between domain consistency and information preservation. To address this trade-off, we introduce a Multi-Scale image Representation (MSR) mapping that exploits structural similarity at coarse scales while suppressing domain-specific variations. We show that MSR achieves a more favorable balance of this trade-off compared to existing approaches. Experiments on real-world denoising benchmarks, including cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM), demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework.

AI.tldr: Proposes LUD-MSR, a latent-variable framework to learn joint distributions from marginals using ELBO optimization and a Multi-Scale Representation (MSR) to balance domain consistency with information preservation, with theoretical error bounds and empirical validation on denoising and cryo-EM data.
AI.motivation: Learning a joint distribution from marginal observations is ill-posed due to ambiguous feasible couplings; a latent-variable approach with structured representations can regularize and enable learning from marginals.
AI.method: Introduce LUD-MSR: a latent-variable probabilistic model with auxiliary representations; optimize evidence lower bounds (ELBO) using only marginal data; propose MSR mapping to exploit coarse-scale structural similarity while suppressing domain-specific variations.
AI.result: Under mild assumptions, derive an upper bound on distribution approximation error; MSR provides a better trade-off between domain consistency and information preservation than existing methods; empirical results on real-world denoising benchmarks, including cryo-EM, show improved performance.
AI.conclusion: The framework offers a principled approach to learning joint distributions from marginals, with a theoretical error bound and practical gains from MSR in challenging denoising tasks, including cryo-EM.

title: Distributed Sketching on Data Partitions for OLS Regression
comment: This work has been accepted at Statistics&Probability Letters, 2026
summary: This paper studies distributed sketching for ordinary least squares (OLS) regression, an approach that distributes small sketches of a large data set over multiple machines to separately construct OLS estimators and average them. Unlike prior studies that consider sketching on the whole data set, we consider sketching on partitioned subsets to further reduce computational cost. Under the fixed design setting, we characterize the exact excess loss of the averaged OLS estimator. Results show that this loss is comparable to the established loss for sketching on the whole data set when the divergence among subset covariances is small.

AI.tldr: Averaging OLS estimators from partitioned data sketches yields an exactly characterized excess risk under fixed design; performance is comparable to full-data sketching when subset covariances are similar.
AI.motivation: Reduce computation for large-scale OLS by sketching on partitioned data and averaging; assess how partitioning affects excess loss relative to sketching the entire data.
AI.method: Derives the exact excess loss of the averaged OLS estimator built from local sketches on partitioned subsets under a fixed design; analyzes how divergence among subset covariances impacts performance.
AI.result: Provides an exact expression for the excess loss; shows it is comparable to the full-data sketching loss when covariance divergence across subsets is small; quantifies the role of heterogeneity.
AI.conclusion: Partitioned-subset sketching is a computationally efficient alternative that preserves statistical guarantees similar to whole-dataset sketching under modest heterogeneity of subset covariances.

title: AutoPersonas: A Multi-Timescale Loop Engine for Open-Ended Persona Evolution
comment: 52 pages, 13 figures/tables, ancillary public-safe evaluation artifacts included
summary: Long-term persona agents must remain identifiable while adapting to new events, relationships, evidence, and social conditions. We identify self-locking as a runtime failure mode in continuing persona-life loops: locally plausible events keep appearing while the generated life collapses toward familiar environments, weak relationships, suspended decisions, and stale life stages. We trace this failure to model-level convergence toward high-probability behavioral channels and system-level context gravity from State, memory, history, and environment summaries. We introduce AutoPersonas, a multi-timescale life-environment engine for bounded persona-level recursive self-evolution. It separates environment-side Occurrences, accumulated Observations, and persona State. Its OSO loop admits divergent future-facing material while requiring evidence-governed absorption before State or reachability changes. A three-year compressed simulation exposed environment watermark shells, occurrence-hardening gaps, slow-change accumulation failures, recursive indecision, and weak relationship persistence. An eight-model 40-day stress test generated 1,600 events and found mean rolling 5-day action-category repetition of 95.2%-97.6%, with all models crossing 90% by day 11. Semantic re-keeping found 79.0%-88.0% macro-theme repetition across all direct-loop runs. In a same-runtime 40-day A/B, context-slice masking plus per-sample divergence targeting reduced macro-theme repetition from 61.8% to 36.3% and roughly doubled cumulative theme count. A juvenile-goblin fictional-world run reproduced the anti-fixation regime without hard real-world intrusions. These results support a bounded claim: separating controlled divergence from evidence-governed absorption can reduce persona-environment self-locking while preserving identity continuity.

AI.tldr: AutoPersonas introduces a bounded, multi-timescale life-environment engine that mitigates self-locking by separating environment signals from persona state and enforcing evidence-based state updates; experiments show reduced macro-theme repetition and increased theme diversity under targeted divergence.
AI.motivation: Identify and mitigate runtime self-locking in continuing persona-life loops, ensuring identity continuity while adapting to evolving events and environments.
AI.method: Propose OSO loop architecture with distinct environment-side components (Occurrences, Observations) and persona State; enable divergent future material but require evidence-governed absorption before state updates; conduct long-horizon simulations (3-year compressed, multi-model 40-day stress tests) and A/B experiments; include a juvenile-goblin world to test anti-fixation behavior.
AI.result: Empirical findings reveal environment watermark shells, occurrence-hardening gaps, slow-change accumulation, recursive indecision, and weak relationship persistence. 8-model 40-day tests show 1,600 events with high short-term repetition; semantic macro-theme repetition 79–88% across direct-loop runs. Context-slice masking and targeted divergence reduce macro-theme repetition (61.8%→36.3%) and roughly double cumulative theme count; juvenile-world run supports anti-fixation regime.
AI.conclusion: Bounded claim supported: separating controlled divergence from evidence-governed absorption reduces persona-environment self-locking while preserving identity continuity.

title: TMI: Text-to-Image Meets Image-to-Image for Complementary Data Synthesis to Boost Long-Tailed Instance Segmentation
comment: Accepted to ECCV 2026. The first two authors contributed equally to this work
summary: Large-vocabulary instance segmentation is constrained by long-tailed category distributions and fine-grained inter-class ambiguity. While data synthesis offers a promising alternative, current paradigms have complementary limitations: text-to-image (T2I) methods inherit noisy pseudo-labels and struggle on rare classes, whereas copy-paste methods compromise contextual realism. To address these issues, we propose a hybrid pipeline coupling T2I generation with context-aware image-to-image (I2I) editing. The T2I branch provides broad category and scene diversity, while a teacher-student scheme ensures label reliability by selectively retaining only prompt-specified categories. To strengthen supervision for rare classes, we introduce VRAIN (Verified Rare-class Augmentation via INstructed editing), a novel I2I editor. VRAIN inserts high-confidence instances at semantically appropriate locations within in-the-wild scenes, yielding semantically coherent and visually natural edits that reduce domain gaps and enable targeted augmentation. On the LVIS benchmark, our method surpasses existing baselines, improving overall AP by up to +4.0 points and rare-class AP by up to +9.5 points, while scaling effectively with backbone capacity. Our project page is available at https://seokhunchoi.github.io/TMI

AI.tldr: A hybrid T2I+I2I editing pipeline (VRAIN) for large-vocabulary instance segmentation that blends generated diversity with semantically coherent, high-confidence rare-class augmentation to improve LVIS performance.
AI.motivation: Address long-tailed category distributions and fine-grained inter-class ambiguity in large-vocabulary instance segmentation. T2I alone yields noisy labels and struggles with rare classes; copy-paste harms contextual realism; need a data-augmentation pipeline that ensures label reliability and semantic coherence.
AI.method: A hybrid pipeline: (1) a text-to-image (T2I) branch providing diverse content; (2) a teacher-student scheme that retains only prompt-specified categories to ensure label reliability; (3) a novel I2I editor, VRAIN, that locally edits real scenes by inserting high-confidence rare-class instances at contextually appropriate locations; (4) evaluation on LVIS, demonstrating gains and backbones scaling.
AI.result: On LVIS, surpasses baselines with overall AP up to +4.0 and rare-class AP up to +9.5, with performance scaling with backbone capacity; project page provided.
AI.conclusion: The proposed hybrid T2I+I2I framework with VRAIN enables reliable, contextually coherent augmentation for large-vocabulary instance segmentation, addressing long-tail and intra-class ambiguity, and yielding strong LVIS gains.

title: Multimodal Unlearning Across Vision, Language, Video, and Audio: Survey of Methods, Datasets, and Benchmarks
summary: With the growing adoption of VLMs, DMs, LLMs, and AFMs, these multimodal foundation models can inadvertently encode sensitive, copyrighted, biased, or unsafe cross-modal associations that originate from their training data. Retraining after deletion requests or policy updates is often impractical, and targeted forgetting remains difficult because knowledge is distributed across shared representations. Multimodal unlearning addresses this challenge by enabling selective removal across modalities while retaining overall utility. This survey offers a unified, system-oriented view of multimodal unlearning across vision, language, audio, and video, grounded in recent advances, emerging applications, and open problems. Our taxonomy enables systematic comparison across model architectures and modalities, clarifying trade-offs among deletion strength, retention, efficiency, reversibility, and robustness. This survey highlights open problems and practical considerations to support future research and deployment of multimodal unlearning. We release a curated repository: https://smsnobin77.github.io/Awesome-Multimodal-Unlearning/

AI.tldr: A survey that unifies multimodal unlearning across vision, language, audio, and video, presenting a system-oriented taxonomy to compare architectures and modalities, and outlining open problems and deployment considerations, with a curated repository for resources.
AI.motivation: Growing multimodal foundation models can leak sensitive or copyrighted associations from training data. Retraining after deletion requests is impractical, and targeted forgetting is hard due to distributed knowledge across representations. Multimodal unlearning aims to selectively remove knowledge across modalities while preserving overall utility.
AI.method: Literature synthesis and taxonomy construction. The paper reviews recent advances in multimodal unlearning across vision, language, audio, and video, proposes a unified taxonomy and comparative framework, analyzes trade-offs (deletion strength, retention, efficiency, reversibility, robustness), and discusses practical deployment considerations. It also provides a curated resource repository.
AI.result: A unified system-oriented taxonomy enabling systematic comparison across multimodal models and architectures. Clarifies trade-offs among deletion strength, retention, efficiency, reversibility, and robustness. Identifies open problems and practical considerations to guide future research and deployment. Provides a curated repository link for resources: https://smsnobin77.github.io/Awesome-Multimodal-Unlearning/
AI.conclusion: Multimodal unlearning is essential in the era of foundation models; the survey establishes a shared framework to evaluate and compare deletion methods across modalities, highlights open challenges, and supports practical deployment with a resource repository.

title: Compete Then Collaborate: Frontier AI Teachers Build a Verifiable Curriculum to Improve a Coding Student Beyond Imitation
summary: Large language models increasingly serve as teachers generating training data for smaller students. Prior multi-teacher knowledge distillation methods merge outputs without determining which frontier model teaches best, often relying on an LLM judge biased toward its own outputs. We introduce a compete-then-collaborate framework where four frontier AI teachers (Claude, Codex-GPT, Grok, Gemini) are ranked head-to-head by an execution-based judge (unit tests and stdin-stdout checks) with fairness controls, and then collaborate to build a verifiable curriculum for a student (Qwen2.5-Coder). We report three findings. (1) Under execution verification, all teachers solve standard problems near-perfectly after self-correction (99-100%) due to a saturation effect, but harder competition problems separate them (Gemini 77% > Claude 69% = Codex 69% > Grok 50%); however, the robust student-side results do not depend on teacher ranking. (2) Imitation (SFT) on verified solutions does not improve, and can degrade, an already-competent student at 7B and 32B (e.g., from 76.7% to 72.7% on MBPP-test, and 5.9% to 2.9% on competition problems). (3) Using the same collaborative curriculum as a reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) environment improves the student (from 5.9% to 8.8% peak on competition problems, a +49% relative gain), reversing SFT's direction. The value of AI-teacher collaboration lies not in pooling answers to imitate, but in jointly constructing a verifiable environment where the student learns by doing. We release a reproducible on-prem pipeline (NVIDIA GB10) with framework patches for running GRPO on a bleeding-edge stack.

AI.tldr: A four-teacher compete-then-collaborate framework uses execution-based judging to build a verifiable student curriculum, showing collaboration and RL-based verifiable rewards improve a student more than imitation; ranking among teachers is not essential for robust student outcomes.
AI.motivation: Address the bias and inefficiency in multi-teacher knowledge distillation where an LLM judge may favor its own outputs, seeking a fair, verifiable curriculum that enhances student learning.
AI.method: Four frontier models (Claude, Codex-GPT, Grok, Gemini) are ranked head-to-head by an execution-based judge with unit tests and stdin-stdout checks and fairness controls, then collaborate to construct a verifiable curriculum for student Qwen2.5-Coder. An on-prem pipeline (NVIDIA GB10) with GRPO-patches is released to enable reproducibility. Evaluation uses SFT and RLVR to assess the student.
AI.result: (1) With execution verification, all teachers reach near-perfect performance on standard problems after self-correction (99–100%), but harder competition problems separate them (Gemini 77% > Claude 69% = Codex 69% > Grok 50%); robust student results do not depend on teacher ranking. (2) Imitation via SFT on verified solutions does not improve and can degrade a 7B/32B student (e.g., MBPP-test 76.7%→72.7%; competition problems 5.9%→2.9%). (3) Using the same collaborative curriculum in an RLVR setting improves the student (5.9%→8.8% peak on competition problems, +49% relative). Value lies in jointly creating a verifiable learning environment rather than pooling answers. Reproducible on-prem pipeline released.
AI.conclusion: The key contribution is the emphasis on a verifiable, outcome-centered collaboration among frontier models to build a learning environment where the student learns by doing, with RLVR offering stronger gains than imitation; this approach shifts the focus from answer aggregation to verifiable learning dynamics and reproducible pipelines.

title: Metrics or Mirage? An Audit of Evaluation Inconsistencies in Colonoscopy Polyp Segmentation Benchmarks
summary: Progress in colonoscopy polyp segmentation is routinely reported through leaderboard comparisons on a small set of public benchmarks. We argue that this apparent progress is difficult to verify: a systematic audit of \textbf{27 papers} published between 2015 and 2026 reveals three structural problems in how the community evaluates models. \textbf{First}, 25 of 27 papers \textit{omit the Hausdorff distance}. Hausdorff distance is a boundary-accuracy metric with direct clinical relevance for detecting flat or small polyps, and is a standard in radiotherapy segmentation. \textbf{Second}, at least five \textit{incompatible train/test split protocols} co-exist across papers reporting results on the same two datasets (Kvasir-SEG and CVC-ClinicDB), making published Dice scores non-comparable even when they appear in the same leaderboard column. \textbf{Third}, 26 of 27 papers make \textit{performance claims without any statistical significance test}. Strikingly, four papers published \emph{after} the Metrics Reloaded framework~\cite{metricsreloaded2024} (Maier-Hein et al., \textit{Nature Methods} 2024) perpetuate these same problems, suggesting that general-purpose metric guidance has not yet reached the colonoscopy sub-community. To show these problems are not merely cosmetic, we re-evaluate five representative models under three controlled protocols with a single uniform scorer, and find that the reported metric conceals large boundary and recall failures, that the ``best'' model changes with the metric, and that near-tied rankings reverse across random splits. We propose a five-point \textbf{Polyp Segmentation Reporting Checklist}~(PSRC) as a lightweight, domain-adapted corrective.

AI.tldr: Systematic audit of 27 colonoscopy polyp segmentation papers (2015–2026) reveals three evaluation flaws: omission of Hausdorff distance, inconsistent train/test splits across datasets (Kvasir-SEG, CVC-ClinicDB), and lack of statistical significance testing. Re-evaluating five models under controlled protocols shows metric-dependent best models and unstable rankings; a five-point Polyp Segmentation Reporting Checklist (PSRC) is proposed to rectify these issues.
AI.motivation: Ensure credible, comparable, and clinically relevant evaluation practices in colonoscopy polyp segmentation; address methodological fragmentation and misalignment with broader medical image analysis standards (e.g., inclusion of Hausdorff distance, consistent data splits, and statistical testing).
AI.method: Systematic audit of 27 papers (2015–2026) on polyp segmentation; identify three structural evaluation problems; examine two public datasets (Kvasir-SEG, CVC-ClinicDB) with incompatible splits; re-evaluate five representative models using three controlled protocols with a single uniform scorer; assess the impact of metric choice on model ranking; propose PSRC
AI.result: Findings: 25/27 papers omit Hausdorff distance; ≥5 incompatible train/test split protocols exist; 26/27 lack statistical significance tests. Even after applying a Metrics Reloaded framework, these problems persist. Re-evaluation under controlled protocols reveals large boundary/recall failures concealed by aggregate Dice scores; best model is metric-dependent; near-tied rankings can reverse with different random splits. Conclusion: Propose a five-point Polyp Segmentation Reporting Checklist (PSRC) as a lightweight, domain-adapted corrective to standardize reporting and enable fairer cross-study comparisons.
AI.conclusion: The abstract advocates standardization of evaluation practices in colonoscopy polyp segmentation through PSRC, highlighting that progress claims are not robust without consistent metrics (including boundary accuracy), reproducible data splits, and statistical validation.

title: Efficient Safety Alignment of Language Models via Latent Personality Traits
summary: Current safety methods for large language models are known to be vulnerable to adversarial attacks, motivating research into robust alternatives. Latent Adversarial Training (LAT) is among the most effective defenses, but can degrade utility and requires training on large datasets of harmful prompts. We introduce Latent Personality Alignment (LPA), which replaces explicit harm refusal with adversarial training on just 66 harm-agnostic statements drawn from psychometric personality literature. We hypothesize that personality-anchored representations share latent structure with harm avoidance, so adversarially stabilizing them implicitly constrains the subspace exploited by jailbreak attacks. LPA achieves near-zero attack success rates on HarmBench across direct requests and five jailbreak methods, despite never seeing harmful content during training and no loss of performance on standard benchmarks. Moreover, the training process is lightweight; the entire procedure completes in minutes on a single GPU and uses 75x fewer examples than standard LAT. Extensive ablations demonstrate the robustness, efficiency, and generalization of our method.

AI.tldr: Latent Personality Alignment (LPA) uses 66 harm-agnostic personality statements to adversarially train latent representations, yielding near-zero HarmBench attack success with no harmful data, preserving utility, and requiring far less data and compute than Latent Adversarial Training (LAT).
AI.motivation: Current safety methods for large language models (e.g., LAT) are susceptible to adversarial prompts and can degrade utility; there is a need for a light-weight, generalizable defense that does not rely on training with harmful content.
AI.method: Adversarial training on 66 harm-agnostic statements drawn from psychometric personality literature to align latent representations; hypothesizes that personality-anchored latent structure shares subspace with harm avoidance; stabilizing these representations indirectly constrains jailbreak exploitability. Evaluation on HarmBench includes direct requests and five jailbreak methods; comparisons to LAT; assesses attack success and standard benchmark performance; training is lightweight and data-efficient.
AI.result: Near-zero attack success rates on HarmBench across direct requests and five jailbreak methods; no loss of performance on standard benchmarks; training completes in minutes on a single GPU; uses 75x fewer examples than standard LAT; extensive ablations support robustness, efficiency, and generalization.
AI.conclusion: LPA offers a lightweight, generalizable defense by leveraging latent personality-informed representations to constrain jailbreak subspaces without exposure to harmful content, achieving strong safety improvements with minimal data and compute and without sacrificing utility.

title: MentalHospital: A Virtual Environment for Evaluating Psychiatric Clinical Encounters
summary: Large language models (LLMs) have shown strong performance on isolated psychiatric tasks, including dialogue, diagnosis, and treatment planning, yet existing benchmarks rarely simulate complete psychiatric clinical encounters. We introduce $\textbf{MentalHospital}$, a virtual evaluation environment for LLM-based psychiatric clinical encounters. MentalHospital instantiates the Subjective Interviewing, Objective Examination, Diagnostic Assessment, and Treatment Planning (S.O.A.P.) workflow, using skill-augmented standardized patients constructed from 1,193 de-identified psychiatric electronic health record (EHR) cases spanning all major ICD-11 categories and 76 disorders. Each encounter is assessed through a dual-track protocol that combines objective comparison against EHR-derived references with subjective assessment of clinical process quality. To scale specialist judgment, we develop $\textbf{MentalEval}$, five domain-specific evaluators covering communication empathy, interviewing professionalism, clinical-note quality, diagnostic rigor, and treatment appropriateness, trained with rubric-grounded SFT and expert-guided DPO. Survey responses from 22 clinicians support MentalHospital's clinical fidelity (3.88/5), while MentalEval achieves strong expert alignment with an average QWK of 0.944. Benchmarking shows that even the strongest LLM trails clinicians by 37.28 percentage points in objective psychiatric competence, with mental status assessment as a key bottleneck.

AI.tldr: MentalHospital creates a virtual psychiatric clinic using S.O.A.P. workflow and EHR-based standardized patients to benchmark LLMs in full encounters, with MentalEval providing domain-specific evaluators. LLMs lag clinicians notably, especially in mental status assessment.
AI.motivation: Address the gap in evaluating LLMs on complete psychiatric encounters, not just isolated tasks, by creating a high-fidelity, scalable evaluation framework.
AI.method: Construct MentalHospital with Subjective Interviewing, Objective Examination, Diagnostic Assessment, and Treatment Planning using 1,193 de-identified EHR cases across ICD-11 categories. Employ dual-track evaluation against EHR references and subjective process quality. Develop MentalEval with five domain-specific evaluators (communication empathy, interviewing professionalism, clinical-note quality, diagnostic rigor, treatment appropriateness) trained via rubric-grounded supervised fine-tuning and expert-guided DPO. Calibrate and validate with surveys from 22 clinicians.
AI.result: Clinicians rated clinical fidelity 3.88/5. MentalEval achieved QWK of 0.944 indicating strong expert alignment. LLMs remained substantially below clinicians, by 37.28 percentage points in objective psychiatric competence; mental status assessment identified as a key bottleneck.
AI.conclusion: The MentalHospital framework and MentalEval evaluators enable principled benchmarking of LLMs in complete psychiatric encounters and reveal specific competency gaps, notably mental status assessment, guiding future improvement priorities and dataset development.

title: Benchmark Evaluation of Feredated Learning on Multi-organ Images
summary: The privacy requirements of medical data and its substantial variations across organs and modalities hinder the clinical implementation of medical AI. Federated learning (FL) is a feasible approach to overcome these challenges. Due to the continuous emergence of FL algorithms and the highly heterogeneous nature of medical data, objectively evaluating their performance in real-world clinical settings remains difficult. Therefore, a comprehensive federated medical imaging benchmark, serving as a unified evaluation standard, is crucial for advancing the technology toward reliable clinical application. Existing federated medical imaging benchmarks have not yet adequately incorporated state-of-the-art algorithms, are limited to data from single organs or modalities, and overly emphasize model accuracy, making it difficult to comprehensively assess the overall efficacy of FL in real-world medical environments. To address these challenges, we developed the MobenFL benchmark. This benchmark integrates 20 cutting-edge FL algorithms and 22 medical imaging datasets, covering 12 critical organs across the human body, surpassing existing benchmark in breadth. In terms of evaluation dimensions, MobenFL not only assesses performance but also systematically incorporates key metrics such as algorithmic efficiency and privacy protection capabilities. Additionally, it conducts specialized evaluations for complex real-world clinical scenarios involving different diseases, devices, and imaging modalities, thereby providing a comprehensive and in-depth evaluation framework for the clinical application of FL in the medical field.

AI.tldr: MobenFL is a comprehensive federated medical imaging benchmark that integrates 20 FL algorithms and 22 datasets across 12 organs, evaluating performance, efficiency, privacy, and real-world clinical scenarios.
AI.motivation: Federated learning for medical imaging must address privacy and data heterogeneity; existing benchmarks are limited in scope and breadth and lack unified evaluation standards.
AI.method: Assembles 20 state-of-the-art FL algorithms and 22 medical imaging datasets spanning 12 organs; assesses performance along with algorithmic efficiency and privacy protection; includes specialized evaluations for real-world clinical scenarios with varying diseases, devices, and imaging modalities.
AI.result: Expands benchmark breadth beyond prior work by covering diverse organs, modalities, and algorithms; provides multi-dimensional evaluation (performance, efficiency, privacy) and scenario-based testing for clinical applicability of FL.
AI.conclusion: MobenFL advances standardized evaluation for federated medical imaging, enabling more reliable assessment of FL readiness for real-world clinical deployment.

title: path_boost: A Python Package for Interpretable Graph-Level Prediction using Path-Based Gradient Boosting
comment: 27 pages, 4 figures, 5 tables. Code available at https://github.com/Claudio-Me/extended_path_boost and on PyPI (path-boost)
summary: We present path_boost, a Python package for interpretable supervised learning on graph-structured input data. The package implements PathBoost, a gradient boosting algorithm that automatically discovers predictive labeled paths within graphs during the learning process. Unlike graph neural networks, which are generally difficult to interpret, PathBoost produces an additive prediction model over path-based features that explicitly reveals which substructures drive predictions. To avoid an exhaustive enumeration of all possible paths, the algorithm iteratively selects and extends paths during learning based on their predictive power, using boosting to combine weak learners into a strong ensemble. The package supports both regression and binary classification. Key features include compatibility with scikit-learn workflows, support for custom base learners and selectors, automatic starting node selection, parallel training across anchor nodes, and built-in variable importance computation. We demonstrate PathBoost on molecular property prediction of transition metal compounds, where atoms serve as nodes and bonds as edges, and further benchmark PathBoost against an established graph neural network and a graph kernel method across six molecular datasets. The package is available on PyPI and GitHub under an open-source license.

AI.tldr: PathBoost is a Python package implementing a gradient-boosting approach that discovers predictive labeled paths in graphs to produce an interpretable additive model, with scalable path selection, scikit-learn compatibility, and open-source availability; demonstrated on molecular-property prediction and benchmarked against a graph neural network and a graph kernel across six datasets.
AI.motivation: The abstract targets interpretability in graph learning by extracting informative substructures (paths) directly during learning, avoiding the opaque representations of many graph neural networks. It also aims to provide a scalable, usable framework compatible with standard ML workflows.
AI.method: PathBoost iteratively grows and selects predictive labeled paths as weak learners, uses boosting to combine them into an ensemble, and integrates path-based features into an additive, interpretable model. It supports regression and binary classification, automatic starting-node selection, parallel training across anchor nodes, custom base learners/selectors, and built-in variable importance. It is designed to leverage scikit-learn workflows and can run with customizable components.
AI.result: The method is demonstrated on molecular-property prediction for transition-metal compounds, with atoms as nodes and bonds as edges. PathBoost is benchmarked against an established graph neural network and a graph kernel method across six molecular datasets, and the package is released on PyPI and GitHub under an open-source license.
AI.conclusion: PathBoost offers interpretable, path-based gradient-boosted predictions on graphs, with scalable learning and good integration into standard ML pipelines. It provides transparent insights into which substructures drive predictions and shows competitive benchmarking in molecular datasets, making it a practical alternative to black-box GNNs in contexts where interpretability is important.

title: Different Teachers, Different Capabilities: Sub-1B On-Device Distillation for Structured Text Enrichment
comment: 12 pages, 5 figures. has a same-size non-reasoning-teacher control, a three-judge LLM-as-a-judge panel with a negative control, full-source faithfulness grading, and a per-field routing analysis
summary: High-volume structured extraction pays a large model's latency on every item, so distilling the task into a small on-device model is attractive: comparable output at a fraction of the time and cost. We measure what that distillation actually delivers, per sub-task. Each news article is mapped to one JSON object with a short summary and five categorical labels. We distill an 8B reasoning teacher (deepseek-r1:8b) into a 0.6B student (Qwen3-0.6B; QLoRA, three seeds), and add two teacher controls: a same-size non-reasoning teacher and a larger managed pipeline. A blinded, reference-free, three-judge panel scores every arm against the full article, alongside two non-distillation baselines, few-shot prompting and constrained decoding. The student runs at about 0.8 s per article against the teacher's 39 s, and recovers 58% of the base-to-teacher gap on summary quality, beating its primary baseline (constrained decoding) by +16.8 points and few-shot prompting by a secondary +4.9. A same-size non-reasoning teacher trains a student no better than the untuned base, so the summary gain follows from the teacher's reasoning nature rather than its scale. Capabilities then split by teacher: the reasoning teacher transfers writing quality and the managed pipeline transfers label diversity, while a same-size instruction teacher's students stay more grounded on the 22 short, thin-source articles in the 93-item test set (74 versus 55 faithful), where the reasoning-lineage student fabricates. That grounding difference is a consistent ordering rather than a significant aggregate effect, and the subgroup is small, so we report it as a direction. Because no single engine wins every field, the deliverable is a per-field routing map for on-device enrichment.

AI.tldr: Distilling an 8B reasoning teacher into a 0.6B on-device student yields substantial latency reductions and partial performance recovery, with per-subtask gains; final deliverable is a per-field routing map for on-device enrichment rather than a single best model.
AI.motivation: High-volume structured extraction is latency-intensive on large models. Distilling into a small on-device model aims to preserve output quality at lower latency and cost. The study measures distillation effectiveness per sub-task using blinded evaluations and multiple teacher controls.
AI.method: Distill an 8B reasoning teacher (deepseek-r1:8b) into a 0.6B student (Qwen3-0.6B; QLoRA, three seeds). Add two teacher controls: a same-size non-reasoning teacher and a larger managed pipeline. Evaluate via blinded, reference-free, three-judge panel on per-article JSON outputs (summary + five labels) with baselines few-shot prompting and constrained decoding. Use 93-item test set; analyze grounding and routing effects across sub-tasks.
AI.result: Student runs ~0.8 s per article vs teacher 39 s, recovering 58% of the base-to-teacher gap in summary quality. Beats constrained decoding by +16.8 points and few-shot prompting by +4.9. Same-size non-reasoning teacher yields no improvement; reasoning teacher boosts writing quality while managed pipeline boosts label diversity. Grounding differences observed in a small sub-group; results are directional rather than aggregate. Deliverable: a per-field routing map for on-device enrichment across sub-tasks.
AI.conclusion: No single engine dominates across all fields. The practical deliverable is a per-field routing map that guides on-device enrichment, leveraging the reasoning-derived writing quality and the pipeline-derived label diversity. Grounding effects warrant cautious interpretation due to a small subgroup sample.

title: LUMI: Tokenizer-Agnostic LLM-Based Lossless Image Compression
summary: Large language model (LLM)-based lossless image compression methods typically represent pixel data through the native text interface of a pretrained model, converting pixel values into token sequences that the LLM processes through its vocabulary head. This design shows that pretrained language models can provide probability estimates for image coding, but it also couples compression to tokenizer behavior, vocabulary-specific numeric tokens, and model-family-specific adaptation. In this paper, we present LUMI (LLM-based Unified Model-agnostic lossless Image compression), a tokenizer-agnostic framework for lossless RGB image compression with frozen LLM backbones. LUMI replaces pixel-as-text tokenization with a pixel embedding module that maps raw intensity and channel information into the continuous embedding space of the LLM. It further introduces intra-patch position encoding to retain two-dimensional spatial structure after flattening, and uses a 256-way prediction head to produce probabilities over the native pixel alphabet. Only the pixel embedding, position encoding, soft-prefix parameters, and prediction head are trained, while the LLM backbone remains fixed. Experiments on natural, medical, and remote-sensing image benchmarks with LLaMA, Qwen, and Gemma backbones show that LUMI provides a unified interface across tokenizer families, achieves competitive compression rates, and improves cross-domain robustness over tokenizer-based LLM compression baselines. These results formulate LLM-based lossless image compression as pixel-space adaptation of frozen foundation models rather than tokenizer-specific language-symbol modeling.

AI.tldr: A tokenizer-agnostic, LLM-based lossless image compression framework (LUMI) that maps pixel data into a frozen LLM's embedding space via a trainable pixel embedding module, intra-patch position encoding, and a 256-way pixel predictor; shows competitive rates and cross-domain robustness across backbones (LLaMA, Qwen, Gemma).
AI.motivation: Tokenization-dependent LLM-based image compression ties performance to tokenizer vocabularies and model families. A tokenizer-agnostic approach using frozen backbones aims to unify performance across tokenizer families and improve cross-domain robustness.
AI.method: Introduce a pixel embedding module that converts raw RGB intensities into the LLM embedding space; apply intra-patch position encoding to preserve 2D spatial structure after flattening; use a 256-way predictor to output probabilities over the native pixel alphabet; train only the pixel embedding, position encoding, soft-prefix parameters, and the prediction head while keeping the LLM backbone frozen.
AI.result: Experiments on natural, medical, and remote-sensing image benchmarks using LLaMA, Qwen, and Gemma backbones show LUMI provides a tokenizer-family–agnostic interface, achieves competitive compression rates, and improves cross-domain robustness relative to tokenizer-based LLM compression baselines.
AI.conclusion: Frames LLM-based lossless image compression as pixel-space adaptation of frozen foundation models rather than tokenizer-symbol modeling, enabling a unified, tokenizer-agnostic approach.

title: Evaluating the Generalizability of Foundation Models for Extreme Environmental Events: Case Study of California Wildfire PM2.5
summary: Wildfire smoke events produce extreme PM$_{2.5}$ concentrations that pose severe public health risks, yet forecasting rare, hazardous-level spikes remains a fundamental challenge. Time series foundation models (TSFMs), pretrained models offering zero-shot inference and efficient adaptation, perform strongly on general benchmarks, but their behavior under extreme out-of-distribution conditions is poorly understood. We present the first systematic benchmark comparing six TSFM configurations (zero-shot TimesFM, Chronos-2, Moirai-2, and Time-MoE, plus LoRA fine-tuned Chronos-2 and Time-MoE) against fully-trained baselines (LSTM, BiLSTM, Transformer) and naive persistence on a 12-year (2013--2025) hourly PM$_{2.5}$ dataset covering 1,375 wildfire incidents across 79 California monitoring sites. A leave-one-incident-out (LOIO) protocol evaluates generalization to unseen fires, using MAE, RMSE, and exceedance F1 at EPA AQI thresholds across 6-, 12-, and 24-hour horizons. Results reveal a consistent hierarchy. The BiLSTM achieves the lowest MAE ($5.16\,μg/m^3$) and the highest exceedance F1 at every threshold, including the Hazardous band ($>225.5\,μg/m^3$), reaching 0.63 versus at most 0.54 for any foundation model. Zero-shot TSFMs improve on persistence only modestly, and zero-shot Chronos-2 exhibits severe RMSE tail instability ($23.4\,μg/m^3$, negative $R^2$) from sporadic large errors. LoRA fine-tuning substantially improves both adapted families and largely repairs this instability, yet no foundation model surpasses the trained recurrent baselines on any metric. These findings challenge the assumption that larger pretrained models universally dominate environmental forecasting and provide actionable deployment guidance for wildfire air quality prediction.

AI.tldr: Foundation models do not outperform trained recurrent baselines for wildfire-related hourly PM2.5 forecasting; zero-shot TSFMs provide limited gains and can exhibit instability; LoRA helps but no TSFM surpasses LSTM/BiLSTM/Transformer, challenging the assumption that bigger pretrained models always win in environmental forecasting.
AI.motivation: Assess how time-series foundation models (TSFMs) behave under extreme out-of-distribution conditions (wildfire-driven PM2.5 spikes) and compare them against traditional trained baselines using a rigorous leave-one-incident-out benchmark.
AI.method: 12-year hourly PM2.5 dataset (2013–2025), 1,375 wildfire incidents across 79 California sites; compare six TSFM configurations (zero-shot TimesFM, Chronos-2, Moirai-2, Time-MoE; LoRA-finetuned Chronos-2 and Time-MoE) against LSTM, BiLSTM, Transformer, and persistence; LOIO protocol; evaluate 6-, 12-, 24-hour horizons; metrics MAE, RMSE, and exceedance F1 at EPA AQI thresholds.
AI.result: BiLSTM achieved the lowest MAE (5.16 μg/m^3) and highest exceedance F1 across all thresholds, including Hazardous (>225.5 μg/m^3) at 0.63; zero-shot TSFMs improved only modestly over persistence; zero-shot Chronos-2 exhibited severe RMSE tail instability (23.4 μg/m^3, negative R^2) due to sporadic large errors; LoRA fine-tuning substantially improved both adapted TSFM families and largely repaired instability, yet no foundation model surpassed trained recurrent baselines on any metric.
AI.conclusion: Larger pretrained TSFMs do not universally dominate environmental forecasting in this setting; practical deployment should favor trained recurrent baselines. LoRA helps mitigate instability and improve adaptation, but careful evaluation indicates limited advantage of base foundation models for extreme wildfire-related PM2.5 forecasting.

title: PolyUQuest: Verifiable Structure-Aware Web RAG over Heterogeneous Graphs
summary: Existing retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems treat web pages as flat text, losing the structural and semantic signals encoded in HTML. We present PolyUQuest, a verifiable, structure-aware web RAG framework built on a heterogeneous graph that unifies hyperlink topology between pages, DOM hierarchy within pages, and entity-relation knowledge across pages. A two-tier router dispatches each query to one of three retrieval modes matched to its structural need, including direct block retrieval, cross-page graph traversal, and multi-hop entity reasoning. Every answer is fully verifiable, as each cited block carries its source page, heading path, and entity links so that users can trace any claim back to its structural evidence. We evaluate on the official websites of the Hong Kong Polytechnic University (PolyU), comprising 4,240 pages, 31,086 DOM blocks, 29,119 entities, and 37,680 relations, together with a multi-type evaluation benchmark. PolyUQuest outperforms existing RAG systems in answer correctness, coverage, and faithfulness, while consuming significantly fewer LLM tokens per query. The demonstration provides an interactive interface for inspecting cited answers, comparing retrieval traces across routing modes, and exploring evidence graph paths. PolyUQuest is being prepared for deployment as a student-facing QA service at PolyU.

AI.tldr: PolyUQuest offers a structure-aware web RAG using a heterogeneous graph to preserve DOM, hyperlinks, and entity relations, with verifiable citations and a tri-mode retrieval strategy; it shows improved correctness, coverage, faithfulness, and efficiency on PolyU site data.
AI.motivation: Conventional RAG treats web content as plain text, losing structural/semantic cues encoded in HTML, hindering faithfulness and verifiability.
AI.method: Construct a heterogeneous graph combining hyperlink topology across pages, DOM hierarchy within pages, and cross-page entity-relations. Implement a two-tier router dispatching queries to three retrieval modes: direct block retrieval, cross-page graph traversal, and multi-hop entity reasoning. Ensure verifiability by attaching source path, heading, and entity links to each cited block.
AI.result: On PolyU's official website (4,240 pages; 31,086 DOM blocks; 29,119 entities; 37,680 relations) plus a multi-type benchmark, PolyUQuest outperforms existing RAG systems in answer correctness, coverage, and faithfulness, while reducing LLM token usage per query.
AI.conclusion: PolyUQuest delivers verifiable, structure-aware web QA via a graph-based retrieval framework; demonstrated interface and ready for deployment as a student-facing QA service at PolyU.

title: INTENT: An LSTM Framework for Vehicle Intention Prediction in Intersection Scenarios with Comprehensive Ablation Analysis
summary: Vehicle intention prediction is a pivotal aspect in the agility and safety of autonomous vehicles in all driving scenarios; if genuine enhancement of autonomous vehicles are required, we need to make them adopt human interpretation of driver's intention especially in cases that require a lot of human interaction as well as complex driving behaviors like the ones at intersections, roundabouts and emergency cases such as sudden stops where vehicle intention prediction helps in taking the correct evasive action within a real time period where every second of action makes an impact and can prevent a catastrophe from taking place. In the worst case, it helps minimize the damage and make safety a priority. Intention prediction can also be used to enhance trajectory prediction (intention conditioned trajectory prediction). In this study, The INTENT framework is proposed using LSTM model to predict the vehicle's intention at intersections 2 seconds ahead of the event occurrence to predict whether the cars in intersections are going straight, turning left, or turning right. Various model experiments and ablation study are thoroughly tested on InD dataset achieving 99.71% accuracy.

AI.tldr: LSTM-based INTENT framework predicts vehicle intent 2 seconds ahead at intersections (straight/left/right); 99.71% accuracy on InD.
AI.motivation: Enhance autonomous driving safety by anticipating other road users' intentions in high-interaction/intersection scenarios to enable timely evasive actions and more accurate trajectory planning.
AI.method: LSTM model trained to classify intended maneuvers; includes intention-conditioned trajectory prediction; conducts ablation studies and extensive experiments on the InD dataset.
AI.result: Achieves 99.71% accuracy on predicting intersection maneuvers, with ablation results supporting the effectiveness of the approach.
AI.conclusion: INTENT framework demonstrates promise for real-time intention-aware planning and improved safety, with potential integration into trajectory prediction pipelines.

title: Multimodal 3D LUT Generation via StatLUT with Statistical Features for Photorealistic Style Transfer
summary: Photorealistic Style Transfer (PST) aims to transfer the color and tonal style of a reference to a content image while strictly preserving its structural integrity. However, existing deep learning-based methods inherently suffer from semantic entanglement caused by pre-trained image encoders, leading to unnatural spatial distortions. Moreover, current pixel-level mapping paradigms often ignore color gamut topology, resulting in color banding, while also lacking the multimodal capability for intuitive text-driven control. To address these bottlenecks, we propose StatLUT, an innovative multimodal framework for 3D LUT generation. First, we bypass traditional encoders and introduce a Lab-Extractor to derive spatially-agnostic statistical features, fundamentally decoupling color distributions from structural semantics to ensure artifact-free rendering. Second, we formulate LUT generation as a Transformer-based Seq2Seq translation task, utilizing a Multi-dimensional Residual Mapper (MR-Mapper) to predict topologically smooth 3D LUTs. Finally, to break the single-modal barrier, we propose the H-Diffuser, a lightweight Diffusion Transformer that directly synthesizes statistical features from natural language prompts, enabling flexible text-driven color grading. Extensive experiments on standard benchmarks demonstrate that StatLUT significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods in both visual quality and quantitative metrics, pioneering a highly robust and flexible paradigm for multimodal photorealistic style transfer.

AI.tldr: StatLUT introduces an encoder-free, multimodal workflow for photorealistic style transfer: a Lab-Extractor for color-structure decoupling, a Transformer-based LUT generator with MR-Mapper for smooth 3D LUTs, and H-Diffuser for text-driven color grading, claiming superior visual quality and multimodal control.
AI.motivation: Address semantic entanglement from pre-trained encoders, color gamut artifacts such as banding, and lack of multimodal (text-driven) control in existing PST methods.
AI.method: 1) Lab-Extractor to derive spatially-agnostic statistical color features, decoupling color distributions from structure. 2) Transformer-based Seq2Seq LUT generation with MR-Mapper to predict topologically smooth 3D LUTs. 3) H-Diffuser, a lightweight Diffusion Transformer, to synthesize statistical features from natural language prompts for text-driven grading.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on standard benchmarks show StatLUT significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods in visual quality and quantitative metrics, demonstrating robustness and flexibility for multimodal PST.
AI.conclusion: Proposes a novel encoder-free, multimodal PST framework that decouples color statistics from structure and enables natural language-driven color grading with high fidelity.

title: Linear Attention Architectures: Mechanisms, Trade-offs, and Cross-Layer Routing
comment: 20 pages, 6 figures, 8 tables. Code available at https://github.com/tommasocerruti/linear-attention-architectures
summary: Self-attention lets each token retrieve information from the full context, but its quadratic cost in sequence length limits training and inference at long context. This paper presents a comparative study of softmax attention and four recent recurrent linear-attention architectures: DeltaNet, Gated DeltaNet, Kimi Delta Attention, and Gated DeltaNet-2. We express these mechanisms in a common recurrent-memory notation, making explicit how they differ in expressivity, memory decay, erase and write control, training throughput, and implementation complexity. Our experiments center on 350M-parameter models trained for 15B tokens, and include optimizer and learning-rate comparisons, hybrid-versus-pure stack comparisons, sequence-length runtime measurements, larger DeltaNet runs at 1.3B and 3B parameters, and a small set of downstream evaluations. The reported speed results measure training throughput and iteration time; we do not provide an empirical inference-speed benchmark. Within the reported 350M-parameter, 15B-token sweep, Kimi Delta Attention with Muon reaches the lowest final validation loss, a pure Gated DeltaNet stack trained with AdamW has the highest normalized training throughput, hybrid stacks generally improve loss at a throughput cost, and Muon consistently lowers final validation loss relative to AdamW in the matched architecture settings we evaluate. We introduce and evaluate lightweight cross-layer routing mechanisms for DeltaNet-style memories. The most natural DeltaNet-inspired formulation, forwarding a lower layer's delta-rule write error into the next layer's value target, does not improve over matched baselines. Routing into the aligned hidden stream and forwarding the write value instead yields a modest improvement in the matched runs we report: Cross-Layer Value Routing (CLVR) lowers final validation loss for both DeltaNet and Gated DeltaNet.

AI.tldr: Comparative study of softmax attention vs four recurrent linear-attention architectures (DeltaNet, Gated DeltaNet, Kimi Delta Attention, Gated DeltaNet-2) expressed in a common memory formalism. Evaluates training-time performance, expressivity, memory control, and routing mechanisms for 350M-parameter models trained to 15B tokens, with larger runs and downstream checks. Key findings: Kimi Delta Attention with Muon achieves lowest final validation loss; pure Gated DeltaNet with AdamW yields highest training throughput; cross-layer routing (CLVR) provides modest gains; no empirical inference-speed benchmarks reported.
AI.motivation: Address the quadratic cost of self-attention by evaluating recurrent linear-attention alternatives within a unified memory framework. Clarify expressivity, memory decay, erase/write control, training throughput, and implementation complexity to guide scalable long-context modeling.
AI.method: Express all mechanisms in a common recurrent-memory notation. Conduct extensive training experiments on 350M-parameter models trained for 15B tokens, comparing optimizers (e.g., AdamW, Muon), hybrid vs pure stacks, and sequence-length runtimes. Extend experiments to larger DeltaNet sizes (1.3B, 3B parameters) and perform downstream evaluations. Introduce lightweight cross-layer routing for DeltaNet-style memories, including Cross-Layer Value Routing (CLVR).
AI.result: No empirical inference-speed benchmark reported. In 350M-parameter, 15B-token sweep: Kimi Delta Attention with Muon achieves the lowest final validation loss; pure Gated DeltaNet with AdamW yields the highest normalized training throughput; hybrid stacks trade some loss improvements for throughput costs; Muon generally lowers final validation loss relative to AdamW in matched settings. CLVR routing lowers final validation loss for both DeltaNet and Gated DeltaNet; the most natural DeltaNet formulation (forwarding a lower layer’s delta-rule write error) does not improve over baselines, while routing into the aligned hidden stream and forwarding the write value yields modest gains.
AI.conclusion: DeltaNet-family recurrent memory architectures can attain competitive training efficiency and validation performance relative to softmax attention within a unified framework. Architectures and optimizer choices drive distinct trade-offs between throughput and accuracy. Lightweight cross-layer routing (CLVR) provides modest but consistent gains, suggesting potential for scalable long-context modeling with DeltaNet variants. Inference-speed benchmarks remain unreported and should be addressed in future work.

title: Understanding Axes of Difficulty For Long Context Tasks Via PredicateLongBench
summary: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated rapidly improving long-context capabilities, prompting a wave of benchmarks designed to evaluate them. However, existing long-context evaluations - from Needle-in-a-Haystack (NIAH) tests to more recent multi-hop reasoning and summarization tasks - predominantly measure average-case performance, and many are either saturated or lack robustness. Notably absent is a systematic way to probe how models perform as we scale up the difficulty of tasks along various axes. We address this gap by proposing PredicateLongBench, a benchmark that stress-tests long-context reasoning by asking models to identify the longest contiguous subsequence of words in a long input that satisfies given predicates/constraints (e.g., lexicographic ordering), drawn from a broader predicate class. The central innovation of our benchmark is the identification and systematic exploration of multiple different axes of difficulty which test multiple aspects of long context understanding. We provide two complementary generation pipelines - a fully synthetic setup using random word-like strings, and a real-world setup that samples words from natural documents while preserving their distributional properties. We find that frontier models struggle to perform well as we scale up the difficulty of tasks along our axes, demonstrating the utility of our benchmark in understanding the limitations of current long-context capabilities. Furthermore, the tasks in PredicateLongBench, though challenging, are conceptually simple and do not require LLM-based generations or judges.

AI.tldr: PredicateLongBench is a benchmark that stress-tests long-context reasoning by finding the longest contiguous subsequence in a long input that satisfies given predicates, with synthetic and real-world generation pipelines; frontier models degrade as task difficulty scales across multiple axes.
AI.motivation: Current long-context benchmarks largely measure average-case performance and often saturate or lack robustness. There is no systematic way to probe model behavior as task difficulty increases along multiple axes of long-context understanding.
AI.method: Defines a predicate-based subsequence task. Two data-generation pipelines are used: (1) fully synthetic random word-like strings and (2) real-world text sampled from natural documents while preserving distributional properties. Multiple axes of difficulty are identified and explored to stress-test long-context reasoning.
AI.result: Frontier models struggle to maintain performance as task difficulty scales along the proposed axes, demonstrating the benchmark's utility in diagnosing long-context limitations. The tasks are conceptually simple and do not require LLM-based generation or judges.
AI.conclusion: PredicateLongBench provides a systematic, multi-axis stress test for long-context reasoning, enabling clearer diagnosis of current LLM limits and guiding future improvements while using simple, non-generative tasks.

title: Swapping Faces, Saving Features: A Dual-Purpose Pipeline for Pedestrian Privacy in ITS
summary: Large-scale and diverse datasets are needed to train AI models to take real-time decisions for autonomous vehicles (AVs), an intelligent transportation system (ITS) application. Pedestrian intention and trajectory prediction are critical models used in AVs, requiring datasets involving diverse pedestrian images. Unrestricted access to these datasets imposes serious security risks, like identity theft and pedestrian tracking. The challenge is to apply privacy preservation procedures while maintaining the image attributes needed to train the models. Existing privacy methods may preserve the pedestrian's privacy, but degrade the image usability, which hinders the models' effectiveness. This work's focus is to implement a five-stage pipeline to protect pedestrians' privacy through face swapping while keeping the essential facial attributes intact. It should be tailored to satisfy the privacy needs of the Egy-DRiVeS dataset. Moreover, Roop and Ghost-v2 face-swapping models are evaluated. Provenly, Roop outperforms Ghost-v2 in various aspects, as will be discussed. Consequently, Roop is the face-swapping model to be used in the pipeline to strike the balance between pedestrian privacy via identity concealment and data usability via facial attribute preservation.

AI.tldr: A five-stage privacy-preserving pipeline for AV pedestrian datasets using face-swapping to conceal identity while preserving facial attributes; Roop outperforms Ghost-v2 and is selected for Egy-DRiVeS implementation.
AI.motivation: To enable large-scale, diverse AV datasets while mitigating privacy risks such as identity theft and pedestrian tracking; preserve image attributes necessary for training pedestrian intention and trajectory models.
AI.method: Develop a five-stage face-swapping pipeline tailored to the Egy-DRiVeS dataset; compare Roop and Ghost-v2 on privacy and attribute preservation; select Roop based on empirical performance for deployment.
AI.result: Roop outperforms Ghost-v2 in multiple aspects, leading to its selection as the face-swapping component of the pipeline for privacy protection and data usability.
AI.conclusion: Roop is the recommended face-swapping model for the proposed privacy-preserving pipeline, balancing pedestrian identity concealment with retention of essential facial attributes in Egy-DRiVeS.

title: TVTA: Trajectory-Aware Viseme-Guided Temporal Aggregation for Event-Based Lip Reading
summary: Event-based lip reading has recently emerged as a promising direction for visual speech recognition, benefiting from the high temporal resolution and motion sensitivity of event cameras. However, existing methods typically perform spatial compression before sufficient temporal modeling, which may suppress sparse and localized motion trajectories that are crucial for distinguishing similar lip movements. Moreover, most current approaches optimize temporal representations mainly at the word-classification level, leaving the underlying articulatory structure weakly constrained. To address these limitations, we propose a temporally enhanced framework for event-based lip reading. First, we introduce Trajectory-Aware Differential Aggregation (TDA), which performs local temporal modeling at each spatial location before adaptive spatial aggregation. Second, we propose Viseme-Guided Aggregation (VGA), a unified temporal module composed of a CTC decoder and a viseme-guided gated aggregation branch, which injects viseme-aware sequence supervision and improves final temporal aggregation for word recognition. Third, we incorporate an EMA teacher--student training strategy to enhance robustness under strong event perturbations. Experiments on the DVS-Lip benchmark verify the effectiveness of the proposed design, and extensive ablation studies further validate the contributions of TDA, VGA, and teacher--student consistency. Qualitative decoding results also demonstrate that the proposed CTC-based temporal modeling learns meaningful viseme-aware structure from event streams.

AI.tldr: Introduces Trajectory-Aware Differential Aggregation (TDA) and Viseme-Guided Aggregation (VGA) for event-based lip reading, coupled with EMA teacher–student learning, yielding improved temporal modeling and viseme-aware supervision validated on the DVS-Lip dataset.
AI.motivation: Address the limitations of spatial compression before temporal modeling and weak articulatory supervision in existing event-based lip reading methods by enabling local temporal modeling and viseme-guided sequence constraints.
AI.method: TDA performs local temporal modeling at each spatial location prior to adaptive spatial aggregation. VGA combines a CTC decoder with a viseme-guided gated aggregation branch to inject viseme-aware supervision into temporal aggregation for word recognition. An EMA teacher–student framework is employed to improve robustness under event perturbations.
AI.result: On the DVS-Lip benchmark, the proposed design improves performance. Extensive ablations confirm the contributions of TDA, VGA, and teacher–student consistency. Qualitative decoding results show that the learned temporal modeling captures meaningful viseme-aware structure from event streams.
AI.conclusion: The framework advances event-based lip reading by introducing per-location temporal modeling and viseme-informed aggregation, enhanced by self-regularization through teacher–student training, achieving robust, viseme-aligned temporal representations for word recognition.

title: KronQ: LLM Quantization via Kronecker-Factored Hessian
summary: Post-training quantization (PTQ) is a widely adopted technique for compressing large language models (LLMs) without retraining. Existing second-order PTQ methods, including GPTQ, construct quantization objectives exclusively from input activation statistics, effectively assuming that all output channels contribute equally to the layer-wise reconstruction objective. We propose KronQ, a PTQ framework that challenges this assumption by introducing the gradient covariance into the quantization pipeline. Under the Kronecker-factored Hessian approximation, the quantization loss depends jointly on both the activation and gradient covariances, and KronQ exploits this at two complementary levels. (1) KronQ introduces bidirectional incoherence processing, extending the existing input-side random rotation to the output dimension using the gradient covariance, reducing weight magnitude variance across both input and output dimensions. (2) KronQ derives a new sensitivity metric for inter-layer mixed-precision allocation, driven by the gradient and activation Hessian traces. Notably, in the case of 2-bit weight-only quantization on LLaMA-3-70B, while GPTQ and GPTAQ diverge or produce degenerate quantizations (>2000 perplexity on WikiText-2), KronQ achieves 7.93 perplexity.

AI.tldr: KronQ adds gradient covariance into post-training quantization (PTQ) using a Kronecker-factored Hessian, enabling joint activation-gradient loss and two-stage quantization enhancements: bidirectional incoherence (input/output) and a gradient-activation-based inter-layer sensitivity metric for mixed-precision. It yields robust 2-bit weight-only quantization on LLaMA-3-70B (WikiText-2 perplexity 7.93) where baselines fail.
AI.motivation: Second-order PTQ methods (e.g., GPTQ) rely solely on input activation statistics and assume equal output-channel contribution, which can misalign the reconstruction objective with actual layer behavior.
AI.method: Under Kronecker-factored Hessian, the quantization loss is a function of joint activation and gradient covariances. KronQ introduces (1) bidirectional incoherence processing by extending input-space random rotation to the output dimension using gradient covariance, reducing weight-magnitude variance across input and output; (2) a new inter-layer mixed-precision sensitivity metric derived from gradient and activation Hessian traces for allocation decisions.
AI.result: For 2-bit weight-only quantization on LLaMA-3-70B, GPTQ and GPTAQ diverge or yield degenerate quantizations (>2000 perplexity on WikiText-2), while KronQ achieves 7.93 perplexity.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating gradient information via a Kronecker-factored Hessian improves PTQ performance by aligning the quantization objective with both activation and gradient statistics, with a robust low-bit option demonstrated; further validation across models and datasets is warranted.

title: Psychological Competence as a Missing Dimension in AI Evaluation
summary: Current AI evaluation frameworks focus primarily on technical performance, including accuracy, robustness, reasoning ability, and policy compliance. These measures remain essential, but they are not sufficient for systems that interact directly with users through natural language. Human-facing AI systems are increasingly used as advisors, coaches, tutors, and companions. In these roles, their responses can shape how users reason, interpret emotions, form beliefs, calibrate trust, and make decisions. The relevant unit of evaluation is therefore not only the model, but the human-AI interaction. This paper introduces psychological competence as a missing dimension in AI evaluation. We define psychological competence as the capacity of a human-facing AI system to support user cognition, emotional interpretation, and behavioral decision-making in ways that are appropriate to the user, context, and purpose of the interaction. This includes interaction properties such as framing, tone, perceived authority, responsiveness, uncertainty handling, and conversational guidance. Existing evaluation approaches capture parts of this problem but rarely assess these psychological effects directly. Drawing on behavioral science and human-AI interaction research, we outline a conceptual framework for psychological competence and its core domains. Rather than proposing a specific benchmark, we define the construct, clarify its boundaries, and describe how it may be assessed through scenario-based probes, structured human evaluation, and model-assisted evaluation methods. We argue that psychological competence should become a core consideration for model providers, deploying organizations, researchers, and regulators concerned with the real-world effects of human-facing AI systems.

AI.tldr: Proposes psychological competence as a missing dimension in evaluating human-facing AI, outlining a conceptual framework and assessment methods to capture how AI affects user cognition, emotion, and decisions.
AI.motivation: Current AI evaluation emphasizes technical metrics; for user-facing systems, interactions shape reasoning, emotion interpretation, trust, and decisions. A framework is needed to assess these effects for real-world use and regulation.
AI.method: Develop a conceptual framework; define the construct and boundaries; identify core domains; propose assessment approaches: scenario-based probes, structured human evaluation, and model-assisted evaluation; grounding in behavioral science and human-AI interaction research; no specific benchmark.
AI.result: Outlines the core domains of psychological competence and concrete assessment avenues, providing a roadmap for implementation and further benchmarking by stakeholders.
AI.conclusion: Psychological competence should be integral for model providers, deployers, researchers, and regulators to address real-world human-AI impact.

title: Latent Memory Palace: Reasoning for Control as Autoregressive Variational Inference
summary: Human decision-making is highly flexible -- some actions are taken immediately; others require longer deliberation. Language models have exhibited a similar capacity for adaptive "reasoning." However, transferring this capability to continuous control policies has been challenging, as directly reasoning in language space may lack the granularity for spatial understanding and precise motions. In this work, we show that reasoning for control policies can emerge by organizing information in an autoregressive latent space reminiscent of a memory palace, where retrieval is iterative and adaptive. Our method, Latent Memory Palace (LMP), formulates reasoning as variational inference with an autoregressive latent distribution. We derive a latent-space reinforcement learning technique to tractably optimize its variational lower bound. The resulting policy, LMP-$π$, achieves strong empirical performance in simulation and real-world domains while exhibiting interpretable, adaptive allocation of test-time compute. We further show that the same framework yields a variable-length action tokenizer, LMP-$\texttt{tok}$, which significantly improves the performance of downstream autoregressive policies. Together, these results present a new perspective on latent reasoning for control through the lens of variational inference.

AI.tldr: Latent Memory Palace (LMP) enables latent, iterative reasoning for continuous control by organizing information in an autoregressive latent space, trained via variational inference. It yields LMP-π for control and LMP-tok as a variable-length action tokenizer, with strong simulation and real-world performance and interpretable compute.
AI.motivation: Bridge the gap between language-model-like reasoning and continuous control policies. Direct reasoning in action space lacks spatial granularity and precise motion control; an autoregressive latent, memory-palace-inspired representation allows adaptive, iterative retrieval and planning for control.
AI.method: Formulate LMP as variational inference over an autoregressive latent distribution. Derive a latent-space reinforcement learning objective to tractably optimize the variational lower bound. Develop LMP-π policy and LMP-tok tokenization for variable-length actions within the same framework.
AI.result: Empirical results show strong performance in both simulation and real-world domains. The method offers interpretable, adaptive allocation of test-time compute and improves downstream autoregressive policies via the variable-length tokenizer.
AI.conclusion: Latent reasoning for control can be realized through an autoregressive latent memory-palace framework optimized via variational inference, providing new insights for efficient, interpretable decision-making and improved policy performance.

title: Closing the Null Space: Guidance-Aware Quantization for Classifier-Free Diffusion
summary: Deploying classifier-free guidance (CFG) diffusion models under real-world compute budgets requires quantization, yet existing post-training quantization (PTQ) methods treat CFG models as single-branch networks, ignoring the paired conditional/unconditional structure that CFG inference fundamentally relies on. This structural blind spot has two consequences. At the system level, the two-pass CFG execution pattern imposes a latency overhead that parameter-count and bit-operation metrics conceal entirely, and commodity INT8 inference stacks fail to realize the theoretical efficiency gains that BOPs calculations promise. At the algorithmic level, calibrating against the guidance gap alone admits an exact null space: a quantized model can achieve perfect gap-fidelity diagnostics while the unconditional branch drifts arbitrarily, corrupting every guided prediction at inference time. This paper terms this the branch-drift trap, proves its existence analytically, and confirms it empirically through a false-positive result in which the best-calibrated model by standard diagnostics simultaneously produces the worst sample quality. To close the trap, Guidance-Aware Mixed Precision (GAMP) is proposed, which calibrates directly on the guided prediction, derives per-layer activation-bit sensitivity from guided-output degradation, and allocates bits via a greedy knapsack -- provably preventing unconditional branch drift by construction.

AI.tldr: Identifies a branch-drift trap in post-training quantization of classifier-free guidance (CFG) diffusion models and proposes Guidance-Aware Mixed Precision (GAMP) to quantize guided predictions directly, preventing unconditional drift and improving real-world efficiency.
AI.motivation: CFG diffusion models rely on a two-branch conditional/unconditional inference; PTQ that treats CFG as a single-branch network misses structural dependencies, causing latency overhead and ineffective bit-precision gains. Calibrating on guidance gaps can yield drift in the unconditional branch, corrupting guided outputs.
AI.method: Proves analytically the existence of a branch-drift trap; empirically demonstrates a false-positive where standard guidance-gap calibration yields the worst samples. Introduces GAMP that (1) calibrates on guided predictions, (2) derives per-layer activation-bit sensitivity from guided-output degradation, and (3) uses a greedy knapsack to allocate mixed-precision bits, thereby preventing unconditional drift.
AI.result: The branch-drift trap is theoretically and empirically validated. GAMP is proposed as a calibration-and-allocation scheme that preserves guided predictions under quantization and closes the trap.
AI.conclusion: GAMP provides a principled, provable method to quantize CFG diffusion models under practical compute budgets, eliminating unconditional drift and delivering reliable guided generation with mixed-precision allocation.

title: Provably Optimal Learning Algorithms for Assistance Games
summary: This paper studies an online variant of the assistance games framework, where an informed agent and an uninformed agent repeatedly interact over $T$ timesteps to optimize a common reward function. While the informed agent (the human) observes a latent state of the world, the uninformed agent (the assistant) observes only the human's actions. We provide the first provably efficient learning algorithms for repeated assistance games. We introduce the notion of assistance regret: the gap between the cumulative utility of interactions and that of the optimal joint policies in hindsight, which map latent states to action pairs. We present decentralized algorithms for both the human and the assistant that achieve a $(1-1/e)$-approximate assistance regret rate of $\widetilde{O}(T^{3/4})$, with runtime polynomial in the size of the action and state spaces. These algorithms are general; in particular, they accommodate any no-regret algorithm for the assistant.
