We prove that achieving a regret approximation factor better than $(1-1/e)$ is computationally intractable. Furthermore, we demonstrate how these generic no-regret algorithms can be tailored to a pseudo-decentralized setting -- using a shared random string -- to achieve a rate of $\widetilde{O}(T^{1/2})$, optimal up to logarithmic factors.

AI.tldr: Online, repeated assistance games with latent world state; defines assistance regret and shows decentralized no-regret algorithms achieve (1-1/e)-approximation with O(T^{3/4}) regret, polynomial runtime; computational hardness prevents better than (1-1/e); pseudo-decentralized variant with shared randomness attains O(T^{1/2}) regret (up to log factors).
AI.motivation: Enable provably efficient learning of cooperative policies when only the human observes latent state; define a meaningful regret metric (assistance regret) and design algorithms that are scalable and robust.
AI.method: Introduce the notion of assistance regret relative to hindsight-optimal joint policies mapping latent states to action pairs; develop decentralized no-regret algorithms for both human and assistant; prove (1-1/e) approximation with O(T^{3/4}) regret and polynomial runtime; establish computational intractability for better-than-(1-1/e) guarantees; adapt to a pseudo-decentralized setting using a shared random string to achieve O(T^{1/2}) regret.
AI.result: Decentralized algorithms achieve ~O(T^{3/4}) regret with (1-1/e) approximation; polynomial-time implementation; no-regret framework compatible with any no-regret algorithm for the assistant; hardness result rules out better factor; pseudo-decentralized variant reaches ~O(T^{1/2}) regret up to logarithmic factors.
AI.conclusion: The work presents a general, efficient framework for online assistance with latent states, balancing regret, computation, and coordination; demonstrates fundamental limits and a path to near-optimal performance via shared randomness, inviting further refinement and specialization.

title: SkelGen4D: Weakly-Supervised Skeleton-Based 4D Generation for Text-Driven Mesh Animation
summary: We study 4D generation to synthesize temporally coherent sequences of 3D geometry for animation and content creation. In contrast to existing SDS-based optimization methods and video-driven animation approaches, we adopt a skeleton-driven animation framework aligned with standard industrial pipelines, which enables explicit control and editing. To this end, we propose SkelGen4D, a weakly supervised feed-forward framework for text-driven mesh animation that generates explicit skeleton motions without requiring per-frame skeleton annotations. SkelGen4D first recovers temporally consistent pseudo-skeletons from animated meshes via differentiable fitting, and then generates text-conditioned skeleton motion sequences in a feed-forward manner, further refined with Motion-GRPO to ensure temporally coherent, physically plausible, and articulated animation. We evaluate our method on two large-scale benchmarks, Truebones Zoo and Diffusion4D. Our results show that our weakly supervised skeleton modeling matches or surpasses fully supervised baselines while scaling to diverse object categories for high-quality text-driven mesh animation. Further, our method supports flexible motion editing and is aligned with standard animation production pipelines.

AI.tldr: Weakly supervised, feed-forward 4D mesh animation via skeleton-driven control that recovers pseudo-skeletons from animated meshes and generates text-conditioned, temporally coherent skeleton motions refined for realism; integrates with standard pipelines and scales across object categories.
AI.motivation: Existing SDS-based optimization and video-driven approaches offer limited explicit control over skeletons and require per-frame annotations or extensive supervision. A skeleton-centric, production-aligned method with weak supervision can provide explicit, editable control, scalability across categories, and compatibility with industry workflows.
AI.method: SkelGen4D consists of (1) differentiable fitting to recover temporally consistent pseudo-skeletons from animated meshes, (2) a feed-forward network that generates text-conditioned skeleton motion sequences without frame-level skeleton annotations, and (3) Motion-GRPO refinement to enforce temporal coherence, physical plausibility, and articulation. The framework is weakly supervised and designed to align with standard animation pipelines, enabling text-driven mesh animation with editable skeletons.
AI.result: On Truebones Zoo and Diffusion4D benchmarks, SkelGen4D matches or surpasses fully supervised baselines while scaling to diverse object categories. It enables high-quality, text-driven mesh animation with explicit skeleton control and supports flexible motion editing.
AI.conclusion: The approach demonstrates that weakly supervised, skeleton-driven 4D animation can achieve production-ready quality and flexibility, offering explicit control, editability, and pipeline compatibility without requiring per-frame skeleton annotations.

title: Collate: Collaborative Neural Network Learning for Latency-Critical Edge Systems
comment: Author's accepted version. Published in the 2022 IEEE 40th International Conference on Computer Design (ICCD)
summary: Federated Learning (FL) empowers multiple clients to collaboratively learn a model, enlarging the training data of each client for high accuracy while protecting data privacy. However, when deploying FL in real-time edge systems, the heterogeneity of devices among systems has a severe impact on the performance of the inferred model. Existing optimizations on FL focus on improving the training efficiency but fail to speed up inference, especially when there is a latency constraint. In this work, we propose Collate, a novel training framework that collaboratively learns heterogeneous models to meet the latency constraints of multiple edge systems simultaneously. We design a dynamic zeroizing-recovering method to adjust each local model architecture for high accuracy under its latency constraint. A proto-corrected federated aggregation scheme is also introduced to aggregate all heterogeneous local models, satisfying the latency constraint of different systems with only one training process and maintaining high accuracy. Extensive experiments indicate that, compared to state-of-the-art methods and under a latency constraint, our extended models can improve the accuracy by 1.96% on average, and our shrunk models can also obtain a 3.09% accuracy improvement on average, with almost no extra training overhead. The related codes and data will be available at https://github.com/ntuliuteam/Collate

AI.tldr: Collate enables federated learning with heterogeneous edge models by dynamically zeroizing and recovering architectures to meet diverse latency constraints, using proto-corrected aggregation to merge heterogeneous local models in one training run, achieving higher accuracy under latency bounds with minimal training overhead.
AI.motivation: Real-time edge FL suffers from device heterogeneity that degrades inference latency; existing FL optimizations focus on training efficiency and neglect latency-constrained inference across diverse devices.
AI.method: Introduce dynamic zeroizing-recovering to adapt each local model’s architecture to its latency budget; apply proto-corrected federated aggregation to combine heterogeneous models in a single training process while satisfying multiple latency constraints.
AI.result: Under latency constraints, extended models show ~1.96% average accuracy improvement; shrunk models achieve ~3.09% average accuracy improvement, with almost no extra training overhead compared to baselines.
AI.conclusion: Collate demonstrates that simultaneous training of heterogeneous models with latency-aware aggregation can meet diverse edge-system constraints while improving accuracy, and provides data/code resources for replication.

title: Blind-Spots-Bench: Evaluating Blind Spots in Multimodal Models
summary: Modern AI models achieve strong performance on many established benchmarks, yet they still fail on tasks that humans find almost trivial, such as manipulating a string or drawing a dog with five legs. These examples suggest that existing benchmarks may under-measure persistent blind spots in current systems. We introduce $\texttt{blind-spots-bench}$, a benchmark designed to expose such blind spots through tasks that appear simple for humans but remain challenging for modern AI. We collect raw questions from students in an AI course, clean and annotate them with structured reference solutions, and propose a task taxonomy tailored to the resulting dataset of 235 samples. We further develop an automated grading pipeline to evaluate a wide range of models, including open-weight and closed-source language, vision-language, and image-generation models. Our analysis on $\texttt{blind-spots-bench}$ reveals that closed-source frontier models can substantially outperform open-weight models with even $\approx10\%$ gap, even when they attain comparable performance on existing benchmarks. A more fine-grained analysis shows that no single model dominates across all task types, and that some tasks remain challenging for all evaluated models. These results highlight the value of $\texttt{blind-spots-bench}$ as a diagnostic stress test for identifying concrete weaknesses in current modern models.

AI.tldr: Blind-spots-bench: a human-intuition-driven benchmark with 235 tasks exposing AI blind spots; finds open-weight models lag behind closed-source frontier models by ~10% on average; no single model dominates; serves as diagnostic stress test.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks under-measure persistent blind spots; need tasks that are trivial for humans but hard for AI to diagnose model weaknesses.
AI.method: Collect raw questions from an AI course; clean & annotate with structured reference solutions; create a task taxonomy; build an automated grading pipeline; evaluate diverse model families (open-weight, closed-source LMs, vision-language, image-gen).
AI.result: Closed-source frontier models outperform open-weight models by about 10 percentage points; some tasks remain hard for all models; no model dominates across all task types; benchmark useful for diagnosing weaknesses.
AI.conclusion: blind-spots-bench provides diagnostic capability to surface concrete weaknesses beyond existing benchmarks and can guide future model development and evaluation.

title: HSA: Hierarchical Slot Attention for Multi-granularity Scene-Decomposition
summary: Slot attention is a powerful framework for object-centric learning, decomposing visual scenes into latent slots through iterative competitive attention. However, existing methods share two critical limitations: they decompose scenes into a flat set of slots at a single granularity, and this decomposition is based on appearance rather than semantics. Yet humans understand scenes through semantic hierarchies: separating foreground from background, recognizing object categories, and identifying individual instances. Crucially, such semantic hierarchies cannot emerge without supervision, because category names are human constructs, not visual patterns. We propose Hierarchical Slot Attention (HSA), which learns multi-granularity semantic scene decomposition from a single model. HSA decomposes scenes at three levels: holistic (foreground/background), semantic (object categories), and panoptic (individual instances). Using only 10\% labeled data, combined with hierarchical alignment loss, HSA learns all three levels jointly. We further introduce grouping purity and containment to measure whether the hierarchy is encoded in representation space, not just output masks. Experiments on COCO and PASCAL VOC demonstrate that HSA outperforms the strongest flat baseline by up to \textbf{$+$41.5} ARI at holistic, \textbf{$+$14.6} at semantic, and \textbf{$+$10.4} at panoptic level on COCO, with even larger gains on Pascal VOC, while requiring a single model instead of three. Code will be made available upon acceptance.

AI.tldr: Hierarchical Slot Attention (HSA) learns multi-granularity semantic scene decomposition (holistic, semantic, panoptic) with a single model using limited supervision (10% labels), via a hierarchical alignment loss, outperforming flat slot attention baselines on COCO and PASCAL VOC.
AI.motivation: Existing slot attention models produce flat, appearance-based scene decompositions and do not capture semantic hierarchies. Humans reason through semantic layers (foreground/background, object categories, instances), but such hierarchies typically require supervision. The paper aims to enable unsupervised-like discovery of semantic structure by leveraging a small amount of labeled data to guide a unified hierarchical model.
AI.method: Extend slot attention to three hierarchical levels: holistic (foreground/background), semantic (object categories), and panoptic (individual instances). Use a hierarchical alignment loss to align representations across levels and co-train with limited labels (10%). Evaluate using alignment-aware metrics and introduce grouping purity and containment to assess whether hierarchy is encoded in representation space, not just outputs.
AI.result: On COCO and PASCAL VOC, HSA outperforms the strongest flat baseline by up to +41.5 ARI at the holistic level, +14.6 ARI at the semantic level, and +10.4 ARI at the panoptic level on COCO, with even larger gains on Pascal VOC. The approach achieves these results with a single model instead of multiple models.
AI.conclusion: HSA demonstrates that a single model trained with limited supervision can learn hierarchical semantic representations of a scene, spanning foreground/background, object categories, and individual instances. It suggests a viable path toward unified, multi-granularity object-centric learning; code will be released.

title: PGD-NO: A Neural Operator with Precomputed Geometry Decomposition for 3D Million-scale Physics Simulations
summary: While neural PDE solvers have demonstrated significant potential for accelerating engineering simulations, existing architectures remain constrained by high memory consumption and the single node bottleneck, where the maximum processable mesh resolution is strictly limited by the VRAM of a single compute unit. To address these challenges, we propose PGD-NO, a neural operator with Precomputed Geometry Decomposition, that relocates the computational overhead of geometric encoding to a deterministic pre-computation phase. By utilizing an iterative geometry decomposition algorithm to extract geometry tokens, our model decouples feature extraction from solution querying. This architecture enables linear memory scalability, allowing high fidelity learning on meshes exceeding 10 million nodes, a scale where existing architectures typically encounter memory exhaustion. PGD-NO demonstrates competitive predictive accuracy across diverse industrial benchmarks and provides intrinsic interpretability through attention mechanisms. By effectively overcoming traditional mesh-size constraints, PGD-NO offers a robust and efficient solution for the next generation of large-scale, high-fidelity industrial design applications.

AI.tldr: PGD-NO introduces Precomputed Geometry Decomposition to decouple geometry encoding from solution querying, enabling linear memory scaling and the ability to handle meshes over 10M nodes with competitive accuracy and interpretable attention.
AI.motivation: Address the memory bottlenecks of neural PDE solvers and the single-node VRAM limitation that restricts mesh resolution.
AI.method: Use an iterative, deterministic pre-computation phase to extract geometry tokens via geometry decomposition; decouple feature extraction from query-stage solution; leverage neural operator with precomputed tokens and attention-based interpretability.
AI.result: Demonstrates competitive predictive accuracy across diverse industrial benchmarks; supports training/inference on meshes exceeding 10 million nodes with linear memory growth; provides intrinsic interpretability through attention.
AI.conclusion: PGD-NO alleviates traditional mesh-size constraints, enabling robust and efficient large-scale, high-fidelity industrial design applications.

title: MobiDiff: Semantic-Aware Multi-Channel Discrete Diffusion for Human Mobility Data Generation
summary: Human mobility data are essential for transportation optimization, urban planning, and resource allocation, yet real-world mobility data are costly to collect and difficult to share due to privacy concerns. Recent diffusion-based methods have shown promise in synthesizing realistic mobility patterns, but they typically rely on continuous or latent spatio-temporal traces, limiting their ability to natively model discrete semantic events with explicit region, activity, time, and interval structures. To address this issue, we introduce MobiDiff, an end-to-end discrete diffusion framework that efficiently generates mobility data by directly denoising multi-channel semantic skeletons, avoiding the costly interpolation, latent trace construction, and coarse-to-fine realization pipelines widely used in existing diffusion-based methods. Specifically, MobiDiff decomposes each human check-in event into spatial, activity, and temporal channels, and employs structured event-, group-, and channel-level masking to jointly capture trajectory-level mobility patterns and within-event dependencies. We evaluate generation fidelity, privacy-preserving, and efficiency on three large-scale real-world datasets from Atlanta, Boston, and Seattle. Results show that MobiDiff effectively preserves trajectory length and temporal interval distributions while remaining competitive across broader mobility statistics; it is also much faster than state-of-the-art methods, e.g., 5.3$\times$ faster than GeoGen on average during inference. These findings suggest that discrete diffusion offers an interpretable and efficient framework for synthetic mobility data generation.

AI.tldr: Discrete diffusion-based generator (MobiDiff) for mobility check-ins that models discrete semantic events (region, activity, time) with multi-channel diffusion and masking, achieving faithful trajectory and interval statistics and faster inference than existing methods.
AI.motivation: Real-world mobility data are valuable but costly to collect and share due to privacy; existing diffusion methods rely on continuous/latent traces, which fail to natively model discrete, semantically structured events.
AI.method: End-to-end discrete diffusion that denoises multi-channel semantic skeletons; decompose each event into spatial, activity, temporal channels; apply event-, group-, channel-level masking to capture trajectory-level patterns and within-event dependencies; avoids interpolation and latent trace construction.
AI.result: Evaluated on Atlanta, Boston, Seattle datasets; maintains trajectory length and temporal interval distributions; competitive on broader mobility statistics; significantly faster than GeoGen (≈5.3x faster at inference).
AI.conclusion: Discrete diffusion on structured semantic skeletons is interpretable and efficient for synthetic mobility data generation.

title: On the Design of Mixture-of-Experts for Dynamic Gaussian Splatting
comment: Accepted by IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence
summary: Dynamic scene reconstruction remains challenging due to the heterogeneous and spatially varying nature of real-world motion. Although recent 3D Gaussian Splatting methods have introduced diverse deformation formulations for dynamic novel view synthesis, each method typically relies on a single deformation model within its representation, which limits robustness across diverse dynamic scenarios. In this work, we study a fundamental problem-multi-deformation modeling for dynamic 3D Gaussian representations-under two distinct integration constraints that differ in when and how multiple deformation experts interact during training. From a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) perspective, we view multi-deformation modeling as the problem of combining multiple specialized deformation models within a unified 3D representation. We first introduce Mixture of Deformation Experts (MoDE), which integrates multiple deformation experts directly into the deformable Gaussian Splatting pipeline through joint optimization. In MoDE, experts operate on a shared canonical Gaussian representation, enabling multi-deformation modeling without introducing additional training stages or modifying the original optimization schedule. In contrast, we further present Mixture of Experts for Dynamic Gaussian Splatting (MoE-GS) under a different integration constraint, where deformation experts are optimized independently and combined through a separate routing stage. As a result, expert interaction occurs over non-canonical Gaussian representations after individual optimization. Together, these two approaches provide alternative strategies for multi-deformation modeling, clarifying how integration constraints shape the design and behavior of deformation experts in dynamic 3D Gaussian representations. Our code is available at: https://github.com/cvsp-lab/MoE-GS-studio.

AI.tldr: Proposes a multi-deformation modeling framework for dynamic 3D Gaussian Splatting using a Mixture-of-Experts approach with two integration schemes for combining deformation models.
AI.motivation: Current dynamic 3D Gaussian methods rely on a single deformation model, limiting robustness to diverse real-world motion. A multi-expert ensemble can capture heterogeneous deformations.
AI.method: Introduce MoDE (joint optimization of multiple deformation experts on a shared canonical Gaussian representation) and MoE-GS (experts trained independently with a separate routing stage to combine non-canonical representations). Both integrate into the Gaussian Splatting pipeline without altering the original optimization schedule for MoDE, while MoE-GS uses a distinct training and routing process.
AI.result: Conceptual formulation and two integration strategies are presented; results are not detailed in the abstract, but the work provides a comparative framework and code availability (GitHub) for implementation and evaluation.
AI.conclusion: Two MoE-based strategies—MoDE and MoE-GS—clarify how integration constraints shape deformation-expert design and interaction in dynamic 3D Gaussian representations, offering robustness benefits and practical guidance for multi-deformation modeling.

title: Rethinking Small VLM Quantization: From Component-Wise Analysis to Hardware-Aware Edge Deployment
comment: 14 pages. Accepted at the ICML 2026 Workshop on Hypothesis Testing
summary: The emergence of vision language models with fewer than 3 billion parameters has accelerated the implementation of on-device multimodal intelligence. However, a detailed understanding of component-wise quantization remains a bottleneck for optimal deployment. This paper presents a systematic evaluation framework for empirically validating five hypotheses across six quantization configurations on the Jetson Orin NX and AGX. By separating the vision encoder, projector, and large language model backbone yields the following results: (1) Quantization sensitivity is governed by the structural paradigm (MoE vs. dense) rather than scale alone, with MoE backbones mitigating INT4 noise where dense backbones degrade; (2) SigLIP encoders incur disproportionate INT8 latency on Jetson Ampere--a deployment-specific encoder-kernel-hardware interaction, not a SigLIP flaw; (3) Although INT4 quantization of LLMs greatly reduces VRAM consumption, it also causes slower token generation due to dequantization overhead; (4) Composite quantization errors are largely additive, except along the modality-alignment path, which is architecture-dependent; (5) The intelligence-per-joule profile varies significantly across platforms owing to memory bandwidth constraints.

AI.tldr: Systematic, hardware-aware evaluation of quantization strategies for vision-language models (<=3B params) across six configurations and two Jetson platforms, revealing architecture-driven sensitivity, deployment-specific kernel interactions, and platform-dependent efficiency.
AI.motivation: To understand how component-wise quantization (vision encoder, projector, LLM backbone) interacts with model architecture (MoE vs. dense) and hardware specifics to guide efficient on-device multimodal AI deployment.
AI.method: Empirical framework evaluating five hypotheses across six quantization configurations, separating vision encoder, projector, and LLM backbone, tested on Jetson Orin NX and AGX.
AI.result: (1) Quantization sensitivity is architecture-driven (MoE mitigates INT4 noise; dense degrades). (2) SigLIP encoders incur disproportionate INT8 latency due to deployment-specific kernel-hardware interaction. (3) INT4 LLM quantization saves VRAM but slows token generation due to dequantization overhead. (4) Quantization errors largely additive except along modality-alignment path (architecture-dependent). (5) Intelligence-per-joule varies with memory bandwidth across platforms.
AI.conclusion: Component-wise quantization effects are architecture- and platform-dependent; guidelines should consider MoE vs dense, encoder-kernel-hardware interplay, and memory bandwidth constraints to optimize for on-device multimodal performance and efficiency.

title: FedOPAL: One-Shot Federated Learning via Analytic Visual Prompt Tuning
summary: With the widespread deployment of basic models in edge intelligence, communication bandwidth has become a core bottleneck restricting the scalability of federated learning. Although one-shot federated learning alleviates this problem by minimizing communication rounds, existing iterative fine-tuning or knowledge distillation methods still face challenges such as high server-side computational costs and hyperparameter sensitivity. Analytical federated learning achieves efficient gradientfree aggregation using least-squares closed-form solutions, but in environments with non-independent and identically distributed data, its static feature assumptions fail, leading to feature manifold misalignment and severely impairing model performance. To address this contradiction, this paper proposes the FedOPAL framework. This framework adapts the visual prompts as feature rectifiers, actively correcting the feature distribution of heterogeneous data to a linearly separable space by applying local proximal constraints, thereby satisfying the theoretical assumptions of analytical federated learning. Experimental results show that FedOPAL not only significantly outperforms the original analytical methods on several benchmarks, but also achieves accuracy comparable to state-of-the-art iterative methods while maintaining zero server-side training costs, providing a new engineering paradigm for efficient collaboration of large models on the edge.

AI.tldr: FedOPAL uses visual prompts as feature rectifiers to align heterogeneous data for analytical federated learning, achieving zero server-side training costs and competitive accuracy.
AI.motivation: To overcome feature distribution misalignment under non-IID data in analytical FL while preserving gradient-free, closed-form aggregation and low communication.
AI.method: Introduce local visual prompts as feature rectifiers with proximal constraints to transform local features into a linearly separable space, aligning with analytical FL assumptions; keep server-side computation zero.
AI.result: Empirical results show improved performance over pure analytical methods and parity with iterative methods on benchmarks, with zero server-side training cost.
AI.conclusion: Offers a new edge-friendly engineering paradigm for efficient large-model collaboration by rectifying feature distributions to enable efficient analytical FL.

title: UniRef-UAV: A Multimodal Benchmark for Universal Referring in UAV Imagery
summary: Unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) increasingly rely on visual grounding capabilities to localize task-relevant targets from diverse instructions in complex aerial scenes. Existing referring expression comprehension (REC) benchmarks and methods, however, are largely built around text-only queries and single-object outputs, which limits their applicability to practical UAV scenarios involving reference images, multimodal instructions, absent targets, and multiple valid target instances. To address this gap, we introduce \emph{Universal Referring}, a generalized UAV referring task that jointly expands the query modality and the output cardinality. We construct \emph{UniRef-UAV}, a multimodal benchmark that supports text-only, image-only, and text+image queries with modality-dependent target cardinality, where text-only and text+image queries admit no-target, single-target, and multi-target grounding while image-only queries focus on existence-aware single-instance grounding. It also provides in-domain and cross-domain evaluation protocols for visual-query generalization. We further present \emph{UAV-URNet}, a detection-style baseline that maps heterogeneous queries into a shared query space and predicts variable-size target sets through set prediction. Extensive experiments show that UAV-URNet provides a stable and reproducible baseline with more consistent no-target discrimination and a more lightweight, reproducible implementation than large general-purpose MLLMs. Additional domain analysis, query-representation analysis, and ablation studies demonstrate that multimodal queries help reduce visual-query ambiguity and promote a more unified query--target alignment space. The annotations, visual query crops/images, train/validation/test splits, evaluation scripts, and baseline code will be made publicly available to facilitate reproducible research.

AI.tldr: Introduces UniRef-UAV benchmark and UAV-URNet baseline for universal referring in UAVs, handling multimodal queries and variable output cardinality (no-target, single, multi) across modalities; provides data, protocols, and baseline code.
AI.motivation: Practical UAV scenarios require grounded references from text and/or images, with absent targets and multiple valid instances. Existing REC benchmarks focus on text-only, single-target queries, limiting real-world UAV applicability and cross-domain generalization.
AI.method: Propose UniRef-UAV: a multimodal benchmark with text-only, image-only, and text+image queries and modality-dependent target cardinality (no-target, single-target, multi-target for text modalities; existence-aware single-instance grounding for image-only). Provide in-domain and cross-domain evaluation protocols. Introduce UAV-URNet, a detection-style baseline that maps heterogeneous queries into a shared query space and predicts variable-size target sets via set prediction. Conduct extensive experiments and ablations to analyze multimodal query benefits and provide a reproducible baseline.”,
AI.result: Experiments show UAV-URNet offers stable, reproducible baselines with consistent no-target discrimination and a lightweight, reproducible implementation compared with large multimodal LLMs. Multimodal queries reduce visual-query ambiguity and align query-target representations more effectively. Domain analysis and ablations validate the proposed design. The authors will publicly release annotations, query crops/images, splits, evaluation scripts, and baseline code.
AI.conclusion: This work fills a gap in UAV visual grounding by enabling universal referring across modalities and output cardinalities. It provides a benchmark (UniRef-UAV), a practical baseline (UAV-URNet), and accompanying resources to support reproducible research and cross-domain generalization.

title: What to Keep, What to Forget: A Rate--Distortion View of Memory Compaction in LLMs and Agents
summary: Large language models, and the agents built on them, spend an ever-growing share of their compute and memory on remembering: caching attention keys and values, carrying long prompts, maintaining recurrent state, and storing what happened in previous turns and sessions. Because none of this memory is free, four largely separate research communities have each learned to compact it. They evict or quantize the KV cache, prune or distill prompts, bound architectural state, and consolidate agent memory. We argue that these are instances of one problem: a rate--distortion decision about what context-derived information to retain versus discard, at what fidelity, under a resource budget, so as to preserve downstream task utility. We make this lens precise with a single compaction objective and a layer-agnostic lower bound, use it to build a seven-axis taxonomy that classifies methods from across the stack uniformly, and use it to transfer mechanisms between layers that have never been connected, from serving-stack KV management to agent long-term memory. Two patterns hold across the survey. At every layer the signal that decides what to keep is attention magnitude or recency, and it fails in the same way everywhere, by discarding, before the query is known and with no way to undo it, information the query later needs. And while compression is measured carefully on single-turn long context, the repeated compaction that agents actually perform is almost never measured, and no benchmark holds one budget axis across all the layers at once. We turn both observations into a benchmark proposal, a small reference experiment, and a set of compaction-aware design principles, and we map the open problems.

AI.tldr: Unifies memory/compression across LLM stacks under a rate–distortion objective, presents seven-axis taxonomy, benchmarks, and design principles to study and transfer compaction methods across layers.
AI.motivation: Growing compute/memory demands for context in LLMs; disparate communities independently compact memory components; need a unified framework to optimize task utility under resource budgets.
AI.method: Proposes a single compaction objective and a layer-agnostic lower bound; builds a seven-axis taxonomy to classify methods across the stack; demonstrates cross-layer transfer and benchmarks; offers a reference experiment and compaction-aware design principles.
AI.result: Identifies recurring patterns: signal for retention is attention magnitude/recency; common failure mode is discarding information before the query is known; notes lack of cross-layer benchmarking; provides a benchmark proposal, a reference experiment, and open problems map.
AI.conclusion: A rate–distortion lens clarifies cross-layer memory management in LLM-based systems, enabling cross-layer transfer of techniques and joint budgeting; highlights need for comprehensive, multi-layer benchmarks and principled compaction strategies.

title: Towards Mechanistically Understanding Why Memorized Knowledge Fails to Generalize in Large Language Model Finetuning
summary: Fine-tuning LLMs to inject new knowledge faces a critical challenge: LLMs can quickly memorize new facts, yet fail to use them for downstream reasoning tasks. We formalize this failure as the \textit{\textbf{Knowing--Using Gap}}, characterized by an accuracy gap and a temporal lag between memorization and generalization. To understand this phenomenon, we fine-tune LLMs with unseen knowledge and monitor the spatial permeation dynamics of the knowledge internally using a novel intervention technique called self-patching. Self-patching identifies activation locations where relocating representations substantially improves failed generalization cases. These results are consistent with a knowledge-circuit misalignment hypothesis: memorized representations can exist internally but may not be routed to computation-effective layers. To demonstrate the practicality of this diagnostic finding, we design a simple heuristic strategy which recovers 58--75\% of the oracle headroom in generalization failure. Experiments are done cross-domain for the robustness of this finding.

AI.tldr: Fine-tuning LLMs with new knowledge reveals a Knowing–Using Gap: memorization occurs quickly but generalization lags in downstream reasoning. The paper introduces self-patching to locate activation loci that, when representations are relocated, improve failed generalization, supporting a knowledge-circuit misalignment hypothesis. A simple heuristic recovers 58–75% of oracle headroom, demonstrated across domains.
AI.motivation: Understand why newly memorized facts do not reliably support downstream reasoning and to develop diagnostic/mitigation tools that bridge the memorization-generalization gap.
AI.method: Fine-tune LLMs on unseen knowledge; monitor internal activation dynamics via self-patching to identify activation locations where relocation of representations aids generalization failures; formulate a knowledge-circuit misalignment hypothesis; propose a heuristic to recover a substantial portion of generalization headroom.
AI.result: Empirical evidence of a consistent accuracy gap and a temporal lag between memorization and generalization; identification of activation loci enabling improved generalization through representation relocation; a heuristic strategy restoring 58–75% of oracle headroom; cross-domain validation supports robustness.
AI.conclusion: The Knowing–Using Gap can be explained by a routing/misalignment between memorized representations and computation-appropriate layers. Self-patching provides a practical diagnostic, and the proposed heuristic demonstrates tangible gains in generalization, suggesting architectural/training adjustments to better align knowledge circuits with computation.

title: Progression as Latent Drift: Generative Forecasting of Slow-Evolving Pathologies
summary: Forecasting the future anatomy of slow-evolving neurodegenerative diseases could enable earlier, more targeted intervention and improve clinical trial design, but it remains challenging because true progression signals are subtle in longitudinal MRI. In this low-signal regime, transferring modern generative sequence models directly is unreliable: training is dominated by stable baseline anatomy and confounded by dense, sample-specific nuisance variation. We first provide a theoretical analysis that explains these failures through two modes. Identity collapse occurs when optimization is driven toward reproducing the current anatomy, which prevents the model from learning faint temporal change. The continuous interpolation trap arises when standard smooth networks cannot separate localized biological drift from pervasive noise, which leads to spurious changes that diffuse across the volume. To address both issues, we propose Latent Drift, a progressive generative framework that learns change in a compressed semantic representation rather than synthesizing full-resolution anatomy. This design removes pixel-level identity from the prediction target and concentrates model capacity on progression-relevant dynamics. We further apply Finite Scalar Quantization to the learned change representation, which suppresses small, high-frequency nuisance fluctuations while preserving consistent structural drift. Experiments on longitudinal 3D brain MRI show that Latent Drift improves patient-specific neuro-forecasting over diffusion and autoregressive transformer baselines across generative fidelity and clinically relevant evaluation metrics. Project page: \href{https://cutepkq.github.io/latent-drift}{https://cutepkq.github.io/latent-drift}.

AI.tldr: Latent Drift is a progressive latent-space generative model with Finite Scalar Quantization for forecasting longitudinal brain MRI progression, addressing subtle signals by learning change in a compressed representation, outperforming diffusion and autoregressive baselines.
AI.motivation: Forecasting slow-evolving neurodegenerative progression from longitudinal MRI is hard because true progression signals are subtle and dominated by stable anatomy and nuisance variation, causing identity collapse and continuous interpolation traps in standard generative sequence models.
AI.method: Latent Drift learns change in a compressed semantic latent space rather than full-resolution synthesis, removing pixel-level identity from targets. It applies Finite Scalar Quantization to the latent change representation to suppress small high-frequency nuisance fluctuations while preserving meaningful structural drift.
AI.result: On longitudinal 3D brain MRI, Latent Drift improves patient-specific neuro-forecasting over diffusion and autoregressive transformer baselines in generative fidelity and clinically relevant evaluation metrics.
AI.conclusion: Latent Drift provides a robust, latent-space forecasting framework for slow neurodegenerative progression, addressing key failure modes and improving clinical usefulness; the approach shows promise for other slow-changing biological sequences.

title: An exact information theory of generalization phase transitions in Bayesian diffusion models
summary: How diffusion models circumvent the curse of dimensionality to learn complex distributions over high dimensional spaces from a finite training set, instead of memorizing it, remains a fundamental mystery. To address this, we introduce analytically tractable Bayesian information restricted diffusion (BIRD) models, in which each pixel observes restricted information about noisy data. A BIRD model time-reverses diffusion by inferring which past training sample produced its current restricted observation using the Bayesian posterior. This model class generalizes existing analytical diffusion models that use spatially local information restriction. We show that spatially local BIRD models closely approximate trained diffusion models \textit{early in training}, across different architectures such as UNets and DiTs. Under minimal assumptions on the data distribution, we identify an information-theoretic phase boundary between memorization and generalization in the joint space of amount of training data, time in the reverse generative process, and amount of information restriction: a BIRD model memorizes when the mutual information between its restricted noisy observations and the training data exceeds the log number of training points, and it generalizes otherwise. Experiments across a range of datasets confirm our theoretically predicted location for the transition. We find that generation proceeds near the edge of memorization: both spatially local BIRD models and early-training diffusion models track the memorization-generalization phase boundary by increasingly restricting information over time. Overall, our results reveal a fundamental role for information restriction in generative AI to circumvent the curse of dimensionality.

AI.tldr: Analytically tractable Bayesian information restricted diffusion (BIRD) models reveal an information-theoretic memorization–generalization phase boundary for high-dimensional diffusion. By restricting per-pixel information and inverting via Bayesian posterior, BIRD explains why diffusion models generalize early in training, with spatially local BIRD approximating trained models; experiments validate a phase transition and edge-of-memorization behavior across datasets and architectures.
AI.motivation: Understand why diffusion models from finite data avoid memorization and how information restriction interacts with high dimensionality to enable generalization, providing an analytically tractable lens on diffusion dynamics.
AI.method: Introduce BIRD models with restricted information per pixel; reverse diffusion by Bayesian inference of which training sample produced the current observation; show equivalence/approximation to spatially local analytical diffusion models; derive an information-theoretic phase boundary between memorization and generalization based on mutual information MI and log N; validate via experiments across datasets and architectures (UNets, DiTs).
AI.result: Spatially local BIRD models closely approximate trained diffusion models early in training; a phase boundary is identified: memorize if MI between restricted observations and training data exceeds log(number of training points), generalize otherwise. Experiments confirm the predicted transition and show generation proceeds near the boundary by increasing information restriction over time.
AI.conclusion: Information restriction is fundamental to circumventing the curse of dimensionality in generative AI; the memorization–generalization balance can be understood via an MI-based threshold, with generation operating near this boundary across architectures and datasets.

title: Game Theory Driven Multi-Agent Framework Mitigates Language Model Hallucination
summary: The application of lightweight Large Language Models in rule-based scientific domains remains severely limited by their tendency to mimic linguistic patterns rather than reproduce axiomatic reasoning, causing frequent hallucinations. Here, we show that G-Frame, an adaptive multi-agent framework integrating Bayesian and team game principles, establishes an automated closed-loop for high-quality data synthesis and model training. By forcing the internalization of domain constraints through structured reasoning, we synthesized a specialized corpus of 363,045 chains-of-thought and 199,589 question-answer pairs. The resulting 7B model OmniChem achieves performance parity with GPT 4o mini on custom benchmarks and ChemBench while exhibiting a 79.46% reduction in hallucinations relative to its base architecture. We further demonstrate the advanced capabilities of OmniChem in molecular design and synthesis planning. This work establishes a scalable paradigm utilizing adaptive multi-agents to overcome inherent reasoning deficiencies, offering a feasible pathway for accelerating knowledge discovery in specialized scientific fields.

AI.tldr: Adaptive multi-agent framework G-Frame enables closed-loop data synthesis and training for rule-based science, yielding 7B OmniChem with parity to GPT-4o mini on benchmarks and substantially fewer hallucinations; demonstrates molecular design/synthesis planning; suggests scalable pathway for domain knowledge discovery.
AI.motivation: Lightweight LLMs struggle in rule-based scientific domains due to tendency to mimic patterns rather than enforce axiomatic reasoning, leading to hallucinations. There is a need for structured reasoning and high-quality data to improve reliability.
AI.method: G-Frame combines Bayesian and team-game principles in an adaptive multi-agent setup to create an automated closed-loop system for data synthesis and model training. It enforces domain constraints via structured reasoning, producing a corpus of 363,045 chains-of-thought and 199,589 question-answer pairs for training a 7B model (OmniChem).
AI.result: OmniChem achieves performance parity with GPT-4o mini on custom benchmarks and ChemBench; exhibits a 79.46% reduction in hallucinations compared with its base architecture; demonstrates advanced capabilities in molecular design and synthesis planning.
AI.conclusion: A scalable, adaptive multi-agent paradigm can overcome inherent reasoning deficiencies in lightweight LLMs, enabling accelerated knowledge discovery in specialized scientific fields.

title: Enhancing the KidSat Model: Integrating Geographical Encoding and Data Quality Assessment for Childhood Poverty Prediction
summary: Accurate poverty mapping using satellite imagery is often hindered by (i) noisy and sparse survey-derived supervision, (ii) image quality issues such as cloud cover and image corruption, and (iii) lack of explicit spatial structure in image-only models. Building on the KidSat framework, we develop an enhanced pipeline that improves predictive accuracy via refined data preprocessing, systematic image quality assessment, and mathematically defined geographic encoding. First, we refine the fine-tuning target matrix by resolving high-cardinality sparsity and reducing one-hot dimensionality from 103 to 51 via DHS re-aggregation. Second, we introduce a simple two-stage quality-screening procedure to filter heavily clouded or corrupted observations. Third, we fuse DINOv2 visual embeddings with Spherical Harmonics (SH) location features. Across extensive experiments, these changes reduce MAE from 0.2167 to 0.1759, corresponding to an 18.83% relative reduction on the cluster-level severe-deprivation proportion scale. When extended from 16 to 33 African countries, the best-performing configuration achieves an overall MAE of 0.1658. We find that SH features consistently improve performance over the image-only backbone, whereas higher-capacity coordinate Multi Layer Perception augmentation (SH+SIREN) can underperform without carefully designed objectives. Finally, gradient-boosted tree heads (XGBoost/LightGBM) most effectively exploit nonlinear interactions in the fused visual-geographic representation. These findings provide a scalable and principled recipe for improving satellite-based socioeconomic predictions using only publicly accessible data.

AI.tldr: An enhanced KidSat-inspired pipeline improves satellite-based poverty prediction by refining the supervision target, filtering low-quality imagery, and fusing DINOv2 visual embeddings with Spherical Harmonics geographic encoding; achieves notable MAE reductions and scales to more countries; SH features outperform image-only baselines, while high-capacity coordinate augmentations require careful objectives; gradient-boosted trees effectively capture nonlinear interactions.
AI.motivation: Tackle noisy, sparse supervision, cloud-related image quality issues, and the lack of explicit spatial structure in image-only poverty mapping. Leverage publicly available data and scalable modeling to improve predictive accuracy across regions.
AI.method: - Refine target matrix by reducing high-cardinality sparsity: DHS-based re-aggregation from 103 to 51 classes. - Two-stage quality screening to filter cloudy/corrupted observations. - Fuse DINOv2 visual embeddings with Spherical Harmonics (SH) location features. - Train with gradient-boosted tree heads (XGBoost/LightGBM) to exploit nonlinear interactions. - Evaluate across 16 and 33 African countries; compare image-only vs SH-enhanced backbones; compare SH vs SH+SIREN; ablation studies to assess components.
AI.result: MAE improved from 0.2167 to 0.1759 (18.83% relative). Cluster-level severe-deprivation proportion scale improved. Extending to 33 countries yields MAE of 0.1658. SH features consistently improve over image-only; SH+SIREN can underperform without carefully designed objectives. Trees (XGBoost/LightGBM) best leverage nonlinear interactions in fused representations.
AI.conclusion: The proposed pipeline offers a scalable, principled approach to satellite-based socioeconomic prediction using public data. Geographic encoding with SH provides robust gains over image-only models, while careful objective design is necessary for higher-capacity coordinate-based augmentations; gradient-boosted trees remain strong baselines for nonlinear fusion.

title: Who Analyses the Analyser? Self-Validating LLM Hazard Analysis with Constitutional Meta-STPA
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly trusted to draft the artifacts of safety analysis such as, losses, hazards, Unsafe Control Actions (UCAs), and safety constraints, inside rigorous processes such as Systems-Theoretic Process Analysis (STPA). Yet a blind spot runs through this fast-growing literature: every system gets analysed except the LLM-assisted tool doing the analysing, which is itself a safety-relevant system that can hallucinate standards, emit unverifiable constraints, and leave no audit trail from prompt to artifact. We take seriously the question the field has skipped -- {who analyses the analyser?} and answer it by turning STPA on the tool itself. We present \{Constitutional Meta-STPA}, an LLM-assisted STPA tool built around a closed loop: the tool runs a {meta-STPA} of the class of AI-assisted safety tools and {derives} rather than asserts, its governance constitution from the resulting loss$\to$hazard$\to$UCA$\to$constraint chain, yielding a published constitution of $21$ Tool Principles and $8$ Meta-Safety Principles, each bound to a code enforcement point. We formalise the measured object as a constitution-marginal coverage operator over a principle set $P$ ($|P|{=}29$) with a soundness lemma that isolates coverage from model and scanner, and report four findings. {(i)~Self-derivation:} a frontier ensemble ({claude-opus-4.8}${+}${claude-sonnet-4}) recovers $18/21$ canonical and all $8/8$ governance principles from the tool's own design, while a weaker pair recovers $12/21$ and $3/8$, so the meta layer is model-limited, not constitution-limited, and the same $8/8$ re-emerge from a second, independently authored tool.

AI.tldr: An LLM-assisted STPA tool audits itself via meta-STPA, deriving a governance constitution with 21 Tool Principles and 8 Meta-Safety Principles (29 total); frontier ensembles recover most canonical and all governance principles, suggesting the meta-layer is model-limited rather than constitution-limited and that governance can be self-derived.
AI.motivation: Address the lack of auditing for safety-analysis tools built with LLMs, ensuring auditable, verifiable governance of the analyser itself.
AI.method: Apply STPA in a closed loop to the tool; derive governance constitution from the tool's loss→hazard→UCA→constraint chain; formalize as constitution-marginal coverage operator over a principle set P (|P|=29); evaluate by testing recovery of principles using frontier ensembles (two Claude models) and a weaker pair; verify whether 8/8 governance principles emerge, and cross-check with an independently authored tool.
AI.result: Four findings reported; (i) self-derivation: frontier ensemble recovers 18/21 canonical and all 8/8 governance principles; weaker pair recovers 12/21 and 3/8; the same 8/8 governance principles re-emerge from an independently authored tool.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates that governance for AI-assisted safety tools can be derived and audited via meta-STPA; the meta-layer appears model-limited rather than constitution-limited; prompts the need for broader validation, generalization to other tool families, and deeper methodological details for reproducibility.

title: OmniFood-Bench: Evaluating VLMs for Nutrient Reasoning and Personalized Health Advice
summary:
The rapid integration of Large Vision-Language Models (VLMs) into critical infrastructure promises to revolutionize
  personalized healthcare and dietary management. However, in the domain of food systems, autonomous agents face a
  unique and persistent challenge: the "Systemic Information Asymmetry" between visual appearance and intrinsic
  nutritional composition. Existing benchmarks primarily focus on coarse-grained classification tasks, such as food
  category recognition, which fail to evaluate the intricate reasoning chain required for real-world dietary management
  -- specifically, the ability to traverse from identifying hidden ingredients to estimating physical mass, and finally
  synthesizing safety-critical medical advice. In this paper, we introduce OmniFood-Bench, a comprehensive benchmark
  constructed from the MM-Food-100K dataset. Unlike previous works, OmniFood-Bench evaluates VLMs across three
  progressive capabilities: Basic Perception (Ingredients & Cooking Methods), Quantitative Reasoning (Portion Size &
  Nutritional Profiling), and Safety-Critical Advisory (Disease-Specific Recommendations). We evaluate six
  state-of-the-art VLMs, including gpt-5.1, gemini-3-flash, and qwen3-vl-8B. Our extensive experiments reveal a
  startling "Semantic-Physical Gap": while models achieve near-human accuracy in naming dishes, they exhibit
  catastrophic failure in mass estimation and frequently hallucinate benign advice for high-risk diabetic profiles. This
  work establishes a rigorous standard for trustworthiness in autonomous agents deployed for public health. The code
  and datasets are available in: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/OmniFood-Bench-7D0B

AI.tldr: OmniFood-Bench introduces a three-stage evaluation for vision-language models on food nutrition tasks, highlighting a semantic-physical gap where models excel at dish naming but fail in mass estimation and safe medical guidance.
AI.motivation: To address Systemic Information Asymmetry between a food item's visual appearance and its intrinsic nutritional content, and to move beyond coarse-grained dish recognition toward a trustworthy, multi-step dietary reasoning pipeline for critical health guidance.
AI.method: Construct OmniFood-Bench from MM-Food-100K and evaluate six state-of-the-art VLMs (e.g., gpt-5.1, gemini-3-flash, qwen3-vl-8B) across three capabilities: Basic Perception (ingredients, cooking methods), Quantitative Reasoning (portion size, nutritional profiling), and Safety-Critical Advisory (disease-specific recommendations).
AI.result: Models achieve near-human accuracy in naming dishes but exhibit catastrophic errors in mass estimation and frequently hallucinate benign safety advice for high-risk diabetic profiles, revealing a significant Semantic-Physical Gap.
AI.conclusion: Sets a rigorous standard for trustworthiness in autonomous health agents by requiring multi-stage, safety-aware evaluation; makes code and datasets available and highlights the need for improvements in quantitative reasoning and safe medical guidance in VLMs.

title: ARGUS: Accelerated, Robust, General, and Unsupervised Cell Tracking Solutions
summary:
Background and Objective: Quantitative analysis of cell dynamics is central to modern biological research, providing critical insights into immune cell interactions, disease progression, and drug mechanisms. Automated cell tracking in time-lapse microscopy remains challenging due to noise, morphological variations, overlapping cells, and dynamic events such as divisions and fusions.
  Methods: We present ARGUS, a framework for Accelerated, Robust, General, and Unsupervised Cell Tracking Solutions. ARGUS combines adaptive cell detection, dense Farneback optical-flow prediction, frame-to-frame linear assignment, and a sequence-level tracklet-refinement step that reconnects trajectory fragments across short temporal gaps.
  Results: On publicly available Cell Tracking Challenge datasets, ARGUS achieved detection accuracy of 0.905-0.971 and tracking accuracy of 0.897-0.964, with runtimes within 1 minute (5-6 seconds for 3 frames).
  Conclusions: ARGUS is a modular, interpretable framework that can be adapted to different imaging modalities and biological applications without training data or GPU infrastructure. The implementation is publicly available at https://github.com/Gitinc/argus

AI.tldr: ARGUS proposes an unsupervised, modular cell-tracking framework that combines adaptive detection, dense optical-flow, frame-to-frame assignment, and tracklet refinement to achieve strong accuracy with fast runtimes on standard datasets.
AI.motivation: Accurate, robust, and efficient cell tracking in time-lapse microscopy remains challenging due to noise, morphology changes, cell overlaps, and dynamic events; there is a need for unsupervised, modality-agnostic approaches with minimal hardware requirements.
AI.method: Adaptive cell detection; dense Farneback optical-flow prediction; frame-to-frame linear assignment; sequence-level tracklet refinement to reconnect fragments across short temporal gaps; modular and interpretable design emphasizing acceleration, robustness, generality, and unsupervised operation.
AI.result: On public Cell Tracking Challenge datasets, detection accuracy 0.905–0.971; tracking accuracy 0.897–0.964; runtimes under 1 minute (5–6 s for 3 frames).
AI.conclusion: ARGUS is a modular, adaptable framework that can operate across imaging modalities without training data or GPUs; the implementation is publicly available at the provided GitHub repository.

title: Reinforcing the Generation Order of Multimodal Masked Diffusion Models
summary: Diffusion Language Models (DLMs) have recently achieved substantial progress in natural language generation tasks. Recent research demonstrates that adaptive token generation ordering can significantly improve performance in mathematical reasoning and code synthesis applications. In this work, we investigate the optimization of generation order for both text-to-image synthesis and multimodal understanding. We first establish that, unlike structured problems in language generation such as Sudoku puzzles, model logits alone are insufficient for determining optimal generation sequences in text-to-image generation and multimodal understanding. To address this challenge, we introduce a learnable control module trained via Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) to determine the generation order. Our results demonstrate that learning this control block substantially improves both text-to-image alignment and multimodal understanding in DLMs. In particular, it enhances the model's ability to capture fine-grained spatial relationships in generated images while also strengthening performance on multimodal reasoning and comprehension tasks. We evaluate our framework on GenEval, an object-focused benchmark for text-to-image alignment, where it achieves 4.08% relative improvements. In addition, experiments on VLMEvalKit confirm 4.85% relative improvements in multimodal understanding, highlighting the broad effectiveness of our approach.

AI.tldr: Learnable control module via Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) to optimize generation order in diffusion language models for text-to-image and multimodal tasks; logits alone are insufficient for ordering; achieves ~4.1-4.9% relative improvements on GenEval and VLMEvalKit, improving spatial reasoning and multimodal understanding.
AI.motivation: Address the limitation that model logits do not reliably determine optimal generation sequences in diffusion-based text-to-image generation and multimodal tasks; improve cross-modal alignment and spatial reasoning by learning generation order.
AI.method: Introduce a learnable generation-order control block trained with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), integrated into diffusion language models for text-to-image synthesis and multimodal understanding; evaluate on GenEval (image alignment) and VLMEvalKit (multimodal understanding).
AI.result: Significant relative gains: 4.08% on GenEval for text-to-image alignment and 4.85% on VLMEvalKit for multimodal understanding; enhanced capture of fine-grained spatial relationships in generated images and stronger multimodal reasoning.
AI.conclusion: Learning the generation order with GRPO substantially improves diffusion-language-model performance in both text-to-image synthesis and multimodal tasks; logits alone are insufficient for ordering, suggesting learning-based control blocks as a robust approach for future work.

title: Applying JEPA-Style Predictive Learning to JA4-Derived Network Fingerprints
summary:
I-JEPA and V-JEPA learn by matching latent predictions to target encoder outputs rather than regenerating the original input, and this has worked well for images and video. We explore whether the same objective works for compact network fingerprints. We built JA4-JEPA, a Transformer-based model trained on JA4, JA4H, JA4S, and JA4X subfields drawn from JA4DB and CIC-IDS- 2017. The training data combines roughly 397K samples from both sources, though no single sample contains all four view families. We evaluated the learned representations with a frozen kNN probe on protocol-family classification across TLS, DNS, and SSH. On 39,416 heldout samples the model achieved a cosine similarity of 0.9899 and a kNN accuracy of 0.9220. These results indicate that JEPA-style predictive learning can produce useful embeddings from JA4-derived fingerprints, even with incomplete view overlap across sources.
  Keywords: JA4, network fingerprinting, JEPA, predictive representation learning, self-supervised learning

AI.tldr: JEPA-style predictive learning can produce high-quality embeddings for JA4 network fingerprints using a Transformer, achieving strong holdout protocol-family classification when evaluated with a frozen kNN probe; performance holds despite incomplete cross-source view overlap.
AI.motivation: Test whether JEPA-style latent-prediction objectives, successful in vision, transfer to compact network fingerprints and multi-source data with incomplete view overlap.
AI.method: Train a Transformer-based JA4-JEPA on JA4/J4H/J4S/J4X subfields from JA4DB and CIC-IDS-2017 (~397K samples from two sources). No single sample contains all four view families. Evaluate using a frozen kNN classifier on protocol-family labels (TLS, DNS, SSH) with 39,416 held-out samples; report cosine similarity between predictions and targets and kNN accuracy.
AI.result: Cosine similarity: 0.9899; kNN accuracy: 0.9220 on held-out samples.
AI.conclusion: JEPA-style predictive learning is effective for producing discriminative embeddings from JA4-derived fingerprints, even with incomplete cross-source overlap; demonstrates applicability of self-supervised latent-prediction objectives beyond visual domains.

title: Texture Representations in Deep Vision Models: Comparing CNNs, Vision Transformers, and Human Perception
summary: In computational vision science, Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have emerged as a popular model of biological vision because of the alignment they can exhibit with neural and behavioral data in humans and animals. However, it remains unclear to what extent this alignment persists for visual tasks that extend beyond the canonical object recognition paradigm based on well defined semantic content. In this study, we diverge from the common object-centric view by focusing on another aspect of vision: texture perception. We consider textures of different complexity generated with three different algorithms from the same source images. Using a rank-based statistic, we quantify the information encoded in the internal representations of a CNN and three Vision Transformers (ViTs), and we compare the similarity of these representations to those inferred from human psychophysics data. We find that the representation of textures is aligned in different ViTs, but not between the ViTs and the CNN; that ViTs form similar representations for textures of different complexity; that human performance in recognizing textures can be better predicted from ViTs representations rather than CNN representations. Taken together, these results suggest that ViTs may capture more faithfully than CNNs how texture patterns are visually processed by humans, and that the representations of texture stimuli in computational models may be driven by the network architecture.

AI.tldr: Vision transformers (ViTs) align with human texture perception better than CNNs; texture representations depend on network architecture and ViTs show consistent representations across texture complexity.
AI.motivation: Assess whether modern vision models (CNNs vs ViTs) capture human texture processing beyond object recognition, by evaluating internal representations to texture stimuli of varying complexity.
AI.method: Generate textures of three complexity levels from the same source images using three texture-generation algorithms. Compare internal representations from a CNN and three ViTs to human psychophysics data using a rank-based statistic to quantify information alignment.
AI.result: ViTs exhibit aligned texture representations across different texture complexities and better predict human texture recognition performance than CNNs; CNN representations fail to align with ViT representations or human data. Texture processing representations appear to be architecture-driven.
AI.conclusion: Architecture shapes texture processing; ViTs may more faithfully model human texture perception than CNNs, suggesting texture representations in models are driven by network design rather than universal perceptual principles.

title: Towards Efficient Large Language Model Serving: A Survey on System-Aware KV Cache Optimization
comment: Accepted to ACL 2026 as a Findings paper
summary: Despite the rapid advancements of large language models (LLMs), LLM serving systems remain memory-intensive and costly. The key-value (KV) cache, which stores KV tensors during autoregressive decoding, is crucial for enabling low-latency, high-throughput LLM inference serving. In this survey, we focus on system-aware KV infrastructure for serving LLMs (abbreviated as sKis). We revisit recent work from a system behavior perspective, organizing existing efforts into three dimensions: execution and scheduling (temporal), placement and migration (spatial), and representation and retention (structural). Furthermore, we analyze cross-behavior co-design affinity and behavior-objective links, highlighting future opportunities. Our work systematizes a rapidly evolving area, providing a foundation for understanding and innovating KV cache designs in modern LLM serving infrastructure.

AI.tldr: A survey introducing a system-aware KV cache infrastructure for LLM serving (sKis), classifying prior work by temporal, spatial, and structural dimensions, and discussing cross-dimension co-design and future opportunities.
AI.motivation: LLM serving demands low latency and high throughput; KV cache of KV tensors is memory-intensive and costly, making efficient KV caching critical for scalable LLM inference serving.
AI.method: Literature survey and taxonomy. Organizes existing work along three dimensions—execution/scheduling (temporal), placement/migration (spatial), and representation/retention (structural)—and analyzes cross-behavior affinities and objective links.
AI.result: A cohesive framework to understand KV cache design in LLM serving, identifying trade-offs, gaps, and opportunities across the three dimensions and their interactions, thereby guiding future sKis research and implementation.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a foundational basis for understanding and innovating KV cache designs in modern LLM serving infrastructure, with emphasis on cross-dimension co-design and actionable directions for future research.

title: Drift-Aware Temporal Graph Rewiring (DATGR) for Adaptive Semantic Modeling in Biomedical Text
comment: 6 pages, 4 figures. Published in the Proceedings of the 2026 IEEE Conference on Artificial Intelligence (CAI 2026)
summary: Biomedical language evolves rapidly as new discoveries emerge, causing traditional text models to lose semantic fidelity over time. Static embeddings and co-occurrence graphs cannot capture such evolution, leading to performance degradation in retrieval and knowledge discovery tasks. This paper introduces a Drift-Aware Temporal Graph Rewiring (DATGR) framework that models concept evolution by dynamically updating co-occurrence edges based on estimated semantic drift. Instead of retraining embeddings for each time slice, DATGR performs lightweight, feedback-driven rewiring using a logistic update rule applied to edge weights. Evaluated on the Biomedical Multi-Relation Corpus (BIOMRC), the method achieved a mean Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic (AUROC) improvement of approximately 0.066 absolute difference (0.699 vs. 0.633) over a static baseline. Area Under the Precision-Recall Curve (AUPRC) remained comparable (0.738 vs. 0.744), showing that drift-aware adaptation enhances link-prediction recall without a loss in precision. These results demonstrate that edge-level adaptation effectively captures temporal semantic change in evolving biomedical text while remaining computationally efficient and interpretable.

AI.tldr: DATGR dynamically rewires temporal biomedical co-occurrence graphs to track semantic drift, avoiding full retraining while improving link-prediction AUROC with stable AUPRC on BIOMRC.
AI.motivation: Biomedical language evolves; static embeddings and co-occurrence graphs degrade semantic fidelity and retrieval/knowledge-discovery performance over time; there is a need for drift-aware, efficient graph adaptation.
AI.method: Drift-Aware Temporal Graph Rewiring (DATGR): updates edge weights via a logistic rule driven by estimated semantic drift, enabling lightweight, feedback-driven edge rewiring across time slices without retraining embeddings; evaluated on BIOMRC.
AI.result: Mean AUROC improved by ~0.066 absolute (0.699 vs 0.633) over a static baseline; AUPRC remained similar (0.738 vs 0.744); demonstrates improved recall with preserved precision; edge-level adaptation captures temporal semantic change while being computationally efficient and interpretable.
AI.conclusion: Edge-level drift-aware adaptation is effective for modeling temporal semantic evolution in evolving biomedical text and offers a computationally efficient, interpretable alternative to full embedding retraining for link prediction.

title: WCog-VLA: A Dual-Level World-Cognitive Vision-Language-Action Model for End-to-End Autonomous Driving
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have advanced end-to-end autonomous driving. However, existing methods either lack comprehensive world cognition or suffer from fragmented world foresight, inherently confining these models to reactive driving. To address this limitation, we propose WCog-VLA, a novel dual-level World-Cognitive VLA framework that successfully bridges semantic world forecasting with generative world evolution to achieve proactive autonomous driving. At the semantic level, WCog-VLA unifies world cognition and reasoning by incorporating 3D spatial perception and injecting agent tokens to capture the world dynamics, while concurrently enabling Game-theoretic Chain-of-Thought (Game-CoT) reasoning. At the generative level, we introduce the Aligned Decoupled Diffusion Transformer (ADDT) as a powerful generative world model that synthesizes physically-plausible joint multi-agent trajectories. Through scene representation alignment, ADDT reduces the number of denoising steps required and thus significantly accelerates inference. To facilitate strategic reasoning, we further construct a large-scale dataset featuring 85k Game-CoT annotations. Extensive experiments on the NAVSIM benchmark demonstrate that WCog-VLA achieves a State-Of-The-Art (SOTA) PDMS score of 92.9.

AI.tldr: WCog-VLA introduces a dual-level World-Cognitive VLA framework that links semantic world forecasting with generative world evolution for proactive autonomous driving. It features a semantic level with 3D spatial perception, agent tokens, and Game-theoretic Chain-of-Thought (Game-CoT) reasoning, and a generative level with the Aligned Decoupled Diffusion Transformer (ADDT) to synthesize joint multi-agent trajectories. A large 85k Game-CoT dataset supports strategic reasoning. On NAVSIM, WCog-VLA achieves SOTA PDMS of 92.9.
AI.motivation: Current Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models for autonomous driving often lack comprehensive world cognition and forward-looking foresight, resulting in reactive behavior. There is a need to unify world cognition with generative world evolution to enable proactive decision-making.
AI.method: Semantic level: integrate 3D spatial perception, inject agent tokens to encode world dynamics, and enable Game-CoT reasoning. Generative level: introduce ADDT (Aligned Decoupled Diffusion Transformer) to synthesize physically plausible joint multi-agent trajectories. Scene representation alignment speeds inference by reducing denoising steps. Dataset: 85k Game-CoT annotations.
AI.result: NAVSIM benchmark results show a state-of-the-art PDMS score of 92.9, indicating superior proactive decision-making performance. ADDT accelerates inference via scene alignment and produces plausible multi-agent trajectories.
AI.conclusion: WCog-VLA advances proactive autonomous driving by coupling semantic world cognition with a generative world model, achieving SOTA performance on NAVSIM while improving efficiency. The large-scale Game-CoT dataset facilitates strategic reasoning.

title: When Thinking Hurts: Epistemic Signals in the Reasoning Chains of Visual Language Models
comment: 7 pages, 2 figures, 5 tables. Oral paper at the 2nd Workshop on Epistemic Intelligence in Machine Learning (EIML@ICML 2026), Seoul, South Korea
summary: Uncertainty quantification for visual language models (VLMs) conventionally targets the answer token distribution. We provide the first three-family empirical characterisation of answer entropy behaviour in thinking-mode VLMs. Running four models on identical POPE adversarial samples, we find three qualitatively distinct patterns: Qwen3-VL-8B-Thinking shows complete collapse (ans H AUROC = 0.492); GLM-4.1V-9B-Thinking shows no collapse (0.716); and InternVL3-8B shows selective thinking (chains on only 50% of samples, ans H = 0.675 full / 0.602 thinking-only). Across all three thinking-mode models, thinking chain entropy outperforms answer entropy on the subset where chains are generated (0.647, 0.759, 0.608 vs. 0.492, 0.716, 0.602 respectively), suggesting chain signals are the more reliable predictor whenever chains are present. This holds strongly for Qwen and GLM, but with only marginal and statistically unreliable advantage for InternVL3 (n_FP = 17). A 300-sample VQAv2 pilot confirms chain entropy (0.680) outperforms answer entropy (0.595) on VQAv2 questions, with the gap largest for free-form answers (0.733 vs. 0.467). On harder reasoning tasks (HallusionBench) both Qwen models show moderate signal (approx. 0.64), consistent with incomplete pre-commitment on difficult questions. We additionally document structured abstention affecting 12-22% of queries with asymmetry toward absent-object queries, and a practical abstention gate raising accuracy from 71.0% to 93.8% at 62.7% coverage with no additional inference cost.

AI.tldr: Empirical study characterizing uncertainty signals in thinking-mode visual language models across three families. Chain-based entropy outperforms answer entropy when chains exist; abstention gating improves practical accuracy with modest coverage; results vary by model, with Qwen showing collapse, GLM stable, InternVL3 selective thinking; validated on VQAv2 and HallusionBench.
AI.motivation: Uncertainty quantification in VLMs has focused on answer-token distributions. This work systematically characterizes thinking-chain (chain-of-thought) uncertainty signals and compares them to final answer uncertainty across multiple models and tasks, revealing when chain signals are more reliable and how abstention can improve practical accuracy.
AI.method: Evaluate four thinking-mode VLMs (Qwen3-VL-8B-Thinking, GLM-4.1V-9B-Thinking, InternVL3-8B, plus a VLM ensemble? not specified) on identical POPE adversarial samples. Compute answer entropy and chain entropy (on thinking chains) for samples where chains are generated; compare AUROC of using chain signals vs answer signals. Extend with a 300-sample VQAv2 pilot and HallusionBench to assess generalization. Document structured abstention patterns and propose an abstention gate that raises accuracy with fixed coverage and no extra inference cost.
AI.result: Three qualitatively distinct patterns across models: complete collapse for Qwen3-VL-8B-Thinking (ans H AUROC 0.492), no collapse for GLM-4.1V-9B-Thinking (0.716), selective thinking for InternVL3-8B (chains on ~50% of samples; full ans H 0.675 thinking-only 0.602).
