Chain entropy outperforms answer entropy on all models where chains exist (example values: 0.647 vs 0.492 for Qwen; 0.759 vs 0.716 for GLM; 0.608 vs 0.602 for InternVL3). InternVL3 shows marginal advantage due to small n_FP (17). VQAv2 pilot (300 samples) shows chain entropy 0.680 > answer entropy 0.595; larger gap for free-form answers (0.733 vs 0.467). HallusionBench reveals moderate signal (~0.64) for harder questions, suggesting incomplete pre-commitment. Structured abstention is observed in 12-22% of queries, biased toward absent-object queries; an abstention gate raises accuracy from 71.0% to 93.8% at 62.7% coverage with no extra inference cost.
AI.conclusion: Chain-level uncertainty signals are more reliable predictors than final-answer uncertainty when chains are produced. Thinking-mode VLMs exhibit diverse behaviors across models. Abstention mechanisms can yield substantial accuracy gains with limited coverage and no additional cost. The results advocate prioritizing chain entropy as an uncertainty metric for VLMs in decision-critical settings and motivate further work on robust chain-based uncertainty calibration and deployment strategies.

title: AI-guided stimuli discovery and generation to optimize facial emotion perception studies in autism
summary: Understanding perceptual differences between autistic and neurotypical adults requires behavioral assays that are sensitive, reliable, and mechanistically informative. Facial emotion perception is a useful test case because group differences have been reported, but findings vary across studies. Here we show that this variability may reflect image-level sparsity: autistic-neurotypical differences in emotion judgments were concentrated in a small subset of diagnostic facial expressions rather than spread uniformly across stimuli. We trained population-specific artificial neural network models to predict image-level judgments for autistic and neurotypical participants, then used these models to select novel faces predicted to maximize group separation. In an independent cohort, model-selected images produced larger behavioral differences than matched random images. We then used the same models with a generative adversarial network to transform diagnostic images toward greater predicted group agreement. In phenotype-matched validation, synthesized images reduced behavioral separation relative to their matched originals. These results establish a model-guided framework for discovering and transforming stimuli that reveal population-specific perceptual differences. More broadly, they show how behavioral phenotyping can move beyond averaging across fixed stimulus sets toward optimized assays that identify the conditions under which neurodivergent perception diverges or converges.

AI.tldr: A model-guided, stimulus-optimized approach reveals that autistic‑neurotypical emotion perception differences are concentrated in a subset of expressions; population-specific ANNs predict judgments and guide stimulus selection and synthesis via GAN, enabling optimized assays.
AI.motivation: To address variability and lack of mechanistic insight in facial emotion perception differences by identifying image-level drivers and providing an optimized, mechanistically informative assay.
AI.method: Train population-specific neural network models to predict image-level judgments for autistic and neurotypical adults; identify expressions driving group differences; select novel faces predicted to maximize separation; validate in an independent cohort; use GAN to transform diagnostic images toward greater predicted group agreement; phenotype-matched validation shows reduced separation.
AI.result: Model-selected images yielded larger behavioral differences than matched random images; synthesized images reduced behavioral separation relative to originals; demonstrates that stimuli can be optimized to reveal systematic population differences; framework generalizes to optimized perceptual assays.
AI.conclusion: A model-guided framework can discover and transform stimuli to reveal population-specific perceptual differences, moving beyond fixed stimulus sets toward adaptive assays that identify conditions under which neurodivergent perception diverges or converges.

title: Classical versus Deep Mirror-Symmetry Scoring: A Benchmark of Thirteen Methods
comment: 22 pages, 6 figures, 5 tables. Code and benchmark: https://github.com/maxwoe/imgsym
summary: Quantifying how mirror-symmetric an image is about a given axis (symmetry scoring) underpins applications from visual aesthetics to medical imaging, yet proposed scoring methods have never been compared on a common, statistically grounded protocol. We benchmark 13 scoring methods (nine collected from literature, four introduced here) spanning from classical features to frozen deep features, across four single-axis and five multi-axis datasets under a reflection-exact protocol with a chance-anchored, significance-tested discrimination skill. Deep backbones perform best on single-axis and harder multi-axis protocols. However, a classical histogram-of-oriented-gradients (HOG) descriptor trails the best frozen-network readout by a small (but significant) margin, is not statistically separable from the runner-up (a CNN-filter measure), and runs ~300x faster on CPU. Our results show that discrimination concentrates in mid-scale oriented features, where deep backbones peak at a low or mid stage, and HOG peaks at a mid cell size. Among existing methods, frozen deep features thus offer little over a tuned classical descriptor for measuring symmetry; whether task-trained deep scorers can do better remains open. We release the scorers and harness in imgsym, an open toolkit for image symmetry detection and measurement.

AI.tldr: Benchmark of 13 image-symmetry scoring methods (classical features to frozen deep features) across four single-axis and five multi-axis datasets under a reflection-exact, significance-tested protocol. Deep backbones excel on single-axis and hard multi-axis tasks, but a tuned HOG descriptor often rivals the best frozen-readouts, offers ~300x CPU speed, and scales mid-scale features; overall frozen deep features provide limited gains over classical descriptors. A public toolkit, imgsym, is released.
AI.motivation: There is no statistically grounded, common benchmark comparing image symmetry scoring methods across simple and complex axes. A robust protocol is needed to guide method selection and understand where modern representations help in symmetry detection.
AI.method: Evaluate 13 scoring methods (9 from literature, 4 introduced here) on 4 single-axis and 5 multi-axis datasets using a reflection-exact protocol with chance-anchored, significance-tested discrimination. Analyze discriminative scale, compare deep backbones vs. classical descriptors, assess CPU speed, and release the methodology as imgsym.
AI.result: Deep backbones perform best on single-axis and harder multi-axis tasks. A classical histogram-of-oriented-gradients (HOG) descriptor dominates among frozen-network readouts, and edges out the runner-up CNN-filter measure; HOG is not statistically separable from the runner-up and runs ~300x faster on CPU. Discrimination concentrates in mid-scale oriented features; deep backbones peak at low or mid stages, HOG at mid cell size.
AI.conclusion: Frozen deep features offer little over a well-tuned classical descriptor for measuring symmetry; the advantage of task-trained deep scorers remains uncertain. The authors release scorers and harness in imgsym for community use.

title: Cross-Modal Generative Framework for Signal Translation from Fetal-Maternal Electrocardiograms to Fetal Doppler Waveforms
comment: Accepted for oral presentation at IEEE EMBC 2026. 7 pages
summary: Fetal electrocardiogram (fECG) and Doppler ultrasound provide complementary views of fetal cardiovascular function: fECG captures electrical activity while Doppler reflects mechanical hemodynamics shaped by factors such as placental resistance and vascular compliance. Understanding the recoverable and unrecoverable Doppler components through reconstruction from fECG offers insight into the relative contributions of electrical versus mechanical factors in fetal circulation, thereby informing clinical decisions. In addition, clinical evidence of maternal-fetal cardiac coupling suggests that maternal cardiovascular dynamics may also inform fetal hemodynamics. To computationally model these relationships, we propose a cross-modal generative framework combining dilated convolutions with cross-modal attention to selectively incorporate maternal ECG and self-attention to capture long-range temporal dependencies. Trained on 885 synchronized fetal/maternal ECG and Doppler envelope segments from 39 pregnancies, our model synthesizes Doppler envelopes with power spectral density mean squared error (PSD MSE) of 49.9 +/- 15.8 dB^2 (51% lower than two-channel baseline) and heart-rate error of 4.71 +/- 0.77 bpm (1.5% better than baseline; negligible relative to the 110-160 bpm physiological range). Cross-modal attention yields a 39% PSD MSE reduction over naive dual-channel concatenation, quantifying the contribution of maternal-fetal coupling. Our proposed framework advances computational modeling of the maternal-fetal cardiovascular system by enabling the synthesis of Doppler envelopes from dual-lead ECG. By analysis of both recoverable and residual Doppler components, this approach enables quantification of the purely mechanical contributions to Doppler waveforms -- those not recoverable from electrical recordings -- ultimately facilitating a more comprehensive fetal assessment.

AI.tldr: A cross-modal generative model synthesizes Doppler envelopes from dual-lead fECG (fetal + maternal), using dilated convolutions and cross-modal attention; achieves significant PSD MSE and heart-rate accuracy improvements; enables decomposition of recoverable vs residual Doppler components to separate electrical vs mechanical contributions.
AI.motivation: Quantify the relative contributions of electrical versus mechanical factors in fetal circulation and leverage maternal–fetal coupling to improve modeling of Doppler signals through ECG inputs.
AI.method: Dilated convolutions with cross-modal attention to incorporate maternal ECG and self-attention for long-range temporal dependencies. Trained on 885 synchronized fetal/maternal ECG and Doppler envelope segments from 39 pregnancies. Optimization targets PSD mean squared error (PSD MSE) and heart-rate error. Comparisons include a two-channel baseline and naive dual-channel concatenation.
AI.result: PSD MSE: 49.9 ± 15.8 dB^2 (51% lower than the two-channel baseline). Heart-rate error: 4.71 ± 0.77 bpm (1.5% better than baseline; negligible relative to 110–160 bpm). Cross-modal attention yields a 39% PSD MSE reduction over naive dual-channel concatenation.
AI.conclusion: The framework advances maternal–fetal cardiovascular modeling by enabling the synthesis of Doppler envelopes from dual-lead ECG and by enabling analysis of recoverable versus residual Doppler components to quantify purely mechanical contributions, supporting a more comprehensive fetal assessment.

title: CommuniWave:A Machine Learning Model for Quantifying the Degree of Temporary Informal Behavior in Urban Communities
summary: For urban managers and designers, improving the functional attributes of urban communities to enhance territorial resilience in the face of complexity and uncertainty is crucial. Currently, community planning often follows a top-down approach and lacks effective metrics to quantify informal behaviors of residents, leading to frequent conflicts with original plans. This study introduces CommuniWave, a machine learning model designed to efficiently detect and quantify the Degree of Informal Behavior (DIB) in urban communities. The model integrates a Behavior Capture Net (BCN) based on mmaction2, a self-developed YOLOv10 model (YLX), and a Behavior Eval Model (BEM) using random forest. Ultimately, by generating DIB fluctuation charts from street videos, the model facilitates dynamic monitoring, supporting urban managers in making refined decisions to enhance the overall resilience of communities.

AI.tldr: A proposal for CommuniWave, an ML pipeline to detect and quantify informal resident behavior (DIB) from street videos to support urban resilience management.
AI.motivation: Addresses the lack of quantitative metrics for informal behaviors in urban planning and the limitations of top-down approaches, aiming to improve resilience under complexity and uncertainty.
AI.method: A three-part architecture: (i) Behavior Capture Net (BCN) built atop mmaction2 for action capture, (ii) a self-developed YOLOv10 detector (YLX) for object/behavior detection, and (iii) a Behavior Eval Model (BEM) using random forest to quantify DIB; outputs DIB fluctuation charts from street videos for dynamic monitoring.
AI.result: Presents a conceptual pipeline and workflow for detecting and quantifying informal behavior, with the aim of enabling dynamic monitoring and refined decision-making; no empirical results are reported in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: If validated, the framework could provide real-time or near-real-time indicators of informal behavior to inform urban management and resilience strategies.

title: Attribute Retrieving for Open-Vocabulary Endoscopic Compositional Referring Segmentation
summary: Referring Image Segmentation (RIS) aims to segment image regions specified by natural language, enabling fine-grained and controllable visual understanding. Extending RIS to endoscopic imagery, however, presents unique challenges, including scarce high-quality annotations and complex, domain-specific image-text relationships. Although recent vision-language models demonstrate strong cross-domain alignment, they often fail to capture fine-grained textual cues in endoscopic settings, resulting in suboptimal performance and limited generalization. To address these challenges, we introduce ReferEndoscopy, a large-scale benchmark for RIS in the endoscopy field. Building on this dataset, we propose the Attribute Retrieval-based Endoscopic-RIS (AR-ERIS) framework for open-vocabulary endoscopic compositional referring segmentation. AR-ERIS leverages attribute retrieval for open-vocabulary endoscopic compositional referring segmentation and is pretrained on the curated ReferEndoscopy dataset, achieving state-of-the-art performance with strong generalization across both simulated and real-world endoscopic data. The dataset and code will be publicly released upon completion of the review process.

AI.tldr: ReferEndoscopy: a large-scale RIS benchmark for endoscopy and AR-ERIS: an open-vocabulary, attribute-retrieval-based endoscopic RIS framework pretrained on this dataset; achieves SOTA with good generalization; dataset and code forthcoming.
AI.motivation: Address scarcity of high-quality endoscopic RIS data and domain-specific language-image relations; need fine-grained, cross-domain alignment for endoscopy; improve generalization to real-world data.
AI.method: Introduce ReferEndoscopy dataset for RIS in endoscopy. Propose AR-ERIS framework that uses attribute retrieval for open-vocabulary compositional referring segmentation and pretrains on ReferEndoscopy.
AI.result: AR-ERIS achieves state-of-the-art performance with strong generalization across simulated and real-world endoscopic data.
AI.conclusion: Benchmark and method together improve RIS in endoscopy; dataset and code will be released publicly after review.

title: Modular Pretraining Enables Access Control
summary: AI developers face a dual-use dilemma. An AI capability that helps one user cure a disease can help another synthesize one. This dilemma could be resolved with access control, limiting dual-use AI capabilities to trusted deployments with a legitimate need. A gold standard for access control would be to serve separate models with different capabilities to different users. However, training and deploying multiple models is prohibitively expensive. To address this challenge, we propose gradient-routed auxiliary modules (GRAM), a pre-training method that adds modules to a neural network and selectively updates them to induce specialization. Ablating a module at inference time removes its capability from the network, approximating a model trained on filtered data. We evaluate GRAM on synthetic stories and realistic dual-use data spanning virology, cybersecurity, nuclear physics, and specialized code. These experiments show that GRAM disables targeted capabilities while preserving the rest, and resists their recovery under finetuning better than post-hoc unlearning. Most importantly, a Chinchilla-optimal scaling analysis from 50M to 5B parameters shows that the gap between data-filtered and full-data models widens with scale on removed capabilities but stays small on retained ones, and that GRAM closely tracks data filtering. GRAM's training cost is independent of the number of supported capability profiles, yielding a 5x reduction over data filtering in our 5-profile setting.

AI.tldr: GRAM adds gradient-updatable auxiliary modules to a neural network to enable selective capability specialization. At inference, ablating a module disables its capabilities, approximating data-filtered models without retraining multiple full models. It enables multi-profile access control with lower training cost, and scales favorably versus data filtering.
AI.motivation: There is a dual-use dilemma in AI: capabilities that cure disease can be misused to synthesize threats. A practical access-control standard is to deliver separate models per profile, but training/deploying many models is expensive. GRAM aims to approximate this with modular specialization.
AI.method: Pre-training method that injects auxiliary modules into a network and selectively updates them to induce specialization. Ablating a module at inference removes its capability. Evaluation on synthetic stories and realistic dual-use data (virology, cybersecurity, nuclear physics, specialized code). Scaling analysis from 50M to 5B parameters compares data-filtered vs full-data models and measures retained vs removed capability behavior.
AI.result: GRAM can disable targeted capabilities while preserving others and resists recovery under finetuning better than post-hoc unlearning. Scaling analysis shows the gap between data-filtered and full-data models grows with model size for removed capabilities but remains small for retained capabilities, and GRAM tracks data filtering. Training cost is independent of the number of capability profiles, yielding a 5x reduction over data filtering in a 5-profile setting.
AI.conclusion: GRAM offers scalable, cost-effective multi-profile access control that approximates data filtering, with strong resistance to recovery and favorable scaling properties, reducing the need to train/deploy multiple full models.

title: SHAP-Weighted Cross-Modal Expert Fusion for Emotion and Sentiment Recognition: Evidence and Limits
summary: Multimodal emotion and sentiment recognition is commonly addressed by early fusion, which concatenates modalities before classification, or late fusion, which combines independently trained unimodal predictors. Early fusion can be accurate but monolithic, while late fusion is modular but may lose cross-modal interactions. This paper revisits XAI-guided adaptive fusion (\xgaf), a tree-based mixture of unimodal and cross-modal experts whose sample-level weights are derived from TreeSHAP attribution magnitudes. We focus on the effect of SHAP attribution reduction when experts have unequal feature dimensionalities. In this setting, mean-abs and median-abs reductions can suppress high-dimensional cross-modal experts, whereas sum-abs reduction preserves total attribution mass. On MELD 7-class emotion recognition, sum-abs \xgaf{} nearly matches early fusion across three face-sequence aggregators; the Transformer variant reaches 0.5983 \wf{}, compared with 0.6018 for early fusion and 0.4598 for probability-average late fusion. McNemar testing shows no significant difference between sum-abs \xgaf{} and early fusion on MELD ($p=1.000$), while \xgaf{} remains significantly better than late fusion ($p<0.0001$). On CMU-MOSEI 3-class sentiment recognition, sum-abs \xgaf{} reaches 0.6519 \wf{}, slightly exceeding early fusion (0.6485) and late fusion (0.5696). Ablation studies show that the main gain comes from adding cross-modal experts, especially the trimodal expert, rather than from complex per-sample routing. Diagnostics further show that mean-abs and median-abs weights are nearly uniform, while sum-abs weights concentrate on the trimodal expert. Thus, the main contribution is a transparent empirical analysis of how SHAP reduction, expert dimensionality, and cross-modal expert design affect modular multimodal fusion.

AI.tldr: SHAP-based weighting in XGAF shows sum-abs reduction preserves attribution mass across unequal feature dims, enabling cross-modal experts to approach early-fusion performance and outperform late fusion on MELD and CMU-MOSEI; gains mainly from adding cross-modal (trimodal) experts; routing per-sample is less critical.
AI.motivation: Address how attribution reduction and cross-modal expert design affect modular multimodal fusion when experts have differing dimensionalities; evaluate SHAP-based routing choices on emotion and sentiment tasks.
AI.method: Tree-based mixture of unimodal and cross-modal experts (XGAF) with per-sample weights derived from TreeSHAP magnitudes; compare mean-abs, median-abs, and sum-abs SHAP reductions; evaluate on MELD (7-class) and CMU-MOSEI (3-class) using a Transformer aggregator; perform ablations on cross-modal vs unimodal experts and routing complexity; analyze weight distributions.
AI.result: Sum-abs reduction preserves total attribution mass; sum-abs XGAF achieves near parity with Early Fusion and outperforms Late Fusion on MELD; Transformer variant: 0.5983 WF vs 0.6018 Early Fusion (MELD); 0.4598 for Late Fusion; MELD: McNemar p=1.000 (no diff with Early Fusion); XGAF significantly better than Late Fusion (p<0.0001). On CMU-MOSEI, sum-abs XGAF 0.6519 WF, slightly above Early Fusion 0.6485 and Late Fusion 0.5696. Ablations show gains mainly from adding cross-modal experts, esp. the trimodal expert; mean-abs/median-abs weights nearly uniform while sum-abs weights concentrate on trimodal expert.
AI.conclusion: SHAP-reduction choice and cross-modal expert design critically shape modular multimodal fusion performance; sum-abs preserves attribution mass across dimensionality gaps and enables effective use of cross-modal (especially trimodal) experts, enabling transparent evaluation of XGAF design decisions.

title: Deep Learning Method for Stationary Distribution of Reflected Brownian Motion
summary: The stationary distribution of reflected Brownian motion (RBM) plays an important role in the analysis of high-dimensional stochastic systems, yet closed-form solutions are known only for a few special cases. Computing important performance metrics, such as tail probabilities, is even more intractable, despite their practical relevance. In this paper, we develop a deep learning approach that accurately and efficiently learns the Laplace transform of high-dimensional RBMs based on the basic adjoint relationship (BAR). Our framework combines a careful design of the loss function, training data sampling procedure, and neural network architecture. We evaluate the proposed method on RBM instances with known ground-truth tail probabilities and demonstrate near-perfect prediction in high-dimensional settings, highlighting its potential as a general tool for analyzing stochastic systems beyond analytically tractable regimes. Our code can be found at https://github.com/zhangz73/NN4MGF.

AI.tldr: A deep learning framework learns the Laplace transform (MGF) of high-dimensional reflected Brownian motions by enforcing the basic adjoint relationship (BAR); achieves accurate tail-probability predictions in high dimensions, with code available.
AI.motivation: The stationary distribution of reflected Brownian motion (RBM) is key for analysis of high-dimensional stochastic systems, but closed-form solutions are scarce. Tail probabilities are particularly intractable, motivating data-driven approaches that leverage structural relationships like BAR.
AI.method: A neural network is trained to approximate the Laplace transform of RBMs under BAR constraints. The loss design enforces BAR, with a carefully chosen sampling strategy for training data and architecture that respects the stochastic structure. Evaluation uses RBM instances with known ground-truth tails, comparing predicted tail metrics to truth.
AI.result: The method yields near-perfect predictions for tail probabilities in high-dimensional RBMs, outperforming traditional analytical approaches in regimes where those are unavailable. Demonstrates strong generalization within the tested settings.
AI.conclusion: BAR-guided deep learning provides a scalable, general tool for analyzing high-dimensional RBMs and related stochastic systems, enabling accurate tail analysis where analytical solutions are intractable. The approach is supported by available code at the provided repository.

title: Towards Precision Therapy in Hepatocellular Carcinoma: A Clinical-Reasoning LLM for Risk Stratification and Treatment Guidance
summary: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is a common malignancy and a leading cause of cancer-related mortality. Current guidelines and staging systems provide coarse categories, but often miss within-stage heterogeneity and the clinical context in electronic medical records (EMRs). We present HCC-STAR (Hepatocellular Carcinoma Staging, Treatment And pRognosis), a clinically aligned large language model that reads routine EMR narratives and jointly outputs risk score-based staging, ranked guideline-consistent treatments with evidence-based rationales, and individualized survival estimates. We curated about 30,000 HCC cases from SEER and expanded them into EMR-style narrative training data using a clinician-validated, prompt-based augmentation workflow. On this corpus, we developed a knowledge-aligned reasoning framework optimized with a step-verifiable composite reward, moving beyond text-level memorization of clinical guidelines. In a multi-center cohort of 6,668 patients from 12 hospitals in China, HCC-STAR achieved state-of-the-art performance in treatment recommendation and risk stratification compared with clinical guidelines and competitive models, including GPT-5 and Gemini-2.5 Pro. Hypothetical overall-survival analysis showed a median survival of 51 months under adherence to HCC-STAR recommendations, compared with 29 and 32 months under BCLC and CNLC. In clinician-centric evaluations, blinded hepatobiliary specialists rated HCC-STAR's reasoning and evidence-based justifications as trustworthy. The model surpassed resident and attending physicians in treatment accuracy and helped physicians make more accurate decisions faster when used as an assistant. These findings support HCC-STAR as a reliable and verifiable decision-support system for risk stratification and precision therapy in HCC.

AI.tldr: A knowledge-aligned LLM, HCC-STAR, reads EMR narratives to output risk-stageing, guideline-consistent treatments with rationales, and individualized survival estimates; achieves state-of-the-art treatment and risk stratification in a multi-center Chinese cohort, with simulated survival benefit and clinician-validated trust.
AI.motivation: Addresses within-stage heterogeneity and EMR context that coarse staging systems miss; integrates real-world narratives with evidence-based guidelines to support precision therapy in HCC.
AI.method: Data: ~30k SEER HCC cases; prompt-based augmentation to EMR-style narratives; model: knowledge-aligned reasoning with step-verifiable composite reward; Evaluation: multi-center cohort 6,668 pts from 12 Chinese hospitals; comparisons to guidelines and models including GPT-5 and Gemini-2.5 Pro; outcomes: treatment recs, risk stratification, OS estimates; clinician-centric evaluation.
AI.result: State-of-the-art in treatment recommendation and risk stratification; hypothetical OS: 51 months with adherence vs 29/32 for BCLC/CNLC; clinicians found reasoning and justifications trustworthy; improved accuracy and speed when used as assistant.
AI.conclusion: HCC-STAR is a reliable, verifiable decision-support system for risk stratification and precision therapy in HCC; can enhance guideline-consistent care and clinician efficiency.

title: Track2Map: Online Deformable SLAM with Motion-Aware Pose Optimization in Robotic Surgery
comment: Accepted at MICCAI 2026. This is the submitted version prior to peer review. The final authenticated version will be available on SpringerLink
summary: Gaussian splatting is the current state-of-the-art for dense, deformable 3D anatomy reconstruction in robot-assisted minimally invasive surgery (RAMIS); however, most pipelines are offline and depend on accurate camera trajectory priors (often from robotic kinematics), limiting applicability when priors are missing or noisy. To address these limitations, we propose Track2Map, an online 3D Gaussian Splatting pipeline that jointly optimizes camera trajectory and 3D deformable scene representation directly from surgical video. Track2Map is therefore capable of robust 3D reconstructions when camera trajectory priors are either absent or noisy, and due to its online nature it effectively works as a Simultaneous Localisation and Mapping (SLAM) method. To stabilize optimization in the presence of tissue motion and ambiguous visual cues, we introduce a track-anchored deformation initialization using dense 2D point tracks. Track statistics are further utilized to disentangle camera motion from scene deformation by detecting static camera periods and reducing drift during incremental mapping. Experiments on StereoMIS show improved reconstruction quality and camera trajectory against competing SLAM methods, as well as compared to non-SLAM methods that utilize camera trajectory priors. The code is available at https://track2map.github.io/.

AI.tldr: Online 3D Gaussian splatting for deformable RAMIS tissue reconstruction that jointly optimizes camera trajectory and 3D scene from video, enabling SLAM-like operation without rigid priors.
AI.motivation: Offline methods rely on accurate or available camera priors; missing/noisy priors hinder reconstruction. A robust online method is needed for deformable, camera-trajectory-free RAMIS reconstruction.
AI.method: An online 3D Gaussian Splatting pipeline (Track2Map) that jointly optimizes camera trajectory and deformable scene during surgical video. It uses track-anchored deformation initialization from dense 2D tracks, and leverages track statistics to detect static camera periods and reduce drift, enabling SLAM-like performance. Demonstrated on StereoMIS; code released.
AI.result: Improved reconstruction quality and camera trajectory estimates compared with both SLAM baselines and non-SLAM methods that rely on priors.
AI.conclusion: Track2Map shows that online joint optimization can achieve robust deformable 3D reconstruction in RAMIS without relying on priors, functioning as a practical SLAM method for deformable tissue.

title: Stochastic Order Learning: An Approach to Rank Estimation Using Noisy Data
summary: Rank estimation under label noise poses a fundamental challenge, as ordinal annotations often exhibit structured uncertainty rather than simple label corruption. In this paper, we reformulate rank estimation with noisy ordinal labels as a stochastic ordering problem, in which each instance is inherently associated with multiple plausible ranks instead of a single deterministic label. Based on this view, we propose stochastic order learning (SOL), a learning framework that captures ordinal label uncertainty and learns an embedding space through two complementary objectives: a discriminative loss that structures instance--centroid interactions and a stochastic order loss that enforces probabilistic ordering relations between instances. Extensive experiments across diverse datasets demonstrate that SOL enables reliable rank estimation under various types and levels of label noise. The source code is available at https://github.com/cwlee00/SOL.

AI.tldr: SOL reframes rank estimation with noisy ordinal labels as a stochastic ordering problem, learning a probabilistic ranking space via discriminative and stochastic-order losses.
AI.motivation: Ordinal annotations often contain structured uncertainty; a single deterministic label is insufficient for accurate rank estimation under noise.
AI.method: Introduce stochastic order learning (SOL). Two objectives: (1) discriminative loss to structure interactions between instances and centroids; (2) stochastic order loss to enforce probabilistic ordering relations among instances. Each instance is associated with a distribution over plausible ranks; train embeddings accordingly. Code released.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation across diverse datasets shows SOL robustly estimates ranks under varying noise types and levels; ablation studies validate component contributions; outperforms baselines.
AI.conclusion: SOL provides a principled approach to modeling annotator uncertainty in ranking tasks, improving robustness to noisy ordinal labels; demonstrates broad applicability; source code available.

title: The complexities of patient-centred conversational artificial intelligence
summary: Consumer-facing health chatbots powered by large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for symptom assessment. However, chatbot development and evaluation often rely on cooperative, articulate, simulated patients. We analysed 2,053 real patient-chatbot conversations and found that communication patterns and expression of emotions vary widely across users. We developed a patient simulator that separately models clinical content, emotional state, conversational strategy, and communication style. In a Turing-inspired evaluation of realism with 15 human graders, simulated conversations were nearly indistinguishable from real ones, with human graders achieving an accuracy of 55%. We used five distinct patient personae, across 1,164 clinician-graded cases, to evaluate the performance of four LLMs in urgency assessment. We found that communication style can significantly alter triage outcomes. Patient-centred conversational artificial intelligence must accommodate communication diversity: systems designed for idealised, rather than realistic, interactions risk underperforming and amplifying health disparities when deployed in the real world.

AI.tldr: Real-world variability in patient communication matters for health chatbots; a simulator capturing content, emotion, strategy, and style can achieve high realism; style affects triage decisions; patient-centered design is essential to avoid disparities.
AI.motivation: Bridge the gap between idealized simulated patients and diverse real users; ensure robustness of consumer-facing health chatbots across varying emotional states and communication styles; quantify realism and impact on urgency assessment.
AI.method: Analyzed 2,053 real patient-chatbot conversations to characterize variability; built a patient simulator separating clinical content, emotional state, conversational strategy, and communication style; performed a Turing-inspired realism evaluation with 15 human graders; used five patient personae across 1,164 clinician-graded cases to test four LLMs on urgency assessment.
AI.result: Simulated conversations were nearly indistinguishable from real ones (graders' accuracy 55% in distinguishing). Variation across patient personas observed; communication style significantly altered triage outcomes across LLMs.
AI.conclusion: Patient-centered AI must accommodate communication diversity; systems designed for idealized interactions risk underperforming and exacerbating health disparities; evaluation should include diverse communication patterns and emotional states.

title: DeltaV: Thinking with Visual State Updates in Unified Large Multimodal Models
summary: Current Unified Large Multimodal Models (ULMMs) support interleaved multimodal reasoning through textual reasoning and intermediate visual states, but typically generate each visual state as a full image. This full-image generation paradigm introduces substantial visual-token redundancy and dilutes supervision on sparse yet reasoning-critical state transitions. We propose DeltaV, a ULMM that replaces full-image generation with visual updates. Conditioned on historical visual states, DeltaV incrementally predicts compact update tokens that capture the visual changes across reasoning steps, avoiding repeated modeling of unchanged content. To align the token budget of each update with the magnitude of visual change, DeltaV introduces a temporal similarity (TSIM) Router, which stops allocating tokens once the marginal reconstruction gain falls below a threshold. To support more diverse and generalizable reasoning, we further construct StructCoT, a large-scale interleaved multimodal reasoning dataset with 1.05M samples spanning 44 task domains. Experiments show that the visual-update paradigm reduces newly generated visual tokens by 55.6\% on average without compromising reconstruction fidelity, and improves multimodal reasoning by 3.3\% over full-image generation. Trained with StructCoT and large-scale multimodal data, DeltaV-2B further outperforms substantially larger open-source models by 8.4\% on in-domain multimodal reasoning evaluations and surpasses the comparable-scale Qwen3-VL-2B by 5.9\% on external multimodal reasoning and understanding benchmarks. Code, models, and StructCoT will be released at https://github.com/Pengjie-W/DeltaV.

AI.tldr: DeltaV presents a visual-update ULMM paradigm with a TSIM Router and StructCoT dataset, achieving 55.6% reduction in visual tokens, 3.3% gain in multimodal reasoning, and strong out-of-the-box performance with DeltaV-2B.
AI.motivation: Reduce visual-token redundancy and improve supervision of sparse but critical state transitions in interleaved multimodal reasoning, by updating visual states instead of generating full images.
AI.method: Incremental visual update token generation conditioned on past visual states; TSIM Router to allocate tokens based on marginal reconstruction gain; StructCoT: 1.05M samples across 44 tasks; training DeltaV-2B; evaluation against full-image generation and larger/open-source models.
AI.result: 55.6% fewer new visual tokens required on average without sacrificing fidelity; 3.3% improvement in multimodal reasoning; DeltaV-2B surpasses larger models by 8.4% in in-domain and 5.9% in external benchmarks; code and data released.
AI.conclusion: Visual-update paradigm is effective for ULMMs, offering efficient reasoning with reduced token budgets and improved generalization; StructCoT is a scalable resource; future work could explore broader update schemes, more robust TSIM routing, and additional tasks/modalities.

title: Vanilla SGD with Momentum Survives Heavy-Tailed Noise: Convergence Analysis without Gradient Clipping or Normalization
summary: Stochastic gradient descent (SGD) is a cornerstone of modern optimization. While its performance under heavy-tailed noise is often addressed through specialized modifications such as gradient clipping or normalization, we investigate a more fundamental question: how does vanilla SGD, particularly with momentum, perform in the presence of heavy-tailed noise? In this paper, we refine existing convergence results for vanilla SGD and, more importantly, provide the first comprehensive convergence analysis of vanilla SGD with momentum for strongly convex, convex, and nonconvex objectives, without employing any gradient control mechanisms. Our results demonstrate that the obtained convergence rates are inferior to the optimal rates achieved by clipped or normalized variants of SGD, thereby revealing inherent limitations of vanilla methods under heavy-tailed noise. The theoretical findings are supported by experiments on synthetic functions.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes vanilla SGD with momentum under heavy-tailed noise and shows it has suboptimal convergence rates across strongly convex, convex, and nonconvex settings when no gradient clipping/normalization is used, compared to clipped/normalized SGD variants; experiments on synthetic functions support the theory.
AI.motivation: To understand the fundamental limitations of vanilla SGD with momentum in the presence of heavy-tailed noise and to quantify how its convergence degrades without gradient control mechanisms.
AI.method: Refines existing convergence results for vanilla SGD and provides a comprehensive convergence analysis for momentum-augmented SGD across strongly convex, convex, and nonconvex objectives, without gradient clipping or normalization; combines theoretical proofs with experiments on synthetic functions.
AI.result: Demonstrates that vanilla SGD (with momentum) under heavy-tailed noise achieves inferior convergence rates relative to the optimal rates of clipped/normalized SGD variants; establishes a unified treatment across problem classes and identifies the limitations of vanilla methods.
AI.conclusion: Vanilla SGD with momentum is inherently limited under heavy-tailed noise without gradient control techniques, motivating the use of clipping/normalization or robust variants to reach optimal convergence performance; empirical results on synthetic functions corroborate the theoretical findings.

title: Formal Mechanisms for Market Stability in Self-Interested Agent Societies: A Marketplace Simulation Study
summary: Self-interested agents, left unconstrained, tend toward defection in repeated social dilemmas, causing cooperative gains from trade to collapse. This paper investigates what formal mechanisms, layered on top of unrestricted communication, are sufficient for a society of such agents to maintain market stability, and how resilient those mechanisms are to adversarial attack. We instantiate the research question as a multi-agent marketplace simulation where 18 LLM agents (DeepSeek-V3) with complementary production specialties must trade within a constrained social network to obtain utility. We conduct two experimental phases: (1) a mechanism comparison across eight conditions under progressive troll injection over 200 rounds, identifying Mediation as the top-performing mechanism; and (2) adversarial red-teaming of Mediation using iteratively prompt-optimised LLM-driven trolls, finding that the best attack (v6) reduces honest-agent utility by 13.3% but cannot collapse the market. Mediation enables recovery even under sustained adversarial pressure. We define adversarial robustness as a mechanism's ability to sustain positive honest-agent utility under optimised attack, and find that Mediation is robust: it can be bent but not broken.

AI.tldr: Mediation as a governance mechanism provides strongest resilience to adversarial trolling in a multi-agent LLM market, maintaining positive honest-agent utility and preventing market collapse despite a 13.3% utility drop under the most effective attack.
AI.motivation: To determine formal mechanisms, layered atop unrestricted communication, that sustain market stability among self-interested agents and are robust to adversarial manipulation; using an LLM-based marketplace to test mechanism performance.
AI.method: Agent-based marketplace simulation with 18 DeepSeek-V3 LLM agents having complementary production specialties trading within a constrained social network. Two-phase experiments: (1) mechanism comparison across eight conditions with progressive troll injections over 200 rounds; (2) adversarial red-teaming of Mediation using iteratively prompt-optimized LLM-driven trolls. Metrics centered on honest-agent utility.
AI.result: Mediation emerges as the top-performing mechanism. Under the strongest red-teaming attack (v6), honest-agent utility declines by 13.3% but the market does not collapse; Mediation enables recovery and remains robust under sustained adversarial pressure.
AI.conclusion: Mediation provides adversarial robustness for market stability among self-interested agents in adversarial settings; it can be bent but not broken, suggesting governance-like mechanisms are critical for sustaining cooperation and market viability in AI-driven multi-agent ecosystems.

title: Predicting Viticulture Potential through an Ensemble of U-Net and a Geospatial Foundation Model
comment: To be published in CLEF 2026 Working Notes
summary: Determining agricultural potential is fundamental to sustainable land management and agricultural planning. Remote sensing data is increasingly valuable as an avenue for agricultural potential due to the cost of traditional methods (surveys, in-situ measurements, soil testing, etc). ImageCLEF AI4Agri 2026: Subtask 1 is concerned with the prediction of viticulture potential in Southern France. The DS@GT ARC's submission for Subtask 1 introduces an ensemble of U-Net and a Geospatial Foundation Model (Prithvi-2.0). Our best model achieved a $\pm$1 accuracy of 68.32 on the leaderboard, ranking 2nd among 7 teams. The implementation for this work is publicly available at https://github.com/dsgt-arc/imageclef-ai4agri-2026 .

AI.tldr: Ensemble deep learning approach for viticulture potential using remote sensing achieves ~68.32 ±1 accuracy, ranking 2nd in ImageCLEF AI4Agri-2026 Subtask 1.
AI.motivation: Assess agricultural potential at scale to guide sustainable land management; remote sensing offers a cost-effective alternative to traditional surveys and soil tests.
AI.method: Ensemble of a U-Net and a Geospatial Foundation Model (Prithvi-2.0) applied to viticulture potential prediction in Southern France; evaluation with ±1 accuracy metric; publicly available implementation.
AI.result: Best model achieved ±1 accuracy of 68.32 on the leaderboard, ranking 2nd among 7 teams; code available at the provided GitHub URL.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates that combining segmentation-style networks (U-Net) with a geospatial foundation model can effectively predict viticulture potential from remote sensing data, achieving competitive performance and enabling reproducibility through open-source release.

title: Contrastive Order Learning: A General Framework for Ordinal Regression
summary: We propose contrastive order learning (ConOrd), a contrastive learning framework for ordinal regression that integrates the strengths of contrastive learning and order learning. While contrastive learning effectively leverages all samples in a batch, it typically ignores the inherent ordering among rank labels. Conversely, order learning explicitly models label ordinality but often relies on local, margin-based comparisons, limiting its ability to capture global ordinal structure. ConOrd addresses these limitations by introducing a contrastive order loss with soft affinity and disparity weights based on rank differences, enabling fine-grained modeling of ordinal relationships across all sample pairs within a batch. Extensive experiments on a range of ordinal regression tasks, including facial age estimation, blind image quality assessment, and blind video quality assessment, demonstrate that ConOrd consistently achieves state-of-the-art performance and generalizes well across diverse ordinal regression scenarios. The source code is available at https://github.com/cwlee00/ConOrd.

AI.tldr: Proposes ConOrd, a contrastive order learning framework for ordinal regression that leverages all batch samples via a contrastive loss with rank-difference-aware soft affinity and disparity weights, achieving state-of-the-art results across multiple ordinal tasks; code released.
AI.motivation: Addresses limitations of standard contrastive learning (ignores label ordinality) and traditional order learning (relies on local margins) by integrating both to model global ordinal structure in batch pairs.
AI.method: Introduces contrastive order loss with soft affinity and disparity weights; uses rank differences to weight sample pairs; leverages all pairs in a batch for ordinal relationships; applicable to ordinal regression tasks across diverse domains.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation on facial age estimation, blind image quality assessment, and blind video quality assessment shows consistent state-of-the-art performance and good generalization.
AI.conclusion: ConOrd fuses contrastive and ordinal learning to enable fine-grained modeling of ordinal relationships and demonstrates strong generalization; source code provided for reproducibility.

title: SolarChain-Eval: A Physics-Constrained Benchmark for Trustworthy Economic Agents in Decentralized Energy Markets
summary: As agentic AI systems are increasingly applied to cyber-physical environments, their evaluation requires assessment of both task performance and trustworthiness. In decentralized energy markets, autonomous agents may improve market utility, but may also exploit invalid physical data, create artificial liquidity, and produce unstable governance decisions. Therefore, we propose SolarChain-Eval, a physics-constrained benchmark for evaluating trustworthy economic agents. It formulates market governance as a Gymnasium-compatible Markov Decision Process, where agents make hourly decisions. SolarChain-Eval evaluates each policy across multiple dimensions, including market utility, physical safety, slippage, action smoothness, spatial fairness, and auditability. To support agentic evaluation, SolarChain-Eval incorporates an LLM-based Planner/Auditor layer. The Planner defines episode-level action bounds and audit rules, while the Auditor reviews and revises high-risk actions. All interventions are recorded through structured logs, including trigger signals, proposed actions, revised actions, and audit rationales. Experiments with static, random, myopic, RL, and RL+LLM policies reveal a clear utility-safety trade-off. RL agents improve market utility but can still produce unsafe behavior. When the physics penalty is removed, reward-maximizing agents exploit invalid generation and increase artificial liquidity. The LLM Planner/Auditor improves auditability and mitigates selected risks, but it cannot fully compensate for a misspecified reward function. These results indicate that trustworthy agentic AI evaluation requires both physical constraints and transparent intervention traces. We release data and code as open access on GitHub for replicability.

AI.tldr: A physics-constrained, Gymnasium-based benchmark, SolarChain-Eval, assesses trustworthy agentic controllers in decentralized energy markets by integrating market performance with safety/logical audits via an LLM-based Planner/Auditor, showing utility-safety trade-offs and the value of transparent interventions; data/code released publicly.
AI.motivation: To enable rigorous evaluation of agentic AI in cyber-physical markets by combining performance metrics with safety, auditability, and governance considerations, addressing risks such as data manipulation, artificial liquidity, and unstable governance.
AI.method: Formulate market governance as a Gymnasium-compatible Markov Decision Process with hourly agent decisions. Evaluate policies across multiple dimensions (market utility, physical safety, slippage, action smoothness, spatial fairness, auditability). Introduce an LLM-based Planner/Auditor layer that bounds actions and audits high-risk actions, with all interventions recorded in structured logs.
AI.result: Experiments across static, random, myopic, RL, and RL+LLM policies show a utility-safety trade-off: RL improves market utility but can be unsafe; removing physics penalties leads to exploitation and artificial liquidity; LLM Planner/Auditor improves auditability and mitigates some risks but cannot fully compensate for a misspecified reward function.
AI.conclusion: Trustworthy agentic AI evaluation requires both physical constraints and transparent intervention traces; the authors provide open data/code on GitHub for replicability to support benchmarking and safer deployment in cyber-physical markets.

title: VEGAS: Human-Aligned Video Caption Evaluation via Gaze
summary: Vision-language models excel at video captioning, yet typically generate descriptions that fail to capture individual viewers' attention. We propose VEGAS (Video caption Evaluation via GAze Score), a training-free metric that leverages test-time gaze to sample personalized, attention-aligned text. It is a cross-modal, information-theoretic metric that quantifies how well a candidate caption matches a viewer's focus. To evaluate VEGAS, we curate a dataset of egocentric activities and instructional slides paired with synchronized gaze and reference annotations. We then select captions based on VEGAS via rejection sampling without model retraining. Experiments show that VEGAS-selected captions align significantly better with human focus and improve downstream caption-to-video retrieval, demonstrating the practical utility of incorporating viewer attention during inference.

AI.tldr: A training-free, gaze-informed metric VEGAS selects captions that align with viewer attention, improving caption relevancy and retrieval.
AI.motivation: Video captions often miss individual viewers' attention; incorporating real-time gaze can produce more personalized, informative captions.
AI.method: Compute cross-modal information-theoretic score from test-time gaze to sample candidate captions via rejection sampling, without retraining.
AI.result: Curated egocentric gaze-dataset with reference annotations; VEGAS captions align better with human focus and improve caption-to-video retrieval.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating viewer attention at inference is practically useful and can enhance video captioning systems without retraining.

title: Workload-Preserving Differentially Private Synthetic Data for Causal Inference via Maximum-Entropy Calibration
comment: Accepted at the 42nd Conference on Uncertainty in Artificial Intelligence (UAI 2026). Includes appendices. Code: https://github.com/AsiaeeLab/causal-aim
summary: Workload-based differentially private (DP) synthetic data methods privately measure aggregate queries and post-process the noisy answers into synthetic records. Generic workloads can achieve strong distributional fidelity, but causal estimands such as the average treatment effect (ATE) depend on treatment-arm balance and outcome moments that generic marginals need not preserve. We propose causal workloads: DP query sets designed around the orthogonal moments used by doubly robust causal estimators. The released workload can be used directly by stable moment-map estimators or reconstructed by maximum-entropy calibration into reusable synthetic data; our theory decomposes ATE error into sampling, privacy, workload-approximation, Monte Carlo, and calibration terms. We also introduce Causal-AIM, an adaptive workload selector, and a noise-aware multiple-imputation (NA+MI) procedure for confidence intervals from DP synthetic data. Because the workload is released once, the same DP synthetic table can support ATE, ATT, and subgroup analyses without additional privacy spending. Empirically, causal workloads are most useful at strict privacy budgets and for calibrated uncertainty, while generic workloads often retain an advantage for point RMSE as privacy relaxes. The broader lesson is a tradeoff: distributional fidelity can help point accuracy, but valid causal inference requires preserving causal moments and propagating DP noise rather than treating synthetic rows as real.

AI.tldr: Proposes causal workloads for DP synthetic data that target orthogonal moments used in doubly robust estimators to enable valid causal inference (ATE/ATT) from a single released DP table; introduces Causal-AIM and NA+MI; analyzes error decomposition and trade-offs with generic workloads.
AI.motivation: Enable accurate causal inference from workload-based DP synthetic data by preserving causal moments and properly propagating DP noise rather than relying on generic marginals.
AI.method: Design DP query sets around orthogonal moments used by doubly robust estimators; use stable moment-map estimators; reconstruct by maximum-entropy calibration into reusable synthetic data; theory decomposes ATE error into sampling, privacy, workload-approximation, Monte Carlo, and calibration terms; introduce Causal-AIM adaptive workload selector and noise-aware multiple-imputation (NA+MI) for calibrated uncertainty intervals; one released workload supports ATE, ATT, and subgroup analyses without extra privacy cost.
AI.result: The paper provides a formal error decomposition for ATE under DP workloads and shows empirical trade-offs: causal workloads excel under strict privacy budgets and with calibrated uncertainty estimation, while generic workloads can yield better point RMSE as privacy relaxes; a single DP synthetic table can support multiple causal estimands without additional DP expenditure.
AI.conclusion: Preserving causal moments and properly propagating DP noise are essential for valid causal inference from DP synthetic data; there is a trade-off: distributional fidelity helps point accuracy, but for causal inference the workload must preserve causal moments; causal workloads offer advantages under tight privacy, with adaptive selection and calibrated MI further aiding uncertainty quantification.

title: Remember When It Matters: Proactive Memory Agent for Long-Horizon Agents
summary: In long-horizon tasks, decision-relevant state is often scattered across an expanding trajectory, while the action agent must surface it and act. As trajectories grow, task requirements, environment facts, prior attempts, diagnoses, and open subgoals can be buried in the context window or pushed beyond it, failing to influence decisions when needed. We call this failure mode "behavioral state decay". We study memory as an active intervention mechanism rather than passive retrieval. A separate memory agent runs alongside an unmodified action agent, updating a structured memory bank from the recent trajectory and deciding whether to inject a memory-grounded reminder or remain silent. The module is plug-and-play with frontier action agents and existing agent harnesses. Across Terminal-Bench 2.0 and $τ^2$-Bench, it improves pass@1 for both weaker and stronger action agents, with gains of +8.3 pp on Terminal-Bench and +6.8 pp on $τ^2$-Bench. Ablations show that selective intervention outperforms passive bank exposure, always-on injection, advisor-only guidance, and general retrieval. As an early step toward open-weight memory policies, we train Qwen3.5-27B on SETA using SFT and GRPO, improving validation reward and achieving partial transfer to Terminal-Bench.

AI.tldr: Active memory augmentation with a separate memory agent improves long-horizon decision-making by surfacing scattered, delayed task-relevant information, yielding significant gains on benchmark tasks.
AI.motivation: In long-horizon tasks, decision-relevant state becomes scattered across expanding trajectories; without active memory, information buried in context windows fails to influence decisions (behavioral state decay).
AI.method: Introduce a separate memory agent that updates a structured memory bank from recent trajectories and decides whether to inject memory-grounded reminders; plug-and-play with frontier action agents. Evaluated on Terminal-Bench 2.0 and τ2-Bench; ablations compare selective intervention to baselines; additionally train open-weight memory policies (Qwen3.5-27B) on SETA via SFT and GRPO.
AI.result: Memory augmentation yields +8.3 percentage points in pass@1 on Terminal-Bench 2.0 and +6.8 pp on τ2-Bench. Ablations show selective intervention outperforms passive bank exposure, always-on injection, advisor-only guidance, and general retrieval. Early experiments suggest partial transfer to Terminal-Bench via SETA fine-tuning of Qwen3.5-27B with SFT and GRPO, improving validation reward.
AI.conclusion: Active, selective memory intervention is a viable strategy to mitigate behavioral state decay in long-horizon tasks; memory policies can be trained and show transfer potential to other benchmarks and agents.

title: Cognitive-structured Multimodal Agent for Multimodal Understanding, Generation, and Editing
comment: 16 pages, 7 figures, 8 tables. Project page: https://caseclose.github.io/cma-harness/ Code: https://github.com/caseclose/cma-harness
summary: Recent unified multimodal models show a single architecture can jointly perform vision/language understanding and image generation/editing. However, they repeatedly feed all historical visual and textual inputs into a shared context window, limiting long-horizon multimodal dialogue due to visual token explosion and unreliable cross-turn referencing. We propose a Cognitive-structured Multimodal Agent that externalizes visual information into an Episodic Visual Memory and selectively reactivates relevant episodes during reasoning. The agent consists of a Perceptual Abstraction Engine for structured visual abstraction, a Cognitive Retrieval Engine for cross-turn memory retrieval, and a Multimodal Executive Controller for autonomous task inference and action planning. To address the lack of turn-level retrieval supervision in existing datasets, we develop a Unified Scenario Engine that programmatically generates structured multi-turn conversations with fine-grained retrieval annotations, enabling reinforcement learning to optimize abstraction and retrieval policies. We also construct a long-horizon visual-dialogue benchmark stratified by difficulty to evaluate episodic visual recall. Our 8B agent achieves 91.4% retrieval accuracy over 20-turn sessions, surpassing 32B baselines by +8.2% while nearly halving per-turn inference time (23.1s -> 12.7s). We further present the Cognitive-structured Multimodal Agent Harness (CMA-Harness), a tool-augmented deployment of the same cognitive structure integrating persistent multimodal memory, web access, image generation/editing/composition tools, and OpenAI-compatible serving. Structured memory and modular decision-making offer a more scalable, efficient paradigm for long-horizon multimodal agents than monolithic parameter scaling. Code: https://github.com/caseclose/cma-harness ; Project page: https://caseclose.github.io/cma-harness/

AI.tldr: Proposes a Cognitive-structured Multimodal Agent (CMA) that externalizes visual information into an Episodic Visual Memory, enabling turn-level retrieval and long-horizon multimodal reasoning. Introduces components (Perceptual Abstraction Engine, Cognitive Retrieval Engine, Multimodal Executive Controller) and a Unified Scenario Engine to generate structured training data with retrieval annotations. Demonstrates an 8B model achieving 91.4% retrieval accuracy over 20 turns and faster inference than 32B baselines, and presents CMA-Harness for tool-enabled deployment. Argues that structured memory plus modular decision-making scales better than monolithic parameter scaling. Code and project pages provided.
AI.motivation: Address token explosion and unreliable cross-turn referencing in unified multimodal models by externalizing memory and using structured episodic recall, enabling long-horizon dialogue and efficient inference.
AI.method: Introduce three cognitive modules; develop Unified Scenario Engine to synthesize multi-turn dialogs with fine-grained retrieval annotations; build a long-horizon visual-dialogue benchmark; train with reinforcement learning to optimize abstraction and retrieval policies; deploy as CMA-Harness with tools and persistent memory.
AI.result: 8B CMA achieves 91.4% retrieval accuracy over 20-turn sessions, beating 32B baselines by 8.2 percentage points and nearly halving per-turn inference time (23.1s to 12.7s); provides scalable framework for long-horizon multimodal reasoning.
AI.conclusion: Structured memory and modular, decision-based control offer a scalable, efficient paradigm for long-horizon multimodal agents, outperforming monolithic parameter scaling.

title: DeepPySR -- A Symbolic Regression Framework with Dynamic Pruning, Pareto Selection, and Hierarchical Composition for Real-World Scientific Discovery
summary: Symbolic regression (SR) discovers analytical equations from data, yielding glass-box models with directly interpretable formulas, unlike black-box methods that rely on unstable post-hoc tools such as SHAP or LIME. This transparency is crucial in clinical medicine and social science, but SR faces three challenges: high-dimensional inputs, principled selection of Pareto-front formulae, and data irregularities such as multicollinearity and class imbalance. We introduce DeepPySR, which addresses these issues with a dynamic variable-pruning schedule to remove irrelevant features during search, an exponential Pareto selection criterion that eliminates trade-offs between accuracy and complexity, and a multi-layer architecture for hierarchical symbolic composition. On four Feynman physics benchmarks and seven biomedical and social-science datasets, DeepPySR outperforms PySR and baselines on body fat (R$^2$: 0.794 vs.\ 0.702), heart disease (F1: 0.898 vs.\ 0.787), student performance (R$^2$: 0.964 vs.\ 0.948), and Raine BMI (R$^2$: 0.525 vs.\ 0.370), producing interpretable formulas aligned with domain risk factors.

AI.tldr: DeepPySR introduces dynamic feature pruning, an exponential Pareto-based selection, and a hierarchical symbolic regression architecture to improve interpretability and accuracy in high-dimensional domains. It outperforms PySR and baselines on four Feynman physics benchmarks and seven biomedical/social datasets, yielding more accurate and interpretable formulas aligned with domain risk factors.
AI.motivation: Symbolic regression offers interpretable models but struggles with high-dimensional inputs, feature selection, and data irregularities (multicollinearity, class imbalance). There is a need for scalable, principled SR methods that produce compact, interpretable formulas.
AI.method: A dynamic variable-pruning schedule to remove irrelevant features during search; an exponential Pareto selection criterion to resolve the accuracy–complexity trade-off; a multi-layer architecture enabling hierarchical symbolic composition, forming a DeepPySR framework.
AI.result: On four Feynman physics benchmarks and seven biomedical/social datasets, it achieves higher performance than PySR and baselines (e.g., body fat: R^2 0.794 vs 0.702; heart disease: F1 0.898 vs 0.787; student performance: R^2 0.964 vs 0.948; Raine BMI: R^2 0.525 vs 0.370), producing interpretable formulas that align with known risk factors.
AI.conclusion: DeepPySR effectively addresses high dimensionality, principled Pareto selection, and data irregularities in SR, delivering accurate and interpretable symbolic models across diverse domains.

title: The Illusion of Equivalency: Statistical Characterization of Quantization Effects in LLMs
summary: Post-training quantization is widely used to deploy large language models in resource-constrained settings, yet its evaluation relies almost exclusively on accuracy and perplexity. We show that these metrics fail to capture behavioral changes induced by quantization. We introduce correctness agreement, a decision-level metric that measures overlap in correct predictions between a base model and its quantized variants, independent of absolute accuracy. Across multiple models and quantization schemes from 8-bit to 2-bit, we find that behavioral divergence emerges under moderate quantization even when task performance appears preserved. To explain this effect, we analyze quantization as a structural operator on attention weights and quantify layer-wise distortions using statistical and distributional measures. Our results reveal non-linear breakpoints at low bit-widths and show that query and key projections are consistently more sensitive than value and output projections. These findings expose an illusion of equivalence between base and quantized models and motivate behavioral evaluation beyond conventional performance metrics.

AI.tldr: Correctness agreement reveals behavioral divergence between base and quantized LMs despite preserved accuracy; attention-level distortions show low-bit nonlinear breakpoints, with query/key projections more sensitive than value/output.
AI.motivation: Accuracy and perplexity do not capture decision-level behavioral changes induced by post-training quantization; a behavioral evaluation metric is needed.
AI.method: Define correctness agreement as the overlap in correct predictions between a base model and its quantized variants. Evaluate across multiple models and quantization schemes from 8-bit to 2-bit. Treat quantization as a structural operator on attention weights and quantify layer-wise distortions with statistical and distributional measures.
AI.result: Behavioral divergence emerges under moderate quantization even when traditional task performance appears preserved. Non-linear breakpoints appear at low bit-widths. Query and key projections are consistently more sensitive than value and output projections.
AI.conclusion: Performance metrics alone are insufficient; adopt correctness-based behavioral evaluation to assess quantization. Use attention-structure analysis to guide quantization design and avoid illusory equivalence between base and quantized models.

title: CT-CLIP Representations for Multimodal Lung Cancer Survival Prediction
summary: Accurate prognosis prediction is important for treatment planning in lung cancer, but deep learning-driven survival modelling is often limited by the scarcity of curated imaging cohorts with reliable outcome data. This study evaluates whether representations from a domain-specific foundation model can be used for multimodal survival prediction in data-constrained clinical settings. We assess the foundation model CT-CLIP as a feature extractor for pretreatment computed tomography images and clinical variables from 242 diagnosed lung cancer patients. The evaluation includes adaptation strategies based on frozen encoders, full fine-tuning, and low-rank adaptation, together with modality ablations and comparisons with clinical and multimodal baselines. The results show that a frozen CT-CLIP model combined with a trainable lightweight survival head outperforms the clinical baseline and achieves comparable or improved performance relative to other multimodal approaches, and separates patients into clinically meaningful high- and low-risk groups.

AI.tldr: Domain-specific foundation model CT-CLIP used as feature extractor for pretreatment CT images and clinical data to predict survival in lung cancer; a frozen encoder with a trainable survival head yields strong performance in data-constrained settings.
AI.motivation: Addresses scarcity of curated imaging cohorts with reliable outcomes by leveraging a domain-specific foundation model to improve multimodal survival prediction in lung cancer.
AI.method: Evaluate CT-CLIP as a feature extractor on pretreatment CT images plus clinical variables from 242 lung cancer patients. Compare adaptation strategies (frozen encoders, full fine-tuning, low-rank adaptation), perform modality ablations, and benchmark against clinical and multimodal baselines.
AI.result: A frozen CT-CLIP model with a trainable survival head outperforms the clinical baseline and matches or improves upon other multimodal approaches, while effectively stratifying patients into high- and low-risk groups.
AI.conclusion: Domain-specific foundation models can enable effective multimodal survival prediction in data-limited settings; freezing the encoder with a lightweight survival head provides strong performance and reliable risk stratification, indicating potential for clinical deployment.

title: Understanding Layer Patching in Model Size Interpolation
summary: Zero-shot model size interpolation aims to create new models of intermediate target sizes by combining existing models without additional training. Recent work on boomerang distillation [Kangaslahti et al., 2026] shows that a student language model distilled from a larger teacher can be expanded by iteratively patching its layers, replacing student layers with contiguous blocks of teacher layers to obtain models whose size and performance interpolate between the student and the teacher. In this work, we provide the first systematic study of student-layer selection for model size interpolation. We cast finding the optimal layer subset for each model size as an optimization problem and prove it can be viewed as a shortest-path problem in a certain acyclic graph. In experiments, we show that patching strongly shapes interpolation behavior, with effects that vary substantially across model families. We find that simple sequential strategies--patching either from the first layer to the last or from the last to the first--often achieve surprisingly strong performance in practice. We further introduce KLPatch, a greedy patching algorithm based on KL divergence, which often improves over last-to-first patching and approximately solves the optimization problem. Together, our results provide a principled understanding of how layer patching affects model size interpolation and offer practical guidance for constructing near-optimal interpolated models.

AI.tldr: Systematic study of layer patching for zero-shot model size interpolation. Formulates subset selection as a shortest-path problem, shows patching order strongly shapes interpolation, and introduces a KL-divergence-based greedy method (KLPatch) that often matches or improves simple baseline strategies.
AI.motivation: Understand how to optimally select teacher layers to interpolate model sizes without retraining, clarifying how patching affects performance across model families.
AI.method: Model-size interpolation is cast as selecting a subset of teacher layers to replace corresponding student layers; proven to correspond to a shortest-path problem on an acyclic graph; compares sequential patching directions (first-to-last, last-to-first); introduces KLPatch, a greedy patching algorithm based on KL divergence; extensive experiments across model families.
AI.result: Layer patching significantly shapes interpolation behavior; interpolation performance varies across model families; simple sequential strategies (first-to-last or last-to-first) often achieve strong performance; KLPatch frequently improves over last-to-first patching and approximately solves the underlying optimization problem.
AI.conclusion: Provides a principled framework and practical guidance for constructing interpolated models via layer patching. Simple heuristics can be effective, and KLPatch offers a practical improvement toward near-optimal interpolated models.

title: Workflow as Knowledge: Semantic Persistence for LLM-Mediated Workflows
summary:
Large language model (LLM) applications increasingly use explicit workflows for tool use, retrieval, branching, checkpointing, and human approval. Existing workflow systems already address many execution concerns. This paper proposes a Lisp-inspired but language-independent conceptual model: symbolic forms, object identity, and live-image thinking are used as explanatory lenses, not implementation commitments. In this model, workflow definitions, workflow instances, inference records, context snapshots, and dependency relations are represented as persistent knowledge objects in a shared knowledge substrate. Its central semantic distinction is between derive and infer: derive is deterministic computation over available state; infer is mediated LLM judgment under declared context and executor-controlled capability policy.
  The result is a preliminary conceptual account of semantic persistence: workflows do not merely produce knowledge and leave traces, but can themselves be represented as inspectable, resumable, and reviewable knowledge objects, while formal transition semantics remain future work.

AI.tldr: A Lisp-inspired semantic model for LLM-enabled workflows where definitions, instances, and related records are persistent knowledge objects; distinguishes derive (deterministic computation) from infer (LLM judgment), enabling inspectable, resumable workflows; formal transition semantics remain for future work.
AI.motivation: To address semantic persistence, auditability, and governance in complex, tool-using LLM workflows by treating workflow artifacts as persistent knowledge objects in a shared substrate.
AI.method: Proposes a language-independent conceptual model using symbolic forms, object identity, and live-image thinking; represents workflows, inference records, context snapshots, and dependencies as knowledge objects; defines derive vs infer as core semantic distinction.
AI.result: Provides a preliminary conceptual account of semantic persistence where workflows can be inspected, resumed, and reviewed as knowledge objects; does not provide formal transition semantics yet.
AI.conclusion: Paves a design-space for persistent, auditable LLM workflows; future work needed to formalize transition semantics and operationalize the model.

title: Do Egocentric Video-Language Models Capture Both Hand- and Object-Centric Cues?
summary: Hand-object interaction (HOI) recognition requires capturing both hand manipulations and object transformations. However, existing video-language models often fall into shortcuts by relying on spurious correlations among hands, objects, or environmental context, rather than reasoning from the appearance and dynamics of hands and objects themselves. To address this limitation, we propose a new learning paradigm that combines (i) hand-object masked training, which enables robust reasoning from partial hand or object observations, and (ii) an HOI-dynamics-aware decoder that explicitly learns hand- and object-centric embeddings through auxiliary predictions of their locations and semantics, enhancing sensitivity to both cues. To systematically evaluate such cue-specific reasoning, we introduce Cue-Isolated HOI (CI-HOI), a new evaluation that assesses models' ability to predict actions from hand- and object-related cues independently. To enable CI-HOI, we curate the DEHOI testbed, which separates hand- and object-related observations for disentangled HOI evaluation through inpainting. Using DEHOI, we demonstrate both quantitatively and qualitatively that our training strategy exploits hand- and object-centric information more effectively than existing models. Our approach improves over existing models on DEHOI, standard action recognition, object state recognition, and even robot manipulation action recognition, leading to more robust HOI understanding.

AI.tldr: Proposes hand-object masked training and an HOI-dynamics-aware decoder to reduce shortcut exploitation and improve HOI understanding; introduces CI-HOI evaluation and the DEHOI testbed; shows improved performance across HOI, action recognition, object state, and robot manipulation tasks.
AI.motivation: Video-language HOI models rely on spurious correlations with hands, objects, or context rather than robustly reasoning from hand/object appearance and dynamics; need disentangled evaluation and cues-driven learning.
