AI.method: Combine hand-object masked training with an HOI-dynamics-aware decoder that uses auxiliary tasks to predict hand/object locations and semantics; introduce CI-HOI to test cue-specific reasoning; curate DEHOI testbed to disentangle hand/object observations via inpainting; evaluate on DEHOI and other tasks.
AI.result: Demonstrates that the training strategy yields improved hand- and object-centric cue utilization; outperforms baselines on DEHOI, standard action recognition, object state recognition, and robot manipulation action recognition.
AI.conclusion: Presents a more robust HOI understanding paradigm by enforcing cue-focused reasoning and disentangled evaluation; generalizes across domains including robotics.

title: Open-ended Multi-agent Autocurricula via Visual Inspection of Policies with Multi-modal LLMs
summary: Open-ended curricula in Reinforcement Learning (RL) aim to train generally-capable agents by identifying tasks that facilitate learning increasingly complex skills. A major challenge when designing such curricula is assessing task difficulty relative to the agent's current learning progress. While previous work has explored using scalar task scores or textual summaries of the agent's behavior, here we study a different approach: directly inspecting policy behavior via recorded episode videos. We introduce a simple yet effective instantiation of this approach which leverages a Video Language Model (VLM) to both process these videos and provide curriculum recommendations, which we call Visual Inspection of Policies (VIP). Since videos can naturally contain any number of controllable agents, we empirically study VIP on the StarCraft Multi-Agent Challenge (SMAC). We show that even with a lightweight and openly accessible VLM (VideoLLaMa2-7B), VIP can use policy videos to generate more effective curricula than both its text-only ablation and methods that rely on scalar task scores.

AI.tldr: A video-based policy inspection approach (VIP) using a VLM to guide RL curricula, achieving better task sequencing than text-only or scalar-score baselines on SMAC.
AI.motivation: Open-ended RL curricula face difficulty in judging task difficulty relative to the agent’s progress; existing scalar scores or textual summaries may be insufficient to capture nuanced policy behavior.
AI.method: Introduce Visual Inspection of Policies (VIP) that uses a Video Language Model (VideoLLaMa2-7B) to process policy videos and generate curriculum recommendations; applied to StarCraft Multi-Agent Challenge (SMAC); compare against a text-only ablation and scalar-task-score baselines.
AI.result: VIP-derived curricula lead to more effective learning progress than baselines; even a lightweight VLM can outperform scalar/text-based signals in shaping curriculum.
AI.conclusion: Directly inspecting policy behavior through videos with a VLM is a viable and effective approach for designing curricula in RL, with potential applicability beyond single-agent settings.

title: AUTOPILOT VQA: Benchmarking Vision-Language Models for Incident-Centric Dashcam Understanding
summary: Recent advances in Vision-Language Models, Large Language Models, and Multimodal Large Language Models have improved autonomous driving tasks such as scene understanding, decision making, trajectory prediction, and visual question answering. However, evaluating whether these models can reliably reason about safety-critical incidents remains challenging. To address this gap, we present AUTOPILOT-VQA, an incident-centric visual question answering benchmark for dashcam video understanding. The dataset evaluates different systems through structured questions designed around real-world driving incidents and near-incidents. The benchmark covers diverse safety-relevant categories, including weather and lighting conditions, traffic environment, road layout, road surface state, signage, involved entities, accident occurrence, impact location, and avoidability-related reasoning. By requiring models to answer grounded questions about both contextual scene properties and event-level incident details, AUTOPILOT-VQA moves beyond object recognition toward temporally grounded, safety-aware reasoning. The dataset is released as part of the AUTOPILOT CVPR 2026 competition and provides a standardized benchmark for assessing the reliability of autonomous driving systems in different scenarios. Our benchmark support developments for more interpretable, robust, and safety-conscious vision-language systems for real-world autonomous driving.

AI.tldr: Introduces AUTOPILOT-VQA, an incident-centric visual question answering benchmark for dashcam videos to assess safety-critical reasoning in autonomous driving; covers weather, traffic, road, signage, incidents, and avoidability; aimed at temporally grounded, safety-aware reasoning; released for the AUTOPILOT CVPR 2026 competition.
AI.motivation: Current vision-language and multimodal benchmarks primarily evaluate recognition and generic reasoning. Autonomous driving requires temporally grounded, safety-critical reasoning about real incidents and near-incidents; a standardized benchmark is needed to evaluate reliability and safety-conscious behavior.
AI.method: Construct a dashcam video VQA benchmark with structured questions centered on real-world driving incidents and near-incidents. Annotate ground-truth contextual properties and event-level details across safety-relevant categories (weather/lighting, traffic environment, road layout, surface state, signage, involved entities, accident occurrence, impact location, avoidability). Requires grounded answers about scene properties and incident details.
AI.result: The paper introduces the AUTOPILOT-VQA benchmark and dataset and positions it as a standardized evaluation tool for safety-critical reasoning in autonomous driving; the abstract does not report empirical results.
AI.conclusion: AUTOPILOT-VQA advances safer, more interpretable vision-language systems for real-world driving by enabling evaluation of temporally grounded, incident-focused reasoning across diverse scenarios.

title: Beyond wheelchairs and blindfolds: Investigating disability stereotypes in T2I models with INCLUDE-BENCH
summary: Text-to-image (T2I) models have been shown to exhibit social biases. Prior work has mainly focused on gender, skin tone, and cultural representation within restricted occupational associations, and emerging benchmarks increasingly incorporate these dimensions. However, disability remains systematically underexplored. Current evaluation practices often fail to align with sociologically grounded definitions of stereotyping, limiting principled assessment of representational harms toward people with disabilities (PWD). To address this, we introduce INCLUDE-BENCH, the first large-scale benchmark for evaluating disability-related bias in T2I models. INCLUDE-BENCH comprises 119K generated images based on prompt design across multiple bias dimensions and both static and dynamic contexts. We evaluate 15 open-source and 2 closed-source models. Our key findings reveal that: (1) mobility-impaired and default disability prompts predominantly yield wheelchair depictions across all models; (2) disability-conditioned generations consistently exhibit less diversity; (3) stereotypical portrayals demonstrate stronger disability-text alignment; and (4) we introduce the Stereotype Content Model (SCM) Score, demonstrating that T2I models reflect real-world stereotypical associations.

AI.tldr: Introduces INCLUDE-BENCH, the first large-scale benchmark for disability-related bias in text-to-image (T2I) models. It analyzes 119K generated images across multiple prompts and contexts, evaluating 18 models (15 open-source, 2 closed-source). Key findings: wheelchair depictions dominate for mobility-impaired and default disability prompts; reduced diversity in disability-conditioned generations; stronger alignment between disability traits and stereotypes; an SCM Score showing T2I models mirror real-world stereotypes.
AI.motivation: Addresses a critical gap in bias benchmarks by focusing on disability representation, which has been underexplored and inadequately assessed due to sociological misalignments in existing metrics. Aims to provide principled, scalable measurement of representational harms toward people with disabilities in T2I systems.
AI.method: Construct prompts designed to probe disability-related biases across static and dynamic contexts. Generate 119K images using 15 open-source and 2 closed-source T2I models. Quantify biases via diverse metrics, including the Stereotype Content Model (SCM) Score, and analyze diversity, disability-prominence, and text-image alignment.
AI.result: Four main findings: (1) mobility-impaired and default disability prompts yield predominantly wheelchair depictions; (2) disability-conditioned generations show less diversity; (3) stereotypical portrayals exhibit stronger disability-text alignment; (4) SCM Score indicates T2I models reflect real-world stereotypical associations.
AI.conclusion: INCLUDE-BENCH provides a principled, scalable framework for evaluating disability bias in T2I models, enabling targeted mitigation and informing dataset curation and model development. It highlights pervasive harms and sets the stage for future work on counter-stereotypical generation and diversity enhancement.

title: PIT-SUN: A Deployable Empirical Marginal Transform Framework with Expectation-Consistent Recovery for Regression in Recommender Systems
summary: Estimating original-space conditional expectations is central to value-driven recommender systems, including dwell time, GMV, and LTV forecasting. Standard MSE is expectation-consistent in principle, but its gradients become unstable on heavy-tailed, zero-inflated, and multimodal targets, causing mean collapse and tail shrinkage. Target transformation alleviates this scale conflict, yet any useful nonlinear marginal transform loses expectation consistency under direct inversion. This is not an implementation oversight: a direct inverse-transform estimator is universally expectation-consistent only when the inverse transform is affine, which cannot simultaneously provide bounded tail compression. Existing conditionally linear recovery methods restore expectation consistency, but still leave open which coordinate, inverse lookup, recovery base, and deployment monitor should be selected for sparse complex marginals. We propose \textbf{P}robability-\textbf{I}ntegral-\textbf{TranS}formed \textbf{Un}biased recovery (\textbf{PIT-SUN}), a deployable empirical marginal recovery framework. PIT-SUN uses one empirical marginal table to define a bounded normal-score coordinate, its inverse-quantile lookup, a variance-controlled recovery base, and drift monitoring, then applies multiplicative SUN recovery to estimate the original-space expectation instead of directly inverting transformed predictions. Experiments on synthetic distributions, public benchmarks, large-scale industrial datasets, and online deployment show robust improvements in point accuracy, calibration, and ranking quality with lightweight deployment overhead.

AI.tldr: PIT-SUN: a deployable empirical marginal recovery framework for estimating original-space expectations in recommender systems, using probability-integral transformed coordinates and multiplicative SUN recovery to achieve unbiased, stable estimates with improved accuracy, calibration, and ranking.
AI.motivation: Mitigate gradient instability and expectation inconsistency of MSE on heavy-tailed, zero-inflated, multimodal targets; provide a practical, deployment-friendly method for recovering original-space expectations without affine inverse transforms.
AI.method: Propose PIT-SUN. Build a bounded normal-score coordinate from a single empirical marginal table. Define an inverse-quantile lookup, a variance-controlled recovery base, and drift monitoring. Apply multiplicative SUN recovery to transform predictions back to original space, ensuring unbiasedness and stable tails.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation across synthetic distributions, public benchmarks, large-scale industrial datasets, and live deployment shows improvements in point accuracy, calibration, and ranking with lightweight overhead.
AI.conclusion: PIT-SUN delivers a practical, expectation-consistent recovery mechanism for complex marginals, balancing tail behavior and deployability; suitable for value-driven recommender tasks.

title: Using AI-based Learning Assistants in Higher Education: A Large-Scale Descriptive Analysis
summary: In this study, we present a large-scale descriptive analysis of the use of an AI-based learning assistant (Syntea) in higher education. Based on objective log data from 77,543 students enrolled in distance studies, we examine usage patterns across gender, age group, study cluster, degree, and study mode. To date, existing research on educational chatbots has largely relied on comparatively small samples and self-reported survey data, while large-scale evidence on actual usage behavior remains limited. Our findings show that Syntea is already embedded in the study routines of many learners, but that usage differs across demographic and structural contexts. By identifying these patterns, our study provides an empirical basis for the further development of AI-based learning support and contributes a large-scale analysis of educational chatbot usage in higher education.

AI.tldr: Large-scale descriptive study of an AI learning assistant (Syntea) using log data from 77,543 distance-learning students; finds integration into study routines with usage varying by demographic and structural factors, addressing the gap of large-scale usage evidence.
AI.motivation: Fill the gap in the literature where educational chatbot research relies on small samples and self-reports; provide empirical, scalable usage patterns to inform AI-based learning support development.
AI.method: Descriptive analysis of objective learning-management-system log data from 77,543 distance-education students; analyze usage across gender, age group, study cluster, degree, and study mode.
AI.result: Syntea is embedded in many learners' routines, but usage varies across demographic and structural contexts, revealing identifiable usage patterns.
AI.conclusion: Provides an empirical baseline for developing AI-based learning supports and contributes a large-scale analysis of educational chatbot usage in higher education.

title: Whareformer: Learning to Track What is Where in Long Egocentric Videos
comment: Accepted at ECCV 2026. Project Webpage: https://jacobchalk.github.io/Whareformer/
summary:
The recently established 'Out of Sight, Not out of Mind' (OSNOM) task for egocentric videos focuses on tracking objects that are moved by the camera wearer, online, maintaining knowledge of instance locations throughout the video even when they leave the field of view or become heavily occluded. In this paper, we propose the first learning-based solution to the OSNOM task: Whareformer, a transformer-based model with two components: an updatable memory of established tracks and a track assignment module that associates observations with existing tracks in a feed-forward manner. Whareformer jointly reasons over evolving object appearance (what) and updated 3D location (where), and employs a dedicated New Track token to reason about novel objects.
  Thanks to its design choices of using relative distances and evolving track representations, Whareformer is trained on a small set of 56 videos but achieves SOTA performance on 260 long test videos from three datasets: EPIC-KITCHENS-100 (unseen videos), IT3DEgo, and HD-EPIC, with significant absolute improvements over prior work.

AI.tldr: Whareformer is a learning-based OSNOM solution using a transformer with an updatable memory of tracks and a feed-forward track assignment module, including a New Track token, achieving state-of-the-art performance on 260 long videos across three datasets with limited training data.
AI.motivation: OSNOM requires online, robust tracking of objects moved by the camera wearer, maintaining instance identities through occlusions and view changes. The problem is data-efficient learning and generalization across diverse environments, with little annotated data.
AI.method: A transformer-based model with two components: (1) an updatable memory of established tracks, and (2) a feed-forward track assignment module that associates observations with existing tracks. The model jointly reasons about appearance (what) and 3D location (where) and uses a dedicated New Track token to represent potential novel objects. It leverages relative distances and evolving track representations and is trained on only 56 videos but evaluated on 260 long videos across EPIC-KITCHENS-100, IT3DEgo, and HD-EPIC.
AI.result: Achieves state-of-the-art performance on 260 long test videos from three datasets, with significant absolute improvements over prior work, despite being trained on a small dataset.
AI.conclusion: First learning-based solution to the OSNOM task, Whareformer demonstrates effective online multi-object tracking under occlusion and leaving the field of view by reasoning over evolving appearance and 3D location, and generalizes well across unseen videos and multiple datasets.

title: RhyMix: A Lightweight Adaptive Multi-Rhythm Network for Long-Term Time Series Forecasting
summary: Real-world time series exhibit complex dynamics characterized by multiple simultaneous temporal patterns: short-term fluctuations, periodic seasonal cycles, long-term trends, and irregular abrupt changes. However, many existing forecasting architectures rely on single-path temporal modeling--transformers capture long-range dependencies but smooth local variations, convolutions capture local patterns but have limited receptive fields, and linear models are efficient but cannot capture nonlinear dynamics. To address this, we introduce RhyMix (RHYthm MIXture), a hybrid neural architecture designed around a parallel dual-path modeling paradigm with adaptive gating mechanisms. RhyMix integrates two complementary encoding branches: (i) a Cyclic Path that incorporates explicit seasonal inductive bias through learnable cyclic embeddings, capturing predictable rhythmic patterns; and (ii) a lightweight Multi-Scale Temporal Convolutional Network with Channel Attention Path that employs multi-scale depthwise dilated convolutions to capture temporal dependencies across different receptive fields. A key innovation is the use of adaptive gating at multiple levels: a path gate dynamically combines four specialized forecasting heads (Direct, Trend-Seasonal Decomposition, Local Convolution, and Periodic Fusion) per sample and channel, while a hybrid gate adaptively balances the Cyclic and MSTCN-CA Paths based on input characteristics. This design ensures the model adapts to specific temporal patterns while maintaining linear complexity in sequence length, channels, and prediction horizon. Across extensive benchmarks on 12 real-world datasets for long-term forecasting, RhyMix achieves state-of-the-art performance on 10 of 12 datasets. The model remains lightweight (~40K params) with linear complexity and low-latency inference (<5ms),suitable for resource-constrained edge devices and real-time deployment.

AI.tldr: Hybrid dual-path RhyMix architecture for long-horizon time-series forecasting; adaptive gating enables per-sample/channel blending of specialized heads; includes Cyclic Path with seasonal embeddings and MSTCN-CA path; achieves SOTA on 10 of 12 real-world datasets with ~40k params and <5ms latency.
AI.motivation: Real-world time series have multiple simultaneous temporal patterns (short-term fluctuations, seasonal cycles, long-term trends, abrupt changes). Single-path models (transformers, convolutions, linear) struggle to jointly model these components efficiently. A parallel, adaptive, low-complexity approach is needed.
AI.method: Parallel dual-path design: (i) Cyclic Path with learnable cyclic embeddings to capture predictable seasonal rhythms; (ii) Lightweight Multi-Scale Temporal Convolutional Network with Channel Attention (MSTCN-CA) using multi-scale depthwise dilated convolutions. Adaptive gating comprises a Path Gate that blends four forecasting heads (Direct, Trend-Seasonal Decomposition, Local Convolution, Periodic Fusion) per sample and channel, and a Hybrid Gate that balances Cyclic vs MSTCN-CA paths by input characteristics. Claims linear complexity in sequence length, channels, and horizon; ~40k params; <5ms inference.
AI.result: Empirical validation on 12 real-world datasets for long-term forecasting; RhyMix achieves state-of-the-art on 10 of 12 datasets; remains lightweight (~40K parameters) with linear scalability and low-latency inference suitable for edge and real-time deployment.
AI.conclusion: The architecture provides an adaptive, efficient solution that captures diverse temporal patterns via parallel specialized pathways and per-sample/channel gating. Its linear complexity and small footprint make it viable for resource-constrained settings, with strong empirical performance on multiple real-world benchmarks.

title: Ideas Have Genomes: Benchmarking Scientific Lineage Reasoning and Lineage-Grounded Idea Generation
summary: Scientific ideas rarely start from a blank page. They inherit mechanisms, repair known limitations, and recombine pieces of earlier work, much like biological genomes. Current benchmarks still say little about whether AI systems can follow this inheritance structure. We present IdeaGene-Bench (IG-Bench), a benchmark for scientific lineage reasoning and lineage-grounded idea generation. IG-Bench is organized around the IdeaGene framework: each paper or proposal is represented as a set of minimal, typed, evidence-grounded Idea Genome objects, and a GenomeDiff aligns these objects to record inheritance, mutation, loss, external import, and novel insertion under six operational evolutionary dynamics. The benchmark contains 1,961 golden lineage traces, 1,085 curated Idea Genome objects, and 920 pairwise GenomeDiff records across 10 scientific domains. It supports two evaluations. IG-Exam (42 task types, 1,029 instances) tests closed-form lineage reasoning across Idea Genome abstraction, inheritance tracing, evolutionary reasoning, and lineage verification. IG-Arena evaluates generation with a lineage-conditioned Population-Evolution Score(PES), asking whether a proposal can be inserted as a coherent descendant of a given lineage population: it should inherit the right Idea Genome objects, vary meaningfully from nearby work, and offer selection value for future research. Experiments on 14 LLM-based scientists expose a compositional bottleneck. The strongest system reaches only 27.3% exact accuracy on lineage reasoning, and structured lineage context reshuffles system rankings rather than helping every participant uniformly.

AI.tldr: IG-Bench introduces IdeaGene framework to benchmark scientific lineage reasoning and lineage-grounded idea generation using typed 'Idea Genome' objects and GenomeDiff across 10 domains. It includes 1,961 golden lineage traces, 1,085 Idea Genome objects, and 920 GenomeDiff records, with two evaluations (IG-Exam and IG-Arena). Experiments with 14 LLM-based scientists show a compositional bottleneck, the strongest achieving 27.3% exact lineage accuracy, and lineage context reshuffles rankings.
AI.motivation: Assess whether AI systems can emulate scientific inheritance and evolutionary processes in idea development; existing benchmarks do not adequately test lineage-grounded reasoning or generation.
AI.method: Represent each paper/proposal as a set of minimal, typed, evidence-grounded Idea Genome objects. Align objects with GenomeDiff to capture inheritance, mutation, loss, external import and novel insertion under six evolutionary dynamics. The benchmark includes 1,961 golden lineage traces, 1,085 curated Idea Genome objects, and 920 pairwise GenomeDiff records across 10 domains. Two evaluations: IG-Exam (42 task types, 1,029 instances) for closed-form lineage reasoning; IG-Arena for lineage-conditioned generation using a Population-Evolution Score (PES). 14 experiments with LLM-based scientists.
AI.result: Demonstrates a substantial compositional bottleneck: the strongest system achieves only 27.3% exact accuracy on lineage reasoning. Introducing structured lineage context reshuffles system rankings rather than uniformly helping all participants. Provides rich data assets (golden traces, objects, diffs) and two evaluation paradigms.
AI.conclusion: IG-Bench reveals clear gaps in current AI capabilities for scientific lineage reasoning and lineage-grounded idea generation. The framework enables systematic evaluation of inheritance-based generation and suggests that improving compositional and lineage-aware reasoning could yield meaningful gains; the benchmark also exposes how lineage context can affect system rankings.

title: VocaDet: Sample-Driven Open-Vocabulary Object Detection and Segmentation via Visual Tokenization and Vector Database Retrieval
summary: Open-vocabulary object detection and segmentation aim to recognize arbitrary objects beyond predefined categories. Although recent vision-language and reference-based approaches have significantly advanced this field, they often rely on text prompts, limited visual examples, or expensive feature matching procedures, making them difficult to scale to large and continuously expanding object repositories. In this work, we propose VocaDet, a sample-driven open-vocabulary object detection and segmentation framework that learns object concepts directly from user-provided positive and negative sample collections without model retraining. The key idea is to transform continuous visual representations into discrete visual vocabularies and perform efficient retrieval-based recognition through a scalable vector database. Specifically, we employ DINOv3 as the visual feature extractor and apply agglomerative clustering with adaptive clustering sensitivity to generate multi-granularity visual tokens. These visual tokens, together with position-debiased representations and spatial topology information, are stored as expandable object memories in a vector database. During inference, query images are converted into visual tokens and efficiently matched against the stored object memories for object localization and segmentation. Furthermore, a background filtering mechanism is introduced to remove frequently occurring background patterns and reduce redundant retrieval operations in practical fixed-camera scenarios. Experiments on the UA-DETRAC dataset demonstrate that VocaDet achieves effective open-vocabulary detection performance without conventional detector training, while supporting continuously expandable recognition capability as additional positive and negative samples are accumulated.

AI.tldr: Sample-driven open-vocabulary detection/segmentation via discrete visual vocabularies stored in a vector database, enabling retrieval-based recognition from user-provided samples without retraining.
AI.motivation: To address open-vocabulary detection/segmentation challenges where predefined categories and heavy prompt-based methods limit scalability; aims to support expanding object repositories and avoid model retraining by leveraging memory-based retrieval of visual concepts.
AI.method: Use DINOv3 as the visual feature extractor; generate multi-granularity visual tokens via agglomerative clustering with adaptive sensitivity; store tokens with position-debiased representations and spatial topology as expandable object memories in a vector database; during inference, query images are converted into visual tokens and matched against memories for localization and segmentation; optional background filtering to remove frequent background patterns in fixed-camera setups; enables continuous expansion by incorporating new positive/negative samples without detector retraining.
AI.result: The approach demonstrates effective open-vocabulary detection on UA-DETRAC without conventional detector training and supports continuous expansion as more samples are accumulated; the method emphasizes scalability and retrieval efficiency, with a practical background-filtering component to reduce redundant retrievals.
AI.conclusion: VocaDet offers a scalable, non-retraining path to open-vocabulary detection/segmentation by converting visual information into discrete tokens stored in a vector memory and retrieved at inference; it enables continuous growth of the recognized set via user-provided samples, though performance depends on token quality, clustering, and background assumptions in fixed-camera scenarios.

title: Structure Learning on Clustered Data
summary: Recent algorithmic advances have made directed acyclic graph (DAG) structure learning scalable for causal discovery. Yet, the currently available techniques assume a completely homogeneous population, precluding their application to clustered data where cluster-specific variations (e.g., patient-specific effects) are common. We address this issue by introducing a new approach that estimates a global structure while accounting for local cluster-level effects. The key idea is to extend the fixed- and random-effects framework of classical mixed models to the structure learning setting. Towards this end, we present a differentiable graph coupling mechanism that guarantees the union of the fixed- and random-effects graphs remains acyclic. Computationally, we provide a provably convergent first-order method and leverage efficient batched updates across clusters. Statistically, we establish identifiability of the model and show that our approach recovers the true structure asymptotically. In experiments on real and synthetic data, our proposal detects dependencies missed by alternative estimators, underscoring its value for structure learning in clustered settings.

AI.tldr: Globally learn a DAG structure in clustered data by coupling fixed- and random-effects graphs with a differentiable, acyclicity-preserving mechanism, yielding a provably convergent optimization and identifiability with asymptotic recovery of the true structure; demonstrates improved detection over homogeneous methods on real and synthetic data.
AI.motivation: Standard DAG structure learning assumes a homogeneous population, which fails for clustered data where cluster-specific effects create heterogeneity in dependencies. There is a need to jointly model a global structure and cluster-level variations.
AI.method: Extend fixed- and random-effects ideas from mixed models to DAG learning. Introduce a differentiable graph coupling that ensures the union of fixed- and random-effects graphs remains acyclic. Develop a provably convergent first-order optimization algorithm with batched updates across clusters. Provide identifiability results and prove asymptotic recovery of the true structure.
AI.result: The approach identifies dependencies missed by alternative estimators, achieves identifiability and asymptotic recovery, and performs well on both real and synthetic data.
AI.conclusion: The proposed clustered-structure learning framework enables accurate, scalable causal discovery in the presence of cluster-level heterogeneity by unifying global and local graph effects with a convergence-guaranteed optimization procedure.

title: Switch-Reasoner: Learn When to Think in Multitask Mixtures via Reinforcement Learning
summary: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) often follow a fixed Think-then-Answer paradigm, which is inefficient in heterogeneous multitask settings because simple inputs may not require explicit reasoning while difficult ones can benefit substantially from it. Learning when to think is also unstable during post-training, where imbalanced rollouts can drive the model toward always-thinking or always-direct behavior. We propose Switch-Reasoner, a GRPO-based framework that learns to adaptively select reasoning modes for MLLMs. It treats thinking as a virtual tool invocation and allows the model to either answer directly or invoke explicit reasoning before answering. To stabilize this decision, we introduce a dual-level regulation mechanism that balances the overall use of Thinking Mode and Direct Mode while providing sample-level supervision based on the relative benefit of the two choices. Experiments on 11 multimodal tasks show that Switch-Reasoner reduces unnecessary reasoning while maintaining strong performance, achieving a better accuracy-efficiency trade-off.

AI.tldr: Switch-Reasoner uses a GRPO-based framework to adaptively switch between direct answers and explicit reasoning for multimodal LLMs; introduces dual-level regulation to stabilize thinking vs direct modes; achieves better accuracy-efficiency across 11 tasks.
AI.motivation: Fixed Think-then-Answer is inefficient for heterogeneous multitask inputs and unstable during post-training due to imbalanced rollouts.
AI.method: Treats thinking as a virtual tool invocation; enables either direct answer or reasoning invocation; uses dual-level regulation balancing Thinking and Direct modes; sample-level supervision based on relative benefit; evaluated on 11 multimodal tasks.
AI.result: Reduces unnecessary reasoning while preserving performance; improves accuracy-efficiency trade-off.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive switching between reasoning and direct answering is beneficial for MLLMs in multimodal multitask settings.

title: An interpretable Good--Turing restart criterion for k-means++
summary: The k-means++ algorithm is commonly restarted multiple times to avoid poor local optima, yet the number of restarts is almost always chosen arbitrarily and applied uniformly regardless of data set difficulty. This undermines any comparison relying on such a choice and wastes computation on easy data sets while potentially under-serving hard ones. We introduce GTRC, a restart criterion combining a Good-Turing estimate, a proven unconditional bound, and a confidence-based bound on the probability that a further restart would improve on the current result, stopping once this probability falls below a user-specified tolerance $\varepsilon$. Across 36 data sets, GTRC reached clustering quality competitive with well-chosen fixed restart counts, while the number of restarts used varied considerably and appropriately with data set difficulty, governed by an interpretable, data-dependent signal rather than a fixed rule. GTRC offers a principled and reportable alternative to fixing the number of $k$-means++ restarts in advance. Software:https://github.com/RCdeAmorim/Good-Turing-Restart-Criterion.

AI.tldr: GTRC combines Good-Turing, an unconditional bound, and a confidence-based bound to determine when to stop k-means++ restarts, yielding data-adaptive restart counts that match fixed counts in quality but vary with dataset difficulty.
AI.motivation: Replace arbitrary, uniform restart counts with a principled, data-dependent criterion to stop restarting, improving efficiency and comparability across datasets.
AI.method: Use a tripartite bound: Good-Turing estimate of unseen outcomes, a proven unconditional bound, and a confidence-based bound on the probability that another restart improves the current result; stop when this probability ≤ ε (user tolerance). Applied to 36 datasets and compared against fixed restart strategies.
AI.result: Achieves clustering quality competitive with well-chosen fixed restart counts; the number of restarts adapts to dataset difficulty; reduces wasted computation on easy datasets and provides a transparent, interpretable stopping rule.
AI.conclusion: GTRC offers a principled, reportable alternative to pre-specifying the number of k-means++ restarts, with software available for implementation.

title: When Structured Sparse Autoencoders Learn Consistent Concepts Across Modalities
summary: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have emerged as a promising technique for mechanistic interpretability by learning a set of sparse latent features in large models, each of which encodes a distinct concept. However, in vision-language models (VLMs), vanilla SAEs struggle to learn modality-consistent concepts, with concepts often exhibiting fragmented coverage (i.e., disjoint regions) in the visual modality. To address this challenge, we propose a Structured Sparse AutoEncoder ($S^2AE$) that enforces concept consistency from both semantic and spatial perspectives in the visual modality. Specifically, we group image patches based on Transformer attention similarity and spatial proximity, and introduce a structured sparsity regularization when training the vanilla SAE. The regularization consists of exclusive sparsity for inter-group concept disentanglement and group sparsity for intra-group concept consistency, which drives the latent neurons by SAEs to specialize in distinct, semantically grounded concepts. Evaluated on the \texttt{Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct} model, the method achieves 6.06% average improvement in semantic alignment (mIoU) and 60.81 in representational efficiency (lower l0 norm) while maintaining near-perfect reconstruction fidelity with an Explained Variance above 99%. Cross-modal analysis further demonstrates that $S^2AE$ enhances neuronal monosemanticity by this visual structural prior, achieving a 3.08% average gain in semantic consistency and a 2.37% average gain in monosemanticity scores for both modalities of multimodal features, thereby fostering more coherent and disentangled representations.

AI.tldr: S^2AE introduces Structured Sparse Autoencoders for vision-language models to achieve modality-consistent, semantically grounded latent concepts by enforcing inter-group exclusivity and intra-group group sparsity through patch grouping based on Transformer attention and spatial proximity.
AI.motivation: Vanilla sparse autoencoders struggle to learn concepts that are consistent across modalities in vision-language models, often producing fragmented coverage in the visual domain. A structured sparsity approach is needed to align semantic concepts with spatial structure and cross-modal representations.
AI.method: Group image patches by Transformer attention similarity and spatial proximity. Train a vanilla SAE with a structured sparsity regularizer consisting of exclusive sparsity to disentangle inter-group concepts and group sparsity to enforce intra-group consistency, guiding latent neurons to specialize in distinct, semantically grounded concepts.
AI.result: On Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct, S^2AE yields a 6.06% average improvement in semantic alignment (mIoU) and 60.81 improvement in representational efficiency (lower l0 norm), while maintaining >99% Explained Variance in reconstruction. Cross-modal analysis shows improvements of 3.08% in semantic consistency and 2.37% in monosemanticity across both modalities of multimodal features.
AI.conclusion: Structured sparsity priors grounded in visual structure (semantic groups via attention and spatial cues) improve concept coherence and disentanglement in VLMs, enhancing cross-modal semantic alignment and monosemanticity without sacrificing reconstruction fidelity.

title: CASL-VAE: Learning Structured Latent Variables from Unpaired Data for Semi-supervised Clustering and Paired Sample Generation
summary: Quantifying variability in a target population relative to a reference population is central to many scientific and clinical problems (e.g., diseased vs. healthy). Yet, without paired data and in the presence of heterogeneous target variation, existing methods struggle to separate multiple modes of target-specific variation. We propose \textit{CASL-VAE}, a deep contrastive latent variable model that learns structured latent generative factors from unpaired data. CASL-VAE factorizes variation into continuous common latent factors shared across populations and hierarchical salient latent factors that model target-specific heterogeneity as discrete subtypes and continuous within-subtype variation. Using variational inference, we show how approximate joint likelihood optimization over reference and target domains can be performed using unpaired data, providing a principled basis for paired-sample generation and cross-domain analysis. We validate CASL-VAE on semi-synthetic neuroimaging data, demonstrating improved subtype recovery and paired-sample generation compared to baseline clustering and generative models. We also validate its ability to reveal biologically plausible heterogeneity in Alzheimer's disease.

AI.tldr: CASL-VAE is a deep contrastive latent variable model that disentangles shared (common) factors from target-specific variation in unpaired data, modeling target heterogeneity as discrete subtypes with continuous within-subtype variation, enabling paired-sample generation and cross-domain analysis.
AI.motivation: Quantify population variability relative to a reference without paired data and with heterogeneous target variation; existing methods struggle to separate multiple modes of target-specific variation.
AI.method: CASL-VAE uses a deep contrastive latent variable model that factorizes variation into continuous common latent factors and hierarchical salient latent factors capturing target-specific heterogeneity as discrete subtypes plus continuous within-subtype variation. It learns from unpaired data via variational inference to approximate a joint likelihood over reference and target domains, enabling paired-sample generation and cross-domain analysis.
AI.result: On semi-synthetic neuroimaging data, CASL-VAE improves subtype recovery and paired-sample generation compared with baseline clustering and generative models; it also reveals biologically plausible heterogeneity in Alzheimer's disease.
AI.conclusion: CASL-VAE provides a principled framework for disentangling shared and target-specific variation from unpaired data, with applications to cross-domain analysis and generation in biomedical contexts, such as characterizing heterogeneity in Alzheimer's disease.

title: Do Transformations Reveal the Truth? Generative Residual Learning for Generalized AI-Generated Image Detection
summary: The rapid advancement of generative AI has enabled the creation of highly realistic deepfake media, posing significant threats, including misinformation, digital identity theft, fraud, and manipulation of public opinion. AI-generated image (AIGI) detection is reliably challenging due to the diversity of generative methods and the subtle artifacts they leave behind. In this work, we propose GenRes, a novel framework for generative residual learning via a neural tensor network, which models fine-grained relational features between original and transformed samples to enhance generalization. To address scenarios involving multiple generative transformations, we introduce GenRes++, which employs a learnable attention mechanism to aggregate relational features across multiple transformed samples and enables the model to focus on the most informative cues. Both models leverage PE-Core as a feature extractor, providing generalized and semantically rich embeddings that improve cross-domain performance and enable the detection of AIGI generated by unseen methods. Comprehensive experiments on multiple benchmark datasets demonstrate that the proposed GenRes++ approach outperforms existing methods.

AI.tldr: GenRes and GenRes++ introduce relational learning for AIGI detection using a neural tensor network to model fine-grained relations between original and transformed samples, with GenRes++ adding attention across multiple transformations and PE-Core features to improve cross-domain/generalization to unseen generators.
AI.motivation: AI-generated imagery is proliferating with diverse generation methods, making reliable detection difficult due to domain shift and subtle artifact variation; robust cross-domain detectors are needed.
AI.method: GenRes uses a neural tensor network to capture fine-grained relational features between original and transformed samples, with PE-Core as a generalized feature extractor. GenRes++ extends GenRes by incorporating a learnable attention mechanism to aggregate relational features across multiple transformed samples, enabling focus on the most informative cues.
AI.result: Experimentation on multiple benchmark datasets shows GenRes++ outperforms existing methods, demonstrating improved cross-domain performance and detection of AIGI generated by unseen methods.
AI.conclusion: A relational-learning framework with neural tensor interactions and attention-based aggregation, built on robust PE-Core features, yields improved generalization for detecting AI-generated imagery across transformations and unseen generators.

title: Classifier Chain-based Pathological Test Recommendation
summary: Accurate and timely diagnoses are essential for quality patient care. However, delayed recommendation of diagnostic tests and physicians' subjective interpretations can hinder effective care. This study introduces a pathological test recommendation system that speeds up the test selection process using patient symptoms before physician consultation. The recommendation task is framed as a multi-label classification problem utilising the Classifier Chain (CC) technique to consider dependencies between tests. We collected data from the SOUTHERN.IML pathology and then created a custom dataset with the help of the expertise. Multiple machine learning algorithms, including Logistic Regression, Decision Tree, and Random Forest, were applied to compare models and identify the best fit for our study context. The Logistic Regression with CC model had the highest overall accuracy at 98.83%, while the Majority Voting ensemble model provided the best balance with a precision of 0.93, recall of 0.85, and F1-score of 0.89. To ensure transparency of the models and clinical interpretability, we used Explainable AI (XAI) techniques utilising SHAP (SHapley Additive Explanations), which identifies how each symptom is contributing to a test recommendation. The diagnostic reasoning revealed by the model was consistent with established medical knowledge of symptoms for the recommended tests, which further adds confidence to the model's reliability for diagnostic purposes. The reasoning could help physicians make logical decisions in critical scenarios. Overall, our findings suggest that CC can improve the efficiency of the traditional algorithms in diagnostic process providing accurate test recommendations.

AI.tldr: Multi-label pathology test recommendation using Classifier Chains (CC) to model dependencies between tests; Logistic Regression with CC achieves 98.83% accuracy; Majority Voting offers best precision/recall balance; SHAP explanations promote interpretability; suggests potential clinical utility but requires rigorous validation.
AI.motivation: Reduce diagnostic delays and subjective test selection by pre-consultation recommendations, improving efficiency and potentially patient outcomes.
AI.method: Constructed a custom dataset from SOUTHERN.IML pathology with expert input. Evaluated multiple ML models (Logistic Regression, Decision Tree, Random Forest). Framed test recommendation as multi-label classification using Classifier Chains (CC) to capture label dependencies. Compared single-model CC variants and ensemble (Majority Voting). Assessed performance with accuracy, precision, recall, and F1. Applied SHAP for model interpretability to show symptom contributions.
AI.result: Logistic Regression with CC achieved the highest overall accuracy at 98.83%. Majority Voting ensemble provided the best balance with precision 0.93, recall 0.85, F1 0.89. SHAP explanations indicated symptom contributions aligned with established medical knowledge, supporting model transparency and potential diagnostic reasoning.
AI.conclusion: Classifier Chains can enhance efficiency and accuracy in pre-consultation test recommendations. The combination of LR+CC and SHAP-based interpretability can aid clinicians, though external validation and reporting of dataset details are needed to confirm generalizability and clinical utility.

title: Multi-Resolution Feature Stem for Diabetic Retinopathy lesion segmentation
comment: 2026 International Conference on Advances in Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning (AAIML), 20-22 March 2026
summary: Diabetic Retinopathy (DR) is a leading cause of preventable blindness worldwide, requiring automated lesion segmentation using deep learning models for early detection and monitoring. However, DR lesions vary dramatically in size from tiny microaneurysms to large hemorrhages and exudates. This variability creates conflicting demands on the model architecture and input resolution, posing a challenge for effective design. This work investigates the impact of input resolution on different lesion types. Through systematic experimentation with multiple architectures (U-Net, UNet++, Vision Transformers, DeepLabV3+) at $512 \times 512$ and $1024 \times 1024$ resolutions, we identify a critical, counter-intuitive phenomenon where increasing input resolution has opposing effects on different lesion types. We demonstrate that while higher resolution is essential for resolving fine-grained microaneurysms, it can unexpectedly degrade performance on larger hemorrhages. This finding challenges the common assumption that higher resolution is uniformly beneficial. To address this, we propose a novel Multi-Resolution Feature Stem, an input-level pyramid integrated with a UNet++ backbone. This architecture processes multiple scales in parallel, capturing fine-grained details without sacrificing contextual information. This work contributes crucial empirical evidence of this complex, resolution-dependent behavior and a practical, parameter-efficient architecture that successfully resolves this trade-off.

AI.tldr: Higher input resolution in DR lesion segmentation yields lesion-type dependent effects; authors propose a Multi-Resolution Feature Stem to capture both micro-level and contextual features, resolving resolution trade-offs.
AI.motivation: Address variability of DR lesion sizes and conflicting demands on architectures and input resolution, enabling accurate segmentation across microaneurysms to hemorrhages.
AI.method: Systematic experiments across architectures (U-Net, UNet++, ViT, DeepLabV3+) at 512x512 and 1024x1024; identification of resolution-dependent effects; propose Multi-Resolution Feature Stem integrated with UNet++ to process multiple scales in parallel.
AI.result: Counter-intuitive finding: higher resolution improves small lesion detection but degrades large-lesion performance; the proposed architecture achieves better trade-off, offering parameter-efficient multi-scale processing.
AI.conclusion: Resolving resolution-dependent trade-offs is crucial; Multi-Resolution Feature Stem provides practical architecture with empirical support for resolution-aware design in DR lesion segmentation.

title: Learning $\mathsf{AC}^0$ under Locally Sampleable Graphical Models
summary:
The problem of learning constant-depth circuits holds profound implications for computational learning theory. In a seminal result, by introducing the low-degree algorithm, Linial, Mansour, and Nisan (J. ACM 1993) presented a quasipolynomial-time learner for $\mathsf{AC}^0$ under the uniform distribution. However, obtaining comparable learning guarantees for broader classes of correlated distributions has remained a longstanding challenge. Recently, Chandrasekaran, Gaitonde, Moitra, and Vasilyan (arXiv 2026) extended these guarantees to Gibbs distributions on bounded-degree graphical models with both strong spatial mixing and polynomial growth.
  In this paper, we give a quasipolynomial-time learner for $\mathsf{AC}^0$ under graphical models that admit efficient local samplers, circumventing the polynomial-growth requirement in prior work. The key ingredient is a new low-degree approximation for Gibbs distributions, established by simulating and suitably truncating the classical Glauber dynamics. As applications, this framework yields learners for two-spin systems, including the hard-core model and Ising model, on arbitrary bounded-degree graphs, in regimes approaching their respective sampling thresholds.

AI.tldr: Quasipolynomial-time learner for AC^0 under graphical models with efficient local samplers, via a new low-degree Gibbs distribution approximation built from truncated Glauber dynamics; applicable to two-spin systems (hard-core, Ising) on bounded-degree graphs near sampling thresholds.
AI.motivation: Extend AC^0 learning from the uniform distribution to correlated Gibbs distributions, removing restrictive growth assumptions from prior work and leveraging local-sampler access to broaden applicability to graphical models.
AI.method: Introduce a low-degree approximation for Gibbs distributions by simulating Glauber dynamics and truncating the process to control complexity, enabling a learning algorithm for AC^0 under graphical-model inputs with efficient local sampling.
AI.result: A quasipolynomial-time learner for AC^0 under graphical models with efficient local samplers; provides applicability to two-spin systems (hard-core and Ising) on arbitrary bounded-degree graphs, in regimes approaching their sampling thresholds.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates that AC^0 learnability extends to a broader class of correlated distributions beyond the uniform case, using sampling-based low-degree approximations; connects learning guarantees with near-threshold sampling behavior for canonical spin systems.

title: SAM-MT: Real-Time Interactive Multi-Target Video Segmentation
summary: Modern Video Object Segmentation (VOS) involves tracking and segmenting user-specified targets. While recent approaches have achieved remarkable performance in single-target scenarios, extending them to multi-target settings typically involves replicating the single-target processing for each individual object, resulting in reduced frame rates (FPS) with unbounded latency as target count increases. Built upon Segment Anything 2 (SAM2), we propose SAM-MT, which addresses this by transforming the model into an interactive framework for real-time Multi-Target video segmentation. SAM-MT uses explicit queries to represent different individual targets, in parallel with a shared representation for global context. It employs decoupled masked attention to keep individual identities distinct from cross-target interference, and sparse memory for stable temporal evolution, along with specialized strategies for occlusion handling and overlap prevention. SAM-MT successfully decouples latency from the number of targets, achieving real-time speed on par with single-target baselines (>36 FPS for 10 targets) while maintaining SAM2's robust video segmentation performance.

AI.tldr: A real-time multi-target video object segmentation framework (SAM-MT) built on SAM2 that uses per-target explicit queries with a shared global context, decoupled masked attention, and sparse memory to achieve scalable, latency-free-with-respect-to-target-count performance, enabling real-time segmentation for multiple targets.
AI.motivation: Extend single-target VOS methods to multi-target scenarios without sacrificing FPS as the number of targets increases; preserve SAM2's segmentation quality while enabling interactive multi-object segmentation in videos.
AI.method: Transform SAM2 into an interactive multi-target framework by introducing explicit per-target queries, a shared global representation, decoupled masked attention to prevent cross-target interference, sparse memory for stable temporal evolution, and specialized strategies for occlusion handling and overlap prevention. The system processes targets in parallel, decoupling computation from target count to maintain real-time performance.
AI.result: The approach achieves real-time speeds (>36 FPS for 10 targets) and maintains SAM2’s robust segmentation performance, effectively decoupling latency from the number of targets and matching single-target baselines in efficiency while handling multiple objects.
AI.conclusion: SAM-MT demonstrates that real-time multi-target VOS is feasible by rearchitecting SAM2 with per-target queries, decoupled attention, and memory mechanisms, enabling scalable, interactive video segmentation with preserved accuracy.

title: Write-Protected Discrete Bottlenecks for Language-Grounded World Models: A Structural Limitation and Sufficient Fix
summary: How should language interface with a world model's discrete symbol system? The dominant paradigm -- end-to-end injection of LLM/VLM features into robot world models (RT-2, Octo, PaLM-E) -- implicitly assumes that language gradients can directly shape physical symbol representations. We ask whether this assumption is safe, find that it is not, and characterize the minimal architectural constraint that prevents the failure. Any language gradient entering a Gumbel-softmax-based discrete symbol bottleneck forces a structural trade-off: the vanilla estimator collapses to 2.2/64 symbols (4/5 seeds), while five anti-collapse strategies maintain diversity but fail to learn semantic labels (all <= 9.2% accuracy). No tested GumbelBottleneck variant achieves both objectives simultaneously. Within this family of discrete bottlenecks, the failure is structural rather than a matter of optimization. We characterize a sufficient set of three constraints that prevent the failure: (1) cut the gradient chain (z.detach()), preventing language signals from reaching the symbol bottleneck; (2) provide a gradient-free semantic channel -- a non-parametric Memory Table (Dict[symbol -> Counter[label]], zero parameters, zero gradients) where co-occurrence counting replaces gradient-based binding; (3) handle symbol collisions via DP-Means streaming clustering for automatic sub-cluster splitting. All three layers together achieve 97.2% grounding accuracy vs. 22.2% without Layer 3. Across two experiments spanning 74 independent runs, we demonstrate zero symbol collapse in all 32 seeds, with the blackboard achieving 79-100% semantic binding across three encoder architectures (CNN, V-JEPA 300M, CLIP ViT-L), two environments, and three texture conditions. The fix trains fewer than 2M parameters and requires no LLM fine-tuning.

AI.tldr: Language gradients entering Gumbel-softmax discrete symbol bottlenecks cause symbol collapse and misbinding; a minimal three-layer architectural fix (detach gradient, a gradient-free semantic Memory Table, and DP-Means sub-cluster splitting) prevents collapse and achieves high grounding accuracy with a small parameter footprint.
AI.motivation: Evaluate whether end-to-end language supervision can safely shape discrete world-model symbols, and identify fundamental architectural constraints that prevent gradient-induced symbol collapse.
AI.method: Theoretical analysis of Gumbel-softmax bottlenecks and empirical evaluation across two experiments with 74 runs, three encoders (CNN, V-JEPA 300M, CLIP ViT-L), two environments, and three textures. Compare vanilla gradient flow, anti-collapse strategies, and the proposed three-layer fix (detach, Memory Table, DP-Means). Grounding accuracy and symbol diversity are measured across 32 seeds.
AI.result: Vanilla Gumbel-softmax collapse: ~2.2/64 symbols (4/5 seeds). Anti-collapse strategies preserve diversity but fail semantic binding (≤9.2% accuracy). No tested variant achieves both diversity and accurate semantics. The three-layer solution (detach, memory table, DP-Means) yields 97.2% grounding accuracy vs. 22.2% without Layer 3. Across 32 seeds, zero symbol collapse; 79–100% semantic binding across architectures, environments, and textures. Parameter footprint <2M; no LLM fine-tuning required.
AI.conclusion: Symbol collapse in discrete bottlenecks under language gradients is structural, not purely optimization. A minimal, three-layer architectural constraint set can safely integrate language with world-model symbols, achieving strong grounding with a small parameter budget and without LLM fine-tuning.

title: HumanForge: A Human-Centric Deepfake Video Benchmark with Multi-Agent Forgery Rationales
summary: Rapid advancements in video diffusion models and temporal editing tools have enabled the generation of highly realistic human-centric videos, posing unprecedented challenges to digital content forensics. Existing benchmarks primarily focus on either face-swapping or global text-to-video synthesis, overlooking the crucial dimensions of human-object or human-human interactions and multi-modal alignment. To address these limitations, we introduce HumanForge, a unified, large-scale, and multi-paradigm human-centric video forgery dataset. To construct and annotate this dataset without labor-intensive manual labeling or hallucinated monolithic prompts, we propose Gen2Anno, a modular active multi-agent pipeline built on LangGraph. Gen2Anno coordinates six specialized agents-ranging from source profiling to MoE-based reference analysis and closed-loop forensic verification-to generate over 18K high-fidelity video segments and produce structured, contrastive omni-annotations containing binary decisions, fine-grained artifact categories, and spatio-temporal localization. Extensive benchmarks using state-of-the-art traditional detectors and Large Multimodal Models (LMMs) demonstrate the significant challenges of zero-shot generalization and fine-grained reasoning on HumanForge. Code and dataset will be publicly released.

AI.tldr: Proposes HumanForge, a large-scale, multi-paradigm human-centric video forgery dataset built with Gen2Anno via a LangGraph-based multi-agent system, producing 18k high-fidelity video segments and rich omni-annotations; demonstrates that zero-shot generalization and fine-grained reasoning remain challenging for detectors and LMMs.
AI.motivation: Addresses gaps in existing benchmarks that neglect human-object/human-human interactions and multi-modal alignment in forgery datasets, enabling more robust forensic evaluation and method development.
AI.method: Gen2Anno: modular active multi-agent pipeline within LangGraph coordinating six specialized agents (e.g., source profiling, MoE-based reference analysis, closed-loop forensic verification) to automatically generate and annotate video forgery data; yields structured, binary/categorical, and spatio-temporal annotations for 18k video segments.
AI.result: Empirical benchmarks show significant challenges in zero-shot generalization and fine-grained reasoning on HumanForge when tested with traditional detectors and LMMs; dataset and code will be released.
AI.conclusion: HumanForge and Gen2Anno offer a unified, scalable resource and workflow to study and improve human-centric video forgery detection, prompting advances in cross-modal reasoning and forensic verification.

title: ArtMine: Discovering and Formalizing Artistic Processes
summary: Understanding how artworks are created requires reasoning about the iterative decisions, material operations, and contextual influences that shape artistic production. While recent generative AI systems can synthesize artworks with high fidelity, they primarily model distributions over finished artifacts rather than the creative processes underlying their creation. In practice, artistic workflows are only partially documented through fragmented sources such as archival records, preparatory studies, correspondence, etc., making process-level understanding difficult to formalize computationally. In this work, we introduce ArtMine, a framework for discovering and formalizing artistic processes from heterogeneous historical evidence. Our approach synthesizes heterogeneous artwork evidence into a structured repository, from which a Peircean abductive agent infers evidence-grounded production steps. These steps are converted into a compositional graph and rendering prompt, then optimized through self-reflection over deviations between the generated and reference artworks. We provide a preliminary proof-of-concept case study using open-domain historical sources across multiple artists and artistic movements, demonstrating that fragmented documentary evidence can support coherent, interpretable, and auditable representations of artistic workflows. By modeling creative processes rather than only final artifacts, our work moves toward process-centred human-AI co-creativity systems that can support artistic interpretation, creative education, reflective collaboration, and computational studies of cultural production.

AI.tldr: ArtMine develops a framework to extract, formalize, and render artistic production processes from fragmented historical evidence via abductive reasoning and compositional graphs.
AI.motivation: To move beyond artifact-level generative AI and enable understanding and collaboration by modeling creative workflows from imperfect historical data, enabling interpretation, education, and cultural studies.
AI.method: Aggregate diverse documentary sources into a structured repository; use a Peircean abductive agent to infer evidence-grounded production steps; encode steps into a compositional graph and rendering prompt; optimize through self-reflection on deviations between generated and reference artworks.
AI.result: Preliminary proof-of-concept across multiple artists and movements shows that fragmented documentary evidence can yield coherent, interpretable, auditable representations of artistic workflows.
AI.conclusion: Shifts focus to process-centered human-AI co-creativity, enabling applications in interpretation, education, reflective collaboration, and computational studies of cultural production.

title: LTM: Large-scale Terrain Model for Wildfire-prone Landscapes
summary: Accurate 3D terrain maps are essential for emergency response when assessing wildfire hazards. However, wildfire-prone regions often span vast areas where conventional reconstruction methods underperform. Airborne LiDAR systems provide high-resolution terrain data, but they are expensive and infrequently updated. Image-based methods offer a lower-cost alternative, but struggle due to sparse visual features and limited image overlap. We propose a multi-modal reconstruction framework leveraging outdated Digital Elevation Models (DEMs) as geometric priors for image-based 3D reconstruction. Our key innovation is physics-based pixel-pixel alignment between images and DEM data, dramatically reducing computational complexity by eliminating expensive feature matching procedures. To validate our approach, we developed a large-terrain simulator based on a real wildfire-prone area, generating realistic images enabling a comprehensive evaluation. Given posed images and legacy DEMs, our method produces high-fidelity depth maps while maintaining real-time performance. We find significant improvements in reconstruction accuracy and computational efficiency over existing techniques, offering a scalable solution for wildfire response.

AI.tldr: A multi-modal 3D reconstruction approach uses outdated DEMs as geometric priors for image-based depth estimation in wildfire-prone terrains, employing physics-based pixel alignment to avoid feature matching, validated on a large-terrain simulator and achieving real-time performance with improved accuracy over existing methods.
AI.motivation: Reconstructing accurate 3D terrain in wildfire-prone regions is challenging with traditional methods: LiDAR is costly and infrequent, while image-based methods suffer from sparse features and limited overlap. Leveraging legacy DEMs can provide structural priors to enable scalable, timely reconstructions.
AI.method: Given posed images and legacy DEMs, perform physics-based pixel-to-DEM alignment to fuse image data with DEM priors, thereby generating dense depth maps without expensive feature matching. A large-terrain simulator based on a real wildfire-prone area creates realistic images for comprehensive evaluation, enabling assessment of accuracy and real-time performance.
AI.result: Reported substantial gains in reconstruction accuracy and computational efficiency compared with existing techniques, indicating a scalable, real-time capable solution for wildfire response.
AI.conclusion: The framework offers a scalable, high-fidelity 3D reconstruction pipeline for wildfire response by integrating outdated DEM priors with image data through physics-based alignment, reducing computation while maintaining accuracy.

title: AutoAnchor: Stable Diffusion Unlearning Using Cross-Attention as a Manifold Surrogate
summary: Diffusion unlearning is essential for mitigating the generation of harmful or copyrighted content in text-to-image models. Current diffusion unlearning techniques determine the model update direction by either using alternatives of the target concept as an anchor or using empty prompts. The anchor-based method relies on manually and semantically-chosen anchors that risk biased unlearning, while the anchor-free method inherently suffers from unrobust unlearning due to unconstrained latent updates. In this work, we theoretically formalize such unstable diffusion unlearning issues under the manifold hypothesis and prove that lacking a manifold-proximal anchor inevitably induces significant normal-space drift that degrades unlearning performance. To achieve stable unlearning, we propose \mysysn, a two-stage framework that automatically synthesizes manifold-proximal anchors. However, direct geometric manifold optimization is computationally intractable. To address this challenge, \mysys introduces a novel cross-attention consistency loss which serves as a highly efficient surrogate of manifold proximity. Experimental results demonstrate that \mysys effectively achieves robust and unbiased unlearning across various state-of-the-art baselines, significantly improving targeted concept removal (by up to 31.04\% in CLIP score) and non-target utility (by up to 4.18\% in CLIP score). Moreover, \mysys can also be easily integrated into existing diffusion unlearning methods to enhance their unlearning performance (by 6.30\% for concept removal and 6.65\% for utility on average).

AI.tldr: A two-stage diffusion unlearning framework that stabilizes unlearning by automatically synthesizing manifold-proximal anchors, using a cross-attention consistency loss as an efficient surrogate for manifold proximity, leading to robust, unbiased concept removal and improved non-target utility across baselines.
AI.motivation: Diffusion models risk generating harmful or copyrighted content. Existing unlearning approaches (anchor-based or anchor-free) suffer from biased or unstable updates. Under the manifold hypothesis, anchors near the data manifold are necessary to prevent drift and achieve reliable unlearning.
AI.method: Propose a two-stage framework (denoted as the method in the abstract) that automatically synthesizes manifold-proximal anchors. Full manifold optimization is intractable, so the framework introduces a cross-attention consistency loss as a computationally efficient surrogate for measuring manifold proximity, enabling stable unlearning. The approach is compatible with existing diffusion unlearning baselines.
AI.result: Empirical results show robust and unbiased unlearning across baselines, with targeted concept removal improving by up to 31.04% in CLIP score and non-target utility improving by up to 4.18% in CLIP score. When integrated into existing diffusion unlearning methods, improvements are 6.30% for concept removal and 6.65% for utility on average.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework effectively stabilizes diffusion unlearning by synthesizing manifold-proximal anchors and employing cross-attention consistency as a surrogate for manifold proximity, achieving strong improvements and compatibility with current unlearning techniques.

title: Pose-to-Biomechanics: Bridging 3D Human Pose Estimation and Biomechanical Attribute Prediction
summary:
Recent progress in 3D human pose estimation has made markerless recovery of skeletal motion increasingly accurate and scalable. However, most pose estimators remain optimized for geometric keypoint accuracy, while many real-world applications in rehabilitation, sports science, ergonomics, and clinical movement analysis require biomechanical quantities that describe how the body moves, loads, and activates. In this work, we propose BioModule, a lightweight plug-in temporal transformer that attaches downstream of any 3D pose estimator and predicts biomechanical attributes from standard 17-joint 3D skeletons. BioModule is estimator-agnostic and requires no modification of the upstream pose model, enabling existing pose estimators to be extended toward physically interpretable motion analysis.
  To train and evaluate BioModule, we construct a large-scale aligned dataset pairing Human3.6M video and 3D keypoints with the biomechanical label space of Human3.6Mplus. We establish and verify anatomical correspondence between coordinate systems of the two datasets, enabling frame-accurate cross-modal supervision. Using this aligned supervision, BioModule predicts biomechanical quantities. We further benchmark BioModule across seven state-of-the-art 3D pose estimators, providing the first systematic analysis of how upstream pose estimation quality propagates to downstream biomechanical prediction fidelity. The results position BioModule as a compact, modular bridge between vision-based pose estimation and biomechanically meaningful human motion analysis.

AI.tldr: BioModule is a lightweight, estimator-agnostic temporal transformer plug-in that outputs biomechanical attributes from standard 17-joint 3D skeletons; trained on aligned Human3.6M / Human3.6Mplus data; demonstrates cross-estimator robustness.
AI.motivation: Real-world biomechanics require interpretable quantities; existing pose estimators optimize geometric keypoints; a bridging module is needed to derive biomechanical signals without modifying upstream models.
AI.method: Attach downstream; temporal transformer; estimator-agnostic; train with aligned cross-modal supervision via aligned coordinate systems between Human3.6M video/keypoints and Human3.6Mplus biomechanical labels; evaluate across seven state-of-the-art 3D pose estimators; analyze propagation of pose quality to biomechanical fidelity.
AI.result: BioModule predicts biomechanical quantities; provides the first systematic analysis of how upstream pose estimation quality affects downstream biomechanical prediction fidelity; demonstrated as a compact, modular bridge between vision-based pose estimation and biomechanical motion analysis.
AI.conclusion: BioModule enables physically interpretable motion analysis on top of vision-based 3D pose estimation with minimal integration effort, acting as a bridge between pose estimation and biomechanical analysis.

title: Spectral Analysis of Dueling Q-Learning
summary: Q-learning is a fundamental algorithm in reinforcement learning (RL) for solving discounted Markov decision processes (MDPs) when the transition kernel is unknown. The deep Q-network (DQN) extends Q-learning by using a deep neural network for Q-function approximation, which makes Q-learning applicable to more practical high-dimensional problems. Dueling Q-learning decomposes the Q-function into a value function and an advantage function and learns the two components jointly, which can improve learning efficiency. However, the theoretical understanding of dueling Q-learning is still limited. Recent work has initiated an analysis of tabular dueling Q-learning, but existing guarantees focus on a regularized formulation and leave the pure tabular update less completely understood. This paper strengthens that line of analysis by adding a direct interpretation of the centered tabular decomposition and by establishing convergence guarantees for the unregularized, unprojected constant step-size recursion. In particular, we derive an exact switching linear system representation for deterministic dueling Q-learning and a finite-time error bound in expectation for the sampled stochastic version. The analysis clarifies how the value and advantage updates act as different gains on the action-common (value function) and action-differential (advantage function) components of the Q-function.

AI.tldr: Exact switching linear system for deterministic tabular dueling Q-learning with finite-time, unregularized convergence guarantees; reveals how value (shared) and advantage (differential) components behave under updates.
AI.motivation: Fill the gap in theoretical understanding of tabular dueling Q-learning, moving beyond regularized analyses to the unregularized, unprojected setting.
AI.method: Derive an exact switching linear system representation for deterministic dueling Q-learning; analyze the unregularized constant-step-size recursion; study the centered tabular decomposition and provide a finite-time error bound for the stochastic (sampled) version.
AI.result: Convergence guarantees for the unregularized, unprojected constant-step-size recursion; finite-time, in-expectation error bound for the sampling-based version; interpretation of value and advantage updates as distinct gains on the common-value and differential components.
AI.conclusion: The analysis clarifies how the value and advantage updates selectively influence the action-common value and action-differential components, enhancing understanding of the dynamics and stability of dueling Q-learning in tabular settings.

title: WaspMOT: A Benchmark for Long-Term Multi-Object Tracking of Trichogramma Wasps
summary:
Multi-object tracking (MOT) has achieved strong performance on benchmarks dominated by short video sequences. However, such datasets do not adequately evaluate long-term identity preservation, where objects must be tracked consistently over extended durations. We introduce WaspMOT, a benchmark designed to address this gap through long-duration tracking of Trichogramma wasps in controlled ecological experiments. The dataset contains 10 sequences of approximately 12,000 frames each (over 8 minutes at 25 FPS), with dense MOTChallenge annotations and oracle detections to isolate association performance.
  Unlike existing benchmarks, WaspMOT forms a closed-set tracking scenario where all individuals remain present throughout the sequence, requiring consistent identity assignment across thousands of frames despite abrupt jumps, occlusions, and highly similar appearance. We establish a benchmark by evaluating five tracking-by-detection methods, including ByteTrack, BoT-SORT, C-BIoU, OC-SORT, and McByte, under a unified protocol. Results show that all methods suffer from significant trajectory fragmentation, highlighting the difficulty of long-term identity preservation even with perfect detections. A simple spatial tracklet stitching baseline consistently improves performance, indicating that substantial gains remain possible.
  WaspMOT provides a new benchmark for studying long-term association and reveals limitations of current tracking approaches that are not observable on conventional datasets. The benchmark will be made publicly available at the project repository: https://github.com/tstanczyk95/WaspMOT/ .

AI.tldr: WaspMOT introduces a long-duration MOT benchmark for Trichogramma wasps to study long-term identity preservation under closed-set conditions; even with oracle detections, trajectory fragmentation remains severe, and simple tracklet stitching offers gains.
