AI.motivation: Current MOT benchmarks focus on short sequences and do not test long-term identity stability; WaspMOT addresses this gap by emphasizing extended tracking in a controlled biological setting to reveal limitations of existing methods.
AI.method: 10 long sequences (~12k frames, ~8 min at 25 FPS) with dense MOTChallenge annotations and oracle detections; evaluates five tracking-by-detection methods (ByteTrack, BoT-SORT, C-BIoU, OC-SORT, McByte) under a unified protocol; includes a simple spatial tracklet stitching baseline.
AI.result: All methods suffer significant trajectory fragmentation under long durations; even with perfect detections, association remains challenging; tracklet stitching yields substantial gains.
AI.conclusion: WaspMOT offers a new benchmark for studying long-term association, exposes limitations of current trackers not visible on standard MOT datasets, and will be publicly available for community use.

title: Certified Interventional Fidelity: Anytime-Valid, Adaptive Evaluation of Causal Claims in Mechanistic Interpretability
comment: Accepted at UAI 2026 (Proceedings of the 42nd Conference on Uncertainty in Artificial Intelligence). Code: https://github.com/AsiaeeLab/certified-interventional-fidelity
summary: Mechanistic interpretability often evaluates explanations by intervening on a model: swapping hidden states, patching activations, ablating components, or comparing a compressed model to the original one. These experiments are usually summarized by a point estimate, even though the evaluation may be monitored while it runs or adapted toward suspected failures. This makes it hard to tell whether a reported fidelity or patching effect is a stable causal claim or a consequence of finite sampling and evaluation choices. We introduce Certified Interventional Fidelity (CIF), a statistical layer for interventional interpretability evaluations. CIF first writes the quantity being reported as a causal estimand: an expectation of a bounded score over a stated input distribution and a stated intervention distribution. It then provides confidence intervals and anytime-valid confidence sequences for this estimand, including under adaptive intervention sampling via bounded mixture importance weighting. We instantiate CIF with Hoeffding-style sequences and variance-adaptive betting sequences, the latter reducing certification cost by 10-30x in our experiments. On MNIST abstractions and GPT-2 Small IOI circuits, CIF certifies high-fidelity claims, shows when apparent method differences are not statistically supported, and makes sensitivity to the intervention distribution explicit.

AI.tldr: CIF provides a statistical layer for interventional interpretability by framing explanations as causal estimands with bounded scores, delivering anytime-valid confidence sequences for adaptive interventions and reducing certification cost, demonstrated on MNIST abstractions and GPT-2 IOI circuits.
AI.motivation: Existing mechanistic interpretability evaluations rely on point estimates, making it difficult to distinguish robust causal claims from sampling noise or evaluation choices. There is a need for formal uncertainty quantification and robustness under adaptive intervention sampling.
AI.method: Define CIF as bounding-score estimands: an expectation over a stated input distribution and a stated intervention distribution. Provide confidence intervals and anytime-valid confidence sequences (e.g., Hoeffding-style, variance-adaptive betting). Handle adaptive sampling via bounded mixture importance weighting. Instantiate with Hoeffding-style and variance-adaptive sequences to lower certification cost.
AI.result: CIF certifies high-fidelity claims on MNIST abstractions and GPT-2 Small IOI circuits, reveals when method differences are not statistically supported, and makes the intervention distribution sensitivity explicit; variance-adaptive sequences reduce certification cost by 10–30x in experiments.
AI.conclusion: CIF offers a rigorous statistical layer for interventional interpretability, enabling stable causal claims and transparent sensitivity analysis under adaptive sampling.

title: OpenCoF: Learning to Reason Through Video Generation
summary: Reasoning has become a core capability for large models, especially when reliable decisions require understanding logical consequences. Recent video generation models offer a reasoning path distinct from previous Chain-of-Thought (CoT): reasoning can unfold through temporally connected frames, known as Chain-of-Frame (CoF) reasoning. However, existing video generators are primarily trained on general video corpora, still lacking diverse supervision and dedicated designs for CoF reasoning. To address this gap, we introduce OpenCoF, a framework comprising the OpenCoF-17K dataset, a reasoning video dataset spanning 11 task families, and Wan-CoF, a fine-tuned video model for studying whether diverse temporal supervision improves CoF behavior. Across four video reasoning benchmarks, Wan-CoF achieves considerable gains over the Wan2.2-I2V-A14B baseline. Building on this, we empirically explore more advanced designs for CoF capabilities, i.e., equipping the model with visual and textual reasoning tokens. This mechanism respectively captures low-level visual cues and high-level semantic priors for spatial and temporal reasoning. Through performance comparisons and attention analysis, we examine how these tokens contribute across model depth, denoising steps, space, and time. Our results suggest that stronger video reasoning requires both broad temporal supervision and explicit mechanisms for organizing intermediate reasoning state. We open-source the dataset, model, and code to facilitate future research on reasoning-oriented video generation.

AI.tldr: OpenCoF introduces a 17K reasoning video dataset (OpenCoF-17K) and a fine-tuned Wan-CoF model to study Chain-of-Frame reasoning, achieving gains over baselines and exploring visual/textual reasoning tokens; code and data are open-sourced.
AI.motivation: Reasoning is critical for reliable decisions by large models, and Chain-of-Frame (CoF) reasoning enables temporally connected reasoning in video. Existing video generators lack diverse supervision and dedicated CoF design, prompting the need for specialized datasets and models.
AI.method: Develop OpenCoF-17K dataset spanning 11 task families for video reasoning; fine-tune a video model (Wan-CoF) to study CoF behavior; evaluate on four video reasoning benchmarks; compare to Wan2.2-I2V-A14B; introduce visual and textual reasoning tokens to capture low-level cues and high-level priors; analyze attention and performance across model depth, denoising steps, and space/time dimensions.
AI.result: Wan-CoF shows considerable gains over the Wan2.2-I2V-A14B baseline across four benchmarks. Token-based designs further enhance CoF capabilities, with attention analyses revealing how tokens contribute across depth, denoising steps, space, and time.
AI.conclusion: Stronger video reasoning requires both broad temporal supervision and explicit mechanisms for organizing intermediate reasoning states; open-sourcing OpenCoF data, model, and code will facilitate future reasoning-oriented video generation research.

title: Self-Adaptive Anomaly Detection with Reinforcement Learning and Human Feedback in Connected Vehicles
comment: Accepted at the 30th IEEE International Conference on Emerging Technologies and Factory Automation (ETFA 2026), Special Session SS10: Evaluation Methods for Autonomous Cyber-Physical Systems' Behavior. 8 pages, 3 figures, 3 tables
summary:
Connected vehicles are autonomous cyber-physical systems whose behavior must be continuously monitored during operation to detect deviations from normal operation before they propagate into failures. Such evaluation is challenging because the systems themselves evolve: over-the-air updates, configuration changes, and shifting workloads alter the definition of normal behavior, causing static diagnostic methods to degrade silently over time. Existing approaches typically address either automated model adaptation or operator integration in isolation, rather than as a single coordinated supervisory loop.
  This paper presents an online anomaly detection framework for autonomous CPS that integrates three coordinated mechanisms. A factorized deep Q-network with self-attention selects the most suitable detector from a candidate pool for each monitored service, exploiting inter-service dependencies in the microservice topology. An ensemble of three statistical drift detectors monitors the input distribution and raises an alarm only when all three concur, prioritizing precision over recall. A human-in-the-loop retraining mechanism, built around a pending transition buffer and a 60/40 prioritized replay strategy, allows the operator to incorporate expert knowledge while preserving the system's learned response to prior data distributions.
  The framework is evaluated on a connected-vehicle testbed running an automated valet parking application across seven backend microservices. The attention-augmented agent achieves an F1 score of 0.69, compared to at most 0.11 for any single detector applied uniformly. Following a real software update that induces measurable concept drift, F1 drops to 0.52; after operator-triggered retraining, performance recovers to 0.65 on the new distribution while remaining at 0.69 on the prior one, demonstrating sustained adaptation without catastrophic forgetting.

AI.tldr: An online, coordinated anomaly-detection framework for evolving autonomous CPS (connected vehicles) combining (1) a factorized, attention-based policy for detector selection, (2) a three-detector ensemble with high precision, and (3) interactive retraining, achieving robust performance under concept drift.
AI.motivation: Static diagnostics degrade as updates and workloads shift normal behavior; a unified supervisory loop is needed to adapt model selection, detection, and operator input.
AI.method: Three components: (a) factorized deep Q-network with self-attention to pick the best detector from a pool for each service, leveraging inter-service topology; (b) ensemble of three drift detectors whose alarm triggers only if all concur to favor precision; (c) human-in-the-loop retraining with a pending transition buffer and a 60/40 prioritized replay to incorporate expert feedback while preserving learned responses.
AI.result: On a connected-vehicle testbed for automated valet parking across seven microservices, the attention-based agent achieves F1=0.69, outperforming any single detector (≤0.11). After a software update causing concept drift, F1 declines to 0.52; operator retraining recovers to 0.65 on the new distribution and remains at 0.69 on the prior, indicating sustained adaptation without catastrophic forgetting.
AI.conclusion: The integrated supervisory loop provides higher precision and drift robustness in evolving autonomous CPS than isolated approaches, enabling durable performance across distribution shifts via detector selection, robust ensemble signaling, and human-assisted retraining.

title: Enhancing In-context Panoramic Generation via Geometric-aware Pretraining
summary: In this work, we present Canvas360, a two-stage framework for in-context panoramic generation that combines geometry-aware pretraining with downstream task-specific fine-tuning. To address the lack of large-scale, high-quality training data tailored to in-context panoramic tasks, we propose Canvas360Dataset, a collection of 1M high-quality paired panoramic samples for style transfer, inpainting, outpainting, and editing, enabling effective supervision across diverse in-context generation scenarios. On the modeling side, Canvas360 enhances text-to-panorama generation through parallel depth generation, velocity circular padding, and similarity loss regularization, enabling the model to learn geometry-aware representations, capture object distortion details, and improve geometric consistency and global coherence. Furthermore, empowered by strong panoramic priors, Canvas360 enables a unified in-context panoramic generation framework that supports diverse downstream tasks via token-level concatenation, surpassing prior methods in both task coverage and modeling flexibility. Extensive experiments show that Canvas360 improves panoramic image fidelity, achieving particularly strong performance on the panorama-specific FAED metric and competitive or leading results across the reported quantitative evaluations. More information can be found on our project page: https://zry000.github.io/Canvas360/

AI.tldr: Canvas360 proposes a two-stage, geometry-aware framework for in-context panoramic generation, backed by a 1M-pair Canvas360Dataset and modeling advances (parallel depth generation, velocity circular padding, similarity loss) to enable a unified, token-driven panormaic task suite with strong fidelity, particularly on the FAED metric.
AI.motivation: Address the data scarcity and modeling challenges in in-context panoramic generation, by providing a large, high-quality panoramic paired dataset and a geometry-aware, flexible model that can handle multiple tasks (style transfer, inpainting, outpainting, editing) in a unified framework.
AI.method: Two-stage approach: (1) geometry-aware pretraining on Canvas360Dataset with 1M panoramic pairs for style transfer, inpainting, outpainting, editing; (2) downstream task-specific fine-tuning. Modeling innovations include parallel depth generation, velocity circular padding, and similarity loss regularization to learn geometry-aware representations, capture distortion details, and improve geometric consistency and global coherence. The framework supports diverse tasks via token-level concatenation, leveraging strong panoramic priors for unified in-context generation.
AI.result: Empirical results show improved panorama fidelity, with particularly strong performance on the panorama-specific FAED metric and competitive/leading results across reported evaluations, surpassing prior methods in task coverage and modeling flexibility.
AI.conclusion: Canvas360 offers a unified, data-efficient path for in-context panoramic generation, combining a large, high-quality dataset with geometry-aware modeling to achieve improved fidelity and broad task coverage. The approach promises enhanced generalization across style transfer, editing, inpainting, and outpainting tasks, with promising results on FAED and other metrics.

title: Eigenvalue Calibration for Semantic Embeddings of Large Language Models
summary: Uncertainty quantification is central to the reliable deployment of large language models (LLMs), and eigenvalues of semantic embeddings have recently emerged as a key tool in state-of-the-art methods. However, conventional calibration results developed for classification probabilities cannot be directly transferred to eigenvalues. We address this gap by proposing a novel framework for calibrating the eigenvalues of semantic embeddings. We interpret LLMs combined with semantic embeddings of their generated answers as density matrix predictors, and we propose a novel approach to calibrate density matrix predictors by applying temperature scaling to their eigenvalues. We establish entropy-risk equivalence under calibration, derive a central calibration inequality specific to eigenvalues, and prove that temperature-scaled eigenvalues optimize calibration when minimizing proper score risks. Experiments on a variety of real-world settings show that current LLMs are systematically overconfident, and validate our theoretical findings. Together, these results advance the foundations and practice of uncertainty quantification for semantic embeddings.

AI.tldr: Calibrates eigenvalues of semantic embeddings via temperature scaling of density-matrix predictors; provides theoretical guarantees and empirical evidence of overconfidence in LLMs.
AI.motivation: Uncertainty quantification for LLMs using semantic embeddings lacks calibration for eigenvalues; conventional calibration does not transfer.
AI.method: Interpret LLMs with semantic embeddings as density matrix predictors; apply temperature scaling to eigenvalues; derive entropy–risk equivalence, a calibration inequality, and optimality for proper scoring rules; validate with experiments.
AI.result: Theoretical results: entropy-risk equivalence, a central eigenvalue calibration inequality, and optimality of temperature-scaled eigenvalues; empirical results show current LLMs are systematically overconfident and calibrations improve reliability.
AI.conclusion: Temperature-scaling of eigenvalues provides calibrated density-matrix predictors for semantic embeddings, advancing uncertainty quantification foundations and practice.

title: OPSD-V: On-Policy Self-Distillation for Post-Training Few-Step Autoregressive Video Generators
summary: We propose OPSD-V, an on-policy self-distillation paradigm for post-training few-step autoregressive (AR) video diffusion models. Existing few-step AR video generators can produce long videos with low latency, but still suffer from error accumulation and weakened motion dynamics during long autoregressive rollout. OPSD-V reduces long-horizon degradation while preserving the original few-step inference path. The key idea is to introduce real long-video data as temporal context during training and use it to provide dense trajectory-level supervision. Specifically, the student follows the exact inference-time rollout, generating each chunk conditioned on its own previously generated KV cache. In parallel, the teacher is evaluated at the same student-visited denoising states, but uses a cleaner AR-consistent temporal cache in which older history can be replaced by real-video context. This provides dense denoising-level corrective targets under on-policy AR cache dynamics, without changing the sampler, number of denoising steps, or inference-time cache mechanism. We apply OPSD-V to representative few-step AR video models, including Self-Forcing and LongLive. Experiments show consistent improvements in visual quality, motion dynamics, and VBenchLong scores. A user study with 10 participants comparing 20 video pairs shows that OPSD-V is preferred over the base models in 66.0% of overall-preference judgments (82.5% excluding ties).

AI.tldr: OPSD-V: an on-policy self-distillation framework for post-training refinement of few-step autoregressive video diffusion models. It uses real long-video context as dense trajectory supervision during on-policy AR rollout, without altering the sampling/inference pipeline, improving visual quality, motion dynamics, and VBenchLong scores; user study reports a preference of 66% (82.5% excluding ties) over base models.
AI.motivation: Mitigate long-horizon error accumulation and degraded motion dynamics in long autoregressive rollouts of few-step AR video diffusion models while preserving the original sampling/inference path.
AI.method: Train a teacher-student on-policy distillation setup. The student follows the exact inference-time rollout with its KV cache. The teacher, evaluated at the same student states, uses a cleaner AR-consistent temporal cache leveraging real-long-video context to provide dense corrective targets. This yields trajectory-level supervision using real data without changing the sampler, number of denoising steps, or cache mechanism. The approach requires real long-video data during training and is applied to representative models like Self-Forcing and LongLive.
AI.result: Consistent improvements in visual quality, motion dynamics, and VBenchLong scores across evaluated models. User study with 10 participants across 20 video pairs shows OPSD-V preferred in 66.0% of judgments (82.5% excluding ties).
AI.conclusion: OPSD-V effectively reduces long-horizon degradation while preserving the existing inference pipeline, by providing dense, on-policy supervision derived from long-video context. It demonstrates practical gains on established few-step AR video models and perceptual preference.

title: Dynamics of Gradient Descent with Large Step Size Near a Manifold of Flat Minima
summary: An important quantity in the theory of gradient descent (GD) is the \emph{sharpness}, defined as the largest eigenvalue of the objective Hessian. Classical analyses typically require the step size to be uniformly smaller than twice the reciprocal of the sharpness, but this condition is frequently violated in the training of deep neural networks. Recent work bridges this gap in the setting of overparametrised least-squares with a \emph{single scalar output}, providing a normal form for large-step GD in a neighbourhood of an \emph{isolated} flat minimum and establishing three corresponding convergence results. In this paper, we extend this theory in two directions: (1) to overparametrised least-squares with \emph{vector-valued outputs} (including regression with arbitrarily many observations), and (2) to a neighbourhood of a \emph{manifold} of flat minima (which we show is essential for applications such as matrix factorisation). We generalise both the normal form and all three convergence theorems of \cite{macdonaldeos} to this broader setting, overcoming several technical challenges, including the solution of a singular partial differential equation via a novel method that may be of independent interest. We further show that our framework applies to deep matrix factorisation under mild assumptions, yielding several new structural results. In particular, we prove that the set of flat minima forms a fibre bundle over a product of spheres, and that the sharpness is Morse-Bott along this manifold.

AI.tldr: Generalizes large-step gradient descent normal form to vector-valued outputs and to manifolds of flat minima; reveals fibre-bundle geometry and Morse-Bott sharpness in deep matrix factorisation.
AI.motivation: Bridging the gap between theory and practice by relaxing the scalar-output and isolated-minimum assumptions; addressing large learning rates that violate traditional bounds in overparameterized deep networks; extending convergent behavior to vector-valued outputs and to manifolds of flat minima.
AI.method: Extend the existing normal form and three convergence theorems for large-step GD from scalar, isolated minima to vector-valued outputs and to manifolds of flat minima. Solve a singular PDE via a novel method, and apply the framework to deep matrix factorisation. Prove structural results: flat minima form a fibre bundle over a product of spheres; sharpness is Morse-Bott along this manifold.
AI.result: Generalized the normal form and convergence results to the vector-output and manifold settings; introduced a new technique for solving the associated singular PDE; demonstrated applicability to deep matrix factorisation; established that the set of flat minima forms a fibre bundle over a product of spheres and that the sharpness is Morse-Bott along this manifold.
AI.conclusion: The work broadens the applicability of large-step GD analyses to more realistic, high-dimensional settings, reveals precise geometric structure of flat minima in overparameterized models, and provides new mathematical tools (PDE method) with potential relevance for optimization and learning dynamics.

title: Geometry and Gradient-based Partitioning for Panoramic Outdoor Reconstruction
summary: Scaling 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) to large outdoor scenes is costly in both data acquisition and computation. Adopting panoramic images with equirectangular projection (ERP) can reduce capture effort via their full $360^{\circ}$ field of view, yet the resulting omnipresent visibility invalidates existing partitioning strategies that rely on local camera frustums, causing block-wise optimization to degenerate into global training. Thus, we propose PanoLOG, a two-stage coarse-to-fine framework equipped with a Geometry and Gradient-based Partitioning Strategy tailored for large-scale panoramic 3DGS reconstruction. In the global coarse stage, PanoLOG leverages sky-sphere modeling and panoramic monocular depth supervision for reliable geometry, while in the refinement stage, G$^2$PS builds adaptive bounding volumes via parallax-driven uncertainty and assigns cameras via gradient-based importance scoring. Furthermore, we construct Pano360, the first benchmark on large-scale panoramic dataset for outdoor scene reconstruction. Extensive experiments demonstrate that G$^2$PS achieves state-of-the-art rendering quality while maintaining scalable, block-parallel training. Our models, training code, and dataset are publicly available.

AI.tldr: PanoLOG introduces a two-stage coarse-to-fine framework for large-scale panoramic 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) reconstruction, with a Geometry and Gradient-based Partitioning Strategy to enable scalable, block-parallel training on omnidirectional imagery; it includes global sky-sphere modeling and panoramic depth supervision, followed by adaptive parallax-driven bounding volumes and gradient-based camera assignment (G^2PS). It also provides Pano360, a first large-scale panoramic outdoor dataset and benchmark.
AI.motivation: To address the high cost and scalability issues of extending 3D Gaussian Splatting to large outdoor scenes using panomtric imagery, which introduces omnidirectional visibility that breaks local-frustum partitioning assumptions.
AI.method: Two-stage coarse-to-fine framework (PanoLOG) with (1) a global coarse stage using sky-sphere modeling and panoramic monocular depth supervision for geometry, and (2) a refinement stage (G^2PS) that builds adaptive bounding volumes via parallax-driven uncertainty and assigns cameras through gradient-based importance scoring; a Geometry and Gradient-based Partitioning Strategy tailored for large-scale panoramic 3DGS; and a new benchmark Pano360.
AI.result: Demonstrated state-of-the-art rendering quality with scalable, block-parallel training; public release of models, training code, and the dataset; extensive experiments support effectiveness of the approach.
AI.conclusion: PanoLOG advances panoramic large-scale 3DGS by enabling efficient, scalable training and accurate reconstruction, and introduces Pano360 as a benchmark for outdoor panoramic scene reconstruction.

title: Beyond Backpropagation: Monte Carlo Method Can Train Deep Neural Networks
summary: Backpropagation (BP) dominates deep learning training, but its reliance on gradients brings inherent troubles -- vanishing and exploding gradients. The pursuit of gradient-free methods has long been a goal in the field of artificial intelligence. This paper shows that indeed the simplest Monte Carlo algorithm implemented on a single GPU -- randomly mutate a parameter, keep it if the loss decreases, otherwise retry -- can practically train deep networks. This gradient-free method does not even need common techniques such as batch normalization or residual connections to directly train sufficiently deep networks. More remarkably, its flexibility extends to several nontrivial scenarios: it enables pure pruning training, supports discrete weights, accommodates unconventional transfer functions such as Gaussian, and reveals the substantial redundancy of deep networks. We have demonstrated its feasibility on deep networks with more than 20 layers, single-hidden-layer wide networks with up to 16,384 hidden neurons, and even a simple Transformer architecture trained on both image classification (MNIST) and character-level language modeling (Tiny Shakespeare). This simple gradient-free method may offer a complementary perspective for understanding the self-organization and learning mechanisms of neural networks, and also provides an alternative route for building physically inspired deep learning systems.

AI.tldr: A simple gradient-free Monte Carlo mutation-with-acceptance method can train deep networks on a GPU without backpropagation, across architectures and tasks, revealing network redundancy and offering a complementary training paradigm.
AI.motivation: To overcome gradient-based optimization limitations (vanishing/exploding gradients) and explore a minimal, gradient-free alternative that can train deep networks and support nonstandard configurations and pruning.
AI.method: Iteratively mutate a single parameter; accept the mutation if loss decreases, otherwise retry. Implemented on a single GPU. Demonstrates training of deep nets (>20 layers), wide networks (up to 16,384 hidden neurons), and a simple Transformer on MNIST and Tiny Shakespeare. Extends to pruning, discrete weights, and unconventional transfer functions (e.g., Gaussian).
AI.result: The approach is shown to be feasible for training deep networks and to work in several nontraditional settings, indicating substantial redundancy in deep networks and offering a gradient-free alternative that does not require common training aids like batch normalization or residual connections.
AI.conclusion: Gradient-free training provides a complementary perspective on neural self-organization and learning mechanisms and may enable physically inspired DL systems; however, questions remain about scalability, efficiency, and performance relative to gradient-based methods across standard benchmarks.

title: LongE2V: Long-Horizon Event-based Video Reconstruction, Prediction, and Frame Interpolation with Video Diffusion Models
summary: Recovering high-quality video from sparse event streams is a challenging task. Regression methods often blur textures, while existing generative models struggle with long-term stability. We propose LongE2V, a novel approach that leverages pre-trained video diffusion priors to jointly handle event-based video reconstruction, prediction, and frame interpolation. By fine-tuning a foundational video model, our approach achieves high data efficiency and superior perceptual quality. We introduce Autoregressive Unrolling and Adaptive Context Switching to mitigate temporal drift in extremely long sequences. We also propose Reencoding Alignment with Cross Residual Correction to ensure precise bidirectional consistency during frame interpolation. Furthermore, Event Voxel Density Augmentation ensures robustness across varying sensor resolutions. Extensive experiments on real-world benchmarks demonstrate that LongE2V outperforms state-of-the-art methods across all three tasks, exhibiting exceptional temporal coherence and zero-shot generalization. Project page: https://cdfan0627.github.io/LongE2V-page/

AI.tldr: LongE2V leverages pre-trained video diffusion priors fine-tuned on event streams to jointly reconstruct, predict, and interpolate event-based video, with novel mechanisms to combat temporal drift and resolution variability; it achieves state-of-the-art results with strong temporal coherence and zero-shot generalization.
AI.motivation: Event cameras produce sparse, high-temporal-resolution data but converting to high-quality, long-range video is challenging due to texture blurring, temporal drift, and sensitivity to sensor resolution. A data-efficient, stable framework for reconstruction, prediction, and interpolation is desired.
AI.method: Fine-tune a foundational video diffusion model on event-based data. Introduce Autoregressive Unrolling for long sequences, Adaptive Context Switching to mitigate temporal drift, Reencoding Alignment with Cross Residual Correction for bidirectional consistency during interpolation, and Event Voxel Density Augmentation to handle varying sensor resolutions.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on real-world benchmarks show LongE2V outperforms state-of-the-art methods across reconstruction, prediction, and frame interpolation, with superior temporal coherence and zero-shot generalization.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates that adapting a pre-trained video diffusion priors to event-based video tasks yields high perceptual quality, data efficiency, and robust performance across long sequences and resolutions; supports a unified framework for reconstruction, prediction, and interpolation.

title: Predicting Male Fertility Using Machine Learning: A Semen Parameters Based Analysis with the VISEM Dataset
summary: Male infertility is a significant yet often underdiagnosed aspect of reproductive health, with semen analysis serving as the cornerstone of clinical evaluation. To address this problem, this study investigates the use of machine learning algorithms to classify male fertility status based on key semen parameters, i.e., sperm concentration, motility, and morphology, using the VISEM dataset. This dataset includes semen samples from 85 participants, classified into three categories, i.e., Fertile, Sub-Fertile, and Infertile, according to the World Health Organization's criteria. After pre-processing and feature engineering, the dataset was used to train and assess multiple classification models using the LazyPredict framework. Among the more than 40 algorithms tested, the Nearest Centroid classifier achieved an accuracy of 94.2%, outperforming other models such as Support Vector Machines and Quadratic Discriminant Analysis. The model's robustness was validated using 5-fold cross-validation and multiclass ROC-AUC analysis. This study illustrates that machine learning models can provide fast, accurate, and objective assessments of semen quality, potentially supporting clinical decision-making in andrology and assisted reproductive technologies. These findings emphasize the growing potential of machine learning to enhance fertility diagnostics and inform patient-specific treatment strategies.

AI.tldr: ML-based semen-parameter classification; Nearest Centroid achieves 94.2% accuracy for Fertile/Sub-Fertile/Infertile on VISEM (85 samples) with 5-fold CV and multiclass ROC-AUC.
AI.motivation: Address underdiagnosis and subjectivity in semen analysis; provide fast, objective decision support for male fertility assessment.
AI.method: Dataset: VISEM with 85 participants; features: sperm concentration, motility, morphology; three WHO-defined classes. Pre-processing and feature engineering. Evaluated with LazyPredict across >40 classifiers; Nearest Centroid selected as best. Validation via 5-fold cross-validation and multiclass ROC-AUC.
AI.result: Nearest Centroid classifier achieved 94.2% accuracy, outperforming SVM and Quadratic Discriminant Analysis; robustness supported by CV and ROC-AUC analyses.
AI.conclusion: ML can offer rapid, objective semen-quality assessment to aid clinical decision-making in andrology and assisted reproduction; potential for patient-specific diagnostic guidance; external validation with larger cohorts recommended due to limited sample size.

title: ZipDepth: Bringing Lightweight Zero-Shot Monocular Depth Anywhere, on Any Device
comment: ECCV 2026. Code: https://github.com/fabiotosi92/ZipDepth - Project page: https://zipdepth.github.io/
summary: Monocular depth estimation has seen remarkable progress through foundation models achieving robust zero-shot generalization, yet their computational demands place them far beyond the reach of embedded and mobile platforms. Lightweight alternatives exist, but have been developed almost exclusively within single-domain, self-supervised paradigms, failing silently under domain shift. We present ZipDepth, a compact monocular depth network that bridges this gap by combining an efficient reparameterizable encoder-decoder with large-scale knowledge distillation from a foundation model over a large multi-domain training set. Comprising just 6.1M parameters, ZipDepth runs at real-time rates from server GPUs to power-constrained devices, achieving the best trade-off between zero-shot accuracy and deployment efficiency among lightweight models across five benchmarks, taking a significant step towards the accuracy of foundation models with 50x more parameters.

AI.tldr: ZipDepth is a 6.1M-parameter monocular depth network that combines an efficient reparameterizable encoder–decoder with large-scale knowledge distillation from a foundation model over a multi-domain training set, achieving real-time performance and strong zero-shot generalization across five benchmarks, closing the gap toward foundation-model accuracy with far fewer parameters.
AI.motivation: Foundation models offer robust zero-shot depth estimation but are computationally prohibitive for embedded/mobile platforms. Lightweight self-supervised methods are prone to performance degradation under domain shift. There is a need for compact, cross-domain capable monocular depth estimators suitable for constrained devices.
AI.method: Introduce ZipDepth: a compact, reparameterizable encoder–decoder for monocular depth estimation trained via large-scale knowledge distillation from a foundation model across a large multi-domain dataset. The architecture enables efficient inference, while distillation signals improve cross-domain generalization.
AI.result: Outperforms existing lightweight models on five benchmarks in zero-shot accuracy vs deployment efficiency, supports real-time inference from server GPUs to edge devices, and demonstrates a substantial step toward foundation-model accuracy with ~50x more parameters.
AI.conclusion: A combination of a parameter-efficient, reparameterizable architecture and cross-domain knowledge distillation yields a compact monocular depth estimator with strong zero-shot generalization and practical edge-device deployment, narrowing the gap to foundation-model performance.

title: MatBind: A Shared Embedding Space for Multimodal Materials Characterization
comment: 24 pages, 12 figures, submitted to npj computational material
summary: Fully characterizing a crystalline material requires integrating heterogeneous data sources -- atomic structures, diffraction patterns, electronic density of states, and natural language -- each of which captures a different facet of the same physical object. In practice, however, these modalities are stored and analyzed in isolation, making it difficult to relate or query materials across representational boundaries. We present MatBind, a contrastive learning framework that aligns four materials modalities -- crystal structure, powder X-ray diffraction (pXRD) simulated from structures, density of states (DOS), and text -- into a unified embedding space using crystal structure as the central physical anchor. The framework induces alignment between modalities never explicitly paired during training, enabling emergent zero-shot cross-modal retrieval as a direct consequence of the shared representation. The learned embedding space organizes materials according to physically meaningful properties without explicit supervision, and retrieval performance improves systematically when modalities are combined at query time. These results demonstrate that treating heterogeneous materials data as complementary projections of a single physical reality, rather than as isolated data sources, is not a practical choice but is consistent with the underlying physics.

AI.tldr: MatBind aligns four materials modalities (crystal structure, pXRD, DOS, text) into a unified embedding with crystal structure as the anchor; enables zero-shot cross-modal retrieval and physics-consistent organization without supervision; fusion of modalities improves retrieval.
AI.motivation: Overcome siloed, heterogeneous materials data and enable cross-modal queries by leveraging a shared physical reality.
AI.method: Contrastive learning that aligns structure, pXRD (simulated from structure), density of states (DOS), and text into a common embedding space, using crystal structure as the central anchor; emergent cross-modal alignment occurs without explicit paired data; retrieval is zero-shot across modalities; performance improves when multiple modalities are queried together.
AI.result: The model yields zero-shot cross-modal retrieval; the embedding space organizes materials along physically meaningful axes without explicit supervision; retrieval performance benefits from combining modalities at query time.
AI.conclusion: Treating heterogeneous materials data as complementary projections of a single physical reality is both physically consistent and practically advantageous for multi-modal materials analytics.

title: Wat3R: Underwater 3D Geometry Learning without Annotations
comment: Accepted to ECCV 2026. The dataset and code are available at https://github.com/LSXI7/Wat3R
summary: Estimating 3D geometry in underwater environments presents unique challenges due to light attenuation, scattering, and the absence of large-scale, high-quality 3D annotations. Pioneering methods rely on massive dense annotations that are impractical in underwater settings. In this paper, we propose Wat3R, a cross-domain semi-supervised learning framework designed to adapt feed-forward 3D reconstruction models from air to underwater scenes. Uniquely, our method eliminates the need for any annotated underwater data following a teacher-student architecture, that learns robust geometry representations merely on abundant unlabeled real underwater video footage. We also design a cross-view consistency loss that leverages geometric cues from other views to compensate for the information degradation in the current view caused by water attenuation and scattering. Furthermore, considering the lack of comprehensive evaluation benchmarks, we construct Water3D, a diverse dataset covering various water bodies and underwater scenarios, designed for geometric task evaluation. Experimental results demonstrate that Wat3R outperforms current state-of-the-art methods in underwater multi-view depth estimation and point cloud reconstruction. The dataset and code are available at https://github.com/LSXI7/Wat3R .

AI.tldr: Wat3R enables cross-domain semi-supervised 3D reconstruction underwater using a teacher–student framework with cross-view consistency, without underwater annotations; introduces Water3D for evaluation and surpasses SOTA in underwater multi-view depth and point-cloud reconstruction.
AI.motivation: Underwater 3D geometry estimation suffers from light attenuation, scattering, and the lack of large-scale, high-quality 3D annotations. Air-trained models struggle underwater, and annotating underwater data is impractical. A semi-supervised cross-domain approach aims to bridge this gap using unlabeled underwater video.
AI.method: A cross-domain semi-supervised learning framework (Wat3R) using a teacher–student architecture trained on unlabeled underwater video to adapt from air to underwater. A cross-view consistency loss leverages cues from multiple views to mitigate information degradation due to water attenuation and scattering. A new underwater 3D dataset, Water3D, is constructed for geometric task evaluation.
AI.result: Wat3R outperforms current state-of-the-art methods in underwater multi-view depth estimation and point cloud reconstruction on the Water3D benchmark; code and dataset are released.
AI.conclusion: The approach reduces the need for underwater annotations while delivering robust underwater 3D geometry, aided by cross-view consistency and a dedicated underwater dataset to enable evaluation and further research.

title: Frequency-Domain Multi-Modality Transportation Modeling
summary: Multi-modality transportation refers to urban systems composed of multiple transportation modes, such as traffic flow and public transit, whose dynamics are coupled by shared temporal patterns. Accurate multi-modality transportation forecasting remains challenging because (1) different modalities exhibit distinct spectral characteristics and (2) interact unevenly across frequencies, whereas most existing methods operate primarily in the time domain or rely on coarse feature fusion. To address these limitations, we propose a lightweight yet effective Frequency-Domain Multi-Modality modeling (FreMo) that explicitly exploits the frequency domain to enable adaptive and selective cross-modality synergy. FreMo disentangles modality-wise spectral refinement from cross-modality synergy and supports plug-and-play integration with general time series backbones. Specifically, FreMo introduces a Modality-Wise Frequency Filter (MFF) to adaptively refine spectral components within each modality, emphasizing informative frequencies while suppressing noise. FreMo further incorporates a Frequency-Guided Synergy Integrator (FSI) that selectively aggregates information across modalities based on their relative contribution at each frequency, facilitating effective cross-modality knowledge sharing while mitigating negative transfer. Extensive experiments on real-world datasets show that FreMo consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, with superior performance and generalization across diverse forecasting scenarios. The code is available at https://github.com/beginner-sketch/FreMo.

AI.tldr: FreMo is a lightweight, frequency-domain framework for multi-modality transportation forecasting that disentangles per-modality spectral refinement from cross-modality synergy. It uses a Modality-Wise Frequency Filter (MFF) and a Frequency-Guided Synergy Integrator (FSI) to selectively refine and fuse information across modalities. The method, compatible with general time-series backbones, achieves superior performance and generalization on real-world datasets, with code released.
AI.motivation: To overcome limitations of time-domain or coarse feature fusion methods in multi-modality forecasting, where modalities have distinct spectral characteristics and interact unevenly across frequencies, leading to suboptimal cross-modal sharing.
AI.method: Introduce MFF to adaptively refine spectral components within each modality; introduce FSI to selectively aggregate information across modalities at each frequency based on their relative contribution. The architecture is designed to be plug-and-play with general time-series backbones, enabling lightweight integration of frequency-domain cross-modality synergy.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on real-world datasets show FreMo consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, with improved performance and generalization across diverse forecasting scenarios.
AI.conclusion: FreMo demonstrates that explicit frequency-domain modeling for multi-modality enables adaptive, selective cross-modal fusion, yielding improved forecasting accuracy while remaining lightweight and transferable; code is publicly available.

title: Ensemble Diversity Optimization for Subjective Supervision
summary: Subjective NLP tasks often exhibit systematic annotator disagreement, requiring models that represent uncertainty rather than collapse it. We introduce Ensemble Diversity Optimization (EDO), a prediction-space framework that jointly optimizes ensemble weights, effective cardinality, and calibration through a unified differentiable objective. EDO learns ensemble composition and size end-to-end via Gumbel-Softmax relaxation and incorporates a signed diversity regularizer, tuned on validation data, to steer optimization toward either preserving or suppressing disagreement. This regularization prevents ensemble collapse and enables controlled navigation of the utility-calibration trade-off. The framework integrates a soft F1 surrogate, class-weighted cross-entropy to address imbalance, and reliability-weighted diversity to regulate intra-ensemble variability. Experiments on four subjective text-classification benchmarks (ArMIS, ConvAbuse, HS-Brexit, MD-Agreement) show that EDO substantially improves probabilistic calibration, reducing cross-entropy (40-78% depending on baseline) and lowering Brier scores relative to Soft-CE, Soft-MD, Top-5 Voting, and WEL, while maintaining competitive F1 and better alignment with annotator distributions. These results demonstrate that jointly optimizing ensemble structure with a signed diversity regularizer provides an efficient, model-agnostic approach for modeling human subjectivity in supervised learning.

AI.tldr: Ensemble Diversity Optimization (EDO) is a differentiable framework that jointly optimizes ensemble weights, effective cardinality, and calibration to model annotator disagreement in subjective NLP tasks, using Gumbel-Softmax and a signed diversity regularizer to avoid collapse and balance utility with calibration.
AI.motivation: Subjective NLP tasks exhibit systematic annotator disagreement, requiring models that represent uncertainty. Traditional ensembles can collapse diversity; there is a need to jointly optimize ensemble structure and calibration to reflect human disagreement and improve probabilistic calibration.
AI.method: EDO introduces a prediction-space ensemble with a unified differentiable objective that optimizes ensemble weights, effective cardinality, and calibration. It uses Gumbel-Softmax to learn ensemble composition and size end-to-end, includes a signed diversity regularizer (tuned on validation) to preserve or suppress disagreement, and combines a soft F1 surrogate, class-weighted cross-entropy, and reliability-weighted diversity to regulate intra-ensemble variability. It is model-agnostic.
AI.result: On four subjective text-classification benchmarks (ArMIS, ConvAbuse, HS-Brexit, MD-Agreement), EDO substantially improves probabilistic calibration (reducing cross-entropy by 40–78% versus baselines like Soft-CE, Soft-MD, Top-5 Voting, WEL) and lowers Brier scores, while maintaining competitive F1 and achieving better alignment with annotator distributions compared to baselines.
AI.conclusion: Jointly optimizing ensemble structure with a signed diversity regularizer provides an efficient, model-agnostic approach to modeling human subjectivity in supervised learning by improving calibration and maintaining performance.

title: Systematic Evaluation of Learning Rate Scheduling Strategies Across Heterogeneous Architectures
summary: Choosing a learning rate scheduling strategy is critical to neural network training, but manual selection is costly and rarely exhaustive. While classical AutoML approaches often treat the scheduler as a secondary hyperparameter, we systematically investigate its impact on classification accuracy across a diverse pool of architectures. We evaluated 30 representative architectures from convolutional and transformer families within the LEMUR neural network dataset. Through automated source-code injection, we applied 25 scheduler configurations across nine PyTorch families, evaluating a total of 3,938 model variants on CIFAR-10. Our best configuration achieved a top-1 accuracy of 86.45%, with 237 variants exceeding 80%. The results show that the choice of scheduler depends heavily on the architecture: CosineAnnealingWarmRestarts and CyclicLR consistently outperform basic decay strategies. The resulting accuracy landscape, contributed to the LEMUR nn-dataset, provides a practical reference for principled scheduler selection.

AI.tldr: LR scheduler choice substantially influences CIFAR-10 accuracy in an architecture-dependent manner; CosineAnnealingWarmRestarts and CyclicLR outperform basic decay; large automated study across 30 architectures on LEMUR dataset yields best top-1 86.45% and 237 variants >80%.
AI.motivation: Manual LR scheduling is costly and often non-exhaustive; a systematic, cross-architecture evaluation is needed to guide principled scheduler selection and inform AutoML pipelines.
AI.method: Automated source-code injection applied 25 schedulers across nine PyTorch families; evaluated 3,938 model variants on CIFAR-10 for 30 CNN/Transformer architectures from the LEMUR dataset; assessed top-1 accuracy.
AI.result: Best configuration achieved 86.45% top-1; 237 variants exceeded 80%; CosineAnnealingWarmRestarts and CyclicLR consistently outperform basic decay strategies; an accuracy landscape is produced.
AI.conclusion: Provides practical reference for principled scheduler selection; scheduler choice is architecture-dependent; contributes the LEMUR nn-dataset for evaluation and benchmarking of schedulers.

title: Stop Guessing When to Stop Testing: Efficient Model Evaluation with Just Enough Data
summary: The inherent rigidity of fixed-size benchmarks makes them an inefficient tool for model evaluation. Diverse evaluation objectives, including model ranking, model selection and testing throughout development, demand varying levels of statistical power. The mismatch between fixed sample sizes and these diverse needs results in either excessive computational cost or compromised reliability - a critical concern for model evaluation. To overcome these limitations, we call for adoption of sequential testing in our field. We provide an adaptive evaluation framework, that provides a principled way to navigate the trade-off between efficiency and reliability in model evaluation. Our framework combines the established statistical paradigm of sequential testing with stopping criteria tailored to common evaluation needs such as diminishing returns detection, and minimum detectable effect size. We demonstrate its ability to adaptively manage the efficiency-reliability trade-off on the Open VLM Leaderboard, including, for example, a 80% reduction in computational cost compared to fixed-size evaluation (with a 2.5-point CI width allowance) while maintaining statistical significance.

AI.tldr: Adaptive sequential evaluation framework for ML model evaluation; demonstrates substantial cost savings (≈80%) with maintained reliability (CI width constraint) on Open VLM Leaderboard.
AI.motivation: Fixed-size benchmarks enforce uniform sample sizes, which is inefficient for diverse evaluation objectives (ranking, selection, progression testing) due to varying statistical power needs; sequential testing offers efficiency-reliability trade-offs.
AI.method: Integrates sequential testing with stopping criteria tailored for common evaluation goals (diminishing returns detection, minimum detectable effect size). Provides an adaptive workflow that adjusts sample size in response to data, allowing early stopping when criteria are met. Evaluation demonstrated on the Open VLM Leaderboard. (e.g., using a 2.5-point CI width allowance for stopping.)
AI.result: Significant reductions in computational cost (≈80%) while preserving statistical significance and required CI width, demonstrating practical efficacy of the adaptive framework.
AI.conclusion: A principled, adaptive evaluation framework can balance efficiency and reliability in ML model evaluation, addressing the limitations of fixed-size benchmarks. Encourages broader adoption for ranking, selection, and development-phase testing, with potential caveats around stopping criteria calibration and generalizability.

title: CAAD: Causality-Aware Multivariate Time Series Anomaly Detection via Multi-Scale Alignment and Structural Causal Consistency
summary:
The operational integrity of complex industrial systems relies on precise anomaly detection and diagnosis. The vast majority of existing methods narrowly focus on capturing temporal similarities of representations, often overlooking the disruption of internal causal relationships, which characterizes system failures and latent anomalies. In this paper, we propose a novel framework (CAAD) that reframes anomaly detection as the continuous verification of Granger causality consistency through exogenous variables.
  Specifically, the CAAD framework models exogenous time-series variables as residuals, identifying anomalies as significant deviations caused by external interventions. The proposed framework leverages multi-scale alignment to internalize system dynamics and utilizes a gradient-based matrix to monitor internal causal relationship breakdowns. By quantifying causal deviations of both dynamic evolution and relational topology, the CAAD is able to capture subtle causal shifts to achieve precise anomaly detection. Extensive experiments on real-world industrial datasets demonstrate that the CAAD achieves high-precision anomaly detection, outperforming most state-of-the-art baselines.

AI.tldr: CAAD reframes anomaly detection as continuous verification of Granger-causality consistency via exogenous variables, detecting anomalies through external interventions by monitoring dynamic and relational causal deviations; uses multi-scale alignment and a gradient-based monitor to achieve high-precision detection that outperforms baselines.
AI.motivation: Most existing anomaly detectors focus on temporal similarity of representations and fail to capture disruptions in internal causal relationships, which are hallmarks of system failures and latent anomalies; there is a need to monitor and quantify causal deviations within complex industrial systems.
AI.method: CAAD models exogenous time-series as residuals and detects anomalies as significant deviations caused by external interventions. It employs multi-scale alignment to internalize system dynamics and uses a gradient-based matrix to monitor breakdowns in internal causal relations. It quantifies causal deviations in both dynamic evolution and relational topology to capture subtle causal shifts.
AI.result: On real-world industrial datasets, CAAD achieves high-precision anomaly detection and outperforms most state-of-the-art baselines.
AI.conclusion: CAAD provides a causality-focused anomaly detection framework that excels at identifying subtle causal shifts induced by external interventions, offering robust, precise detection suitable for industrial deployments.

title: Contravariance Theory: Strong Alignment for Minimal Solutions to Hard Tasks
summary: A series of results from the NeuroAI over the past fifteen years have raised core questions both about how to compare Deep Neural Network (DNN) models to the brain, and about how much convergent evolution to expect between artificial networks and real brain networks. Here, we show that for any two minimal DNN solutions to a sufficiently hard task: (i) "weak" alignment of network representations based on affine mappings guarantees "strong" alignment of privileged axes, and (ii) alignment "zippers" up the network hierarchy, causing the emergence of privileged axes from end-to-end task optimization. These results formalize the notion of contravariance from Cao and Yamins [2024], and illustrate important consequences for the theory of NeuroAI: with sufficiently strong tasks, choice of metric for inter-network comparison is not all that sensitive, and that convergent evolution is probably inevitable.

AI.tldr: Affine alignment between two minimal DNN solutions guarantees strong alignment of privileged axes; hierarchical alignment ('zippers') yields privileged axes from end-to-end optimization; formalizes contravariance; strong tasks imply metric-insensitive cross-network comparison and likely convergent evolution between DNNs and brain networks.
AI.motivation: Assess how to compare DNNs to the brain and evaluate the extent of convergent evolution, by formalizing contravariance in NeuroAI and clarifying when comparison metrics matter.
AI.method: Theoretical analysis of two minimal DNN solutions to a sufficiently hard task; derive conditions under which affine alignment leads to privileged-axis alignment and how hierarchical 'zippers' propagate alignment; formalize contravariance in this context.
AI.result: (1) Weak alignment based on affine mappings guarantees strong alignment of privileged axes. (2) Alignment propagates up the network via 'zippers', enabling privileged axes to emerge from end-to-end task optimization. (3) These findings formalize contravariance (Cao & Yamins, 2024) and imply that with sufficiently strong tasks, inter-network comparison metrics become less sensitive and convergent evolution is likely.
AI.conclusion: Under sufficiently hard tasks, convergence between DNN representations and brain-like representations is probably inevitable, and the choice of comparison metric becomes less critical; the contravariance framework gains empirical support.

title: Spectral Stability of Pseudoinverse-Based Extreme Learning Machine
summary: Extreme Learning Machine (ELM) computes output weights analytically using the Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse. Although this leads to fast training, its numerical stability depends strongly on the conditioning of the hidden layer matrix. This paper studies pseudoinverse-based ELM from a spectral perspective. We show that the smallest singular value governs perturbation amplification in the output weights, while the condition number provides a quantitative measure of hidden-layer instability. We compare SVD-based pseudoinverse computation with iterative hyperpower methods and discuss width-dependent conditioning through a random feature interpretation. Experiments on synthetic matrices and ELM benchmarks show that SVD-based methods remain the most reliable under ill conditioning, while iterative methods are more sensitive to spectral properties. The results suggest that ELM stability is fundamentally governed by the singular value structure of the hidden layer matrix.

AI.tldr: Spectral analysis reveals ELM output weights are most sensitive to the smallest singular value of the hidden-layer matrix; SVD-based pseudoinverse is more robust to ill-conditioning than iterative hyperpower methods. Width through random features affects conditioning, linking stability to singular-value structure.
AI.motivation: Explain and quantify the numerical stability of Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse in ELM training, relate conditioning of the hidden layer to perturbation amplification, and compare computational schemes.
AI.method: Spectral analysis of the hidden-layer matrix for perturbation amplification via singular values; compare SVD-based pseudoinverse with iterative hyperpower methods; interpret width effects using a random feature perspective; validate via experiments on synthetic matrices and standard ELM benchmarks.
AI.result: Smallest singular value governs perturbation amplification in the output weights; condition number measures hidden-layer instability; SVD-based inversion outperforms iterative methods under ill-conditioning; iterative methods are more sensitive to spectral properties; width-related conditioning aligns with the random feature interpretation; overall, stability is dictated by the singular-value structure of the hidden layer.
AI.conclusion: ELM numerical stability is governed by the singular value spectrum of the hidden-layer matrix; to maximize robustness, prefer SVD-based pseudoinverse in ill-conditioned regimes and be mindful of width-induced conditioning as explained by random feature theory.

title: Robust Bayesian Decision Making under Adversarial Uncertainty
summary: Scientific experiments are often designed to maximize information gain, yet in many applications the primary objective is to support reliable downstream decision-making. Existing decision-aware experimental design and active learning methods typically assume well-specified outcome models and implicitly rely on the stability of the optimal decision under real-world perturbations. In practice, however, experimental outcomes are frequently influenced by hidden or weakly modeled effects, which can substantially alter decision optimality and lead to misleading conclusions. We study sequential adversarially robust decision-aware experimental design, where data acquisition has to take into account information gain against plausible worst-case unexpected effects, modeled here as variation in adversarial variables. Building on Bayesian decision theory, we formalize an adversarially robust optimal decision under this setting and derive a principled Bayesian experimental design criterion. The criterion explicitly targets decision stability rather than nominal optimality. Experiments on synthetic and real-world scientific datasets show that conventional decision-aware design can converge rapidly to high confidence yet fragile decisions, while our robustness-aware approach yields decisions that are significantly more stable and reliable under adversarial variation.

AI.tldr: Adversarially robust decision-aware experimental design for stable, reliable decisions under hidden/unmodeled effects, using Bayesian sequential design to optimize stability rather than nominal information gain.
AI.motivation: Decision-aware experimental design often assumes well-specified outcome models; hidden/weakly modeled effects can shift optimal decisions and mislead conclusions. This work aims to ensure decision stability under plausible adversarial perturbations.
AI.method: Sequential Bayesian experimental design with worst-case adversarial variation. Formalizes an adversarially robust optimal decision within Bayesian decision theory and derives a criterion that targets decision stability rather than pure information gain.
AI.result: Compared to conventional decision-aware design, which rapidly converges to high-confidence but fragile decisions, the proposed robustness-aware design yields decisions that are more stable and reliable under adversarial variation, demonstrated on synthetic and real-world datasets.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating adversarial robustness into decision-aware experimental design improves reliability of downstream decisions in the presence of unmodeled effects, potentially at the expense of nominal information gain but with greater practical stability.

title: Federated Deep Learning for Privacy-Preserving Cardiovascular Disease Risk Prediction
comment: 15 pages, 2 figures, 2 tables. Submitted to Frontiers in Applied Mathematics and Statistics, Research Topic "Enhancing Healthcare through Federated Learning: Privacy, Security and Performance"
summary: Cardiovascular disease risk prediction models often rely on data from a single institution or centrally pooled datasets. Extending these models across institutions could be limited by privacy regulations and constraints on sharing patient-level data. Federated learning enables collaborative model development without transferring sensitive patient data, but its application in healthcare remains challenging because datasets often differ in size, population characteristics, and outcome definitions. In this study, we present a federated deep learning approach for privacy-preserving cardiovascular disease risk prediction that integrates two population-based cohorts with different characteristics: Lifelines, including 148,230 participants meeting the study inclusion criteria with self-reported outcomes, and the Rotterdam Study, including a smaller cohort of 10,155 participants with digitally linked clinical outcomes. Model performance was primarily evaluated on the Rotterdam Study because of its complete follow-up. Deep survival models trained using federated learning achieved higher predictive performance than models trained locally without federation. For the Rotterdam Study, the C-statistic increased from 0.728 (95% CI: 0.717-0.739) to 0.739 (95% CI: 0.728-0.749). For Lifelines, the C-statistic increased from 0.783 (95% CI: 0.775-0.791) to 0.787 (95% CI: 0.780-0.792). These findings suggest that federated deep learning across heterogeneous cohorts can improve cardiovascular disease risk prediction while preserving the privacy of individual-level patient data.

AI.tldr: Federated deep learning across two population cohorts (Lifelines and Rotterdam Study) improves cardiovascular disease risk prediction over local models while preserving patient privacy; small gains in C-statistic observed, with comprehensive outcomes and heterogeneity in data.
AI.motivation: Overcome privacy and data-sharing barriers in building robust, generalizable CVD risk models across institutions; address heterogeneity in size, population characteristics, and outcome definitions by using federated learning.
AI.method: Deep survival models trained with federated learning on two cohorts (Lifelines: 148,230 participants with self-reported outcomes; Rotterdam Study: 10,155 with digitally linked outcomes). Evaluation prioritized on Rotterdam due to complete follow-up; comparison against locally trained models.
AI.result: Federated models outperform local models: Rotterdam C-statistic 0.728→0.739; Lifelines 0.783→0.787; both with 95% CIs; indicating privacy-preserving cross-cohort learning can enhance predictive performance.
AI.conclusion: Federated deep learning across heterogeneous cohorts can improve cardiovascular risk prediction while preserving privacy, demonstrating viability of privacy-preserving multi-institutional risk modeling.

title: Steering Neural Network Training through Interpretable Constraints Based on Partial Dependence
summary: Over the last few years, there has been an increased interest in making machine learning models more interpretable. Although a great deal of effort goes into developing techniques for interpreting the interactions learned by a given model, fewer studies focus on assessing the quality of such explanations. Even fewer focus on how to adjust the model to produce explanations faithful to prior knowledge, a process known as explanation-guided learning. Furthermore, most approaches in this area focus on classification problems and usually assume prior knowledge about which input features or regions are most important. In this work, we introduce a new approach to steering neural networks based on partial dependence, such that their average response to certain features aligns with specific functional domain knowledge about the problem. We empirically demonstrate on a range of regression problems, including dynamical systems forecasting, that models whose training has been controlled using our method perform better than unconstrained models and are more data-efficient. Moreover, we highlight that interpretations obtained from the former actually align with the user-provided knowledge, whereas those obtained from the latter do not.

AI.tldr: A novel explanation-guided learning approach using partial dependence to align a model's average response over selected features with domain knowledge, yielding better accuracy and faithful explanations in regression tasks.
AI.motivation: Interpretability research often evaluates explanation quality but seldom enforces explanations to reflect prior knowledge; existing methods mainly address classification and rely on assumed important features. There's a need for mechanisms to steer models so their explanations are faithful to domain knowledge, improving data efficiency.
AI.method: Train neural networks with a partial dependence constraint: enforce that the average predicted response over specific features matches a user-specified target function, effectively embedding domain knowledge into the model's behavior (a regularization term). Applied to regression tasks including dynamical systems forecasting.
AI.result: Across several regression problems, including dynamical systems forecasting, the constrained models outperform unconstrained ones and are more data-efficient; their explanations align with user knowledge, whereas explanations from unconstrained models do not.
AI.conclusion: Partial dependence-guided learning provides a practical means to inject domain knowledge into models, improving both predictive performance (data efficiency) and faithfulness of explanations; the approach can be generalized to other settings.

title: BiSCo-LLM: Lookup-Free Binary Spherical Coding for Extreme Low-Bit Large Language Model Compression
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly constrained by memory capacity, weight bandwidth, and checkpoint storage during deployment. Existing low-bit compression methods mainly follow two directions. Scalar or group-wise quantization is simple and compatible with efficient low-precision kernels, but its representation capacity becomes limited when the target budget approaches 2 bits per weight. Vector-quantized weight compression provides a richer block-level representation, but usually introduces explicit codebooks, index lookup, and additional storage accounting. This paper presents BiSCo-LLM, a codebook-free binary spherical coding framework for extreme low-bit LLM weight compression. The core pipeline is built on three components. First, local weight chunks are mapped onto a unit hypersphere and binarized into compact spherical codes, so that the main payload is a bit-packed sign stream rather than explicit VQ centroids. Second, a residual BSQ stage encodes the reconstruction error left by the base spherical codec, providing an explicit rate-distortion path without stored codebooks. Third, category-wise recovery distillation is performed after replacing each Transformer module category, reducing the mismatch between local weight reconstruction and assembled model behavior. A small 8-bit protected-channel path is used as an auxiliary stabilization mechanism for sensitive channels and is counted separately from the BSQ payload. The reported storage budget includes binary codes, neural decoders, protected-channel payloads, LoRA adapters, and metadata.

AI.tldr: BiSCo-LLM introduces a codebook-free binary spherical coding framework for extreme low-bit LLM weight compression, avoiding explicit codebooks via spherical binarization and a residual stage, plus category-wise recovery distillation and a small 8-bit protected-channel path; reports a comprehensive storage budget including codes, decoders, channels, LoRA adapters, and metadata.
AI.motivation: LLMs are hampered by memory, bandwidth, and checkpoint storage in deployment. Scalar/group quantization loses capacity near 2 bits/weight; vector quantization adds explicit codebooks and extra storage. A codebook-free, high-density, rate-distortion aware approach is needed for extreme low-bit compression.
AI.method: Three components: (1) map local weight chunks to a unit hypersphere and binarize into compact spherical codes, producing a bit-packed sign stream without explicit centroids; (2) a residual BSQ stage encodes the reconstruction error to provide a rate-distortion path without stored codebooks; (3) category-wise recovery distillation after replacing each Transformer module category to reduce mismatch between local reconstruction and full model behavior. An 8-bit protected-channel path serves as an auxiliary stabilization mechanism counted separately from the BSQ payload. The reported storage budget includes binary codes, neural decoders, protected-channel payloads, LoRA adapters, and metadata.
AI.result: The abstract does not report numerical results. It claims a practical pipeline achieving extreme low-bit compression with a codebook-free approach and explicit rate-distortion control, leveraging residual encoding and distillation to preserve performance; quantitative metrics are not provided in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: BiSCo-LLM presents a novel, codebook-free alternative to vector quantization for LLM weight compression, combining binary spherical coding with a residual encoding stage and category-wise recovery distillation, and accounting for auxiliary protected-channel data within the storage budget.

title: Multi-Modal, Multi-Environment Machine Teaching for Robust Reward Learning
summary: As autonomous agents are increasingly deployed across diverse operational contexts, aligning their behavior with human intent demands reward functions that remain robust to such changes rather than overfitting to any single environment. Inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) provides a principled way to infer such objectives from human feedback. However, existing analyses of optimal teaching approaches for IRL focus on single-environment, demonstration-only settings, leaving underexplored how heterogeneous feedback modalities and environment dynamics jointly constrain reward functions that generalize across multiple environments. Because demonstrations in one MDP entangle reward information with that environments specific structure, the resulting rewards frequently fail to generalize when the agent is deployed in a new setting. We first analyze how different feedback modalities constrain rewards, showing that, in the unlimited-data regime, comparisons impose strictly stronger global constraints than other modalities. Beyond this theoretical analysis, we introduce a hierarchical machine teaching algorithm for reward learning that operates across multiple MDPs. The algorithm first greedily selects informative environments that expose complementary reward constraints, then strategically queries low-cost feedback within those environments. Empirically, our method achieves substantially lower regret and stronger generalization to held-out environments than uniform teaching baselines under identical feedback budgets, demonstrating the importance of multi-environment, multi-modal teaching for learning dynamics-robust reward functions.

AI.tldr: Multi-environment, multi-modal teaching for IRL yields robust rewards that generalize across MDPs; theoretical result shows comparisons provide stronger global constraints in the unlimited-data regime; hierarchical teaching across environments with low-cost queries achieves lower regret and better generalization than uniform baselines.
AI.motivation: To learn reward functions in IRL that generalize across diverse environments and feedback modalities, avoiding overfitting to environment-specific structure.
AI.method: Theoretical analysis of how feedback modalities constrain rewards, proving that comparisons impose stronger global constraints in the unlimited-data regime. Introduces a hierarchical machine teaching algorithm that selects informative environments exposing complementary reward constraints, then queries low-cost feedback within those environments. Empirical evaluation compares to uniform teaching baselines under identical feedback budgets.
AI.result: In the unlimited-data regime, comparison-based feedback imposes strictly stronger global reward constraints than other modalities. The hierarchical teaching algorithm achieves substantially lower regret and stronger generalization to held-out environments compared with uniform teaching baselines under equal budgets.
AI.conclusion: Multi-environment, multi-modal teaching is essential for learning dynamics-robust reward functions in IRL and improves generalization to new environments.

title: Secure Decentralized Federated Learning via Gossip and Virtual Voting
summary: Decentralized federated learning (DFL) removes the central server by letting nodes exchange model updates through peer-to-peer gossip, but existing gossip-based methods often lack provenance finality and resilience to Byzantine or lazy participants. Ledger-assisted federated learning (FL) improves auditability, yet blockchains, shards, or settlement committees can reintroduce global coordination costs that conflict with DFL locality. This paper proposes \emph{gspDAG-FL}, a secure DFL framework that derives consensus from the same gossip history used to disseminate models. Nodes exchange model payloads only with neighbors, while full nodes collect event certificates and receiver-endorsed accepted gossip proofs, reconstruct a compact Topology directed acyclic graph (DAG), and run Hashgraph-style virtual voting followed by compact full-node certificates. Finality is over unique model-origin tuples, not identical local parameter states. To improve resilience, gspDAG-FL combines payload validation, accepted-proof validation, and private semantic audit before aggregation. We formalize the adversarial setting, prove safety and conditional liveness of the control plane, and give a convergence guarantee for certified perturbed gossip under time-varying effective mixing.
